tests.label: Species of different genera and classes change at different rates
tests.hypothesis: If different classes and genera change at different rates, then taxonomic turnover measured as the stratigraphic duration of extinct genera in the Paleobiology Database should differ substantially among major animal classes, and, within classes, among orders.
tests.pass: Using PBDB genus-rank taxa with first- and last-appearance ages for 14 higher taxa (Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Cephalopoda, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Crinoidea, Ostracoda, Bryozoa, Mammalia, Reptilia, Actinopterygii, Chondrichthyes), restricted to extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences, genus duration = midpoint of first-appearance range minus midpoint of last-appearance range. Clause A (between classes): a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across the higher taxa has p < 0.001 AND epsilon-squared effect size >= 0.02 AND the ratio of the largest to the smallest group median duration is >= 2. Clause B (between genera grouped by order, within classes): within each higher taxon having >= 3 orders with >= 20 qualifying genera each, a Kruskal-Wallis test of genus duration across orders has p < 0.001 and epsilon-squared >= 0.02; clause B passes if this holds in a majority of eligible higher taxa. Verdict 'supports' if A and B pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if neither.
tests.fail: Clause A fails if genus durations are statistically indistinguishable across classes (p >= 0.001), or the effect is trivial (epsilon-squared < 0.02), or every class median lies within a factor of 2 of every other. Clause B fails if orders within a class differ significantly and non-trivially in half or fewer of the eligible classes. Both failing refutes the claim. A sensitivity re-run with >= 20 occurrences per genus is reported; if the sign of either clause flips under that filter the result is downgraded to 'mixed' regardless.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'rate of change' of species is read, following the Grok assessor, as taxonomic turnover: shorter genus durations mean faster replacement of forms. 'Classes' are mapped to PBDB classes or, where PBDB class structure is unstable (brachiopods, bryozoans), phyla. 'Species of different genera' is approximated by genera grouped into orders, because species-level ranges in PBDB are too noisy and species durations are strongly tied to the genus concept. Durations are taxonomic, not morphological; the morphological reading (rates of character change) is not tested. Differences in preservation potential and taxonomic splitting between classes can mimic rate differences, which is why the pass criterion requires a non-trivial effect size and a two-fold spread of medians rather than mere significance.
tests.method: For each of 14 higher taxa the PBDB genus list with appearance ages was downloaded; accepted extinct genera with >= 5 occurrences were kept and duration computed as the difference between first- and last-appearance midpoints. Clause A: Kruskal-Wallis across higher taxa with epsilon-squared effect size and the ratio of extreme group medians. Clause B: within each higher taxon with >= 3 orders of >= 20 genera, Kruskal-Wallis across orders. The whole procedure was repeated with >= 20 occurrences as a sensitivity check.

measured.unit: ratio of largest to smallest median genus duration among the 14 higher taxa (Myr/Myr)
measured.uncertainty: Kruskal-Wallis H = 3080.0, p = 0.00e+00, epsilon2 = 0.203

caveats: Genus duration is a taxonomic proxy for rate of change; it conflates true evolutionary rate with preservation potential, sampling intensity and how finely each class is split by taxonomists.
Durations of genera with few occurrences are truncated; the >= 5 occurrence filter (and the >= 20 sensitivity run) reduces but does not remove range truncation, which differs among classes.
Groups are not all of class rank (Brachiopoda and Bryozoa are phyla) because PBDB class membership is unstable for them.

Only extinct genera are included (extant genera have open-ended durations), which excludes the long-lived 'living fossil' lineages Darwin also had in mind and so is conservative with respect to the spread of rates.
Darwin's phrase covers rate 'or degree' of change; morphological degree of change is not measured here.

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database taxa lists (genus rank, show=app,class) for 14 higher taxa

tests.label: Groups rise gradually in species number to a maximum, then gradually decline
tests.hypothesis: For extinct marine-invertebrate families, the number of genera recorded per geological stage rises from a low value at the family's first appearance to an interior maximum and then declines to a low value at its last appearance, rather than appearing or disappearing at or near maximal diversity or showing several separate peaks.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: a family's trajectory is scored 'Darwinian' when, with R_i = range-through genus richness in stage bin i (from the family's first to last bin) and M = max R_i: (a) R_first <= 0.5 M, (b) R_last <= 0.5 M, and (c) the set of bins with R_i > 0.5 M is contiguous (a single peak). The claim is SUPPORTED if at least two thirds (>= 0.667) of qualifying families are Darwinian, where qualifying = extinct family within the sampled higher taxa with >= 10 genera having occurrences and a duration spanning >= 6 stage bins.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTED if fewer than half (< 0.5) of qualifying families are Darwinian. A fraction in [0.5, 0.667) is MIXED. If fewer than 50 families qualify the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'group' is read as a family and 'number of species' as number of genera per stage (the level with usable fossil coverage, as both assessors note). 'Gradual increase to a maximum, then gradual decrease' is operationalised as the three shape conditions (a)-(c): low start, low end, single peak. The sampled higher taxa are fixed in advance: Trilobita, Brachiopoda, Cephalopoda, Bivalvia, Gastropoda, Crinoidea, Anthozoa, Echinoidea, Bryozoa. Only extinct families are used because the decline-to-extinction half of the claim is only observable for them. Counts are raw range-through counts from the Paleobiology Database diversity endpoint at stage resolution; no sampling standardisation is applied, which is recorded as a caveat.
tests.method: For each of 9 higher taxa the accepted extinct families with occurrences were listed from PBDB taxa/list. For every family whose recorded span was >= 5 Myr, occs/diversity (count=genera, time_reso=stage) gave per-stage counts; range-through richness R = X_bt + X_Ft + X_bL + X_FL was taken from the first to the last stage with R > 0, and the number of genera = sum(X_Ft + X_FL). Families with >= 10 genera and >= 6 stage bins qualified (n = 313). Each trajectory was scored for low start (R_first <= 0.5 max), low end (R_last <= 0.5 max) and a single peak (bins with R > 0.5 max contiguous); the fraction scoring all three was compared with the pre-registered thresholds (>= 0.667 supports, < 0.5 refutes), with a Clopper-Pearson 95% CI.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying extinct families with low start, low end and a single peak
measured.uncertainty: 95% Clopper-Pearson CI [0.528, 0.640]

caveats: The two 'gradual' components of the claim are strongly supported: 93% of families start and 95% end at <= half their maximum genus richness, and only 2.6% peak in their first and 1.0% in their last stage. What fails is the single-maximum component: 34% of families have two or more separate peaks above half-maximum, so the overall fraction (0.58) falls in the pre-registered MIXED band.

Range-through counting at stage resolution structurally favours low first and last bins (a family's first bin can only contain genera that originate in it), so the start/end components are partly a counting artefact; peak position (median 0.43 of the way through the family's duration) and the medians of 6 bins of rise and 8 bins of fall are more informative.

Raw PBDB counts were used without sampling standardisation; uneven rock record and research effort produce spurious secondary peaks and troughs, which bias against the single-peak condition. Stage bins vary in length (about 2-15 Myr).

Only extinct families were used, so the result says nothing about families still at or before their maximum. 'Group' was read as family and 'number of species' as number of genera; species-within-genus counts were not tested.

59 of 313 families have at least one interior stage with no genus recorded or ranging through (Lazarus gaps); they were kept as pre-registered (the criterion did not provide for dropping them) and are less often single-peaked (49% vs 61%).

Bivalvia (0.33, n=27) and Crinoidea (0.45, n=20) fall below 0.5; Brachiopoda, Trilobita, Cephalopoda, Anthozoa and Bryozoa are all between 0.61 and 0.69. Echinoidea contributed no qualifying extinct family.
The PBDB is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as occurrences are added. Response checksums at retrieval time are in derived/fetch_log.csv.gz.

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database data service 1.2: taxa/list (family sampling frame) and occs/diversity (range-through genus counts per stage)

tests.label: Species and groups disappear gradually, place by place, not by global catastrophes
tests.hypothesis: If Tertiary extinctions were gradual and place-by-place rather than catastrophic, the last occurrences of extinct genera should be spread across many Tertiary stages rather than concentrated in one or two, and genera recorded on several continents should usually disappear from those continents at demonstrably different times, more often than genera killed in the known K-Pg catastrophe.
tests.pass: Two groups are analysed separately with Paleobiology Database genus-level occurrences from the Campanian through the Pliocene: Mollusca and Mammalia. Clause A (no catastrophic concentration): among PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence (midpoint of its age range) falls in the Tertiary (Danian to Piacenzian, 17 ICS stages), the single stage holding the most last occurrences holds < 1/3 of them, and at least 4 stages are needed to accumulate 50% of them when stages are ranked by count. Clause B (place by place): among those Tertiary-extinct genera that have >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents (PBDB continent codes), the fraction whose regional last occurrences are staggered (the earliest-vanishing continent's last-occurrence minimum age is older than the last-vanishing continent's last-occurrence maximum age, i.e. non-overlapping age ranges) is > 0.5 AND exceeds the same fraction computed for the K-Pg control set (PBDB-extinct genera whose global last occurrence midpoint falls in the Maastrichtian, using Campanian-Maastrichtian occurrences). A clause passes only if it passes in both groups. Verdict 'supports' if both clauses pass, 'mixed' if exactly one passes, 'refutes' if neither passes.
tests.fail: Clause A fails if, in either group, one Tertiary stage holds >= 1/3 of the genus last occurrences or <= 3 stages hold 50% of them. Clause B fails if, in either group, the staggered fraction is <= 0.5 or does not exceed the K-Pg control's staggered fraction (which would mean the apparent staggering is no greater than what incomplete sampling produces in a known simultaneous extinction). Both clauses failing refutes the claim; the K-Pg control itself is outside the claim's Tertiary scope and is used only as a sampling-artefact baseline.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'species and groups of species' are tested at the genus level because genus-level identifications are far more complete and less affected by taxonomic noise in PBDB. 'Disappearing from one spot, then another' is read as non-overlapping last-occurrence age ranges on different continents (modern continents, PBDB cc codes). 'Swept away together by catastrophes' is read as a strong concentration of last occurrences in one or two stages. The Signor-Lipps effect makes any extinction look gradual and staggered in an incomplete record; the Maastrichtian (K-Pg) control set provides an empirical baseline for how staggered a real catastrophe looks in the same database, so clause B requires Tertiary staggering to exceed that baseline. Scope is the Tertiary, as Darwin stated; the K-Pg event itself is not used to judge the claim.
tests.method: Genus-resolved PBDB occurrences of Mollusca and Mammalia from the Campanian to the Pliocene were downloaded for each of nine PBDB continents. For each genus flagged extinct in PBDB taxonomy, the last occurrence (smallest minimum age) was located and its age midpoint assigned to an ICS stage; genera whose database-wide last appearance is younger than the Tertiary were excluded. Clause A measured the concentration of Tertiary last occurrences across the 17 Tertiary stages (largest single-stage share; number of ranked stages needed to reach 50%). Clause B took Tertiary-extinct genera with >= 2 occurrences on each of >= 2 continents and called their disappearance staggered when the first-vanishing continent's last-occurrence age range lies entirely before the last-vanishing continent's; the same statistic was computed for genera with a Maastrichtian last occurrence as a K-Pg catastrophe control.

measured.unit: mean over the two groups of the fraction of multi-continent Tertiary-extinct genera with staggered regional last occurrences

caveats: Regional staggering is only detectable at the resolution of the occurrence dating: when a genus's last occurrences on two continents are both dated only to the same stage (common for mammals, whose records are often dated to land-mammal ages spanning several stages, and for all Maastrichtian records in the control), the ranges overlap and the genus is scored 'not staggered'. The mammal result for clause B is therefore partly a dating-resolution result, and the K-Pg control's zero staggering reflects the same effect as much as the catastrophe itself.
The Mammalia K-Pg control set is empty (no extinct mammal genus with >= 2 Maastrichtian occurrences on each of two continents), so for mammals clause B rests only on the > 0.5 condition.

Genus last occurrences in PBDB are truncated by sampling (Signor-Lipps), so both the spread across stages and the regional staggering are biased toward looking gradual; the Maastrichtian control set calibrates this for clause B but not for clause A.
The Tertiary window ends at the Piacenzian; genera that actually died out in the Pleistocene but have no PBDB Pleistocene record are counted as Piacenzian extinctions, inflating the youngest stage.
Stage assignment uses the midpoint of the last occurrence's age range; poorly dated occurrences spanning several stages add noise to clause A.
Modern continents are used as 'places'; a genus vanishing from one basin while persisting in another on the same continent is not visible, which biases clause B toward 'not staggered'.
PBDB coverage is heavily weighted to Europe and North America; staggering between continents can reflect unequal sampling rather than real sequential disappearance.

The test is at genus level, not species level, and is confined to Darwin's stated Tertiary scope; the K-Pg (Maastrichtian) set shows what a catastrophic horizon looks like in the same data and is deliberately excluded from the verdict.

tests.label: The extinction of a group is generally slower than its origination
tests.hypothesis: Extinct animal families in the fossil record are bottom-heavy: their genus diversity peaks early in their history and tapers over a longer decline, so the centre of gravity of the diversity trajectory lies in the first half of the family's duration.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: from the Paleobiology Database taxa API, all accepted animal (Metazoa) genera with first and last appearance ages and family assignment. A family is extinct if none of its genera is flagged extant and every genus has lastapp_min_ma > 0. Each genus ranges from firstapp_max_ma to lastapp_min_ma; the family's range is the union. Diversity D(t) = number of genera ranging through t on a 0.1 Myr grid. Centre of gravity CG = sum(D(t) * tau(t)) / sum(D(t)), tau = (family origin - t) / (family origin - family end), so CG < 0.5 means diversity is concentrated early and decline is slower than rise. Families qualify with >= 5 genera and duration >= 10 Myr. SUPPORTS if the median CG < 0.5, the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of CG - 0.5 < 0 has p < 0.01, and at least 55% of families have CG < 0.5.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if the median CG >= 0.5. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 100 qualifying families: inconclusive (underpowered); PBDB API unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). Descriptive secondary statistics: median CG and share below 0.5 for families ending at the five big mass extinctions (end-Ordovician 443.8, Late Devonian 372.2, end-Permian 251.9, end-Triassic 201.4, end-Cretaceous 66.0 Ma, within 2 Myr) versus all others, and for Paleozoic-, Mesozoic- and Cenozoic-originating families.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'complete extinction of the species of a group is generally a slower process than their production' is read through clade shape (Gould et al. 1977): if production is fast and extermination slow, the diversity trajectory rises steeply and tapers, giving a centre of gravity in the first half of the clade's duration. Groups are extinct animal families as classified in PBDB (Darwin's 'groups' of genera and families); diversity is counted in genera, because Darwin's species are rarely resolved in the fossil record. Range-through ranges from database first and last appearances are used without sampling correction; the Signor-Lipps effect pulls last appearances earlier and can shorten or lengthen the tail, so the test measures the record as compiled.
tests.method: All 79,166 accepted Metazoa genera were fetched from the PBDB taxa API; genera without ages or family were dropped. A family was taken as extinct when none of its genera is flagged extant and none has a last appearance at 0 Ma. Each genus ranges through from firstapp_max_ma to lastapp_min_ma; genus diversity D(t) was counted on a 0.1 Myr grid between the family's first origin and final extinction, and the centre of gravity CG of D over relative time (0 = origin, 1 = extinction) was computed for the 1,866 extinct families with >= 5 genera and >= 10 Myr duration. The median CG, the share below 0.5 and a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of CG - 0.5 were compared with the pre-registered thresholds; families ending within 2 Myr of the five big mass extinctions and families by era of origin are reported separately.

measured.unit: median centre of gravity of range-through genus diversity of extinct animal families (0 = origin, 1 = extinction; < 0.5 = slow decline)
measured.uncertainty: Wilcoxon one-sided p (CG < 0.5) = 1.06e-18; IQR 0.409-0.547

caveats: The asymmetry is real but small: median CG 0.477 (IQR 0.41-0.55), 59% of families below 0.5. It holds in every large phylum (Chordata 0.485, Arthropoda 0.473, Mollusca 0.462, Brachiopoda 0.489, Echinodermata 0.456, Cnidaria 0.473) and in Paleozoic-, Mesozoic- and Cenozoic-originating families (0.477, 0.482, 0.475). The test passes the pre-registered thresholds, but 'generally a slower process' is supported only as a modest tendency, not a strong rule.

As Darwin himself noted for ammonites, families ending at the big five mass extinctions are the exception: their median CG is 0.523 and only 41% are below 0.5 (n = 359), against 0.468 and 64% for families ending at other times (n = 1,507).

No sampling correction was applied. Range-through ranges from database first and last appearances are affected by the Signor-Lipps effect (last appearances drawn earlier); the 'pull of the Recent' does not apply because only extinct families are used. The grok assessor warned that sampling bias can manufacture slow-looking declines; the opposite bias (late-Lazarus truncation) also exists, so the direction of net bias is not known.

Genus first and last appearance ages are taken at the outer bounds of the first and last intervals (firstapp_max_ma, lastapp_min_ma), which lengthens every genus range by up to one interval at each end symmetrically.
Families are PBDB's classification, which includes paraphyletic families; Darwin's 'group' could also be read at the order or class level, which was not tested.
PBDB is a live database; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.

datasets.name: Paleobiology Database data service 1.2, taxa/list: accepted Metazoa genera with first and last appearance ages (show=app) and classification (show=class)

tests.label: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world
tests.hypothesis: Marine faunas on different continents change in step: the genus composition of a stage on one continent identifies the same (or an adjacent) stage on the other continents, and the magnitude of faunal change between consecutive stages is correlated across continents.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per ICS stage (stages >= 1 Myr) for each of six PBDB continents (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia), (A) for every continent-stage with >= 100 genera, find the stage whose pooled genus list from the other five continents has the highest Jaccard similarity with it; and (B) for every continent, compute the series of proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (fraction of genera in stage i absent from stage i+1, both stages >= 100 genera) and the Spearman correlation of this series between every pair of continents. The claim is SUPPORTED if in (A) the best-matching stage is the same or an adjacent stage for >= 85% of continent-stages, AND in (B) the mean pairwise Spearman correlation is > 0 with permutation p < 0.01 (independent permutation of stage order within each continent, 2000 permutations).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the same-or-adjacent matching rate in (A) is < 60%, or the mean pairwise correlation in (B) is <= 0. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Exact-stage matching rate, matching rate within two stages, and per-continent-pair correlations are reported as supplementary numbers.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world' is operationalised by its own consequence, which he states: that formations in distant regions can be correlated by their fossils. Test (A) is that correlation exercise done with genera: a continent's fauna from one stage should pick out the same stage elsewhere in the world. Test (B) checks that the amount of change between consecutive stages co-varies across continents (synchronous turnover). 'Almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense' is read as within one stage (typically 2-10 Myr). PBDB continents are the geographic units; marine environments only. Known limitation stated up front: PBDB stage assignments rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, which makes some agreement across continents expected by construction; a failure of test (A) would nevertheless be possible if faunas were strongly provincial, and test (B) uses magnitudes of change that are not used in dating.
tests.method: PBDB data service 1.2: ICS stage list (intervals/list.json?scale=1, type 'age'; 95 stages with duration >= 1 Myr) and, for each stage and each of six PBDB continents (cc=NOA, SOA, EUR, AFR, ASI, AUS), the marine Metazoa genus list from occs/taxa.json (rank=genus, envtype=marine, timerule=major): 570 API calls, cached and hashed individually (derived/files.json). (A) For every continent-stage with >= 100 genera (357 of them), the Jaccard similarity of its genus list with the pooled genus list of the other five continents was computed for all 95 stages and the best-matching stage recorded (derived/stage_matching.csv). (B) For every continent, proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (1 - |G_i & G_i+1| / |G_i|, both stages >= 100 genera) was computed; Spearman correlation of these series between every continent pair with >= 10 shared boundaries (13 pairs), and a permutation test of the mean pairwise rho (stage order permuted independently within each continent, 2000 permutations, seed fixed in analysis.py). Verdict follows the pre-registered rule: supported requires (A) >= 85% same-or-adjacent and (B) mean rho > 0 with p < 0.01; refuted if (A) < 60% or (B) mean rho <= 0; otherwise mixed.

measured.unit: fraction of continent-stages (>= 100 genera) whose fauna best matches the same or an adjacent stage on the other continents

caveats: Test (A) fell short of the pre-registered 85% bar: 78.4% (95% Wilson CI 73.9-82.4%) of continent-stages are best matched by the same or an adjacent stage elsewhere (53.8% exact, 87.4% within two stages, median offset 0). Test (B) passed clearly: mean pairwise Spearman rho of proportional genus loss = 0.31, permutation p = 0.0005; 12 of 13 continent pairs positive. The pre-registered rule therefore gives 'mixed'.

Matching success depends strongly on sampling: Europe 88%, Asia 86%, North America 85% (the three continents with median > 300 genera per stage) versus Africa 66%, Australia 55%, South America 54% (median 165-185 genera per stage). The failures are mostly a sampling-depth problem rather than faunal provinciality: for the 77 mismatched continent-stages the true stage's Jaccard is on average 79% of the best stage's, i.e. the correct stage is nearly tied.

Mismatches concentrate in the Neogene-Quaternary (e.g. Calabrian faunas of three continents best match the Aquitanian) where genus-level turnover is low and many genera persist for the whole period, and in thin Permian/Oligocene records. Low turnover is the opposite of what would falsify Darwin's claim (asynchronous change), so the 'mixed' verdict understates support for synchrony of change while correctly recording that genus lists alone cannot date stages to within one stage on poorly sampled continents.

PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, so some cross-continent agreement in (A) is expected by construction; test (B) uses magnitudes of turnover, which are not used in dating, and is the more independent test. The PBDB is a live database; the retrieved responses are hashed and dated so the run can be audited but later runs may differ.

Darwin's claim is about marine forms changing 'almost simultaneously throughout the world'; it is here reduced to genus composition of marine Metazoa on six continental units at stage resolution (typically 2-10 Myr). It does not test synchrony at finer than stage resolution.

tests.label: Fossils from consecutive formations are more alike than those from remote ones
tests.hypothesis: The taxonomic similarity of marine fossil faunas from two geological stages decreases with the time separating them, consecutive stages being far more similar than widely separated ones, and the fauna of each stage is intermediate between the faunas of the stages before and after it.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per international stage (ICS 2020 scale as served by PBDB; stages shorter than 1 Myr excluded; stages with fewer than 200 genera excluded), compute Jaccard similarity between all stage pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the Spearman correlation between pairwise Jaccard similarity and the separation of stage midpoints (Myr) is <= -0.5 with Mantel permutation p < 0.001, (ii) the mean Jaccard similarity of consecutive stage pairs is at least 2 times the mean similarity of pairs separated by 5 or more intervening stages, and (iii) for at least 80% of stages i with both neighbours, J(i-1, i+1) <= min(J(i-1, i), J(i, i+1)) (intermediacy).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the Spearman correlation is > -0.2, or the consecutive/remote similarity ratio is < 1.2, or intermediacy holds for fewer than 50% of stages. Other outcomes are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'formations' are read as international chronostratigraphic stages (the finest global units with ages), 'fossils ... closely related' as sharing of genera (the finest rank that is comparable across regions in PBDB), and 'remote' as separation by five or more stages. 'Intermediate' is read as: two stages bracketing a third never share more genera with each other than either shares with the middle stage. Only marine environments are used because marine faunas have the most continuous record. Modern reinterpretation: PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphy, which could inflate within-stage faunal homogeneity; the pass criterion therefore requires a large, graded effect over multi-stage separations, not merely a within-stage one.
tests.method: The 101 ICS stages of PBDB time scale 1 were retrieved; the 6 stages shorter than 1 Myr (Holocene and Pleistocene) were excluded and the Fortunian (139 genera) fell below the 200-genus floor, leaving 94 stages. For each stage the list of marine Metazoa genera with at least one occurrence (occs/taxa, envtype=marine, timerule=major) was downloaded (38,533 distinct genera; median 1,070 per stage). Jaccard similarity was computed for all 4,371 stage pairs and correlated (Spearman) with midpoint age separation, with significance from 2000 permutations of stage labels; mean similarity of consecutive pairs was compared with pairs separated by five or more stages; and for each interior stage the bracketing stages' similarity was compared with their similarity to the middle stage.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between pairwise Jaccard genus similarity of stages and their midpoint age separation (Myr)
measured.uncertainty: Mantel permutation p = 0.0005 (2000 permutations)

caveats: PBDB collections are assigned to stages partly by biostratigraphy, so some of the within-stage homogeneity is built into the data; the graded decay over 2-20 stages (0.29, 0.22, 0.17, ... 0.02) is not explicable by that alone, and the ratio at exactly five stages' separation (0.29 / 0.12) still exceeds the pre-registered factor of 2.
The 'remote' mean (gap >= 5 stages, 0.023) is dominated by very distant pairs; the profile by separation is given in measured.extra so the reader can choose a different threshold.

Genus sharing is a proxy for Darwin's 'closely related'; shared genera undercount relatedness between remote stages that share families but no genera, so the measured decay is steeper than a phylogenetic distance would be.
Intermediacy failed for 12 of 92 stages, mostly short or poorly sampled stages where sampling noise makes the two neighbours marginally more similar to each other than to the middle stage.
Stage durations vary (1-20 Myr) and sampling intensity varies strongly between stages; neither was corrected for, consistent with Darwin's claim being about raw faunal lists.

tests.label: Each region's fossils are succeeded by allied living forms in the same region
tests.hypothesis: If each area's later-Tertiary inhabitants left modified descendants in the same area, then the families of terrestrial mammals recorded as fossils on a continent in the Miocene-Pliocene should have living members on that same continent more often than they have living members on any other continent.
tests.pass: Fossil side: PBDB Miocene-Pliocene (23.03-2.58 Ma) occurrences of Mammalia on each of five continents (Africa, Eurasia = PBDB EUR+ASI, North America, South America, Australia), excluding marine orders/families (Cetacea, Sirenia, Desmostylia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae), giving for each continent the set of fossil families with >= 2 occurrences there. Living side: GBIF non-fossil, non-captive occurrence facets by family for Mammalia on each GBIF continent (Europe+Asia merged), a family counting as living on a continent if it has >= 20 such records there (same marine exclusions). For each continent X, S(X) = fraction of X's fossil families that are living on X, and O(X) = mean over the other four continents Y of the fraction of X's fossil families living on Y. Pass if S(X) > O(X) for all five continents AND the pooled ratio mean S / mean O >= 1.2 AND, in a permutation test that randomly reassigns the five living-family sets to continents (all 120 permutations, i.e. exact), the observed sum of S(X) is the maximum or tied maximum (p <= 1/120 + ties). The same statistics at genus level (fossil genera that are extant and living on the same continent) are reported as an extra and do not enter the verdict.
tests.fail: Fails if fossil families are no more likely to survive on their own continent than elsewhere: S(X) <= O(X) for two or more continents, or the pooled ratio is < 1.2, or the observed sum of S(X) is not the maximum over the 120 continent-label permutations. One continent failing with the other conditions met gives 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'closely allied' is read as membership in the same family (his examples, marsupials and edentates, are order- or family-level alliances, so family is a conservative choice). 'Later Tertiary' is read as Miocene plus Pliocene. 'Same continent or area' uses modern continents, merging Europe and Asia. Birds and molluscs, also in the stated scope, are not tested because their later-Tertiary fossil record in PBDB is far sparser and their family-level taxonomy less stable; islands are not tested. The GBIF side measures where families live today, which includes recent introductions (e.g. Muridae everywhere), a bias toward sharing with other continents that works against the claim.
tests.method: Miocene-Pliocene mammal occurrences were downloaded from PBDB for each continent and reduced to families (and genera) with >= 2 occurrences, excluding marine orders and families. Living families (and genera) per continent were taken from GBIF family/genus occurrence facets (>= 20 non-fossil, non-captive records). For each continent the fraction of its fossil families living there today (S) was compared with the mean fraction living on each other continent (O), and the sum of S was compared with all 120 reassignments of living-family sets to continents.

measured.unit: ratio of mean same-continent survival fraction to mean other-continent survival fraction, later-Tertiary mammal families
measured.uncertainty: exact permutation p = 0.0083 (1 of 120 label permutations >= observed)

caveats: Family-level alliance is coarse; cosmopolitan families (Bovidae, Felidae, Canidae, Muridae) raise both same- and other-continent fractions and dilute the signal, while endemic families (marsupial and xenarthran families) carry it, as in Darwin's own examples.
GBIF 'living on a continent' includes introduced and feral species (e.g. Muridae and Leporidae in Australia), which biases toward sharing with other continents and so against the claim.
PBDB family assignments and GBIF backbone family names are mostly but not entirely harmonised; mismatched spellings or re-ranked families count as 'not living', equally on all continents.

The Great American Biotic Interchange (c. 3 Ma) means part of South America's Pliocene fauna is of North American origin, which Darwin could not know; it makes the North/South America comparison conservative.
Birds, molluscs and islands, also in the claim's scope, were not tested.

tests.label: Physical conditions do not explain the similarity or dissimilarity of regional biotas
tests.hypothesis: Across regions of the world, the taxonomic similarity of their biotas is explained by which land mass they belong to (shared history and barriers) rather than by the similarity of their climates; in particular, climatically matched regions on different continents (e.g. the Mediterranean-climate belts of Australia, South Africa and Chile) share fewer taxa than climatically different regions on the same continent.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For the 23 regions in derived/regions.csv (5x5 degree boxes, pre-assigned to a continent and to one of six climate classes), genus lists of mammals, birds and vascular plants are taken from GBIF occurrences (genera with >= 3 georeferenced records in the box), and climate from the NASA POWER climatology (annual mean 2 m temperature, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range at five points per box). For each taxon group, pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity between regions is regressed on standardised climate distance and a same-continent indicator (permutation test over region labels, 2000 permutations). The claim is SUPPORTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, (a) the same-continent effect is significant (p < 0.05) and its partial R-squared exceeds that of climate distance, and (b) the mean Jaccard similarity of climate-matched pairs on different continents is lower than the mean similarity of climate-mismatched pairs on the same continent.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if, in at least 2 of the 3 taxon groups, climate distance has the larger partial R-squared and the same-continent effect is not significant, or climate-matched cross-continental pairs are more similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. If GBIF returns fewer than 20 genera for a region/group, that region is dropped for that group; if fewer than 15 regions remain for a group, the group is not evaluated.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'inhabitants of various regions' are read as the genus-level composition of three well-recorded groups (Mammalia, Aves, Tracheophyta); 'climatal and other physical conditions' as the NASA POWER temperature and precipitation climatology; 'similarity' as Jaccard similarity of genus lists. His 'accounted for' is read comparatively: climate distance should explain less of the variation in biotic similarity than does being on the same land mass, and his own example (Australia, South Africa, western South America at 25-35 degrees S) is tested directly as the climate-matched cross-continental pairs. The absolute wording ('neither ... nor ... can be accounted for') is not testable as stated because climate obviously limits distributions within a continent; the comparative reading is the one tested. Regions and climate classes were fixed before any data were retrieved. GBIF records include introduced species, which inflate cross-continental similarity and therefore work against the claim.
tests.method: Genus lists for Mammalia, Aves and Tracheophyta were obtained for the 23 pre-registered 5x5 degree regions from GBIF genus facets (genera with >= 3 georeferenced, non-flagged, present records); climate was summarised from NASA POWER climatology at five points per box (annual mean T2M, annual precipitation, seasonal temperature range), standardised (log precipitation) and converted to Euclidean climate distance. Pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity (253 pairs) was regressed on climate distance and a same-continent indicator with a Mantel-type permutation test (2000 permutations of region labels), and partial R-squared values compared; separately, the mean similarity of climate-matched cross-continental pairs was compared with climate-mismatched same-continent pairs. Central Arabia was dropped for mammals (17 genera < 20).

measured.unit: taxon groups (of 3) in which same-continent membership outweighs climate distance and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are less similar than climate-mismatched same-continent pairs
measured.uncertainty: permutation p-values per group in extra

caveats: For vascular plants the result is reversed: climate distance explains more of the genus-level dissimilarity (partial R2 0.36) than continent (0.08), although the same-continent effect is still significant and climate-matched cross-continental pairs are still (non-significantly) less similar than mismatched same-continent pairs. Genus-level plant composition is strongly shared across continents (cosmopolitan and Holarctic genera, plus introduced species in GBIF), so the claim holds for mammals and birds but not, at genus rank, for plants.

GBIF occurrences include introduced and vagrant taxa and uneven sampling; the >= 3 record filter removes only the rarest. Introduced species inflate cross-continental similarity and bias the test against the claim.

Climate is summarised by three variables from a 0.5 degree reanalysis-based climatology at five points per box; finer climatic structure (soils, topography) is not represented. The 'same continent' indicator also absorbs geographic distance, which Darwin treated as part of the same explanation (barriers and history).

Darwin's own triad (SW Australia, Western Cape, central Chile) shares a mean of 16% of mammal genera and 24% of bird genera, versus 30% and 57% for climatically different regions on the same continent.
The absolute wording of the claim is not tested; the comparative reading (continent outweighs climate) is.

tests.label: Barriers to migration correspond closely to differences between regional biotas
tests.hypothesis: Across pairs of regions of similar size, the species-level dissimilarity of their terrestrial faunas increases with the impassability and age of the barrier separating them (none < large river < shallow recently-dry strait < mountain range or desert < deep never-bridged strait < ocean basin), and this ordering persists after controlling for the geographic distance between the regions.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: 26 fixed region pairs are assigned a barrier rank (0 none, 1 large river, 2 shallow strait dry at glacial low stands, 3 mountain range or desert, 4 deep strait never bridged, 5 ocean basin). For each pair and each of three groups (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia) the Sørensen dissimilarity (1 - 2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|)) of species sets (GBIF occurrences, >= 3 records per species in the box) is computed and averaged over the three groups. SUPPORTS if Spearman's rho between mean dissimilarity and barrier rank is >= 0.5 with p < 0.01 (n = 26), AND the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log centroid distance is > 0 with p < 0.05, AND mean dissimilarity of the rank-0 (no barrier) pairs is lower than that of every barrier class with rank >= 2.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if Spearman's rho <= 0, or if the no-barrier pairs are on average at least as dissimilar as the deep-strait and ocean pairs (ranks 4-5). Any other outcome is MIXED. A pair in which any group has fewer than 10 species in either box is dropped for that group; if fewer than 20 pairs retain all three groups, groups are averaged over those available and this is reported; if fewer than 15 pairs remain the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'barriers of any kind' are represented by six classes with replicate pairs, ranked by a pre-registered judgement of how impassable and long-standing they are: contiguous land (0), the Amazon main stem (1), straits shallower than ~120 m that were land during Pleistocene low stands (English Channel, Palk Strait, Bass Strait, Malacca Strait, Torres Strait, Gulf of Paria, Sunda Strait) (2), high mountain ranges (Andes twice, Sierra Nevada) and wide deserts (Nullarbor, Sahara) (3), deep straits with no Pleistocene land bridge (Makassar Strait, Lombok Strait, Mozambique Channel, Yucatán Channel) (4), and ocean basins (Atlantic, Indian) (5). 'Difference between the inhabitants' is species-level Sørensen dissimilarity of three terrestrial, non-volant, non-marine vertebrate groups; bats and birds are excluded because they fly over barriers, and marine mammals because the barriers are their habitat. Distance is a confound Darwin himself names ('distance... is of less importance than barriers'), so the partial correlation controlling for distance is part of the criterion. Introduced species (notably Rattus, Mus, Hemidactylus, Rhinella marina) cannot be removed from GBIF data in general; Rattus and Mus species are removed explicitly, the rest remain and bias against the claim by making distant regions look similar.
tests.method: For each of 52 pre-registered boxes and three groups (Rodentia minus Rattus and Mus, Squamata, Amphibia) the GBIF occurrence API returned speciesKey facet counts (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, PRESENT, 1900-2026, fossil/living specimens excluded); species with >= 3 records formed the box's set. For each of the 26 pairs the Sørensen dissimilarity was computed per group (pairs with < 10 species in a box were dropped for that group) and averaged over the available groups; the Siberian control pair had too few species in every group and was dropped (n = 25). Spearman's rho between mean dissimilarity and the pre-registered barrier rank, and the partial Spearman correlation controlling for log centroid distance, were computed and compared with the pre-registered thresholds, together with the mean dissimilarity per barrier class.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between barrier rank and mean species-level Sørensen dissimilarity (Rodentia, Squamata, Amphibia)
measured.uncertainty: one-sided p=1.40e-05; partial Spearman controlling log distance rho=0.800, one-sided p=1.34e-06

caveats: Rodentia reached the 10-species minimum in only 13 of 25 pairs (islands and arid regions are thinly recorded), so most pairs are averaged over Squamata and Amphibia; all three groups individually show positive rank correlations (0.51, 0.70, 0.70).

Distance is only partly controlled: the desert and ocean pairs are much farther apart (2000-8600 km) than the others, and climate differs across the Sahara, Nullarbor and Sierra Nevada pairs. The partial correlation (0.80) and the fact that the mountain and deep-strait pairs (240-910 km) are more dissimilar than the no-barrier pairs at 560-1120 km address but do not remove this.
Barrier ranks are a pre-registered judgement; replicate counts per class are small (river 1, desert 2, ocean 2, mountains 3).
Introduced species remain in the data except Rattus and Mus; they lower dissimilarity across the widest barriers and so bias against the claim.
The Bali-Lombok pair is the least dissimilar deep-strait pair (0.49), consistent with the known weakness of Wallace's line for reptiles and amphibians; it is reported, not removed.
Boxes are bounding boxes with uneven sampling intensity; poorly sampled boxes inflate dissimilarity regardless of barrier.
GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.

tests.label: Species of the same continent or sea are related despite differing stations
tests.hypothesis: Within one continent, the genus-level composition of the fauna/flora of two strongly contrasting habitats (hot desert vs. humid tropical forest) is more similar than the composition of the same habitat type on two different continents; i.e. geographic region, not habitat, is the primary predictor of taxonomic affinity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for each of five taxonomic groups (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Amphibia, Magnoliopsida), compute the Sørensen similarity of genus sets (2|A∩B|/(|A|+|B|), GBIF occurrence-derived genus lists, genera with >= 5 records per region) for (i) the 5 within-continent / different-habitat region pairs and (ii) the 20 between-continent / same-habitat region pairs. The claim is SUPPORTED if the mean of (i) exceeds the mean of (ii) in at least 4 of the 5 groups AND a one-sided Mann-Whitney U test pooling all groups' pairs (i) vs (ii) gives p < 0.01.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTED if the mean of (i) exceeds the mean of (ii) in 2 or fewer of the 5 groups, or if the pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney test in the opposite direction ((ii) > (i)) gives p < 0.05. Any other outcome is MIXED. If fewer than 4 groups have >= 20 genera in every region, the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'productions of the same continent' are taken as the native genera recorded in GBIF within fixed bounding boxes on five continents (South America, Africa, Australia, North America incl. Central America, mainland Asia). 'Different stations' is operationalized as two habitat types with the strongest possible contrast on each continent: a hot desert/semi-desert box and a humid tropical forest box. 'Affinity' is operationalized as sharing genera (and, secondarily, families), which is the pre-phylogenetic measure of relatedness Darwin himself used. The 'same sea' half of the claim is not tested here. Regions are fixed before any data are downloaded; genera of domestic and commensal species that humans have spread worldwide (Homo, Rattus, Mus, Canis, Felis, Bos, Ovis, Capra, Sus, Equus, Columba) are excluded, as are fossil and living (zoo/garden) specimen records, because the claim concerns natural distribution.
tests.method: For each of 5 groups (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Amphibia, Magnoliopsida) and 10 pre-registered regions (a hot-desert and a humid-forest box on each of 5 continents) the GBIF occurrence API was queried for facet counts of genusKey and familyKey (hasCoordinate, no geospatial issue, PRESENT, 1900-2026, fossil and living specimens excluded). Genera with >= 5 records formed the regional genus set; 11 domestic/commensal genera were removed. Sørensen similarity was computed for all 45 region pairs per group and pairs were classed as within-continent/different-habitat (5 per group), between-continent/same-habitat (20) or between-continent/different-habitat (20). Means were compared per group and a pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney U test (within-continent/different-habitat > between-continent/same-habitat) was run on the 25 vs 100 genus-level pair similarities.

measured.unit: groups (of 5) where within-continent/different-habitat mean genus Sørensen > between-continent/same-habitat mean
measured.uncertainty: pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney (within > between-same-habitat), genus level: U=2086, p=1.22e-07

caveats: Magnoliopsida is the one group where the same habitat on another continent is as similar (0.307) as a different habitat on the same continent (0.295); introduced weeds and genuinely cosmopolitan plant genera both contribute, and GBIF cannot flag introductions reliably.

Amphibia is underpowered (as few as 4 genera in the Thar desert box) but the criterion was still met in 4 groups with >= 20 genera everywhere (Mammalia, Aves, Squamata, Magnoliopsida); Amphibia is reported but did not decide the verdict.
Genus sharing is a pre-phylogenetic proxy for 'affinity'; no phylogenetic beta-diversity was computed.
Introduced and vagrant species other than the 11 excluded commensal genera remain in the lists; they bias toward between-continent similarity, i.e. against the claim.

Bounding boxes approximate habitats; each box contains some other habitat. Sampling intensity differs by orders of magnitude between boxes (e.g. Asian desert mammals 2.5k records vs North American desert 237k), which depresses similarity for poorly sampled regions regardless of category.
The 'same sea' half of the claim was not tested.
GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added. Response checksums at retrieval time are in derived/fetch_log.json.

tests.label: Many genera are confined to one region and the most natural genera are local
tests.hypothesis: Across well-recorded classes of animals and plants, most genera (and a larger share of genera than of families) have essentially all of their modern occurrence records within a single continental region; and among mammal genera, those whose species are most closely related (youngest crown age in a dated phylogeny) occupy fewer regions and are more often confined to a single region than genera whose species are more distantly related.
tests.pass: Clause 1 (regional confinement by rank): in each of the analysed classes (Mammalia, Aves, Amphibia, Reptilia, Magnoliopsida, Liliopsida, Pinopsida; GBIF backbone), the fraction of assessable genera that are confined to one region (>= 95% of their continent-assigned, non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records in one of six regions: Africa, Eurasia, North America, South America, Oceania, Antarctica) is > 0.50 in at least five of the seven classes, and in at least five of seven classes the confined fraction for genera exceeds the confined fraction for families. Clause 2 (natural genera are local, mammals): the Spearman partial correlation between genus crown age (MRCA age of the sampled congeneric species in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree) and the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records, controlling for log(number of sampled species in the genus), is positive with p < 0.05, AND the single-region fraction among genera in the youngest crown-age tercile exceeds that in the oldest tercile. The claim is 'supports' if both clauses pass; 'mixed' if exactly one passes; 'refutes' if both fail.
tests.fail: Clause 1 fails if the confined fraction of genera is <= 0.50 in three or more of the seven classes, or genera are not more confined than families in three or more classes. Clause 2 fails if the partial Spearman correlation between crown age and number of regions is <= 0 or not significant at p < 0.05, or the youngest-tercile single-region fraction does not exceed the oldest-tercile fraction. Both clauses failing refutes the claim.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'region' is read as a continental biogeographic region (six regions, with Europe and Asia merged into Eurasia following Sclater's Palaearctic). 'Confined to a single region' is read with a 5% tolerance for misidentified, vagrant, introduced or mislabelled records. Sub-families and sections of genera are not available in the GBIF backbone and are not tested; the rank gradient is tested only between family and genus, with species reported as an extra. 'Most natural genera (species most closely related)' is read, following the assessors, as genera with the youngest crown age in a dated molecular phylogeny; this is a modern phylogenetic reinterpretation of a pre-evolutionary taxonomic notion. Only genera with >= 20 qualifying occurrence records are assessed, so that poorly recorded taxa do not appear confined merely through lack of records.
tests.method: For seven GBIF backbone classes and each of seven GBIF continents, one faceted occurrence search (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, fossil and living specimens excluded) returned record counts per genus, family (and species for the smaller classes). Europe and Asia were merged into Eurasia. Taxa with >= 20 records were scored as confined if >= 95% of records fell in one region, and the fraction of confined taxa was compared between genera and families within each class. For mammals, genus crown ages were computed as the MRCA age of sampled congeners in the Upham et al. 2019 DNA-only MCC tree, genus names were matched to GBIF genus keys, and crown age was correlated (Spearman, and partial Spearman controlling log sampled richness) with the number of regions holding >= 5% of the genus's records; single-region fractions were compared between youngest and oldest crown-age terciles.

measured.unit: mean across classes of the fraction of assessable genera with >= 95% of records in one region

caveats: GBIF 'Reptilia' (classKey 358) is a pro-parte synonym with no occurrences in the current backbone, so the pre-registered reptile class was run as Squamata (classKey 11592253), which holds most reptile genera.

GBIF continents are a coarse proxy for Darwin's biogeographic regions; merging Europe and Asia follows the Palaearctic but leaves Wallace's line and the Nearctic/Neotropical boundary at the continental edge.

Genus-level 'assessable' counts include extinct genera that have non-fossil basis-of-record entries and genera whose records are introductions or captives not flagged as LIVING_SPECIMEN; both bias against confinement, so clause 1 is conservative.

Recording effort is very uneven (Europe and North America dominate); the >= 20 record floor reduces but does not remove under-recording of tropical taxa, which could make some truly widespread genera look confined.

Clause 2 is a modern reinterpretation: 'most natural genera' was read as young crown age in a dated molecular tree. Crown age depends on which species were sampled (DNA-only tree) and on taxonomic lumping/splitting, and only 577 of 1890 assessable mammal genera had >= 2 sampled species. The negative partial correlation (older genera occupy fewer regions, controlling for richness) is significant but small.

Sub-families and sections of genera, which Darwin names explicitly, are not represented in the GBIF backbone and were not tested; the family-to-genus-to-species gradient is consistent with his rank ordering.
