tests.label: Continents and oceanic islands were not united by land in the recent period
tests.hypothesis: If now-separate continents and the existing oceanic islands were not continuously or almost continuously joined by land during the period of existing species, then even at the lowest Quaternary sea level (about -130 m) the sea floor between them should remain submerged: oceanic islands should not connect to any continent, and the Atlantic, Indian and Southern Ocean gaps between continents should not close.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the NOAA ETOPO 2022 global relief model exported from the NCEI image service onto a 0.1-degree grid, cells with elevation >= -130 m are treated as potentially emergent and labelled into connected components (with longitude wrap). The 45 pre-registered oceanic islands in derived/sites.csv are checked for membership of a continental component (continent seeds in the same file). Five continental gaps are tested for connection at -130 m: (T1) Eurasia-North America via the Atlantic, with the Bering region (lat > 55 N, lon 160 E to 160 W) masked as deep; (T2) Africa/Eurasia-South America; (T3) Australia/New Guinea-Asia; (T4) Antarctica-South America; (T5) Antarctica-Australia. The claim is SUPPORTED if none of T1-T5 is connected at -130 m and at least 90% of the oceanic islands are unconnected. A set of 20 continental (shelf or fragment) islands is run as a positive control and is not part of the verdict.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if two or more of T1-T5 are connected at -130 m, or if 25% or more of the oceanic islands connect to a continent at -130 m. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. The Bering connection between Eurasia and North America is reported separately with its sill depth (the shallowest threshold at which the two connect) because Darwin's wording concerns continents that are 'now quite separate' and he explicitly accepted a near-continuous circumpolar land connection during the glacial period (Chapter XI); it does not enter the verdict.
tests.interpretation: 'The recent period' / 'period of existing species' is read as the Quaternary, for which the maximum glacio-eustatic sea-level fall (about 120-130 m below present) is the most generous possible allowance for land exposure; a gap that remains submerged at -130 m cannot have been bridged by land at any time in that period without vertical crustal movement, which Darwin's opponents (Forbes) invoked and Darwin doubted. 'Oceanic islands' are the volcanic and coral islands listed in derived/sites.csv (one representative point each). 'Continuously or almost continuously united' is approximated by connectivity at the extreme lowstand; connections that exist only near -130 m were at most intermittent, which already satisfies Darwin's denial, so the test is conservative with respect to the claim. The 0.1-degree grid (about 11 km) cannot resolve straits narrower than a cell; bilinear resampling smooths sills, which is noted as a limitation.
tests.method: ETOPO 2022 (60 arc-second, surface) was fetched from the NCEI THREDDS NetCDF Subset Service in six 60-degree longitude bands with horizStride=6, giving a 1800 x 3600 global grid at 0.1 degree (nearest-sample subsampling; the six NetCDF files, 26 MB in total, are cached in data/ and hashed in result.json). Cells with elevation >= -130 m were labelled into 4-connected components with longitude wrap-around (scipy.ndimage.label plus union-find across the +-180 meridian). Six continent seed cells and 45 oceanic and 20 continental islands are listed in derived/sites.csv; each island is located by the nearest present-day land cell (z >= 0) within +-5 cells, or failing that the nearest cell emergent at -130 m (its bank). An island is 'connected' if its -130 m component contains a continent seed. Five continental gaps were tested for connectivity at -130 m, each restricted to the relevant ocean: T1 Eurasia-North America on cells north of 20 N with the Bering region (lat > 55 N, lon 160 E to 160 W) masked; T2 Africa-South America on cells south of 30 N; T3 Eurasia-Australia, T4 Antarctica-South America and T5 Antarctica-Australia on the full grid. For every gap, the Bering connection and every island, the sill depth (shallowest sea level at which the pair joins) was found by bisection on the threshold (14 steps, lower bound -6000 m for gaps and -1000 m for islands). Outputs: derived/island_connectivity.csv and derived/measured.json. Verdict by the pre-registered rule.

measured.unit: fraction of pre-registered oceanic islands whose emergent component at -130 m contains no continent seed
measured.uncertainty: 36 of 45 islands resolved as present-day land on the 0.1-degree grid (the rest located by their -130 m bank); 0 of 5 continental gaps connected at -130 m; 43 of 45 oceanic islands not joined to any continent even at -1000 m

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration, disclosed: the plan named the NCEI ArcGIS ImageServer (DEM_all mosaic) exportImage as the access route; it was replaced by the NCEI THREDDS subset service of the ETOPO 2022 60 arc-second file itself because the ImageServer mosaic blends ETOPO with higher-resolution coastal DEMs and resamples bilinearly, whereas the THREDDS route delivers unmodified ETOPO 2022 samples. The dataset (ETOPO 2022, DOI 10.25921/fd45-gt74), grid resolution and all analysis rules are as pre-registered.

Result: 0 of 5 continental gaps are connected at -130 m (sill depths: Eurasia-North America via the North Atlantic -757 m, Africa-South America -3750 m, Australia-Asia -1321 m, Antarctica-South America and Antarctica-Australia -3422 m); 0 of 45 oceanic islands join a continent at -130 m, and 43 of 45 remain isolated even at -1000 m (the two exceptions, Iceland and the Faroes, join Europe only at -608 m across the Greenland-Scotland Ridge). The Bering connection, excluded from the verdict as explained in the pre-registration, has a sill of -45 m and joins Eurasia and North America at -130 m, as Darwin himself allowed.

Positive controls behave as expected: 14 of 20 continental islands connect at -130 m with shallow sills (Great Britain -30 m, Ireland -53 m, Borneo -35 m, Sumatra -20 m, Java -32 m, New Guinea -13 m, Tasmania -58 m, Newfoundland -63 m, Taiwan -56 m, Hainan -21 m, Trinidad -14 m, Sakhalin -3 m, Sri Lanka -8 m, Honshu -119 m), while the continental fragments (Madagascar, New Zealand, New Caledonia, Seychelles) are isolated to -1000 m, Cuba joins only at -728 m and the Falklands at -163 m. The method therefore discriminates shelf islands from isolated ones at the resolution used.

Nine small oceanic islands (Ascension, Diego Garcia, Cocos Keeling, Amsterdam, Juan Fernandez, Pitcairn, Norfolk, Lord Howe, Raoul) are not sampled as land on the 0.1-degree grid; six were located by their -130 m bank and three (Cocos Keeling, Amsterdam, Pitcairn) have no emergent cell within 0.5 degrees, so they are counted as unconnected because the surrounding sampled sea floor is far below -130 m. Excluding them changes nothing (36/36 resolved islands unconnected).

The test is of bathymetry, not of history: it shows that no glacio-eustatic sea-level fall within the Quaternary range (about -120 to -130 m) could have joined the tested continents or oceanic islands to one another without vertical crustal movement of hundreds to thousands of metres. It does not rule out Forbes-style subsidence hypotheses by itself, and the 'period of existing species' is read as the Quaternary. The 0.1-degree nearest-sample grid can miss sills narrower than about 11 km in either direction (making a strait appear closed or open); the positive controls suggest the effect is small, and the margins in the main results (hundreds to thousands of metres) are far larger than any plausible resolution artefact.

The ETOPO 2022 surface layer includes ice-sheet and ice-shelf surfaces around Antarctica and Greenland; this can only enlarge the Antarctic component and so works against the claim for T4 and T5, which nevertheless remain unconnected.

datasets.name: NOAA NCEI ETOPO 2022 Global Relief Model, 60 arc-second surface elevation (ETOPO_2022_v1_60s_N90W180_surface.nc), accessed through the NCEI THREDDS NetCDF Subset Service with horizStride=6 (0.1-degree nearest-sample grid)

tests.label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right that the temperature of the whole world was simultaneously cooler during the Glacial period, then within one and the same dated interval of the last glaciation (the Last Glacial Maximum chronozone, 19-23 ka) surface temperature should have been below modern values everywhere: in both hemispheres, at all latitudes, and in every ocean basin, not only in the northern regions where glacial geology was first described.
tests.pass: In the MARGO gridded compilation of LGM (19-23 ka) sea-surface temperature anomalies (modern minus LGM, annual mean, 5x5 degree cells), (i) >= 90 % of cells with data show cooling (anomaly > 0), (ii) in every 30-degree latitude band of each hemisphere with >= 5 cells, and in each of the Atlantic, Indian and Pacific basins, >= 80 % of cells show cooling and the area-weighted mean anomaly is > 0 with a one-sample t-test p < 0.01, and (iii) the area-weighted global mean anomaly is >= 1 degree C.
tests.fail: Refutes if any hemisphere, or any 30-degree band of a hemisphere with >= 5 cells, or any basin, has a majority of cells warmer than modern, or if the global fraction of cooling cells is < 60 %. Any other outcome is mixed.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'Glacial period' is read as the last glaciation and 'this period' as its culmination; the MARGO project's LGM chronozone (19-23 ka, defined on independent radiocarbon and stratigraphic age models) is the standard operationalisation of a single simultaneous interval, so testing whether cooling is found in every region within that window tests simultaneity directly. 'Temperature of the whole world' is tested with sea-surface temperature because the ocean compilation is global, gridded and has quantified errors; land temperatures are not tested here. Darwin's own hedge ('or at least along broad longitudinal belts') is covered by the per-band and per-basin criteria. A cell counts as 'cooler' if the central anomaly estimate is positive; a sensitivity count using only cells whose anomaly exceeds its total error is reported but is not part of the rule.
tests.method: analysis.py downloads the MARGO supplementary zip, parses Table S9 (307 ocean grid cells with LGM reconstructions), computes cooling = modern WOA98 SST minus LGM SST per cell (the table's own 'anomaly' column is LGM minus modern despite the caption, so the two temperature columns are used directly), and evaluates the fraction of cooler cells, the cosine-latitude weighted mean cooling and a one-sided t-test globally, per hemisphere, per 30-degree latitude band and per ocean basin (basins assigned from longitude). The verdict follows the pre-registered thresholds.

measured.unit: fraction of 5x5 degree ocean grid cells with LGM (19-23 ka) annual SST below modern
measured.uncertainty: area-weighted mean cooling 2.063 C; 0.433 of cells cooler by more than the stated total error

caveats: Within the single LGM chronozone 84.4 % of 307 ocean cells were cooler than today (area-weighted mean cooling 2.06 C, p = 2e-39), both hemispheres (82 % and 88 %), every latitude band and every basin cooled on average with p < 1e-9, except the 60-90 N band (50 % of cells, p = 0.10). No subset shows majority warming, so the refutation condition is far from met; the 'supports' thresholds (>= 90 % globally, >= 80 % in every subset) are missed by the global figure, the Atlantic (79.5 %), the Pacific (79.3 %) and the Nordic Seas. Darwin's hedged version ('along broad longitudinal belts from pole to pole') is clearly supported; the literal 'whole world' is supported as a mean statement but not cell by cell.

Of the 48 cells warmer than modern, only 5 are warmer by more than MARGO's stated total error, and 142 of 307 cells rest on a single record; among cells with >= 2 records 88.5 % are cooler. The warm cells cluster in the Nordic Seas and the north-west Pacific, where foraminiferal transfer functions are known to give ambiguous LGM estimates (sea-ice and seasonality effects), i.e. where the proxy is least reliable rather than where the climate was demonstrably warmer.

Only sea-surface temperature is tested; terrestrial pollen- and glacier-based LGM reconstructions show cooling on all continents but were not used here because no comparable gridded text-format compilation with quantified errors was located.

Simultaneity is inherited from the MARGO chronozone (19-23 ka, independently dated at each site); the test shows that the same dated interval was cold almost everywhere, which is what Darwin asserted, but it does not test the longer onset/termination phasing between hemispheres.

The first run used the table's anomaly column with the sign read from the captions, which inverted every result; the sign was verified against the raw temperature columns and the script now derives cooling from those columns. The pre-registered criterion was not changed.

datasets.name: MARGO Project Members (2009) Constraints on the magnitude and patterns of ocean cooling at the Last Glacial Maximum, Nature Geoscience 2:127-132; supplementary Table S9 (MARGO_all_LGM_SST, 5x5 degree grid), archived at PANGAEA

tests.label: The Glacial period was simultaneous across the whole world
tests.hypothesis: If the Glacial period lasted a very long time at each place and was at least in part simultaneous across the whole world, then (a) a globally mixed marine proxy of ice volume and deep-water temperature (benthic d18O) shows prolonged cold, ice-rich states lasting well over 10 thousand years and recurring through the Pleistocene, with the last glacial maximum in such a state, and (b) a southern-hemisphere high-latitude temperature record (Antarctic ice core) is cold at the same times as the global proxy is ice-rich, within age-model uncertainty.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: (1) LR04 benthic d18O stack of Lisiecki and Raymo (2005), the LR04stack.txt file served by the author (columns: age in ka, benthic d18O in per mil, error), and (2) EPICA Dome C deuterium-derived temperature anomaly on the EDC3 age scale (Jouzel et al. 2007), the NOAA paleoclimatology file edc3deuttemp2007.txt. Criterion A (long-lasting cold states): with d18O linearly interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-2600 ka, d18O >= 4.0 per mil during at least 20% of the interval AND at least 5 separate contiguous intervals with d18O >= 4.0 per mil each lasting >= 10 kyr. Criterion B (last glacial maximum): mean d18O over 18-26 ka >= 4.5 per mil. Criterion C (simultaneity, north-dominated ice volume vs southern temperature): both series interpolated to a 1-kyr grid over 0-800 ka; the maximum Pearson correlation between EDC temperature anomaly and negative d18O across lags of -6 to +6 kyr (to allow for independent age models) is >= 0.6. SUPPORTS if A, B and C all hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if d18O >= 4.0 per mil covers < 10% of 0-2600 ka, OR fewer than 2 contiguous >= 4.0 per mil intervals last >= 10 kyr, OR the 18-26 ka mean d18O is < 4.2 per mil, OR the maximum lagged correlation in criterion C is < 0.3 (southern temperature not in step with global ice volume). MIXED otherwise (values between the support and refute thresholds, or A and B holding while C is between 0.3 and 0.6). INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if either file cannot be downloaded.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's Glacial period is mapped to the Pleistocene glacial stages. 'Lasted a very long time' is read as cold states of at least 10 kyr; 'simultaneous across the whole world' is read as the Antarctic (southern high-latitude) temperature record being in step with the benthic d18O stack, whose glacial signal is dominated by northern-hemisphere ice sheets; this is a two-hemisphere test of simultaneity at the resolution of orbital cycles, not of the sub-millennial bipolar seesaw. Darwin implied one long glacial episode; the data show many cycles, so the test asks whether long, globally cold intervals recur and co-occur. The 4.0 and 4.5 per mil thresholds and the 0.6 correlation threshold were fixed before any data were read. Criteria A and B follow the swarm thread's draft plan; criterion C was added to address the simultaneity clause the draft could not test.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads both text files. analysis.py interpolates LR04 d18O to a 1-kyr grid over 0-2600 ka, measures the fraction of time at or above 4.0 per mil and the contiguous intervals at or above 4.0 per mil lasting 10 kyr or more, the mean d18O over 18-26 ka, and, over 0-800 ka, the maximum Pearson correlation between the EDC temperature anomaly and negative d18O across lags of -6 to +6 kyr. The pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: fraction of the last 2.6 Myr with benthic d18O >= 4.0 per mil (pre-registered threshold 0.20)
measured.uncertainty: LR04 standard errors are 0.03-0.1 per mil per point, small relative to the 4.0 threshold

caveats: Darwin pictured one long Glacial period; the record shows dozens of glacial cycles. The test asks only whether long (>= 10 kyr), globally registered cold states recur and whether the southern high latitudes are cold at the same times, which they are (correlation 0.88 at a 2 kyr lag).

Benthic d18O mixes ice volume (mostly northern hemisphere ice sheets) with deep-water temperature; the Antarctic record is a single site. Simultaneity is shown at orbital (10-100 kyr) resolution and does not speak to millennial-scale bipolar anti-phasing.
The 4.0 and 4.5 per mil thresholds are absolute values of a stack whose mean level drifts over 2.6 Myr; early Pleistocene glacials are shallower, which the 20% criterion absorbs.
Darwin's 'whole world' includes the tropics and the ocean, which these two records do not resolve.

datasets.name: LR04: Pliocene-Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic d18O records (Lisiecki and Raymo 2005), author's distribution file LR04stack.txt
datasets.license: not stated on the file; published data, cite the paper

datasets.name: EPICA Dome C ice core 800 kyr deuterium and temperature estimates on the EDC3 age scale (Jouzel et al. 2007), NOAA World Data Service for Paleoclimatology file edc3deuttemp2007.txt
datasets.version: NOAA file last updated 2007-11-26 (EDC3 age model)

agent.run: scienceclaw-c4 (claims thread, ScienceClaw hack); drafts by the swarm thread (claude-sonnet-5-5) were used as starting points where noted

tests.label: Plants of high mountains and temperate lowlands worldwide are identical or closely related
tests.hypothesis: The vascular-plant floras of high tropical mountains share a few identical species and many more genera with the temperate lowland floras of both hemispheres, and they share more genera with those temperate floras than the tropical lowlands at the foot of the same mountains do; the temperate lowland floras of the two hemispheres are likewise related at the genus level beyond what tropical lowlands share with them.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Regions: 4 tropical high-mountain regions M (GBIF records with elevation >= 3500 m in the N Andes and Trans-Mexican volcanic belt, >= 3000 m in the East African mountains and New Guinea highlands), their 4 tropical-lowland controls C (same bounding box, elevation <= 800 m), 3 northern (N) and 3 southern (S) temperate lowland regions L (elevation <= 600 m). Species/genus present if >= 3 records. For a pair (X, L): f_sp = |species(X) ∩ species(L)| / |species(X)|, f_gen = |genera(X) ∩ genera(L)| / |genera(X)|. SUPPORTS requires all of: (A) in >= 20 of the 24 (M, L) pairs, 0 < f_sp < 0.5 f_gen (identical species exist but are the minority of allied relationships); (B) in >= 20 of 24 (M, L) pairs f_gen(M, L) > f_gen(C_M, L) (one-sided binomial sign test vs 0.5, p < 0.01); (C) in >= 7 of the 9 (N, S) pairs f_gen(N, S) exceeds the mean over k of f_gen(C_k, S).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if (B) holds in <= 12 of 24 pairs or (C) holds in <= 4 of 9 pairs. Any other combination is MIXED. If any mountain region yields fewer than 50 species, that region is dropped; with fewer than 3 mountain regions remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: 'Plants' = Tracheophyta (GBIF phylum key 7707728). 'Lofty mountains' including tropical ones = GBIF records above 3500 m (3000 m for Africa and New Guinea, whose summits are lower and more sparsely recorded) inside fixed tropical bounding boxes. 'Temperate lowlands of the northern and southern hemispheres' = fixed lowland boxes at 41-55 N and 34-55 S. 'Identically the same' = same GBIF backbone species; 'specifically distinct though related' = different species in the same genus (Darwin's own unit of alliance). Because 'remarkable' relatedness needs a reference, the tropical lowlands at the foot of each mountain range are the pre-registered control: Darwin's glacial-dispersal explanation implies the alpine flora, not the surrounding tropical lowland flora, is the one allied to temperate floras. Introduced species cannot be excluded from GBIF occurrence data; this inflates species identity (A) and is listed as a caveat.
tests.method: For 14 pre-registered regions the GBIF occurrence API was queried for Tracheophyta facet counts of speciesKey and genusKey restricted to the region's bounding box and elevation band (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, PRESENT, 1900-2026, fossil/living specimens excluded); taxa with >= 3 records formed each region's species and genus set. For every (tropical mountain M, temperate lowland L) pair the fraction of M's species also in L (f_sp) and of M's genera also in L (f_gen) was computed, and f_gen was compared with the same quantity for the tropical lowland control C at the foot of the same mountains. For the 9 (north, south) temperate pairs f_gen was compared with the mean f_gen from the four tropical lowland controls to the same southern region. Criteria (A), (B), (C) were counted and (B) tested with a one-sided binomial sign test.

measured.unit: of 24 (tropical mountain, temperate lowland) pairs in which the mountain flora shares a larger fraction of its genera with the temperate flora than the adjacent tropical lowland flora does
measured.uncertainty: one-sided binomial sign test vs 0.5: p=5.96e-08

caveats: Introduced species inflate species identity: e.g. 28% of the Central European lowland species set is also recorded in lowland New Zealand, mostly European weeds and crops. Criterion (A) (identical species exist but are a minority) is therefore satisfied partly for the wrong reason; the genus-level criteria (B) and (C) are less affected because the comparison is against tropical lowland controls that also receive introductions.

f_gen normalises by the source region's genus count, so the very genus-rich Andean lowland control (2206 genera) is penalised relative to the Andean alpine set (595); the Mexican and East African controls, which are similar in size to their mountain sets, show the same ordering, so the result does not depend on this.

Elevation comes from the GBIF 'elevation' field, which is missing on many records; regional sets are therefore samples of the flora, not checklists, and are unevenly sampled (e.g. 12.8k records in lowland Patagonia vs 1.0M in lowland New Zealand).
Genus sharing is a pre-phylogenetic proxy for 'related in a most remarkable manner'; no phylogenetic distances were computed.
Only four tropical mountain systems and six temperate lowland regions were sampled; temperate mountains ('the more lofty mountains' generally) were not tested separately.
GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added. Response checksums at retrieval time are in derived/fetch_log.json.

datasets.name: GBIF occurrence search API (facet counts of speciesKey/genusKey for Tracheophyta within bounding boxes and elevation bands; GBIF Backbone Taxonomy for keys)
datasets.license: varies by publisher (CC0 / CC BY / CC BY-NC); API output is aggregated counts

tests.label: Northern species naturalise far more often in the south than the reverse
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, many more European species have become naturalised in La Plata (and, to a lesser degree, in Australia) than species from those southern regions have become naturalised anywhere in Europe: the Europe-to-south naturalisation count should exceed the south-to-Europe count several-fold for each region.
tests.pass: Using World Checklist of Vascular Plants native and introduced distribution records by TDWG level-3 unit: A_LP = number of species native in Europe (TDWG level-1 region 1) and not native in La Plata that are recorded as introduced in La Plata (units AGE Argentina Northeast and URU Uruguay); B_LP = number of species native in La Plata and not native in Europe that are recorded as introduced in any European unit; likewise A_AU and B_AU for Australia (TDWG level-2 region 50: WAU, NTA, SOA, QLD, NSW, VIC, TAS). Supports if A_LP >= 5 * B_LP and A_AU >= 5 * B_AU.
tests.fail: Refutes if A_LP < 2 * B_LP or A_AU < 2 * B_AU (no strong asymmetry, or reversed). Otherwise mixed. The secondary clause 'in a lesser degree in Australia' is evaluated as A_LP > A_AU and reported, but is not part of the verdict rule because absolute counts now depend on two centuries of differing colonisation history.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'productions' is tested for vascular plants, the group for which native and introduced status is coded worldwide at consistent regional units; his La Plata examples (cardoon, thistles, fennel) are plants. 'Naturalised' is mapped to WCVP's 'introduced' flag, which records established alien occurrences in a unit (casual records and cultivated plants are excluded by WCVP's criteria). 'Europe' is TDWG level-1 region 1 (Iceland to the Urals, including the Mediterranean islands and European Russia; Macaronesia is in Africa in TDWG). 'La Plata' is the Rio de la Plata basin lowlands, mapped to Argentina Northeast (which includes Buenos Aires and Entre Rios provinces) plus Uruguay. Species native to both source and recipient regions are excluded. Counts are reported raw (Darwin's 'very many' versus 'extremely few') and as a fraction of each source flora. The claim is about the pattern, not its cause; propagule pressure is discussed in caveats only.
tests.method: analysis.py reads the WCVP distribution table for accepted species, defines Europe as TDWG level-1 region 1, La Plata as level-3 units AGE (Argentina Northeast) + URU (Uruguay), and Australia as level-2 region 50. A_LP is the number of species native in Europe, not native in La Plata, and flagged introduced in La Plata; B_LP is the number native in La Plata, not native in Europe, and flagged introduced in any European unit; A_AU and B_AU likewise for Australia. The pre-registered rule compares A/B ratios with thresholds 5 (supports) and 2 (refutes). Two sensitivity analyses are reported but do not enter the verdict: a wider La Plata (AGE, AGW, AGS, URU, PAR) and a restriction of each source pool to species whose entire native range lies in one TDWG continent (Europe, South America, Australasia).

measured.unit: ratio of European plant species naturalised in La Plata to La Plata species naturalised in Europe (WCVP)
measured.uncertainty: exact counts from WCVP status flags; depends on completeness of introduced-status coding

caveats: Primary result: A_LP = 465 European species naturalised in La Plata versus B_LP = 341 La Plata species naturalised in Europe (ratio 1.36, below the refute threshold of 2); A_AU = 837 versus B_AU = 274 (ratio 3.06, between the thresholds). Darwin's direction of asymmetry holds for both regions, but its magnitude ('very many' versus 'extremely few') does not: hundreds of South American and Australian species are coded as introduced in Europe.

Per source species the pattern is reversed for La Plata: 58 of every 1000 La Plata natives are naturalised in Europe, versus 17 of every 1000 European natives naturalised in La Plata, because the European native pool (27,000 species) is far larger than that of AGE+URU (5,832).

WCVP's 'introduced' flag mixes long-established invaders with regionally established aliens whose European foothold may be small; many Australian species recorded as introduced in Europe (Atriplex, Austrostipa, Calotis, Acacia) were historically wool or garden aliens, and some may now be casual or extinct. WCVP intends to exclude casuals, but its coding leans on regional floras of varying strictness, so B counts may be inflated relative to Darwin's 'naturalised'.

Conversely, the South-American-to-Europe list includes pantropical or widespread weeds (Amaranthus, Alternanthera, Bidens pilosa) that are native in La Plata but may have reached Europe from elsewhere. The continent-confined sensitivity removes these and gives ratios of 0.09 (La Plata) and 0.43 (Australia), but that restriction is biased against Europe, whose natives are mostly shared with Asia or North Africa (only 15 Europe-confined species are naturalised in La Plata), so it is a lower bound on the asymmetry, not a preferred estimate.

The secondary clause 'in a lesser degree in Australia' is not borne out: more European species are coded introduced in Australia (837) than in AGE+URU (465), in part because Australia is a continent-sized recipient with seven level-3 units and an intensive alien-flora census, whereas La Plata here is two units.

Darwin's observation dates from the 1830s; naturalisation counts now reflect two centuries of horticultural, agricultural and wool-trade propagule pressure in both directions, which Darwin could not have anticipated. The test addresses the present-day pattern, not whether Darwin's 1859 reading of it was reasonable.
Only vascular plants are tested; Darwin's 'productions' could include animals, for which no comparably coded global native/introduced checklist exists at regional resolution.

datasets.name: World Checklist of Vascular Plants (WCVP), Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: wcvp_names.csv and wcvp_distribution.csv in wcvp.zip

tests.label: Fresh-water species range widely and allied species occur worldwide
tests.hypothesis: Within each of three classes (insects, molluscs, flowering plants), species of fresh-water families occupy more continents than species of related terrestrial families, and fresh-water genera are more often spread over several continents than terrestrial genera.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for every family in the fixed fresh-water and terrestrial lists, GBIF occurrence facets give the set of species and genera recorded (>= 3 records) on each of the six inhabited continents. Per class, compute P_sp = proportion of species recorded on >= 3 continents and P_gen = proportion of genera recorded on >= 3 continents, separately for the fresh-water and the terrestrial family set. SUPPORTS if in all three classes P_sp(fresh-water) > P_sp(terrestrial) AND P_gen(fresh-water) > P_gen(terrestrial), and the pooled species-level continent counts differ in the fresh-water direction (one-sided Mann-Whitney, p < 0.001).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if, in at least two of the three classes, P_sp(fresh-water) <= P_sp(terrestrial) or P_gen(fresh-water) <= P_gen(terrestrial). Any other outcome is MIXED. A class with fewer than 200 species in either habitat set is dropped; with fewer than two classes remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: 'Fresh-water species of quite different classes' is operationalised with three classes Darwin names in this section (insects, molluscs, plants), using families whose members live in fresh water, each paired with terrestrial families of the same class and, where possible, the same order (aquatic Adephaga beetles vs. Carabidae; aquatic Heteroptera vs. terrestrial Heteroptera; freshwater snails and mussels vs. land snails; aquatic angiosperm families vs. a fixed list of common terrestrial angiosperm families). 'Enormous range' is given a comparison group as both assessors demanded: a species recorded on three or more continents. 'Allied species prevail throughout the world' = the genus is recorded on three or more continents. Continents follow GBIF's continent field (derived from coordinates), excluding Antarctica. Human-mediated introductions are present in both habitat sets and cannot be separated in GBIF; this is a caveat, not a filter.
tests.method: Each pre-registered family was resolved to a GBIF backbone key and, for each of six continents, the occurrence API returned facet counts of speciesKey and genusKey (coordinates present, no geospatial issue, PRESENT, 1900-2026, fossil/living specimens excluded); a species or genus was scored present on a continent with >= 3 records. Per class and habitat set the proportion of species (P_sp) and of genera (P_gen) recorded on >= 3 continents was computed and the fresh-water and terrestrial sets compared; continents-per-species distributions were compared with one-sided Mann-Whitney tests per class and pooled.

measured.unit: classes (of 3 usable) in which both the proportion of species and of genera on >= 3 continents is higher for fresh-water than for terrestrial families
measured.uncertainty: pooled one-sided Mann-Whitney on continents per species (fresh-water > terrestrial): p=3.42e-17

caveats: The species-level effect in insects is small (P_sp 0.021 vs 0.018, mean continents 1.14 vs 1.12) although the genus-level effect is large (0.22 vs 0.12); the verdict for insects rests mainly on genera, which is the 'allied species prevail throughout the world' half of the claim.

Human-mediated introductions inflate multi-continent occurrence in both sets (e.g. Physa acuta, Pomacea, Sphaeriidae among fresh-water taxa; Helicidae, Achatinidae, Rosaceae and Solanaceae crops and weeds among terrestrial taxa) and cannot be separated in GBIF.
GBIF 'continent' is interpreted from coordinates; records of Oceania and islands are coarse, and species with >= 3 records on 3 continents is a crude proxy for 'enormous range'.

Family lists were fixed in advance but are a judgement sample, not the whole class; several fresh-water families (Hydrophilidae, Elmidae, Haloragaceae, Menyanthaceae) include terrestrial or amphibious members, which dilutes the contrast.
Taxonomic splitting differs between groups (e.g. cryptic diversity in fresh-water snails and mussels) and the GBIF backbone's synonymy decides what counts as one species.
GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.

tests.label: Fresh-water fish species are not shared between distant continents
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous fish species has a native range that includes two continents separated by ocean (e.g. Eurasia and North America, Africa and South America, Asia and Australia).
tests.pass: Among FishBase species flagged as fresh-water only (Fresh = 1, Brack = 0, Saltwater = 0) and not anadromous, catadromous, amphidromous or oceanodromous, zero species have 'native' or 'endemic' country status (FishBase country table) in at least one country on each side of any ocean-separated continent pair. Ocean-separated pairs are all pairs among {Eurasia (Europe + Asia), Africa, North America (incl. Central America and the Caribbean), South America, Oceania (Australia + New Guinea + Pacific)} except Eurasia-Africa and North America-South America, which are joined by land.
tests.fail: Five or more such species have native status in >= 2 countries on each side of an ocean-separated pair (robust counterexamples, not single-country errors): refutes. Between 1 and 4 robust species, or only single-country cases: mixed. The share of strictly fresh-water species that are shared across an ocean is reported to distinguish 'never' from 'rarely'.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'fresh-water fish' is mapped to FishBase species that are flagged fresh-water only and are not diadromous, because he treats migratory marine-linked fishes separately and the claim concerns fish confined to fresh water. 'Distant continents' is mapped to continents separated by sea today; Eurasia is one landmass and North and South America are joined, so those pairs are not 'distant' for this test (a sensitivity count over all pairs of FishBase's six continents is also reported). Native status comes from FishBase's country status field (native, endemic), which excludes introductions, the main modern confound Darwin could not have foreseen. The second clause (within a continent, river systems share some species and not others) is near-tautological and is not tested here.
tests.method: analysis.py downloads the FishBase 24.07 species, country and countref CSVs, keeps species flagged fresh-water only (Fresh, not Brack, not Saltwater) whose AnaCat is not anadromous/catadromous/amphidromous/oceanodromous (16,213 species, 16,174 with native country records), joins their native/endemic country records to FishBase's Continent field, collapses Europe+Asia into Eurasia, and counts species with native records on both sides of each ocean-separated landmass pair. A species is 'robust' if it has >= 2 native countries on each side. Two post-hoc checks, labelled as such in measured.extra.post_hoc, were added after inspecting the output: removing Indonesia/Timor-Leste from the Asian side of the Eurasia|Oceania pair (Indonesian Papua is on New Guinea), and re-running the Eurasia|North America pair with brackish-tolerant non-diadromous species admitted.

measured.unit: strictly fresh-water, non-diadromous fish species native (>= 2 countries each side) on both sides of an ocean-separated continent pair
measured.uncertainty: exact count from FishBase 24.07 status fields; FishBase status errors can move single species in or out

caveats: The pre-registered mechanical count is 6 robust species (>= 5, 'refutes'), but inspection shows that count is partly artefactual: Upeneus guttatus is a marine goatfish mis-flagged as fresh-water only, Cichlasoma bimaculatum's 'native' Eurasian records are status errors, and three Indo-Pacific gobies/pipefishes (Glossogobius clitellus, Redigobius oyensi, Lophocampus retzii) reach Oceania from the Philippines/Indonesia; such island gobioids have marine larval phases that FishBase does not always code as amphidromous. 72 of the 77 Eurasia|Oceania 'shared' species are Indonesian-Papua vs Papua New Guinea/Australia records on the single landmass of New Guinea/Sahul, an artefact of FishBase filing Indonesia under Asia.

The verdict nevertheless stands on the genuine Holarctic cases: under the strict filter Thymallus arcticus (robust), Prosopium coulterii and Dallia pectoralis are native in both Siberia and North America; admitting brackish-tolerant non-diadromous species (post hoc) adds Esox lucius, Lota lota, Catostomus catostomus, Cottus cognatus and Prosopium cylindraceum (10 species listed, of which Atractosteus spatula and Gasterosteus microcephalus look like status errors). Northern pike and burbot in both England and Canada falsify 'never' on Darwin's own terms.

Darwin's generalization is nonetheless very nearly true: 6 of 16,174 species (0.04 %) meet the robust rule and 83 (0.5 %) share any country pair across an ocean, almost all of them artefacts; genuine sharing is confined to the Bering Strait region, where a Pleistocene land connection joined river systems, which is the mechanism Darwin himself proposed for dispersal of fresh-water fish.

FishBase treats Alaska, Canada and USA as separate 'countries', which makes North American counts easier to satisfy than Russian ones (a single country for all of Siberia); this biases the robust rule against Eurasia|North America cases, not in favour of them.
The within-continent clause of the claim (river systems share some species and not others) was not tested.
FishBase is licensed CC BY-NC; the data are not redistributed here, only fetched and summarised.

tests.label: Oceanic islands have fewer species than equal continental areas
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, an oceanic island supports far fewer native species than a continental area of the same size, after allowing for the physical conditions he thought could not explain the difference; for vascular plants (de Candolle's case) native species richness of oceanic island units should fall well below the continental species-area relationship.
tests.pass: Fit log10(native vascular plant species) = a + b*log10(area km2) + c*|centroid latitude| by ordinary least squares on continental (mainland-connected) TDWG level-3 botanical countries from the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, then predict richness for each pre-registered oceanic island unit at its own area and latitude. Supports if (i) the median ratio of observed to predicted richness across oceanic units is <= 0.5, (ii) >= 80 % of oceanic units lie below the continental prediction, and (iii) a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the oceanic log-residuals against zero gives p < 0.01.
tests.fail: Refutes if the median observed/predicted ratio is >= 1.0 or fewer than 60 % of oceanic units lie below the prediction. Any other outcome is mixed. Oceanic units whose area lies outside the range of continental areas used in the fit are excluded from the test and listed.
tests.interpretation: 'Species of all kinds' is tested for vascular plants, the group Darwin cites de Candolle for and the only group with a complete, native-status-coded global checklist at consistent regional units. 'Oceanic islands' are the TDWG level-3 units that are volcanic hot-spot islands, atolls or intra-oceanic arc islands never joined to a continent: AZO, MDR, SEL, CNY, CVI, STH, ASC, TDC, BER, GAL, HAW, MID, FIJ, SAM, TON, SCI, MRQ, TUA, TUB, COO, NUE, PIT, EAS, JNF, VAN, NFK, MAU, REU, ROD, COM, GGI, CRL, MRN, MRS, GIL, LIN, PHX, WAL, TOK, TVL, NRU, WAK, HBI, KER, CRZ, ASP, HMD, MPE, BOU, ICE, OGA, KZN, MCS, CGS, MDV, LDV, XMS, CKI, SGE, TRT, SOL (Solomon Is., oceanic arc), SCZ (Santa Cruz Is.), ALD (Aldabra). Units that are continental fragments or shelf islands (e.g. NWC New Caledonia, SEY Seychelles, FAL, NZN, NZS, MDG, GRB, JAP, SRL, CUB, FOR) are excluded from both groups; 'continental' means a level-3 unit whose polygons lie within 2 km of another unit's polygons (i.e. part of a connected mainland block), Antarctica excluded. Area is the spherical area of each unit's polygons; |latitude| of the area-weighted centroid is the only 'physical condition' covariate available at this resolution, so the physical-conditions clause is only crudely addressed. Native richness counts accepted species (rank Species) with a WCVP distribution record that is not introduced, extinct or doubtful. Small continental units (city-states, small countries) and the smallest oceanic islands may be undersampled in different ways; this is noted rather than corrected.
tests.method: analysis.py computes the spherical area and area-weighted centroid latitude of each of the 369 TDWG level-3 units and marks a unit 'continental' if any boundary point lies within 2 km of another unit's boundary (241 units after excluding Antarctica), 'oceanic' if in the pre-registered list, and 'other island' otherwise. Native richness per unit is the number of accepted WCVP species with a distribution record flagged neither introduced, extinct nor doubtful. An OLS fit log10 S = a + b log10 A + c |lat| on continental units (b = 0.199, c = -0.0088, R2 = 0.33) predicts richness for each oceanic unit; 28 of 60 oceanic units fall inside the continental area range (196 to 3.84 million km2) and enter the test. The measured value is the median observed/predicted ratio; the rule also requires the fraction below prediction and a one-sided Wilcoxon test.

measured.unit: median ratio of observed native vascular plant species on oceanic island units to the richness predicted for a continental area of equal size and latitude
measured.uncertainty: Wilcoxon one-sided p = 3.73e-09; interquartile range of ratio 0.185-0.612

caveats: All 28 oceanic island units (Hawaii 0.52, Fiji 0.66, Galapagos 0.21, Vanuatu 0.58, Samoa 0.46, Iceland 0.58, South Georgia 0.03, Canary Is. 1.00, ...) lie at or below the continental prediction; median ratio 0.44 (IQR 0.19-0.61), Wilcoxon p = 3.7e-9. The area-only model gives the same answer (median 0.45). Shelf and continental-fragment islands (n = 66, median 0.80, 61 % below) show a much weaker deficit, which matches Darwin's distinction between oceanic and continental islands.

Two codes in the pre-registered oceanic list were transcription errors discovered when the first run printed unit names: 'TVL' is Northern Provinces (South Africa), not Tuvalu ('TUV'), and 'TRT' is Trinidad-Tobago, a shelf island, not Trindade (which has no level-3 unit). They were corrected before the reported run; in the first run the only units at or above prediction were those two mis-coded units and the Canary Islands (ratio 1.00), so the verdict does not depend on the correction.

32 oceanic units smaller than the smallest continental unit (196 km2) are excluded by the pre-registered range rule; all of them have far fewer species than any continental unit, so the exclusion is conservative. TDWG polygons for some small remote islands are coarse (Kerguelen is drawn at 40 km2 against a true 7,200 km2), another reason to keep the small-island exclusion.

Only vascular plants are tested; Darwin's 'species of all kinds' extends to animals, for which no native-status-coded global checklist at consistent regional units is public. de Candolle's plant case is, however, the one Darwin cites.

The continental species-area slope across political/botanical units (0.20) is shallow and R2 is 0.33 because unit boundaries are arbitrary; the Canary Islands, the one oceanic unit at parity, are old, high and near Africa. |Latitude| is a crude stand-in for 'physical conditions'; the test cannot separate isolation from climate, area and age as thoroughly as Darwin's clause implies.
The Solomon and Santa Cruz Islands and Iceland are counted as oceanic on geological grounds; removing them would not change the median materially (all three are below prediction).

tests.label: Oceanic islands have a very high proportion of endemic species
tests.hypothesis: Oceanic islands have few native vascular plant species but a high proportion of them are endemic (found nowhere else), higher than mainland regions have, even though the islands are far smaller.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the World Checklist of Vascular Plants, for every TDWG level-3 area compute the native accepted species count S and the proportion E/S of those species that are native to no other level-3 area. Oceanic islands are the 63 level-3 areas pre-registered as 'oceanic' in derived/island_classes.csv; the mainland comparison set is every level-3 area not listed in that file as any kind of island. Areas (km2) are computed from the TDWG WGSRPD level-3 polygons. The claim is SUPPORTED if (i) the median S of oceanic islands is below the median S of mainland areas ('scanty'), (ii) the median E/S of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species is at least twice the median E/S of mainland areas, and (iii) at least 70% of oceanic islands with at least 20 native species lie above the mainland regression line of logit(E/S) on log10(area) ('extremely large relative to their area'). Islands with fewer than 20 native species are excluded from (ii) and (iii) because a proportion is unstable for them.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the median E/S of oceanic islands is not greater than the mainland median, or if fewer than 50% of oceanic islands lie above the mainland area regression line. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Supplementary: the fraction of oceanic islands with E/S >= 0.25, and the same statistics for the 'other-island' class (continental and arc islands), are reported.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'oceanic islands' are read as islands of volcanic or coral origin that have never been connected to a continent (list fixed in derived/island_classes.csv before any data were inspected; continental fragments, island arcs adjacent to continents and shelf islands are placed in a separate 'other-island' class). 'Kinds of inhabitants' is restricted to native vascular plant species because that is what WCVP records; introduced species are excluded. 'Found nowhere else in the world' is read as native to exactly one level-3 area, so for mainland areas 'endemic' means endemic to that botanical country, which is the fairest available analogue. Area is included because the claim says the proportion is large relative to the islands' size.
tests.method: Native (non-introduced, non-doubtful) occurrences of 358,113 accepted non-hybrid WCVP v16 species were tabulated by TDWG level-3 area; a species native to exactly one area was counted as endemic to it. Areas (km2) were computed from the WGSRPD level-3 GeoJSON by spherical polygon area. Islands were classified in advance (derived/island_classes.csv): 63 oceanic, 61 other islands, the rest mainland (Antarctica excluded). Medians of native richness and endemic proportion were compared between the 60 oceanic islands with >= 20 native species and 247 mainland areas; logit(endemic proportion) was regressed on log10(area) for mainland areas and the fraction of oceanic islands above that line computed; a one-sided Mann-Whitney test compared the distributions.

measured.unit: median proportion of native vascular plant species endemic to a single level-3 area, oceanic islands with >= 20 native species
measured.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney one-sided p vs mainland = 2.32e-05; IQR 0.031-0.248

caveats: Endemism at level-3 scale for mainland areas depends on political boundaries (e.g. 'Peru', 'India') and is inflated in Scandinavia and other parts of Europe by apomictic microspecies (Hieracium, Taraxacum, Ranunculus auricomus group) that WCVP accepts as species, so the mainland baseline is biased upward and the test is conservative with respect to the claim.

Eleven oceanic islands, nearly all low coral atolls (Cocos-Keeling, Maldives, Laccadives, Marshall, Tuvalu, Phoenix, Nauru, Howland-Baker, Marcus) or recently glaciated sub-Antarctic islands (Crozet, Heard), have no endemic species; the claim's 'often extremely large' is borne out by the high-island group (Hawaii 86%, St Helena 58%, Juan Fernandez 49%, Tristan da Cunha 47%) rather than by every oceanic island, and 25% of oceanic islands exceed 25% endemism.

Continental and arc islands (the 'other-island' class) show similar endemism (median 11%), so high endemism is a property of isolation generally, not exclusively of oceanic origin; the claim as stated concerns oceanic islands only and is supported for them.
Island groups are single level-3 units (e.g. the whole Hawaiian archipelago), so single-island endemics within an archipelago are pooled; this does not affect the comparison with mainland units.

WCVP inventory completeness is uneven, and a species recorded from only one area may sometimes reflect incomplete recording elsewhere rather than true endemism; this affects islands and mainland alike.

tests.label: Frogs, toads and newts are absent from oceanic islands
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no geologically oceanic island or archipelago (volcanic hot-spot island, atoll or intra-oceanic island arc that has never been joined to a continent) has a native amphibian species; every amphibian recorded there is a human introduction.
tests.pass: Across a pre-registered list of 40 oceanic island units (see planned unit list in interpretation), zero units have an amphibian species that is endemic to the unit by GBIF occurrence data, where 'endemic' means the species has >= 10 non-fossil, non-captive occurrence records worldwide and >= 95 % of them fall inside the unit. An endemic species cannot be a human introduction, so endemism is used as a conservative proof of native status.
tests.fail: Two or more independent oceanic island units each have at least one endemic amphibian species by the rule above: the universal statement is refuted. Exactly one such unit: 'mixed' (a single counterexample Darwin himself might have disputed, like his New Zealand frog). The proportion of units with native amphibians is reported in either case to characterise the 'general absence' Darwin also asserted.
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'islands with which the great oceans are studded' is read as geologically oceanic islands, which he distinguishes from continental islands elsewhere in the chapter (he explicitly excludes New Zealand and the Falklands as continental). Batrachians = class Amphibia (GBIF classKey 131). 'Never been found' is read as no native population; introductions, which Darwin himself discusses (Madeira, Azores, Mauritius), are excluded by requiring endemism. Pre-registered oceanic units (ISO code or bounding box): Fiji FJ, Samoa WS, American Samoa AS, Tonga TO, Palau PW, Micronesia FM, Marshall Is. MH, Northern Marianas MP, Guam GU, French Polynesia PF, Cook Is. CK, Vanuatu VU, Niue NU, Tuvalu TV, Kiribati KI, Nauru NR, Wallis & Futuna WF, Tokelau TK, Pitcairn PN, Norfolk I. NF, Bermuda BM, St Helena/Ascension/Tristan SH, Iceland IS, Sao Tome & Principe ST, Cape Verde CV, Comoros KM, Mayotte YT, Mauritius MU, Reunion RE, Christmas I. CX, Cocos (Keeling) CC, Hawaii (box), Galapagos (box), Canary Is. (box), Azores (box), Madeira (box), Juan Fernandez (box), Fernando de Noronha (box), Ogasawara/Bonin (box), Easter I. (box), Lord Howe I. (box). Excluded as continental fragments or shelf islands: New Zealand, Seychelles (granitic), Socotra, New Caledonia, Solomon Is., Bioko, Falklands, Faroes, Japan, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Taiwan, British Isles, Caribbean Greater Antilles. Classification follows the standard volcanic/arc versus continental distinction used in island biogeography (e.g. Weigelt et al. 2013 PNAS) and is a judgement made before any data were examined.
tests.method: analysis.py queries the GBIF occurrence API for class Amphibia (classKey 131) within each of 41 pre-registered oceanic island units (ISO territory code or WGS84 bounding box), excluding fossil and living/captive specimens, and facets by speciesKey. For each species recorded in a unit it fetches the species' global record count (for bounding-box units both counts are restricted to georeferenced records without geospatial issues, so that un-georeferenced museum specimens do not deflate the fraction) and flags the species endemic to the unit if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % of them inside the unit. The measured value is the number of units with at least one endemic amphibian; the verdict follows the pre-registered rule (0 supports, 1 mixed, >= 2 refutes).

measured.unit: oceanic island units with >= 1 endemic (hence native) amphibian species
measured.uncertainty: endemism rule: >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % inside the unit; counts are GBIF snapshot values at retrieval time

caveats: Three independent oceanic units have endemic, hence native, amphibians: Fiji (Cornufer vitiensis, 207 of 210 records; C. vitianus at 86 % narrowly misses the rule), Palau (Cornufer pelewensis, 1482 of 1505) and Sao Tome and Principe (six endemic species including the caecilian Schistometopum thomense). Mayotte's Boophis nauticus (93 %) and Blommersia transmarina (89 %) fall just under the 95 % rule and are not counted, so the count of 3 is conservative.

Darwin's wider point also holds in the data: 38 of 41 oceanic units (92.7 %) have no endemic amphibian, and in the well-sampled ones (Hawaii, Bermuda, Canaries, Azores, Madeira, Mauritius, Reunion) every recorded amphibian is a widespread species consistent with introduction. The universal statement is false; the strong tendency is real.
The pre-registration text says 40 units but the enumerated list (unchanged) contains 41; the count in the text was a miscount.
Endemism is a sufficient but not necessary proof of native status; non-endemic native species are not detected, which can only make the test more conservative.

Whether Fiji and Palau are 'oceanic' in Darwin's sense is a geological judgement: both are intra-oceanic island arcs never connected to a continent, but Fiji includes some old arc crust. Sao Tome and Principe are unambiguous volcanic hot-spot islands.

GBIF counts are a live snapshot; occurrence totals will drift between runs, but the identity of endemic species is stable. Species-level misidentifications in GBIF are mitigated by the >= 10 record rule.

tests.label: No native terrestrial mammals on islands more than 300 miles from a continent

(CX; 105.65,-10.5), Cocos (Keeling) (CC; 96.85,-12.15), Andaman and Nicobar (box; 92.8,12), Maldives (MV; 73.5,3.2), Chagos (IO; 72.4,-7.3), Seychelles (SC; 55.5,-4.6), Mauritius (MU; 57.55,-20.3), Reunion (RE; 55.5,-21.1), Comoros (KM; 43.8,-12.0), Mayotte (YT; 45.15,-12.8), Socotra (box; 54,12.5), Kerguelen/French Southern (TF; 69.3,-49.3), Iceland (IS; -18.5,65), Faroe Is. (FO; -6.9,62). Units nearer than 482.8 km are excluded from the main count and reported separately. Present-day distances are used, as Darwin did.
tests.method: analysis.py downloads Natural Earth 1:50m land polygons, computes spherical areas, keeps the 23 landmasses >= 100,000 km2, and measures the great-circle distance from each pre-registered unit's representative point(s) to the nearest densified vertex of those landmasses (excluding a polygon containing the point). 43 of the 52 units lie beyond 482.8 km. For each far unit it facets GBIF Mammalia occurrences by species (country code or bounding box; fossil and living specimens excluded), drops Chiroptera, Cetacea, Sirenia, pinniped and cetacean families and Hominidae via the species API, and flags a species endemic if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % inside the unit (for box units both counts are restricted to georeferenced records without geospatial issues, a correction made after the first run showed un-georeferenced museum specimens deflating the fraction). Verdict follows the pre-registered rule.

measured.unit: island units > 300 miles from a continent or great island with >= 1 endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal species
measured.uncertainty: distances from 1:50m coastlines and a representative point per unit (tens of km); endemism rule >= 10 records, >= 95 % inside unit; GBIF snapshot counts

caveats: The Galapagos (1,068 km from Ecuador) carry five endemic rice rats detected by the rule, Aegialomys galapagoensis and Nesoryzomys indefessus, N. narboroughi, N. fernandinae and N. swarthi (all records inside the archipelago), plus N. darwini and Megaoryzomys curioi below the 10-record threshold. Darwin visited the Galapagos and collected Aegialomys galapagoensis and Nesoryzomys darwini himself (Waterhouse 1839 described them), so this is a counterexample he had in hand; he may have regarded their native status as doubtful.

The first run used all records as the denominator for box units, which made the Galapagos rodents fall below 95 % because many museum specimens lack coordinates; restricting both numerator and denominator to georeferenced records is a correction of the measurement, not of the criterion, and is recorded here.

Only 1 of 43 far units (2.3 %) has detectable native non-volant mammals; the remaining 42 (Hawaii, Bermuda, Azores, Madeira, Cape Verde, Mascarenes, Seychelles, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga, Polynesia, Micronesia, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Falklands, etc.) show only cosmopolitan introduced species. Darwin's generalisation is very nearly right; the universal is not.

The Solomon Islands (1,006 km from New Guinea by this method, since New Britain is below the 100,000 km2 cut-off) have native murids (Solomys, Uromys, Melomys) but each has < 10 GBIF records or records split with Bougainville (politically Papua New Guinea), so the rule does not count them; counting them would strengthen the refutation. The Falkland Islands' extinct native fox Dusicyon australis (642 km) has no modern GBIF occurrence records.
Endemism is a sufficient but not necessary proof of native status, so the test under-detects native mammals. GBIF counts are a live snapshot and will drift between runs.
Distances are present-day, as Darwin used; Pleistocene sea-level lows do not connect any of the far units to a continent.

tests.label: Bats occur on almost every island, often as endemic species
tests.hypothesis: If Darwin is right, bats are recorded on almost every remote oceanic island group that has been reasonably surveyed, and a substantial share of those groups have bat species found nowhere else, in sharp contrast with the near-absence of native non-volant land mammals on the same islands.
tests.pass: Using the 43 pre-registered island units lying > 300 statute miles from any landmass >= 100,000 km2 (the far units of darwin1859-ch12-09, same GBIF filters and representative points), a unit counts as 'surveyed' if GBIF holds >= 500 non-fossil, non-captive bird (class Aves) records for it. A surveyed unit 'has bats' if at least one Chiroptera species has >= 5 non-fossil, non-captive GBIF records inside the unit (single records are treated as possible vagrants). A bat species is 'endemic' to a unit if it has >= 10 records worldwide and >= 95 % of them inside the unit (same rule as ch12-09). Supports if >= 80 % of surveyed far units have bats AND >= 33 % of the surveyed far units with bats have >= 1 endemic bat species.
tests.fail: Refutes if < 50 % of surveyed far units have bats, or if < 10 % of the bat-occupied surveyed units have an endemic bat species. Otherwise mixed. The contrast with non-volant mammals is reported descriptively: the number of far units with an endemic bat species is compared with the number having an endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal from the same GBIF endemism rule (1 of 43 in darwin1859-ch12-09).
tests.interpretation: Darwin's 'almost every island' is read as 'almost every remote oceanic island group that naturalists have actually searched', since he was generalising from the islands then known; the Aves-record threshold is a proxy for survey effort independent of bats. 'Their own species' is operationalised as GBIF endemism at the unit level; subspecies-level endemics (e.g. the Hawaiian hoary bat, treated by GBIF as Lasiurus cinereus or Aeorestes semotus depending on the backbone) are counted only if the backbone treats them as species. 'Remote' uses the ch12-09 distance rule (> 482.8 km from any landmass >= 100,000 km2), so the test is on the same 43 units for which the absence of terrestrial mammals was tested. Units are archipelago-level (country codes or bounding boxes), so a bat endemic to one island within a group counts as endemic to the unit. The threshold of >= 5 records per species is intended to exclude storm-blown vagrants (e.g. North American bats recorded in Iceland or Bermuda) while keeping genuinely resident but poorly recorded species; a sensitivity with >= 1 record is reported.
tests.method: analysis.py reads the 43 far island units (> 482.8 km from any landmass >= 100,000 km2) and their GBIF filters from ../darwin1859-ch12-09/derived/units.json. For each unit it counts GBIF bird records (survey proxy, threshold 500), then facets Chiroptera records by speciesKey; for each bat species it fetches the global record count (georeferenced-only for bounding-box units, all records for country-code units) and flags endemism at >= 10 records and >= 95 % inside the unit. A surveyed unit has bats if any species has >= 5 records in it. The pre-registered rule compares the occupancy fraction (thresholds 0.80 / 0.50) and the fraction of bat-occupied units with an endemic bat (0.33 / 0.10). Sensitivities: any single record counts as presence; endemism at >= 80 %.

measured.unit: fraction of surveyed far island units (>= 500 GBIF bird records) with a bat species having >= 5 GBIF records
measured.uncertainty: GBIF snapshot counts; endemism rule >= 10 records and >= 95 % inside unit; units are archipelago-level

caveats: Occupancy: 25 of 40 surveyed far units (62.5 %) have a bat species with >= 5 records, between the supports (80 %) and refutes (50 %) thresholds; counting any single record gives 32 of 43 units (74 %). Bats are nearly universal on tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean archipelagos but absent from the remotest eastern Polynesian groups (French Polynesia, Pitcairn, Easter Island), from the South Atlantic islands (St Helena, Ascension, Tristan da Cunha, Falklands, South Georgia), from the subantarctic (Kerguelen) and from Iceland, so 'almost every island' is an overstatement for the most isolated islands Darwin did not know well.

Endemism: 5 of 25 bat-occupied units (20 %) have an endemic bat by the strict 95 % rule (Azores, Hawaii, Ogasawara, Reunion, Solomon Islands); 5 far units have an endemic bat versus 1 (Galapagos) with an endemic non-volant mammal in darwin1859-ch12-09, which is the contrast Darwin draws.

The 95 % endemism cut-off is too strict for country-code units: well-known single-archipelago endemics such as Pteropus ornatus (94.9 % of records in New Caledonia), Notopteris neocaledonicus (93.3 %), Pteropus anetianus (92.5 %, Vanuatu), Pteropus aldabrensis (89 %, Seychelles) and Mormopterus acetabulosus (85 %, Mauritius) fall just below it because some museum records lack a country code. At >= 80 % the count rises to 9 of 25 bat-occupied units (36 %) and 18 endemic species, which would satisfy the endemism half of the supports rule; the occupancy half would still fail.

Several Pacific units are undersurveyed for bats even above the bird threshold: Niue (0 bat records) and Wallis and Futuna (4 records) are both known to hold Pteropus tonganus; Norfolk Island's Chalinolobus gouldii (2 records) is a historical resident. Correcting these three would raise occupancy to 28 of 40 (70 %), still short of 80 %.

Bermuda's seven bat species (24 records) are all North American migrants or vagrants with no resident population; the >= 5 record rule nonetheless counts Bermuda as occupied, which inflates occupancy slightly in Darwin's favour.

Hawaii's endemic is counted via the GBIF backbone species Aeorestes semotus (Hawaiian hoary bat), which many authorities treat as a subspecies of the hoary bat; Darwin's 'their own species' is sensitive to such taxonomic rank decisions.
Units are archipelago-level (country codes or boxes), so 'island' here means island group; bat-free individual islands within occupied groups are not counted against the claim.

tests.label: Sea depth between island and mainland predicts their mammalian affinity
tests.hypothesis: Across continental and near-continental islands, the fraction of an island's terrestrial mammal species that also occur on the neighbouring mainland decreases with the maximum depth of the sea channel separating them, and this relationship holds after controlling for the width of the channel; islands whose channel is shallower than the Pleistocene low stand (about 120 m) share more species than islands whose channel is deeper.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: for each of 28 fixed islands, (i) the terrestrial mammal species set (GBIF Mammalia occurrences with >= 3 records inside the island box, minus bats, cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and 12 domestic or commensal genera), (ii) the same for a fixed neighbouring-mainland box, (iii) channel depth = greatest water depth (GEBCO 2020 via the OpenTopoData API, 100 points) along a fixed straight transect between the nearest island and mainland shores, and (iv) channel width = transect length. f = |island ∩ mainland| / |island|. SUPPORTS if all of: Spearman rho(f, log depth) < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; partial Spearman of f on log depth controlling log width < 0 with one-sided p < 0.05; mean f of islands with depth <= 120 m exceeds mean f of islands with depth > 120 m.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if Spearman rho(f, log depth) >= 0 or if mean f of shallow (<= 120 m) islands is <= mean f of deep (> 120 m) islands. Any other outcome is MIXED. Islands with fewer than 5 qualifying species are dropped; with fewer than 12 islands remaining the result is inconclusive (underpowered). If the bathymetry API is unreachable the result is inconclusive (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: 'Terrestrial mammals' excludes bats (Darwin treats them separately), marine mammals and species carried by humans (domestic stock, commensal rodents, Homo); other introductions remain in GBIF and bias against the claim by making deep-water islands look similar to the mainland. 'Depth of sea' is the present maximum depth along a straight line between the nearest shores; Darwin's reasoning is about former land connections, so the 120 m Pleistocene low-stand depth is the pre-registered dividing line, and present depth is an imperfect stand-in for past connection (caveat). 'Same or allied species' is measured at the species level only (shared species fraction); genus-level affinity is recorded as a secondary descriptive measure. For Wallacean islands (Sulawesi, Lombok) the Sunda-shelf islands Borneo and Bali serve as the 'mainland', and for Hokkaido and Ireland the larger neighbouring islands (Honshu, Great Britain) do, as Darwin himself discusses Britain and its islands; this is noted.
tests.method: For each of 28 islands the GBIF occurrence API returned speciesKey and genusKey facet counts for Mammalia in the island box and in the mainland box, and the same for Chiroptera, Cetacea, Sirenia, Phocidae, Otariidae, Odobenidae and 12 domestic or commensal genera, which were subtracted; species with >= 3 records formed the sets. f = fraction of island species also present in the mainland set. Channel depth = greatest depth among 100 GEBCO 2020 points along the pre-registered straight transect (OpenTopoData API); width = transect length. Three islands with < 5 qualifying species (Pemba, Lombok, Cyprus) were dropped (n = 25). Spearman's rho between f and log depth, the partial Spearman correlation controlling log width, and the shallow (<= 120 m) vs deep (> 120 m) means were compared with the pre-registered thresholds.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between log channel depth and the fraction of island terrestrial mammal species shared with the neighbouring mainland
measured.uncertainty: one-sided p=0.139; partial rho controlling log channel width=-0.116, one-sided p=0.295

caveats: The direction is as Darwin stated (rho = -0.23; shallow islands share 59% of species with the mainland, deep islands 50%; the three deepest continental fragments, Cuba, Sulawesi and Madagascar, share 9%, 5% and 1%), but neither the correlation nor the shallow-deep difference reaches the pre-registered significance levels, so the verdict is MIXED.

The deep-water islands with high sharing are the Mediterranean islands (Corsica-Sardinia 0.72, Crete 0.73, Balearics 0.81, Sicily 0.39) plus Ireland (0.94) and Vancouver Island (0.86). The Mediterranean islands' present mammal faunas consist overwhelmingly of species introduced by humans since the Neolithic after their endemic faunas went extinct, and Ireland's fauna includes many Holocene introductions; GBIF has no reliable native-status flag, so these introductions could not be removed and they work directly against the claim. Vancouver Island was glaciated and its present channel depth overstates its Pleistocene isolation.

Several shallow-channel islands show low sharing for reasons unrelated to depth: New Guinea (0.20) and Sulawesi-adjacent Borneo (0.52) have large endemic radiations and small mainland reference boxes; Taiwan (0.36), Hainan (0.33) and Bioko (0.39) carry many island forms raised to species rank in recent taxonomy, which lowers species-level sharing while genus-level sharing stays higher (Hokkaido 0.47 vs 0.90 at genus level).

Channel depth is the maximum depth along one straight line between two pre-registered points, not the true sill depth; several transects cross land (e.g. 70 of 100 points for Sakhalin, 59 for Trinidad), and present depth is only a proxy for Pleistocene connection, which is what Darwin's argument actually concerns.
For Sulawesi and Lombok the Sunda-shelf islands Borneo and Bali stand in for the mainland, and for Hokkaido and Ireland the larger neighbouring islands do.
Bounding boxes of very different size and sampling intensity were used for islands and mainland regions; a mainland box that is too small or too thinly recorded lowers f regardless of depth.
GBIF is a live resource; re-running reproduces the method but counts drift as records are added.

tests.label: Island endemics are related to species of the nearest continent
tests.hypothesis: For endemic vascular plants of oceanic islands, the nearest relatives outside the island group on an independent synthetic phylogeny are, in a large majority of cases, native to the nearest continent or to the island group's own neighbouring islands.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: endemics of island group A = WCVP accepted non-hybrid species whose non-doubtful native records (introduced = 0) all lie in A. For each genus containing such an endemic, all WCVP accepted species are matched exactly to Open Tree (TNRS, context 'Land plants') and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree is fetched. For a focal endemic, the outside relatives O are the non-A tips of the smallest clade containing the focal tip and >= 1 non-A tip. The focal endemic is 'near-related' if more than half of O have a native record in A's pre-registered near source S_A (the TDWG level-1 continent nearest to A, plus A's own TDWG level-2 region, i.e. other near islands). s_A = fraction near-related. Island groups with < 10 focal endemics are dropped. SUPPORTS ('almost universal rule') if pooled s >= 0.75 AND s_A >= 0.6 in at least 75% of remaining island groups.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: REFUTES if pooled s < 0.5 or if s_A < 0.5 in a majority of remaining island groups. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 5 island groups remaining: inconclusive (underpowered). WCVP or Open Tree unreachable: inconclusive (data-unavailable). As a descriptive control, the fraction of all non-A congeners native to S_A is reported for each island group.
tests.interpretation: 'Related to those of the nearest continent, or of other near islands' is read as: the closest non-island relatives (sister clade on the genus tree) are native to the nearest continent, with near islands meaning the TDWG level-2 region the island group belongs to. Nearest continents (TDWG level 1) are fixed in advance by great-circle proximity: Galápagos 8 (Southern America), Juan Fernández 8, Cape Verde 2 (Africa), Canaries 2, Madeira 2, Azores 1 (Europe), Hawaii 7 (Northern America), Bermuda 7, Mascarenes (MAU+REU+ROD) 2, Seychelles 2, Tristan da Cunha 2, Fiji 5 (Australasia). Darwin's own contrast with climatically similar distant regions (assessors' suggestion) is not modelled; the test asks only whether the nearest continent dominates. Plants only; genus-level trees, so endemics of island-endemic genera are not scored.
tests.method: Island endemics were WCVP accepted species whose native records all fall in one of the 12 pre-registered island groups (3,928 species in 871 genera). All accepted species of those genera were matched exactly to Open Tree and the induced subtree of the synthetic tree was fetched per genus (783 trees). For each endemic in a genus tree that has species outside the island group (2,918 endemics), the outside relatives were the non-island tips of the smallest clade containing the endemic and at least one outside species; the endemic was near-related if more than half of them are native to the nearest continent (TDWG level 1) or the island group's own level-2 region. Shares per island group and pooled were compared with the pre-registered thresholds; the share of all outside congeners native to the near source is reported as a control, and the subset whose nearest outside clade is a single species is reported as a post-hoc check.

measured.unit: pooled fraction of island endemics whose nearest outside relatives (smallest clade on the Open Tree genus subtree) are mostly native to the nearest continent or the island group's own region
measured.uncertainty: island groups with s >= 0.6: 0/12; with s < 0.5: 9/12; endemics scored: 2918

post_hoc_single_outside_relative.note: not pre-registered; endemics whose nearest outside clade is a single species

caveats: The pre-registered criterion is met for refutation (pooled near-related share 0.29; 9 of 12 island groups below 0.5, none at or above 0.6), but this mostly reflects the resolution of the synthetic tree rather than biogeography: the median nearest outside clade contains 80 species, because species absent from every input phylogeny are placed as unresolved members of their genus, so the majority rule then scores the geographic spread of the whole genus. In most groups the near-related share barely exceeds the share of all outside congeners native to the near source (e.g. Galápagos 0.54 vs 0.53; Juan Fernández 0.33 vs 0.31), i.e. the test has little power beyond genus membership.

Post hoc (not pre-registered): among the 313 endemics whose nearest outside relative is a single resolved species, 63% are near-related, and Darwin's rule holds well for the Canaries (0.83, n = 77), Galápagos (0.90, n = 10), Mascarenes (0.91, n = 57), Madeira (0.73, n = 22) and Juan Fernández (0.67, n = 12), but fails for Hawaii (0.23, n = 74) and Fiji (0.43, n = 35), whose floras derive largely from Malesia, Australasia and the Pacific rather than from the nearest continent. This post-hoc pattern does not change the verdict but suggests the claim holds for Atlantic and Indian Ocean islands near continents and fails for remote Pacific archipelagos.

'Near islands' was operationalised as the island group's own TDWG level-2 region; for Hawaii and Fiji this excludes other Pacific archipelagos that Darwin might count as near islands, which makes these groups harder to pass.
Darwin's specific contrast (Galápagos with America rather than with climatically similar Cape Verde, and vice versa) was not modelled; the test only asks whether the nearest continent dominates.
Plants only; genus-level trees, so endemics of island-endemic genera (e.g. many Hawaiian lobeliads) were not scored.
