tests.label: Variability of stature and weight tracks the rate of growth
tests.hypothesis: The coefficient of variation (CV = SD / mean) of human stature and of weight at a given age tracks the mean rate of growth at that age: it falls through childhood as growth decelerates, rises again during the adolescent growth spurt, and falls after it. Hence, across ages, CV should be positively associated with growth velocity, within childhood as well as over the whole span, and the CV peak should coincide with the velocity peak.
tests.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using the CDC 2000 growth-chart LMS reference tables for stature-for-age and weight-for-age (2-20 years, half-month grid, each sex), compute at each age the CV of the fitted Box-Cox distribution (mean and SD obtained by numerical integration over z in [-4, 4]; the LMS S parameter is reported as a check) and the growth velocity dM/dt (central differences of the median M, per year). For each of the four series (stature boys, stature girls, weight boys, weight girls), over ages 2.5-19.5 years: (T1) Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive with P < 0.01; (T2) the age of maximum CV between 8 and 19 years lies within 1.5 years of the age of peak velocity (the adolescent spurt), and CV at that peak exceeds the pre-pubertal minimum CV (ages 4-11) by at least 5% of its value; (T3) within childhood, from 2.5 years to the age of minimum velocity before the spurt, Spearman rho between CV and velocity is positive (CV falls as growth decelerates). The claim is supported if T1, T2 and T3 all hold in at least 3 of the 4 series.
tests.fail: Pre-registered (claim refuted). T1 fails (rho <= 0, or P >= 0.01) in at least 3 of the 4 series, or T3 shows a significant negative rho (CV rising while growth decelerates, P < 0.01) in at least 3 of the 4 series. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. the adolescent rise T2 holds everywhere but the childhood decline T3 does not). If the CDC tables cannot be retrieved the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's evidence was Bowditch's and Boas & Wissler's cross-sectional CVs of Boston schoolchildren, ages 5-18 (stature CV about 4.8% at 5, 4.4% at 9, 5.8% at 14, 3.7% at 18). Modern reference charts are smoothed cross-sectional distributions of the same kind, so the LMS S parameter (approximately the CV) by age is the direct analogue. 'Rate of growth' is read as the absolute velocity of the median (cm/yr, kg/yr), Thompson's own usage (his Fig. 4 is the curve of annual increments). The WHO 2007 reference (5-19 years, height-for-age, both sexes) is a secondary replication, and the CDC infant tables (length and weight for age, 0-36 months) a descriptive check of Pearson's statement that variability decreases from birth; neither enters the verdict. Known confound (assessors): the adolescent CV rise is produced largely by variation in the timing of the spurt rather than by the rate itself; this does not affect the empirical association tested here. Before this pre-registration a reachability probe fetched statage.csv and wtage.csv and printed their header and first two rows (age 24 and 24.5 months); nothing else was inspected.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the six files and writes derived/lms.csv (series, sex, age, L, M, S). analysis.py uses the LMS S parameter as the age-specific coefficient of variation and the central-difference derivative of the median M as growth velocity (cm/yr, kg/yr); for each of the four primary series (CDC stature and weight, boys and girls, ages 2.5-19.5) it computes T1 (Spearman rho of CV vs velocity over all ages), T2 (age of the CV maximum in 8-19 y within 1.5 y of the age of peak velocity in 8-19 y, CV peak >= 5% above the pre-pubertal minimum in 4-11 y) and T3 (Spearman rho of CV vs velocity from 2.5 y to the age of minimum velocity before the spurt). Deviation from the pre-registration: the pre-registered 'exact CV by numerical integration of the Box-Cox distribution' is used only as a check for stature (L between -0.39 and 2.24, where it agrees with S to 4 decimals and gives identical test outcomes) because for weight L is -0.21 to -1.87 and the Box-Cox distribution has infinite variance for L <= -0.5, so that CV does not exist. WHO height (5.5-18.5 y) and CDC infant tables are secondary and do not enter the verdict.

measured.unit: primary series (of 4) in which CV rises into the adolescent spurt (T1 and T2 pass); 0 of 4 pass the childhood test T3
measured.uncertainty: half-month age grid, 204 ages per series; T1 P-values 2.8e-6 to 2.2e-75; T3 (stature) P = 1e-97 (boys) and 9e-19 (girls) in the wrong direction

caveats: The adolescent half of the claim is confirmed cleanly: in all four CDC series and in WHO boys the CV peaks within 0.5-1.2 years of peak velocity and 17-54% above its pre-pubertal minimum, and CV is positively correlated with velocity over the whole 2.5-19.5 y span (rho 0.32-0.90). The childhood half is contradicted: between 2.5 y and the pre-spurt velocity minimum (10.4 y boys, 9.3 y girls), stature CV rises monotonically (0.041 to 0.048) while velocity falls from 8.4 to 4.9 cm/yr (rho -0.996 boys, -0.79 girls; WHO: -1.0 both sexes), the opposite of Thompson's 'descends when the rate of growth diminishes'. For weight no childhood deceleration exists in the 2-20 y reference (velocity rises steadily from 1.6 kg/yr at 2.5 y to the spurt), so T3 is undefined and the childhood claim cannot be tested for weight there; in the CDC infant tables (0-36 months) weight CV does fall with falling velocity (0.15 to 0.11, rho 0.68 boys, 0.05 girls), while length CV falls (0.053 to 0.041) but not monotonically with velocity (rho -0.29, -0.37).

Deviation from the pre-registration: the CV is taken as the LMS S parameter rather than the quadrature CV of the Box-Cox distribution, because that distribution has infinite variance for L <= -0.5, which holds for weight at essentially all ages. For stature both definitions agree to 4 decimals and give identical outcomes. The verdict rule itself was applied as pre-registered; under it the weight series could never pass T3, so 'supports' was unreachable once stature failed T3, and the pre-registered 'refutes' condition (3 of 4 series with significantly negative childhood rho) could not be met either because only 2 series have a defined T3. The honest summary is: adolescent part supported, childhood part refuted for stature and untestable for weight in this range.

Thompson's own table (Bowditch) shows stature CV falling from 4.76 at age 5 to 4.40 at age 9; the modern US and WHO references show the opposite trend over the same ages (CDC boys 0.0425 at 5 to 0.0462 at 9). Bowditch's values are cross-sectional school data of the 1870s with small per-age samples; the LMS references are smoothed and much larger, and pool secular trend and mixed ancestry, which may inflate childhood variance.

Reference LMS curves are smoothed fits, not raw sample statistics, and the S curve is itself smoothed over age; Spearman P-values on a half-month grid treat each grid point as an observation and overstate the evidence, so they are reported for the sign and ordering, not as exact probabilities. The adolescent CV rise is widely attributed to variation in the timing of the spurt rather than to the rate of growth per se (the assessors' confound); this test cannot separate the two.

tests.label: Plaice weight-length coefficient peaks near the size of sexual maturity
tests.hypothesis: In North Sea plaice sampled in late winter, the weight-length coefficient k = W/L^3 averaged by length class rises with length to a maximum near 30 cm, close to the length at which sexual maturity begins, and then declines slowly at larger sizes.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ICES DATRAS exchange-format CA (age/biology) records for the North Sea IBTS, quarter 1 (January-February, the closest survey season to Thompson's March 1907 sample), years 2015-2019, species Pleuronectes platessa (Aphia 127143), individual weight > 0, lengths converted to cm. Compute k = 1000 W/L^3 (W in g, L in cm) per fish, average by 1-cm length class over 15-50 cm keeping classes with >= 30 fish, smooth with a 3-class running mean, and let L* be the length of the maximum smoothed k. Maturity: from the same Q1 CA records with a maturity code, classify immature (scale code ending in 1) vs mature (codes ending 2-5), fit a logistic of maturity on length (sexes pooled; by sex reported) and take L50. Supports if all hold: (1) hump: L* is at least 3 cm above the smallest and 3 cm below the largest analysed class, and smoothed k(L*) exceeds smoothed k at both ends of the analysed range by >= 3%; (2) 25 <= L* <= 35 cm; (3) |L* - L50| <= 5 cm. Secondary (reported): the same by sex, and for quarter 3 (2017-2019).
tests.fail: Refutes if smoothed k is flat (max - min over classes < 3% of the mean) or monotonic (maximum at an end of the analysed range), or if L* lies outside 22-38 cm. Mixed if a hump exists in the right place but is more than 5 cm from L50, or if the hump exists only in one sex or season.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's k is the Fulton condition factor computed by length class from mean weights of trawl-caught plaice 'in a particular locality and at a particular time'. Modern survey fish are weighed individually, so class means of individual k are used, which is equivalent for the purpose. 'Near 30 cm' is read as 25-35 cm; 'about the size at which sexual maturity begins' is read as within 5 cm of the length at 50% maturity in the same samples, since the onset of maturity is not sharply defined. North Sea plaice today mature at smaller sizes than in 1907, so criterion (3) tests the coupling to maturity rather than the fixed 30 cm figure, while (2) tests the figure itself.
tests.method: Downloaded eight NS-IBTS CA XML files from the DATRAS web service, kept Pleuronectes platessa records (Aphia 127143; Q1 2015-2019: 12504 records, Q3 2017-2019: 9514), converted mm length classes to cm, and computed k = 10,000 W/L^3 per fish (11474 Q1 fish of 15-50 cm with weight). Class means of k by 1-cm length class (>= 30 fish) were smoothed with a 3-class running mean and the maximum located; the same was done by sex, by year and for Q3. Maturity codes were mapped to immature (…1) / mature (…2-5) and a maximum-likelihood logistic ogive gave L50 pooled and by sex (10464 Q1 fish with maturity codes).

measured.unit: cm, length class of maximum smoothed k in Q1 (upper end of analysed range 16-43 cm); k x 10^4 falls from 97.9 at 16 cm to a minimum of 93.1 at 26-27 cm and rises to 100.2 at 43 cm
measured.uncertainty: class means based on 36-646 fish per class; standard deviations in derived/k_by_length.csv; the same U-shape appears in each year, each sex and in Q3

caveats: The modern pattern is the inverse of Thompson's: k is highest in the smallest fish, falls to a minimum at 24-28 cm and rises again toward 40+ cm (a U, not a hump), in Q1 pooled, in each year 2015-2019, in each sex, and in Q3 (minimum 25-27 cm). No class near 30 cm is a maximum.

Scope difference: Thompson's 1907 fish came from 'a particular locality' in March with k from class mean weights; here fish are pooled across the whole North Sea survey and weighed individually. Spatial pooling can blur a local hump but cannot manufacture a minimum, and the by-year and by-sex replicates agree.

Maturity has shifted: North Sea plaice now reach 50% maturity at ~18 cm pooled (females 22.5 cm, males 15.2 cm) in Q1, far below the ~30 cm Thompson cited, so criterion (3) could not have been met at 30 cm even if a hump existed there. The k minimum (~26 cm) lies near the female L50, the opposite sign of the association Thompson proposed.
Notation: the pre-registration wrote k = 1000 W/L^3; the analysis reports k x 10^4 as Thompson did (plaice k ~ 100). The scaling does not affect any criterion.
Q3 maturity codes are sparse (1,652 fish) and Q3 L50 (~25 cm) differs from Q1; Q1 is the pre-registered primary season.

tests.label: Seasonal cycle in fish weight at fixed length is caused by spawning
tests.hypothesis: At fixed length, plaice (Pleuronectes platessa) lose weight from about November to March/April (spawning) and regain it from May/June to November, and this cycle is caused wholly by spawning and the rebuilding of tissues and gonads. In the ICES North Sea IBTS, whose Q1 cruises run mid-January to early March (during and just after the North Sea plaice spawning season) and whose Q3 cruises run July to September (recovery), this predicts for MATURE plaice: (P1) the condition factor K = 100 W / L^3 declines with date within Q1; (P2) K rises with date within Q3; (P3) in Q1, spent fish have lower K than maturing or spawning fish of the same length. If spawning is the WHOLE cause, IMMATURE plaice should show (M) no comparable within-Q1 decline.
tests.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using NS-IBTS CA records (individual weights, CANoAtLngt = 1, maturity staged, length 15-55 cm) joined to HH records for haul dates, with log10 K regressed on day-of-year with fixed effects for 1-cm length class and sex: (P1) the Q1 slope for mature fish is negative with 95% CI excluding 0 and implies a decline of at least 2% of K per 30 days; (P2) the Q3 slope for mature fish is positive with 95% CI excluding 0; (P3) in Q1, spent fish have mean log10 K at least log10(1.05) below maturing fish at the same length and sex (95% CI excluding 0); and (M) the within-Q1 decline per 30 days in immature fish is less than 50% of that in mature fish (point estimate), or is not distinguishable from 0 at the 95% level.
tests.fail: Pre-registered (claim refuted). (P1) fails with the opposite sign (a significant within-Q1 increase in K for mature fish), OR (P1) holds in mature fish but immature fish show a within-Q1 decline per 30 days that is at least 80% of the mature decline with 95% CI excluding 0 (the seasonal cycle is not confined to spawners, so it is not caused wholly by spawning). Any other combination (e.g. the pattern holds but immature fish show 50-80% of the mature decline, or P2 or P3 fails while P1 and M hold) is 'mixed'. If fewer than 500 mature plaice with individual weight, maturity and haul date are available in Q1, the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's table is for 55-cm fish from the 1909 Plaice Report, month by month. DATRAS does not give monthly coverage of the North Sea (NS-IBTS samples only Q1 and Q3), so the test uses the within-quarter trends that Thompson's smoothed curve predicts (decline Jan->Mar of roughly 7% per month; rise Jul->Sep of roughly 3-4% per month) and the maturity-stage contrast that is the direct signature of his mechanism. The word 'wholly' is tested with immature fish as the control that the assessors proposed: immature plaice do not spawn, so under the claim they should not share the cycle. Feeding and temperature covary with season and would produce a cycle in immature fish too; that is exactly what would refute 'wholly'. Planned years 2015-2024 (10 years, Q1 and Q3). Maturity codes are mapped before the data are seen: immature = {1, 61, A, I}; maturing = {2, 62, B}; spawning = {3, 63, C}; spent = {4, 64, D}; resting/skipped = {5, 65, E}; other codes (-9, 66, 6, F) excluded; mature = maturing + spawning + spent + resting. Length: LngtCode '1' means LngtClass in cm; '.' or '0' means mm (divided by 10). Fish with |residual log10 K| > 0.3 from the length-class/sex means are dropped as recording errors (pre-registered cleaning). A single probe request (NS-IBTS 2019 Q1 CA, HTTP status and first record only, a herring) was made before this pre-registration to confirm that the web service is reachable; no plaice data were inspected.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the 40 XML files (875 MB, not committed) and derives: (i) plaice cells per quarter x ISO-style week x sex x maturity group x 1-cm length class with n, sum of day-of-year, sum and sum of squares of log10 K (K = 100 W/L^3), after mapping maturity codes as pre-registered and dropping 21 fish with |log10 K - cell mean| > 0.3; (ii) the same per year. analysis.py fits weighted least squares on cell means (weights n; exact individual-level OLS except that day-of-year is the weekly mean) of log10 K on day-of-year with length-class and sex fixed effects, separately for mature (maturing+spawning+spent+resting) and immature fish in Q1 and Q3, plus stage contrasts in Q1 and the adjusted Q3-Q1 difference; the pre-registered rules then give the verdict.

measured.unit: ratio of the within-Q1 (Jan-Feb) decline of log10 K per 30 days in immature plaice to that in mature plaice (pre-registered threshold for 'wholly spawning': < 0.5)

caveats: The descriptive half of the claim is strongly confirmed: at fixed length, mature plaice lose about 4.4% of their weight per 30 days through January-February (P1), regain about 4.7% per 30 days through July-September (P2), and in Q1 spent fish are 7.7% lighter than maturing fish of the same length and sex (P3); the adjusted Q3-Q1 difference is +10.9% for mature fish and is positive in every year 2015-2023 (5-14%). What is refuted is the word 'wholly': immature plaice, which do not spawn, show the same cycle (Q1 decline -5.7% per 30 days, 1.29 times the mature decline; Q3 rise +3.3%; Q3-Q1 +9.2%, positive in every year), so most of the seasonal weight cycle at fixed length is somatic (winter fasting and summer feeding), not gonadal. Within mature fish the stage pattern agrees: fish still 'spawning' lose 5.6% per 30 days while 'spent' fish are flat (+0.6%), i.e. the gonadal loss happens at spawning and then stops, whereas the somatic loss continues in all non-spent groups.

Thompson's own inference, that the spawning season can be read from length-weight data alone, is therefore not safe in general: an immature stock would show a comparable winter trough without spawning. The maturity-stage contrast (P3) does identify spawning, but it requires dissection, which is what Thompson claimed could be avoided.

Within-quarter trends mix calendar date with survey geography (different nations survey different parts of the North Sea at different dates), and fish are treated as independent (haul clustering ignored), so the standard errors are too small; the conclusion does not rest on them but on the comparison of immature with mature fish, which share the same geography and dates, and on the Q3-Q1 contrast, which replicates in every year.

Maturity is taken from the DATRAS codes at face value with the pre-registered mapping; 1480 fish with sub-staged old IBTS codes (Ba, Bb, Ca, Cb, Da, Db) and 29084 weighed plaice without a maturity stage were excluded as pre-registered. Some 'immature' fish of 25-35 cm could be mis-staged late maturers, but at that size the immature group is large (hundreds per week) and the pattern holds across weeks.

NS-IBTS samples only January-March and July-September, so the months Thompson named for the trough (March-April) and the peak (November) are not observed directly; the test uses the direction of change inside each quarter, which his smoothed curve predicts unambiguously.

tests.label: Arizona tree rings show a regular 150-year climate periodicity
tests.hypothesis: Annual ring-width chronologies of Arizona ponderosa pine over roughly 1390-1910 contain a regular oscillation with a period of about 150 years, visible as a significant spectral peak near 150 yr and as century-smoothed maxima recurring every ~150 yr.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Primary series: ITRDB chronology az572 (Flagstaff, Arizona, Pinus ponderosa, 'Modern + Archaeological', AD 570-1987), the standard index over the window 1390-1910 (521 yr). Replicate: ITRDB az547 (Walnut Canyon, Pinus ponderosa, 1420-1987) over 1420-1910. Test 1 (spectral): periodogram of the mean-removed annual index; null = AR(1) with the series' lag-1 autocorrelation and variance, 5000 surrogates; pass if the largest periodogram ordinate at periods 120-200 yr exceeds the pointwise 95th percentile of the surrogate periodograms and its period lies in 130-170 yr. Test 2 (regularity of century-smoothed maxima, Douglass's own procedure): 101-yr centred running mean of the index (using data from 1340 on so the smoothed series spans 1390-1910); find local maxima of the smoothed series separated by at least 50 yr; pass if there are at least two intervals between successive maxima and every interval lies in 125-175 yr. Supports if both tests pass on az572.
tests.fail: Refutes if both tests fail on az572 (no significant 120-200-yr spectral peak against red noise, and smoothed maxima spaced irregularly or outside 125-175 yr). Mixed if exactly one test passes, or if az572 passes but the az547 replicate fails both tests.
tests.interpretation: Thompson relayed Douglass's (1909, 1914) reading of century-smoothed Flagstaff pine ring widths as showing a ~150-yr climatic cycle. 'Regular period of almost exactly 150 years' is read as a spectral line in the 130-170-yr band that is significant against a red-noise background, together with smoothed maxima recurring at 150 +/- 25 yr. The moisture-versus-temperature attribution is not tested. Modern ITRDB chronologies are standardized indices (age trend removed) built from many trees, not the few raw series Douglass had; they are the best available record of the same trees' growth signal. A 521-yr window holds only ~3.5 cycles of 150 yr, so the spectral test is low-powered and is complemented by the smoothed-maxima test.
tests.method: Downloaded the two Tucson-format .crn chronologies from NCEI, parsed the standard index (x1000, 9990 = missing) and sample depth, and took 1390-1910 (az572, 521 yr, complete) and 1420-1910 (az547, 491 yr). Test 1: raw periodogram of the mean-removed index against 5000 AR(1) surrogates matched in lag-1 autocorrelation (0.45, 0.52) and variance; the largest ordinate at 120-200 yr was compared with the pointwise 95th percentile (and with a band-maximum null). Test 2: 101-yr centred running mean (51-yr as sensitivity); local maxima at least 50 yr apart; intervals between successive maxima.

measured.unit: yr, mean interval between successive maxima of the 101-yr-smoothed Flagstaff index 1390-1910 (intervals 73, 57, 70, 68, 109); strongest 120-200-yr periodogram ordinate at 174 yr has power 1.33 vs AR(1) 95th percentile 1.64
measured.uncertainty: 521-yr window holds ~3.5 cycles of 150 yr; spectral test low-powered by design, so the smoothed-maxima test was pre-registered alongside

caveats: Both pre-registered tests fail at both sites: no 120-200-yr spectral ordinate exceeds the red-noise 95th percentile (Flagstaff 174 yr: 1.33 vs 1.64; Walnut Canyon 164 yr: 2.21 vs 3.39), and century-smoothed maxima recur every 57-133 yr (means 75 and 89 yr), not every 150. The smoothed series do oscillate, but irregularly and roughly twice as fast as Thompson's figure; a 51-yr smoothing gives the same conclusion.

Sample depth is thin early in the window (Flagstaff: 1-3 trees before 1400, 3-6 in the 1400s; Walnut Canyon: 2-4 trees before 1600), so the 15th-16th-century part of the index is noisy; this weakens any periodicity test but cannot create a regular 150-yr cycle where none is detected.

ITRDB standard chronologies remove the age trend by curve fitting; Douglass smoothed raw widths of a few trees. Detrending with conservative curves preserves century-scale variance in most chronologies but could damp a very long oscillation; the 521-yr window itself limits detectable periods to well under ~260 yr for two cycles.

Not pre-registered, reported as observation only: both sites show a ~70-yr spectral peak (Walnut Canyon 70 yr at 2.4x the AR(1) 95th percentile; Flagstaff 74 yr at 1.4x), in the range of known multidecadal drought variability in the Southwest, not the 150-yr cycle claimed.
The moisture-versus-temperature attribution in the claim was not tested.

tests.label: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
tests.hypothesis: Across plant and animal species, the gametic (haploid) chromosome number n lies mostly between 6 and 16: the fraction of taxa with n < 6 is small and the fraction with n > 16 is smaller still.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Plants: species-level gametic numbers from the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB) statistics service for all four major groups (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes), using each species' median parsed n. Animals: the Animal Chromosome Count Database (ACC) table (haploid N where given, else 2N/2), one median value per species. For each kingdom compute f_low = fraction of taxa with n < 6, f_mid = fraction with 6 <= n <= 16, f_high = fraction with n > 16, at two resolutions: species level, and genus level (median of species values per genus, the primary resolution, to damp sampling bias toward well-studied genera). Supports if at genus level, in both kingdoms, f_low <= 0.10 and f_high <= 0.10 and f_high <= f_low.
tests.fail: Refutes if at genus level f_high >= 0.25 in either kingdom (more than a quarter of genera above 16 is not 'fewer still'), or if f_high > f_low in both kingdoms (the upper tail is the larger tail, inverting the claim). Mixed otherwise (e.g. one kingdom satisfies the bounds and the other does not, without reaching the refutation thresholds).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'germ-nuclei' chromosome number is the gametic number n (half the somatic 2n), which both databases provide or allow (CCDB parses counts to gametophytic n; ACC lists N or 2N). 'Few' and 'fewer still' are read as tail fractions of at most 10%, with the upper tail no larger than the lower. The claim is about organisms generally, so species (or genera) are the units, each counted once, with no phylogenetic weighting; the species-level figures are reported alongside the primary genus-level ones. Databases are biased toward studied taxa (crops, insects, vertebrates), which is noted but not corrected beyond the genus-level aggregation.
tests.method: Fetched the CCDB statistics CSV for each of the four plant major groups (69,948 species rows; median parsed n per species) and parsed the ACC data table embedded in its download page (12,221 animal records; haploid N where given, else 2N/2). Collapsed to one median value per species and per genus, then computed the fractions of taxa with n < 6, 6 <= n <= 16 and n > 16 for plants and animals at both resolutions, plus breakdowns by plant major group and animal phylum and a histogram (derived/histograms.csv).

measured.unit: fraction of animal genera with haploid n > 16 (plant genera: 0.320); fraction with n < 6: animals 0.080, plants 0.011
measured.uncertainty: database census; genus-level n = 8414 plant and 5285 animal genera, species-level n = 64926 and 12221

caveats: The lower bound holds (only 1.1% of plant genera and 8.0% of animal genera have n < 6) and the modal haploid number (9-13) sits inside Thompson's 6-16 window, so the claim is half right; what fails is the upper bound: 32% of plant genera and 41% of animal genera have n > 16, so the upper tail is roughly 30 and 5 times larger than the lower tail, the reverse of 'fewer still'.

Both databases over-represent studied taxa (crops, insects, vertebrates) and plants are counted as gametophytic numbers including polyploids (hexaploid wheat is n = 21). Even taking the most favourable subsets (gymnosperms 5.8% > 16; bryophytes 11%), ferns (96% > 16), vertebrates (74%) and molluscs (60%) leave the general claim refuted.
ACC records with non-numeric or range entries for 2N and N were dropped; odd 2N values (XO systems) give half-integer n, which does not affect the 6-16 binning.
Thompson wrote in 1917 from a handful of counted species; the finding reflects a century of counting rather than an error in his reading of the data available to him.

tests.label: Chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen
tests.hypothesis: If chromosome numbers of germ-nuclei mostly lie between six and sixteen, with few below six and fewer still above sixteen, then across plant species the haploid (gametic) number n has most of its mass in 6 <= n <= 16, a small lower tail (n < 6) and a still smaller upper tail (n > 16).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the Chromosome Counts Database (CCDB, Rice et al. 2015), 'statistics' API output (one row per resolved species name with the median gametophytic/sporophytic counts) retrieved per major group (Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Pteridophytes, Bryophytes) in CSV. One n per species: the median resolved gametophytic count; where only a sporophytic (2n) count is given, n = 2n/2; species with no usable count excluded. SUPPORTS if all three hold: (a) at least 70% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; (b) fewer than 15% have n < 6; (c) the share with n > 16 is smaller than the share with n < 6.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if any holds: fewer than 50% of species have 6 <= n <= 16; the share with n > 16 is >= the share with n < 6; or the share with n > 16 is >= 15%. MIXED otherwise. INCONCLUSIVE (data-unavailable) if the API cannot be read; INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 1000 species have a usable n.
tests.interpretation: 'Germ-nuclei' chromosome number is the reduced (haploid, gametic) number n. Thompson wrote before polyploidy was understood; using the median count per species keeps polyploid cytotypes within a species from counting as extra species. The database covers land plants only, so this decides the plant half of the claim ('plants and animals'); the animal half is not tested. 'Few' and 'fewer still' are read as the two tails of the distribution with the lower tail larger than the upper. Follows the swarm thread's draft plan with the data access route specified. READINGS CHECK (added after the result, at the hub's request; the pre-registered rule and thresholds are unchanged). Operationalization: Thompson's 'germ-nuclei' number is the haploid number n; 'organisms' are species; 'few' and 'fewer still' are the two tails of the species distribution, compared with each other and with the 6-16 core. Stated scope: 'plants and animals'; only the plant half is tested (CCDB is plant-only), so the verdict is for plants. Alternative readings computed post hoc: (i) lowest count per species rather than the median, which strips polyploid cytotypes within a species: 30.3% above 16 vs 2.2% below 6, still refuted; (ii) one value per genus (median of species medians), which damps polyploid species radiations: 32.0% of 8414 genera above 16 vs 1.1% below 6, still refuted; (iii) angiosperms only: 33.0% above 16, still refuted. (iv) Animals, untested here: the claim would not be rescued by them, since most vertebrates have n above 16 (humans 23, most birds about 40), but no animal dataset was analysed and this is background knowledge, not evidence from this test. The verdict is 'refutes' under every reading computed.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads four CSV files (2.7 MB). analysis.py takes the median count per resolved species name, confirms on six reference species (Arabidopsis n=5, maize 10, wheat 21, rice 12, Scots pine 12, silver fir 12) that the column is at the haploid level, drops duplicates and non-numeric rows, and computes the shares of species with n < 6, 6 <= n <= 16 and n > 16, overall and by major group. The pre-registered rule is applied.

measured.unit: share of plant species with haploid number n > 16 (claim: 'fewer still' than the share with n < 6, which is given in extra)
measured.uncertainty: binomial standard error below 0.002 at this sample size

caveats: Thompson's central range is roughly right (64% of species have 6 <= n <= 16, mode n = 9), but the upper tail is 20 times larger than the lower tail (34% above 16 versus 1.7% below 6), the opposite of 'fewer still have more than sixteen': polyploidy, unknown in 1917, puts a third of angiosperms and 96% of ferns above 16.
Plants only; the animal half of the claim is untested here (animal karyotype compilations were not pursued in this batch).
The CCDB is a compilation of published counts with uneven taxonomic coverage; the median per species name hides within-species cytotype variation, which is the intended treatment of polyploid races.
Species with only a sporophytic count: the CCDB statistics service reports counts at the gametophytic level (confirmed on reference species), so no halving was applied.

Readings check: the refutation holds whether species are scored by their median or lowest count, whether genera rather than species are counted, and within angiosperms alone; it is a refutation for plants, the only half of Thompson's 'plants and animals' scope that was tested.

tests.label: The biconcave red blood corpuscle is not a surface-tension equilibrium figure
tests.hypothesis: Measured red blood cells have a biconcave thickness profile whose upper surface has mean curvature of opposite sign at the central dimple and at the rim crest, so the cell surface is not of constant mean curvature (not a liquid-drop equilibrium figure), whereas rigid spheres imaged and analysed the same way show no such sign change.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: ground-truth quantitative phase maps of red blood cells (gt_phase1.mat ... gt_phase100.mat, red_blood_cell/train) and of 3 um polystyrene beads (gt_phase1.mat ... gt_phase50.mat, polystyrene_bead/train) from Figshare 21378744. Phase is proportional to optical thickness; the upper surface is taken as z = t/2 (cell symmetric about its mid-plane). Isolated objects are segmented by thresholding the background-subtracted phase, keeping connected components not touching the patch border, with aspect ratio <= 1.3 and footprint diameter >= 12 px. For each object the azimuthally averaged profile t(r) is computed about its centroid; r_crest = radius of maximum t; the centre curvature sign is the sign of b in a fit t(r) = a + b r^2 over r <= 0.3 r_crest. On the upper surface the mean curvature at the crest is negative (convex, since t'(r_crest) = 0 and t'' < 0) and at the centre it is positive (concave) when b > 0 and r_crest >= 0.25 r_edge; that sign change does not depend on the lateral or phase-to-height calibration. SUPPORTS if >= 70% of analysable RBCs show the sign change and <= 10% of analysable beads do.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if <= 30% of analysable RBCs show the sign change while <= 10% of beads do (RBCs are dome-like, consistent with a drop). MIXED if between 30% and 70%. INCONCLUSIVE (underpowered) if fewer than 30 analysable RBCs or 10 analysable beads; INCONCLUSIVE (other) if > 10% of beads show a sign change (the method manufactures dimples).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's argument is that a fluid drop held by surface tension alone must have constant mean curvature 1/r1 + 1/r2 everywhere, and the biconcave corpuscle does not. We test the geometric premise on measured cells: a closed surface whose upper face is concave at the centre and convex at the rim cannot have constant mean curvature. The thickness map from quantitative phase imaging is used with the standard mid-plane symmetry assumption. The second clause, that corpuscles become spherical in diluted blood, and the suggested osmotic or fluid-crystal causes are not tested here. Species of the donor blood is taken from the data source's description; scope is mammalian red cells.
tests.method: analysis.py range-extracts 100 RBC and 50 bead ground-truth phase maps, subtracts each map's median, thresholds at 0.25 x the 99th percentile, labels 8-connected components, fills holes, and keeps objects not touching the border with aspect ratio <= 1.3 and footprint diameter >= 12 px. For each object it builds a 1-px radial profile about the centroid, takes r_crest at the profile maximum, fits t = a + b r^2 over pixels with r <= 0.3 r_crest (at least 4 pixels needed), and scores a centre-rim sign change when b > 0 and r_crest >= 0.25 r_edge. Fractions with a sign change in RBCs and beads are judged against the pre-registered thresholds. A sensitivity run with a 4 px bead diameter minimum (not pre-registered) is reported. Per-object rows are in derived/objects.csv, the summary in derived/summary.json.

measured.unit: fraction of analysable red cells whose upper-surface mean curvature changes sign between the central dimple and the rim crest
measured.uncertainty: 1148 RBC profiles from 100 unique phase maps; pre-registered bead control: 41 analysable beads

caveats: The bead control failed: 38 of the 41 analysable bead objects (93%) show the same centre-rim sign change as the red cells, with a similar central dip (median 51% of the crest). Under the pre-registered rule this means the method manufactures dimples, so the 73% of red cells showing a sign change (1148 profiles; 70% was the pass mark) cannot be counted as support.

Why the control fails: single 3 um beads are only ~7.6 px across in these maps, too small to give the 4 central pixels the centre fit needs, so none of them is analysable. The beads that pass the 12 px size cut are 12-16 px objects with ring-shaped phase profiles, probably clusters or reconstruction artefacts rather than single spheres. The control therefore tests a different object class from the one intended, and a sphere control at red-cell scale (>= 12 px) would be needed. The 4 px sensitivity run changes nothing, because the extra beads are still too small for the centre fit.

The pre-registration listed bead files as gt_phase{1..50}.mat; in the archive they are named bead_gt_phase{1..50}.mat, which were used. It listed RBC files gt_phase{1..100}.mat; the archive numbers RBC files in blocks of 50 (1-50, 501-550, 1001-1050, ...), so the first 100 in numeric order (1-50 and 501-550) were used. Both are naming deviations, not changes of criteria.
Descriptively, most red cells do have a central thickness minimum and a rim maximum, as Thompson says. This test only fails to separate that from what the method finds in non-cell objects.

The dataset description does not state the donor species of the red cells; scope is assumed to be human or mammalian blood. Phase maps are network-training ground truths from one instrument; mid-plane symmetry (z = t/2) is assumed.
The sphering-in-diluted-blood clause and Thompson's suggested causes are not tested.

preregistered_at is the time of the pre-registration commit (0db9ed6a); the committed pre-registration carried an estimated time (21:40Z) written before committing. Data were first fetched after that commit (21:42Z); criteria are unchanged.

tests.label: Tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120°, regardless of cell size
tests.hypothesis: If tissue cell walls meet three at a time at 120 degrees regardless of cell size, junction angles in real tissues cluster near 120 degrees more tightly than in a random partition of the plane, T-shaped junctions are rare, four cells do not meet at one point, and angle deviation does not depend on cell size.
tests.pass: Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test. A tissue conforms if its junction-angle SD and its fraction of T-like junctions (largest angle >= 160 deg) are both below the random-Voronoi control. Supports if every usable tissue conforms; mixed if some do and some do not; refutes if none do.
tests.fail: Refutes if no tissue has both an angle SD and a T-junction fraction below the random-Voronoi control.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'tissue cell walls' are taken as segmented cell outlines in 2D images of epithelia and epidermes; the angle is the angle between wall directions near the junction. The compound eye is included as a packing of ommatidia, not of single cells.
tests.method: Cells in each image were segmented with Cellpose CPSAM v2 on the Nebius Scientific AI Platform (claim-sources/cell-geometry/segment.py; operation IDs and model checksum in claim-sources/cell-geometry/results/<image>/cellpose.json). claim-sources/cell-geometry/analyze.py closes inter-cell gaps, finds points where three or more cells meet, estimates each wall's direction from wall pixels 0.08-0.25 median cell diameters from the junction, counts neighbours of cells fully surrounded by segmented cells, and runs the same measurement on three synthetic tilings (hexagonal lattice, brick wall, random Voronoi) as calibration.

measured.unit: tissues (of those usable) whose junction-angle SD and T-junction fraction are both below the random-Voronoi control, as measured on Cellpose-SAM output (see revisions for segmenter bias)
measured.uncertainty: one image per tissue

not_used.arabidopsis-shoot-section: crop missed the intended panel; segmentation unusable

caveats: Segmenter bias (added 2026-10-31 after external review): Cellpose-SAM pulls non-hexagonal packings toward 120-degree junctions (brick wall 100% -> 3-16% T-junctions). Conforming tissues are consistent with 120-degree packing but their margin over the random control is inflated; see revisions[0].

Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test.
One image per tissue, all from Wikimedia Commons; tissues were chosen by availability, not sampled.
Four-way junction fractions are upper bounds: the random-Voronoi control, which has no true four-way vertices, scores 8.6% because close three-way junctions merge.
Weak negative size-deviation correlations in some tissues also appear in the random control, so they are attributed to measurement noise in small cells.
The Drosophila eye image is an SEM of a curved surface; projection distorts its angles.

tests.label: Hexagons are regular only where cells are equal in size and forces uniform
tests.hypothesis: If regular hexagonal packing arises only where cells are uniform in size (and forces uniform), then within an epithelium that Thompson names as the showcase of regular hexagons, the retinal pigment epithelium, the local regularity of the cell polygons must track the local uniformity of cell size: regions whose cells are more uniform in area must have a higher fraction of six-sided cells and a lower spread of neighbour numbers than regions whose cells vary more in area.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For every corrected RPE segmentation ROI of the 10 participants in Granger et al. 2018 (in vivo adaptive-optics imaging of the human RPE mosaic), identify the cells not touching the ROI border, their pixel areas and their numbers of neighbours. For ROIs with >= 30 interior cells compute the coefficient of variation of cell area (CV_A), the fraction of six-sided cells (f6) and the standard deviation of neighbour number (SD_n). The claim is supported if, across ROIs, Spearman's rho between f6 and CV_A is <= -0.3 with p < 0.01, and the mean f6 of the quartile of ROIs with the lowest CV_A exceeds that of the highest-CV_A quartile by at least 0.10 (ten percentage points). SD_n versus CV_A (expected positive) is reported as a consistency check.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if Spearman's rho between f6 and CV_A is >= 0, or if the relation is not significant (p >= 0.05) with the quartile difference in f6 below 0.05, i.e. hexagon regularity does not track size uniformity. Intermediate results (e.g. significant but weak, rho in (-0.3, 0)) are 'mixed'. If fewer than 20 ROIs qualify the verdict is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's statement is comparative across tissues: perfectly regular hexagons where cells are uniform (retinal pigment epithelium) and irregular polygons where cell sizes vary (intestinal epithelium, parenchyma). No public dataset gives comparable per-cell segmentations of all three tissues, so the test is run within the tissue he names as the regular case, using natural variation in cell-size uniformity between regions of the human RPE mosaic (different retinal eccentricities and individuals). 'Regular hexagons' is operationalized topologically as the fraction of six-sided cells and the spread of neighbour numbers; 'uniform in size' as the coefficient of variation of apical cell area within the same region. 'Uniform forces' is not measured; the RPE as a non-proliferating monolayer under hydrostatic pressure is Thompson's own example of uniform forces, so the test isolates the size-uniformity part of his claim. Before this pre-registration only the Dryad file listing, the dataset README and the TIFF header tags (image size, bit depth, compression) of one participant's files were inspected, to confirm the segmentation images are readable; no cell outlines or measurements were examined. Post hoc data-cleaning rule (needed once the images were seen): the corrected segmentations cover only part of each 184 x 184 px ROI, leaving one large unsegmented component around the segmented patch; components with area > 3x the median interior cell area were treated as unsegmented regions and cells adjacent to them were excluded because their neighbour counts are incomplete.
tests.method: Each corrected-segmentation TIFF was decoded with a minimal TIFF reader; cells were taken as 4-connected components of non-boundary pixels and two cells counted as neighbours when their labels co-occur in the 3 x 3 neighbourhood of a boundary pixel. Cells touching the image border, oversized components (unsegmented area) and cells adjacent to oversized components were excluded, leaving 813 fully-surrounded cells in the 21 ROIs (8 participants) with at least 30 counted cells. Per ROI, CV of pixel area, fraction of six-sided cells and SD of neighbour number were computed; Spearman correlations across ROIs and the f6 difference between the lowest- and highest-CV_A quartiles were evaluated against the pre-registered thresholds. A non-pre-registered sensitivity analysis repeated the correlation with 15- and 20-cell minimum thresholds.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between fraction of six-sided cells and coefficient of variation of cell area, across RPE regions
measured.uncertainty: p = 3.1e-4 (n = 21 ROIs, 813 cells)

caveats: Within-tissue test only: the comparative part of Thompson's statement (RPE versus intestinal epithelium and parenchyma) was not tested because no comparable public per-cell segmentations of those tissues were found; what is tested is the stated rule that hexagonal regularity tracks uniformity of cell size, inside the tissue he names as the regular case.

Only 21 ROIs (8 of 10 participants) reach the pre-registered 30-cell minimum, because the grader-corrected segmentations cover only part of each ROI and peripheral cells adjacent to unsegmented area had to be dropped. With looser thresholds (15 or 20 cells, 57-82 ROIs) the correlation keeps its sign but weakens to rho = -0.24 to -0.27 (p = 0.03-0.05), as expected when per-ROI estimates become noisier; within-participant correlations are also negative but weak (mean rho about -0.15).

Even the most uniform regions are far from 'perfectly regular': the fraction of six-sided cells ranges 0.42-0.77 (mean 0.54), so Thompson's 'regular hexagons' in the RPE holds only as a statistical tendency.

A negative relation between area dispersion and side-number dispersion is partly expected from the geometry of space-filling tessellations (Lewis's law and related size-topology relations); this test confirms that geometric regularity, which is what Thompson asserted, without identifying forces.
Cell areas are pixel counts inside hand-corrected 1-px boundaries at ~0.85 um/px; segmentation error adds noise to both variables, which attenuates rather than inflates the correlation.
Dryad downloads are served behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically.

tests.label: Cylinders or spheres pressed into full surface contact form hexagons
tests.hypothesis: If cells of similar size in complete surface contact under a uniform force (cortical tension) tend to form a pattern of hexagons, then in a living, expert-segmented and cell-tracked epithelium (Drosophila wing imaginal disc pouch, cultured ex vivo over hours) hexagons must be the clearly dominant polygon class (well above the ~0.29 six-sided fraction of a random Poisson-Voronoi partition and at least a majority), the hexagon fraction must not fall over time while the force keeps acting, and a cell's neighbour number should follow its relative size and local force rather than its division history.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the five movies, use the TissueMiner database (tables cells, directed_bonds, vertices, cell_histories) to compute, per frame, the number of neighbours of every interior cell (cells sharing a bond with the margin/background cell are excluded), its area and whether it or its sister arose from a division within the preceding 60 min. Per movie report the time-averaged fraction of six-sided cells f6, mean and SD of neighbour number, the Spearman rho between f6 and frame time, and the coefficient of variation of cell area CV_A. The claim is supported if in at least four of the five movies f6 >= 0.60 (hexagons dominate as in the retinal pigment epithelium and the compound eye) and rho(f6, time) >= 0 (packing does not drift away from hexagons while tension acts), with mean neighbour number in [5.8, 6.2] and interior junctions predominantly three-way (>= 95%).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if in at least four of the five movies f6 < 0.50 (hexagons are not even a majority in a tissue that satisfies Thompson's conditions of complete contact and uniform cortical tension) or rho(f6, time) < -0.3 with p < 0.05 (packing drifts away from hexagons). Results between the two thresholds (f6 in [0.50, 0.60), or movies split) are 'mixed'. As a pre-registered guard on Thompson's 'similar size' condition: if CV_A >= 0.6 (the level of a random partition) in the majority of movies the cells are not of similar size and the verdict is inconclusive with reason not-operationalizable. Diagnostic, not part of the verdict: the mean neighbour number of cells that divided within the preceding 60 min versus all other interior cells, and the Spearman rho between neighbour number and area relative to the frame median; a gap of >= 0.5 sides between recently divided and other cells, exceeding what area predicts, attributes departures from hexagons to division topology rather than to packing forces.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's statement names epithelia in its scope and gives the sufficient conditions: similar size, complete surface contact, a uniform force. The Drosophila wing disc pouch is a columnar monolayer whose apical surfaces tile the plane without gaps under actomyosin cortical tension, so the conditions hold apart from the size uniformity that the pre-registered CV_A guard checks. 'A pattern of hexagons' is read as hexagons being the clearly dominant polygon class; the thresholds 0.60 and 0.50 are chosen so that the tissues Thompson cites as regular (RPE 0.67, compound eye 0.99 in claim-sources/cell-geometry) pass and a random partition (0.29) fails. The Lean proof of this claim (ThompsonLaws.Cells.hexagon_of_120) shows that 120 degree three-way junctions force six neighbours on average; this test asks whether living cells meeting Thompson's conditions actually are hexagons, and uses the lineage information to see whether departures come from cell division, a cause Thompson does not mention.
tests.method: For each of the five TissueMiner databases, every directed bond was joined to its conjugate to list each cell's neighbours per frame; cells sharing a bond with the margin cell (id 10000) were dropped, leaving 1,900-2,700 interior cells per frame (1.76 million cell-frames in all). Per frame: fraction of six-sided cells f6, mean and SD of neighbour number, CV of cell area; per movie: their time averages, Spearman rho of f6 against time, the fraction of interior vertices with three bonds, the polygon distribution, and the mean neighbour number of cells that appeared by division within the preceding 60 min versus other cells, plus Spearman rho between neighbour number and area relative to the frame median. A Poisson-Voronoi partition of 20,000 points (interior 12,812 cells) gave the random baseline. Two non-pre-registered sensitivity analyses were added after the main run: the division effect at matched relative area (mean over area quintiles), and the junction angles at interior three-way vertices in every 20th frame, taken between straight chords from the vertex to the far end of each bond.

measured.unit: median over movies of the time-averaged fraction of six-sided interior cells
measured.uncertainty: range 0.379-0.403 across movies

extra.literature_reference: Gibson, Patel, Nagpal & Perrimon 2006 Nature 442:1038 report about 46% hexagons, 29% pentagons and 21% heptagons in the proliferating Drosophila wing disc and similar distributions in Hydra and Xenopus.

caveats: Pre-registered refutation criterion met in 5 of 5 movies: f6 = 0.379-0.403, below 0.50, while hexagons are still the modal class (pentagons 0.27, heptagons 0.21) and f6 exceeds the Poisson-Voronoi baseline (0.29). Three of five movies also show a significant decline of f6 over culture time (rho -0.41 to -0.58); the other two are flat. Mean neighbour number (5.90-5.93) and three-way vertices (98.4-98.8%) satisfy the supporting sub-criteria, as topology requires.

Thompson's 'similar size' condition is only marginally met: the CV of apical cell area is 0.49-0.66 (pre-registered guard 0.6 tripped by one movie only), as variable as a random partition (0.53) and far above the tissues where Thompson's regular hexagons are seen (compound eye 0.09, corneal endothelium 0.30 in claim-sources/cell-geometry). Neighbour number correlates with relative area at rho 0.43-0.51 (Lewis's law), so much of the departure from hexagons is the size variation of cycling cells, which is what the companion claim thompson1917-ch07-08 predicts. The verdict therefore refutes the claim as a sufficient rule for epithelia in general; it does not touch post-mitotic epithelia with uniform cells.

Division is a cause Thompson does not mention: cells that appeared by division within the last 60 min have 0.16-0.42 fewer sides than other cells (pre-registered diagnostic gap below the 0.5 threshold), and 0.21-0.31 fewer at matched relative area (non-pre-registered sensitivity), so division lowers the hexagon fraction beyond its effect through size.

Junction angles (non-pre-registered) have SD 24-28 degrees with 42-48% of angles within 15 degrees of 120 and only 16-21% of junctions with all three angles within 15 degrees, close to the random control of claim-sources/cell-geometry (14%) and far from corneal endothelium (75%); but the angle here is between straight chords between vertices, which misstates the angle at curved bonds, and the method differs from the cell-geometry pipeline.

Tissues were cultured ex vivo in Grace's medium with ecdysone (Dye et al. 2017); the slow decline of f6 in three movies may reflect culture rather than in vivo dynamics. Mean neighbour number below 6 reflects the ~1.5% four-way vertices and tracking gaps.

Analysis uses TissueAnalyzer segmentations corrected by the authors; no Cellpose step, so the junction-rounding bias documented in claim-sources/cell-geometry does not apply. Data were downloaded after the pre-registration commit (e77f4bcf) and are not committed (2.9 GB); SHA-256 of each zip is recorded.

tests.label: Close-packed corallites of varying size are on average hexagonal
tests.hypothesis: If close-packed cells of varying size are on average hexagonal, the mean number of neighbours of fully surrounded cells is 6.
tests.pass: Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test. A tissue conforms if its mean neighbour number is within 0.1 of 6. Supports if most usable tissues conform.
tests.fail: Refutes if most usable tissues have a mean neighbour number more than 0.1 from 6.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's example is coral corallites; this tests the same statement on plant and animal cell sheets. Euler's formula forces a mean of 6 for any large planar tiling with three cells at every vertex, so agreement confirms the claim without testing a biological mechanism.
tests.method: Cells in each image were segmented with Cellpose CPSAM v2 on the Nebius Scientific AI Platform (claim-sources/cell-geometry/segment.py; operation IDs and model checksum in claim-sources/cell-geometry/results/<image>/cellpose.json). claim-sources/cell-geometry/analyze.py closes inter-cell gaps, finds points where three or more cells meet, estimates each wall's direction from wall pixels 0.08-0.25 median cell diameters from the junction, counts neighbours of cells fully surrounded by segmented cells, and runs the same measurement on three synthetic tilings (hexagonal lattice, brick wall, random Voronoi) as calibration.

measured.unit: usable tissues with mean neighbour number within 0.1 of 6
measured.uncertainty: one image per tissue

not_used.arabidopsis-shoot-section: crop missed the intended panel; segmentation unusable

caveats: Exploratory, not pre-registered: the images were segmented and inspected before the pass criterion was written. Treat the verdict as hypothesis-generating; a pre-registered replication on new images is needed before it counts as a test.
A mean of 6 is a topological necessity for trivalent planar tilings (Euler), reproduced by the random-Voronoi control; it is not evidence for any biological mechanism.
Grass epidermis falls short of 6, most likely because unsegmented stomata and hairs hide some neighbours.
Corallites, Thompson's own example, were not tested.

tests.label: The bee’s cell is a hexagonal prism capped by rhombic-dodecahedral facets
tests.hypothesis: If a hive-bee comb cell is a hexagonal prism closed by three rhombic facets of a rhombic dodecahedron, then in 3-D measurements of bee-built cell bases (not foundation-formed bases) the three basal facets must be planar rhombi meeting pairwise at dihedral angles close to 120 degrees, with each rhombus having obtuse angles close to 109 degrees 28 minutes (arccos(-1/3)) and acute angles close to 70 degrees 32 minutes.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. From a public micro-CT or 3-D scan of natural (foundationless) worker comb, fit planes to the three basal facets of each measurable cell and compute the rhombus obtuse angle at the apex of the base. The claim is supported if the median apex angle over >= 20 cells lies within 109.47 +/- 3 degrees and the facet-plane fit residuals are small relative to wall thickness (planar facets), with the prismatic walls meeting at 120 +/- 5 degrees in cross-section.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. Refuted if the median apex angle differs from 109.47 degrees by more than 6 degrees (e.g. if bases are rounded or formed of a single curved surface with no three-facet structure in the majority of cells), or if fewer than half of the cells show three identifiable planar basal facets. Results in between are 'mixed'. If no public 3-D data of bee-built cell bases can be obtained, the verdict is inconclusive with reason data-unavailable.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's claim has two parts: a geometric description of the cell (hexagonal prism, three rhombic basal facets meeting at the tetrahedral angle 109 deg 28 min) and a minimal-surface rationale. Only the geometric description is tested here; the minimal-surface statement is a theorem about the rhombic dodecahedron (and is in fact not the true minimum, as Toth 1964 showed), not an empirical matter. The test requires 3-D geometry of bee-built cell bases. The two Dryad datasets listed were identified as the only public comb datasets found on Dryad, Zenodo and figshare on 2026-10-31; their README files were read to determine whether they contain basal-facet geometry before any data were downloaded.
tests.method: No analysis was run. The file inventories and README files of the two candidate Dryad datasets were examined via the Dryad API (datasets endpoint and /files listing) and the README of dryad.z8w9ghxmw was read. Neither contains 3-D geometry of bee-built cell bases: dryad.z8w9ghxmw (Peleg lab, 19.2 GB) holds X-ray microscopy of comb built on 3-D-printed plastic foundation frames, whose cell bases are the printed plastic, plus cell-size tables and cell tilt angles; dryad.r4xgxd2f3 (Yang 2022) holds cell orientation (in-plane rotation) angles and cell counts of natural combs in spreadsheets, with no basal geometry. MorphoSource and other scan repositories require a login. No other public micro-CT or 3-D scan of natural comb was located.
caveats: Dryad file inventory for doi:10.5061/dryad.z8w9ghxmw on 2026-10-31: s_1_raw_xrm_data.zip (11.99 GB), processed_XRM_data.zip (6.88 GB), 3D_reconstruction_movies.zip (220 MB), 2D_images.zip (61 MB), cell_size_data.zip, angle_data.zip (cell tilt angles only), angle_raw_data.zip, figure data zips, README.md (file id 4176003). The README states the comb was built on 3-D-printed foundation frames of varying cell size, so the cell bases are not bee-built and cannot test the rhombic-cap geometry.

Dryad file inventory for doi:10.5061/dryad.r4xgxd2f3 on 2026-10-31: README_file.txt and five spreadsheets of cell orientation angles and cell numbers for Eastern and Western honey bee combs; no 3-D data.
The claim remains testable: a micro-CT of foundationless natural comb (or Toth-style measurements of the three basal rhombi) would resolve it with the pre-registered criteria above.

tests.label: Minimal bisecting walls cut the longest axis and alternate at right angles
tests.hypothesis: In dividing plant cells, the new wall cuts across the mother cell's longest axis (its normal is near-parallel to that axis), and when two successive divisions are both recent, the second wall is near-perpendicular to the first.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the same 8 Arabidopsis shoot-apex archives as thompson1917-ch08-02 (first 8 archive names, alphabetical, of Zenodo record 18711581). Sister pairs = the two cells separated by a wall in *_new_walls.tif; mother = their union; sisters >= 40 um^3, not touching the border. Part 1 (longest axis): theta = angle between the new wall's normal (smallest principal axis of the shared-interface voxel coordinates, in um) and the mother's longest principal axis (largest-variance axis of its voxel coordinates, in um); analysed for elongated mothers (sqrt(lambda1/lambda2) >= 1.2), all mothers reported too. Under random orientation the median theta is 60 deg. Part 1 passes if median theta <= 30 deg and >= 60% of elongated mothers have theta <= 30 deg. Part 2 (alternation): triples X, Y1, Y2 where Y1|Y2 is a new wall and Y1 and Y2 each also share a new wall with the same cell X (so Y divided after X|Y formed); phi = angle between the normals of wall Y1|Y2 and wall X|(Y1 u Y2), folded to [0, 90]. Part 2 passes if median phi >= 75 deg and >= 50% of triples have phi >= 70 deg. SUPPORTS if both parts pass.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. Part 1 fails if median theta >= 50 deg; Part 2 fails if median phi <= 60 deg. REFUTES if both parts fail. MIXED for any other combination of pass/fail/neither. If Part 2 has fewer than 15 triples it is underpowered; the verdict is then Part 1's outcome (supports if it passes, refutes if it fails, mixed otherwise) with that limitation noted and confidence capped at 0.6. If Part 1 has fewer than 30 elongated mothers: inconclusive (underpowered). Secondary, reported but not used for the verdict: in eLife 79224 Figure 8 source data 2 (Laruelle et al. 2022, Arabidopsis embryo apical cells at 16C), the fraction of horizontally dividing cells whose longitudinal length exceeds their maximal radial length, and of longitudinally dividing cells whose longitudinal length is below it.
tests.interpretation: Thompson derives the rule for an ideal rectangular parallelepiped bisected by a least-area plane: the plane is perpendicular to the longest edge, and successive bisections alternate at right angles. Real meristem cells are not rectangular, so 'longest axis' is the largest principal axis of the cell volume and the test is restricted to mothers that are measurably elongated (principal-axis ratio >= 1.2), where the axis is defined. Successive divisions are identified only where both walls are still flagged as recent in one snapshot, so Part 2 samples rapid successive divisions. Division orientation in the shoot apex is also influenced by tissue stress, which can mimic or mask the geometric rule; the test measures the outcome, not the cause.
tests.method: analysis.py range-extracts the five members per archive and, for each wall flagged new whose two flanking cells are >= 40 um^3 and whose bounding boxes do not touch the image border, takes the mother as the union of the two cells. The wall normal is the smallest principal axis of the midpoints of the voxel faces shared by the two cells (um coordinates); the mother's longest axis and elongation sqrt(lambda1/lambda2) come from the covariance of its voxel coordinates. theta is the folded angle between them. Part 2 searches for cells X sharing a new wall with both cells of another new wall Y1|Y2. As a control that was not pre-registered, 1000 randomly sampled walls per apex that are not flagged new are analysed identically. Secondary: the eLife table is read and fractions are computed by division type. Per-wall rows are written to data/part1.csv (regenerated, not committed); derived/part1_theta_histogram.csv has theta counts by wall kind and elongation bin.

measured.unit: median angle (deg) between the new wall's normal and the mother cell's longest principal axis, elongated mothers (axis ratio >= 1.2)
measured.uncertainty: IQR 20.3-58.4 deg; random-orientation median 59.8 deg; per-apex medians 27.2-52.9 deg across the 8 apices

extra.part1_outcome: neither (median <= 30 not met, fraction >= 0.6 not met, median < 50)

caveats: Part 1 is between the pre-registered pass and fail bands. New walls are better aligned with the mother's long axis than random planes (median 35.9 deg against 59.8 deg), but short of the 30 deg median and 60%-within-30-deg needed to pass (41%). Alignment increases with elongation: median 26.7 deg for mothers with axis ratio >= 2, and 42-48 deg for nearly isodiametric ones, as the rule predicts if 'longest axis' only matters when one is clearly longest.

Part 2 could not be tested. The dataset's new-wall detection pairs each cell with at most one sister (no cell lies on two new walls in any of the 8 apices), so no successive-division triples exist. Under the pre-registered rule the verdict is Part 1's outcome (mixed), with confidence capped at 0.6. The alternation half of the claim is untested.

A control that was not pre-registered weakens the support from Part 1. Walls not flagged as new, between arbitrary neighbouring cells, score better (median 26.5 deg, 59% within 30 deg) than new walls do. The union of any two adjacent cells is elongated across their shared wall, so this measure favours the rule by construction. New walls lining up less well than that geometric baseline suggests that the observed alignment is not evidence for a division rule beyond geometry.

Sister identification relies on the dataset's own new-wall filter, which flags 4,365 walls in the first apex (8,730 of 12,499 cells), more than a single recent round of division would give. It probably includes older walls, which this test cannot separate from recent ones.

The 'cell crosses image border' field in *_cell_data.csv is 0 for every cell, so border contact was judged from each cell's bounding box touching the image edge. Mothers whose sister volumes the segmentation already limits to >= 40 um^3 all pass the volume filter.

Secondary (eLife 79224, embryo apical cells at 16C, not part of the verdict): 136 of 140 longitudinal divisions are in cells whose radial length exceeds their longitudinal length, as the rule predicts. All 9 transverse divisions are also in such cells, against the rule. Nearly all these cells are radially longer (median ratio 0.73), so the table cannot show cells choosing their division by length.
Shoot-apex division orientation is also influenced by mechanical stress and growth direction, which this test does not separate from geometry.

preregistered_at is the time of the pre-registration commit (9e0ec83d); the committed pre-registration carried an estimated time (21:40Z) written before committing. Data were first fetched after that commit; criteria are unchanged.
