tests.label: A new cell wall has the least area that can enclose the given volume (Errera)
tests.hypothesis: In recently divided plant cells, the new wall between two sister cells has close to the least area of any planar cut that divides the reconstructed mother cell in the same volume ratio, and much less area than a cut of random orientation.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: the 8 alphabetically first meristem archives of Zenodo record 18711581 (Yates et al. 2026, Arabidopsis inflorescence shoot apices, 3D confocal, watershed-segmented). For each wall marked in *_new_walls.tif, the two cells it separates are sisters; the mother is their union (including the wall voxels between them). Both sisters must have volume >= 40 um^3 and must not touch the image border. Observed area A_obs = area of the voxel faces shared between the two sister regions in the mother mask (anisotropic voxel face areas from Metadata.txt). For 500 plane orientations spread uniformly over the hemisphere (Fibonacci lattice), the plane offset is set so the smaller side holds the observed smaller-sister volume fraction, and the cut area A(n) is measured with the same voxel-face rule. A_min = min over orientations; q = A_obs / A_min; percentile p = fraction of orientations with A(n) < A_obs. SUPPORTS if the median p over all divisions is <= 0.10 AND at least 50% of divisions have q <= 1.10.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if the median p is >= 0.35 (observed walls are no smaller than typical random-orientation cuts) OR fewer than 20% of divisions have q <= 1.10. Any other outcome is MIXED. Fewer than 30 analysable divisions: inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Errera's rule as Thompson states it: the incipient partition has the least area that can divide the given space-content. The 'given space-content' is the observed volume split of the two sisters, so asymmetric divisions are included. Real walls may be curved; the minimum is taken over planes, so a curved minimal wall can have q < 1, which still counts as consistent. Sisters are identified from the dataset's own detection of recently formed walls (its pipeline flags thin, recent walls), not from lineage tracking; mis-identified pairs work against the claim. Sachs's subordinate rule (right-angle alternation) is tested separately under thompson1917-ch08-01. The test is on one model plant tissue (Arabidopsis shoot apex), within the claim's scope 'dividing cells, especially plant cells'.
tests.method: analysis.py: for each wall flagged in *_new_walls.tif, the mother is the union of the two sisters; the observed interface area (anisotropic voxel faces) is compared with planar cuts at 500 Fibonacci-lattice orientations at the observed volume fraction. Per-division rows in derived/divisions.csv (regenerated by analysis.py, not committed); per-archive figures in derived/summary.json.

measured.unit: median over divisions of the percentile of the observed new-wall area among 500 planar cuts of the mother at the observed volume ratio (voxel-face areas)
measured.uncertainty: 27249 divisions in 8 shoot apices; IQR of percentile 0.016-0.156

control_not_preregistered_old_walls.note: up to 150 randomly sampled walls per apex not flagged as new, union of the two flanking cells analysed identically

sensitivity_not_preregistered_orientatio.note: voxel-face area divided by |n_z|+|n_y|+|n_x| of the cut normal (observed wall: normal of its interface face centres)

caveats: Mixed by the pre-registered thresholds: median percentile 0.062 passes (<= 0.10), but only 24.7% of divisions have q <= 1.10 (needs >= 50%; refutes below 20%). New walls are far smaller than random cuts (median 0.68 of the median random-cut area) but usually 10-40% above the least-area plane.

The q criterion is sensitive to how area is measured. The voxel-face rule inflates staircase surfaces that are oblique to the voxel grid. A sensitivity analysis that was not pre-registered (dividing face area by |n_x|+|n_y|+|n_z|) gives median q 1.04 and 65% within 1.10, which would pass. The pre-registered verdict stands.

Old walls (not flagged as new, analysed identically, not pre-registered) give median q 0.96 and 89% within 1.10. Either established walls relax towards least area after division, or the new-wall flags from the dataset pipeline pick thin, irregular walls that are measured less accurately.
Sisters are identified from the dataset flag for recently formed walls, not from lineage tracking; 3990 divisions touching the image border were excluded.
One tissue (Arabidopsis inflorescence shoot apex, 8 apices, 27,249 divisions); the minimum is taken over planes only.
Completed by the parent agent from the tester run output after the tester subagent stopped; the analysis ran unmodified.

datasets.name: Image processing data for manuscript: Control of plant organ growth through cell division orientation in inner tissues (Yates & Sablowski)

tests.label: The suture of a turreted shell is a conical geodetic with coils closing toward the apex
tests.hypothesis: If the sutural line of a turreted shell such as Turritella is a geodesic of the shell's enveloping right cone, then the number of whorls the suture makes cannot exceed the number of turns a conical geodesic can make: a geodesic on a right cone of apical angle alpha develops into a straight line on a sector of angle 2*pi*sin(alpha/2), sweeps at most pi of that sector, and therefore turns at most N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) times in total (and only half of that while approaching the apex). Measured whorl counts of Turritella shells must therefore satisfy N_obs <= N_geo.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. From published per-specimen measurements of Turritellidae giving both the apical angle alpha and the total whorl number N_obs (Pandita et al. 2013, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6, 50 specimens of 5 species), compute N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)) and the ratio R = N_obs / N_geo for every specimen with both values. SUPPORTS if at least 90% of specimens have R <= 1 (whorl count within the geodesic bound).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least 90% of specimens have R > 1, i.e. the suture coils more times than any geodesic of the enveloping cone can, so the sutural line cannot be a conical geodesic. Between 10% and 90% is 'mixed'. If the tables cannot be retrieved or parsed, inconclusive with reason data-unavailable. The claim's first part (coils tighten toward the apex) is shared by a geodesic and by the logarithmic helico-spiral and is not discriminating; the verdict rests on the identification of the suture with a geodesic.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'spiral geodetic' on a right cone is taken literally (a curve of zero geodesic curvature on the enveloping cone), and 'the sutural line ... such as Turritella ... is a geodetic of this kind' as the claim that the suture follows such a curve. The enveloping surface of a turritellid is close to a right circular cone whose apical angle is the measured alpha. The test uses only two gross measurements per shell, apical angle and whorl number, because the geodesic bound on the number of turns depends on nothing else. Whorl counts in the source include the early (protoconch/juvenile) whorls, where the cone approximation is roughest; the result is checked for sensitivity by also subtracting two whorls from every count.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the article PDF, records its SHA-256 and transcribes Tables 2-6 with pdfplumber into derived/pandita2013_turritellidae.csv (49 rows; all published ratio columns Wang:L and Wsut:L were recomputed from the transcribed measurements and agree, confirming the transcription). analysis.py computes for each of the 34 specimens with both apical angle and whorl number the maximum number of turns of a geodesic on a right cone of that apical angle, N_geo = 1/(2 sin(alpha/2)), the ratio R = whorls/N_geo, the same ratio after subtracting two whorls (allowance for the protoconch/early whorls), and the apical angle that would have been needed for the observed whorl count to fit a geodesic.

measured.unit: median ratio of observed whorl number to the maximum number of turns a conical geodesic can make (R = N_obs / N_geo); R > 1 is impossible for a geodesic
measured.uncertainty: R ranges from 1.63 to 3.39 across all 34 specimens (4 species); every specimen exceeds the bound

caveats: The test refutes the identification of the suture with a geodesic of the enveloping right cone; it does not test Thompson's purely geometric statement that a conical geodesic coils more closely toward the apex (true) nor whether the suture is locally geodesic-like over a fraction of a whorl.

The bound assumes the shell envelope is a right circular cone, which is what Thompson states; real turritellid envelopes are slightly convex or concave, but the Clairaut relation on any such surface of revolution still forbids a geodesic from winding many times toward a narrowing apex unless the sides are almost parallel.

Specimens are Neogene fossils from West Java, not the type species Turritella terebra; fossil apices are often incomplete, so whorl counts are if anything underestimates, which makes the test conservative. Apical angles are the authors' gross measurements to 0.5 degree.
Whorl counts include early whorls where the cone approximation is roughest; subtracting two whorls from every count leaves all 34 specimens above the bound.
The published tables list 50 specimens in the text but 49 rows were present (Table 6 lacks a specimen 5B); 15 rows lack an apical angle and were excluded.
Transcription from the PDF needs pdfplumber (not in the standard tool list); the transcribed table is committed so analysis.py runs with pandas and numpy only.

datasets.name: Pandita, Zaim, Aswan & Rizal (2013) Relationship of Biometrical Aspect of Turritellidae with Geochronological Aspect in West Java, Int. J. Geosciences 4:777-784, Tables 2-6 (biometric measurements of 49 turritellid specimens from five Neogene localities)

tests.label: Horns, molluscan shells, foraminifera and sunflower florets follow the logarithmic spiral
tests.hypothesis: If the permanent spiral forms of organisms (ruminant horns, molluscan and foraminiferal shells, sunflower capitula) are logarithmic spirals, then for any such structure the linear size of the growing edge (radius vector or whorl size) must increase exponentially with angle of rotation about the spiral's pole, r = a e^(b theta), and must do so better than the alternative simple spirals (Archimedean r = a + b theta, which grows linearly; Fermat / parabolic r = a sqrt(theta + theta0), which decelerates).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Only the molluscan-shell class can be tested with public data located (see interpretation). For every gastropod specimen in Collins et al. 2021 with >= 5 digitised successive half-whorl apertures, take the square root of aperture area as the linear whorl size at angles 0, pi, 2 pi, ...; for every ammonoid species in Korn & Walton 2018 with >= 5 half-whorl diameters, take conch diameter at each half whorl. Fit the three two-parameter models by least squares in the size domain and compare root-mean-square residuals. The claim (for molluscan shells) is supported if the logarithmic model has the lowest RMSE in >= 80% of gastropod specimens and in >= 80% of ammonoid species, and the median ratio RMSE(Archimedean) / RMSE(logarithmic) exceeds 1.5 in both groups. Because horns, foraminifera and sunflower capitula remain untested, the confidence attached to a supporting verdict is capped at 0.5.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted (for molluscan shells, and hence as a universal) if the logarithmic model is best in fewer than 50% of specimens in either group, or if the median RMSE ratio Archimedean / logarithmic is below 1.0 in either group. Intermediate results are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's statement is a universal over four classes of structure plus a stated exception (the cordate leaf). Public coordinate data were found only for molluscan shells: no digitised floret positions of sunflower capitula (the Swinton et al. 2016 citizen-science deposit gives parastichy counts and annotated photographs, not coordinates), no horn centre-line or outline data, and no foraminiferal chamber-position tables were located on Dryad, Zenodo or figshare; MorphoSource meshes require a login. The test therefore covers only the molluscan class, and its verdict is explicitly a test of that class with the caveat that a logarithmic fit for molluscs cannot establish the universal. 'Logarithmic spiral' is operationalized as exponential growth of linear whorl size with rotation angle: in a gastropod, the square root of aperture area at successive half whorls; in an ammonoid, conch diameter at successive half whorls (for a planispiral conch the diameter is the sum of two opposite radius vectors and grows exponentially if and only if the radius does). Both datasets were already downloaded for claim tests thompson1917-ch11-05 and thompson1917-ch11-15; those tests examined allometry of conch proportions and whorl-expansion and apical angles, not the comparison of spiral models made here.
tests.method: For 145 gastropod specimens (>= 5 apertures) the series sqrt(aperture area in mm^2) versus angle (0, pi, 2pi, ...) and for 179 ammonoid species the series conch diameter versus whorl angle were each fitted by nonlinear least squares with a logarithmic spiral a e^(b theta), an Archimedean spiral a + b theta and a Fermat spiral a sqrt(theta + theta0); the model with the lowest RMSE was recorded per series and the median RMSE ratios Archimedean/logarithmic and Fermat/logarithmic computed per group. Pre-registered thresholds were then applied.

measured.unit: fraction of gastropod specimens for which the logarithmic spiral has the lowest RMSE (ammonoids: 1.000)
measured.uncertainty: gastropods n = 145 specimens / 21 species; ammonoids n = 179 species

gastropod_species_where_Archimedean_fits: Pelicaria vermis (36 specimens, log best in 14%)

caveats: Only the molluscan-shell class of Thompson's universal was tested; ruminant horns, foraminiferal shells and sunflower capitula (and the cordate-leaf exception) remain untested for lack of public coordinate data, so even a clean pass could not have established the universal claim.

Within molluscs the result is itself mixed: every one of 179 ammonoid species is fitted far better by the logarithmic spiral (median RMSE ratio 15 against Archimedean), but only 68% of gastropod specimens (14 of 21 species) are, and in the Struthiolariidae genus Pelicaria (36 specimens) and a handful of other species the whorl size grows closer to linearly than exponentially with angle over the digitised whorls. Collins et al. (2021) themselves report that struthiolariid coiling departs from constant-rate (logarithmic) growth.

Gastropod series are short (median 8 half-whorl apertures spanning ~3-4 revolutions with a median expansion of 1.54 per revolution), which limits discrimination between exponential and linear growth; the median RMSE ratio of 1.39 reflects that limited leverage as well as genuine departures.

Tenagodus is a siliquariid whose coiling loosens and uncoils in adulthood, so its non-logarithmic fit is expected; removing it does not change the gastropod percentage materially (it contributes 2 of 145 specimens).

The Fermat (parabolic) spiral, which modern work (Vogel 1979) uses for sunflower capitula, is the worst of the three models for every mollusc group here (median RMSE ratio 3-25), i.e. molluscs are not sunflower-like; the sunflower class itself could not be tested.
Dryad downloads are served behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically and must download the 521 MB archive (only the 1.5 MB .tps inside is read).

datasets.name: Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods (Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines 2021, Paleobiology)
Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology)

tests.label: The shell grows in size without changing its shape
tests.hypothesis: If a coiled shell grows by terminal accretion without changing its shape, then within a species the dimensionless conch proportions (whorl width / diameter, whorl height / diameter, umbilical width / diameter) and the whorl expansion rate are constant across ontogeny, i.e. each linear conch dimension scales isometrically (log-log exponent 1) with conch diameter through the measured growth stages.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each species with measurements at >= 4 growth stages (diameters), fit ordinary least squares of log(ww), log(wh) and log(uw) on log(dm) across its stages. The claim is supported if (a) the across-species median exponent for each of the three dimensions lies in [0.90, 1.10], and (b) at least two thirds of species have all three exponents in [0.90, 1.10] (shape changes by less than ~25% over a ten-fold size range). The same test on Nautilus pompilius (Thompson's showcase) is reported separately and must also meet (a) for the species-level exponents from individual trajectories.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if the across-species median exponent for any of ww, wh or uw lies outside [0.80, 1.20], or if fewer than half of the species have all three exponents in [0.90, 1.10]. Results between pass and fail thresholds are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'shell' is the externally coiled molluscan shell; he uses Nautilus as the type case and the claim is stated for shells growing by terminal accretion generally (horns included). 'Does not change its shape' is mapped to isometry of conch dimensions with diameter across post-embryonic growth stages, which is exactly the self-similarity that defines the logarithmic spiral (whorl expansion rate and whorl-section proportions constant). Ammonoid conch-parameter trajectories (Korn's ww, wh, uw, dm measured at successive diameters) and Nautilus pompilius 3D ontogenetic morphometry are the public data; all stages present in the data are used, with a sensitivity analysis excluding dm < 2 mm (embryonic / earliest juvenile shell) reported in measured.extra. Species-level values (not every specimen) are the unit of analysis. The dataset file listings on Dryad were viewed to plan this test; no measurement values were downloaded or inspected before this pre-registration. Deviation noted after download: the released ammonoid table carries conch width index (ww/dm), umbilical width index (uw/dm) and whorl expansion rate WER rather than raw ww, wh, uw; ww and uw were reconstructed as index x dm, and the aperture height ah = dm(1 - WER^-1/2), the radial increment over the preceding half whorl, was used in place of the pre-registered whorl height wh (the same test of constant radial growth per turn). Nautilus has no umbilical measurement, so its test uses ww and ah only.
tests.method: For each of 179 ammonoid species, ww = CWI x dm, uw = UWI x dm and ah = dm(1 - WER^-1/2) were computed at every half whorl with data, and the OLS slope of log(dimension) on log(dm) was fitted across all stages (median 16 stages per species, dm from ~0.5 to ~30 mm). Isometry predicts slope 1. The across-species median and the fraction of species with all three slopes in [0.9, 1.1] were compared with the pre-registered thresholds, and repeated using only stages with dm >= 2 mm. For Nautilus pompilius, the same slopes were fitted per specimen and pooled across all 1408 stage observations of the 6 specimens.

measured.unit: across-species median log-log exponent of umbilical width on conch diameter (isometry = 1)

caveats: Both pre-registered fail conditions fire for ammonoids: the median umbilical-width exponent (0.705) is far below 0.8, and only 8.9% of species are isometric in all three dimensions; 59% of species have uw exponents below 0.8 (whorls become relatively more involute with growth).

Whorl width and aperture height are close to isometric (medians 0.96-0.97; 69-79% of species within [0.9, 1.1]), so the departure from self-similarity is concentrated in the coiling tightness, not in the whorl section.

Nautilus pompilius, Thompson's own exemplar, passes (pooled exponents 0.946 and 1.055; all 6 specimens within [0.9, 1.1]), so the claim holds approximately for the type case even though it fails as a general statement about coiled shells.

Early whorls (ammonitella and first juvenile whorls, dm < 2 mm) are included in the primary test because Thompson states the claim for the shell as a whole; excluding them makes the umbilical allometry stronger (median 0.633), not weaker.

Thompson himself notes a few lines later that the spiral angle 'is not always, nor rigorously, a constant angle' in some ammonites; the data show that such ontogenetic change is the rule rather than the exception in this sample, which is biased toward pachyconic and globular Palaeozoic-Mesozoic ammonoids.
Gastropods and horns, also within the stated scope, were not tested.
Dryad serves downloads behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically. Dryad API downloads without a token returned HTTP 401 at the time of the test.

datasets.name: Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology)

Data from: Intraspecific variation in cephalopod conchs changes during ontogeny: perspectives from three-dimensional morphometry of Nautilus pompilius (Tajika, Morimoto, Wani & Klug 2018, Paleobiology)

tests.label: Each increment of a spirally grown structure is a gnomon to the whole before it
tests.hypothesis: If every increment of a spirally grown shell is a gnomon to the whole structure before it (the enlarged whole stays similar to itself), then a molluscan shell is geometrically self-similar through growth: dimensionless shape indices of the conch measured at successive diameters along one specimen's ontogeny (conch width index CWI = ww/dm, umbilical width index UWI = uw/dm, whorl expansion rate WER) stay constant, apart from measurement noise, from the end of the embryonic shell to maturity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Data: Walton & Korn (2018) ontogenetic conch-parameter series for 177 Devonian-Jurassic ammonoid species (Dryad 10.5061/dryad.c17p8), measured on median cross-sections at successive diameters dm. For each species keep the post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and require at least 4 points spanning at least a fourfold range of dm. For each retained index compute the log-range D = max ln(index) - min ln(index) over the series. A species is 'gnomonic' if D <= ln(1.25) (at most 25% change) for CWI, UWI and WER alike; 'allometric' if D >= ln(1.5) (at least 50% change) for at least one index; otherwise intermediate. SUPPORTS if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are gnomonic. As a secondary descriptor, the fraction of species whose indices show a monotonic trend with ln dm (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05, for at least one index) is reported; it does not enter the verdict.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if at least two thirds of the qualifying species are allometric (at least one shape index changes by 50% or more over post-embryonic growth, so successive increments are not gnomons of the pre-existing conch). Otherwise 'mixed'. Fewer than 30 qualifying species: inconclusive (underpowered). File unobtainable: inconclusive, data-unavailable.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's gnomon is 'an addition that leaves the enlarged whole similar to what it was before'; for a coiled conch, continued similarity means that the ratios describing its shape are unchanged by growth, which is exactly what constant CWI, UWI and WER along an ontogenetic trajectory express (constant WER is the constant spiral angle; constant CWI and UWI fix the whorl-section proportions and the umbilicus). Ammonoid conchs are molluscan shells, within the stated scope. The embryonic ammonitella (dm below about 1-2 mm) formed inside the egg rather than by the accretion Thompson describes, so points below 2 mm are excluded. Thresholds of 25% and 50% are chosen before analysis to separate measurement noise in cross-sections from genuine shape change; the measurement protocol (Korn 2010) reports typical errors of a few percent.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the Dryad version zip and records its SHA-256. analysis.py reshapes the four parameter sheets to one long table (species, half-whorl, dm, CWI, UWI, WER), keeps post-embryonic points (dm >= 2 mm) and the 179 series with >= 4 points spanning >= 4x in diameter, and for each index computes the log-range over the series (percent change), a Spearman correlation with ln dm, and classifies each series as gnomonic (all three indices change <= 25%), allometric (any index changes >= 50%) or intermediate. Sensitivity runs use dm >= 5 mm and drop UWI.

measured.unit: fraction of qualifying ammonoid series in which at least one conch shape index changes by >= 50% over post-embryonic growth (pre-registered refutes threshold 2/3); fraction gnomonic = 0.006 (supports threshold 2/3)
measured.uncertainty: 168 allometric, 10 intermediate, 1 gnomonic (Eurites permutus); 93.9% of series show a monotonic trend (|Spearman rho| >= 0.7, p < 0.05) in at least one index

caveats: The refutation is carried almost entirely by the umbilical width index: UWI changes by >= 50% in 92% of series (median change 204%), whereas the whorl expansion rate, which encodes the spiral angle, stays within 25% in 80% of series (median change 17%). The spiral itself is therefore close to logarithmic (gnomonic in Thompson's sense), while the whorl section and the degree of involution change through growth, so the enlarged conch is not similar to its earlier self. Dropping UWI, only 34% of series (27% at dm >= 5 mm) are allometric and the pre-registered rule would give 'mixed'.

Walton & Korn chose their 177 species to study pachyconic and globular ammonoids with phased ontogenies, so the sample is probably enriched in species with strong ontogenetic shape change relative to ammonoids at large.

UWI is the noisiest index at small diameters (small umbilical widths); the 2 mm cut-off and the requirement of a monotonic trend (met by 94% of series) limit but do not remove this effect; at dm >= 5 mm the allometric fraction is still 84%.

Scope: Palaeozoic-Jurassic ammonoid conchs only; Thompson's gnomon claim also covers gastropod and bivalve shells, opercula, foraminiferal chambers, horns and tusks, which were not tested. The 25% and 50% thresholds are pre-registered conventions, not derived from Thompson.

Thompson himself notes elsewhere (ch. XI, changes of spiral angle with age) that some ammonoids change their spiral angle during growth; this test shows that even where the spiral angle is nearly constant, the conch shape generally is not.

datasets.name: Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology 61, doi:10.1111/pala.12308)
datasets.version: Dryad version id 7242 = dataset version 1 (published 2018-05-16), the only publicly listed version

tests.label: Whorl breadths of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod shells form a geometric progression
tests.hypothesis: Along a radius, successive whorl breadths (and hence conch diameters measured at successive half-whorls) of Nautilus, ammonoids and spiral gastropods form a geometric progression: log(diameter) is linear in whorl number, so the whorl expansion rate is constant through ontogeny; for Nautilus the ratio per whole whorl is about 3.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For every specimen with at least four successive half-whorl conch-diameter measurements (ammonoids: stages with diameter >= 5 mm, excluding the embryonic ammonitella; Nautilus: all measured post-embryonic stages): (1) fit log(dm) against half-whorl index by least squares; the median R^2 across specimens must be >= 0.99, and the exponential (geometric) model must have lower residual sum of squares on the dm scale than a straight-line (arithmetic) model in at least 75% of specimens; (2) strict constancy: the median across specimens of the within-specimen relative range of WER, (max - min)/median over post-embryonic stages, must be <= 0.20, and no systematic ontogenetic drift (median within-specimen Spearman correlation of WER with stage between -0.5 and 0.5); (3) the median Nautilus WER (per-revolution diameter ratio) must lie in [2.6, 3.5]. 'supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the geometric model beats the arithmetic model in fewer than 50% of specimens, or the median R^2 < 0.95, or the median Nautilus WER is outside [2.2, 4.0]. 'mixed' if the geometric progression holds approximately ((1) and (3) pass) but the strict constancy test (2) fails, i.e. WER drifts systematically during growth. Gastropods are included only if a public dataset gives successive whorl measurements per specimen; otherwise the gastropod part is reported as data-unavailable and the verdict rests on nautiloids and ammonoids with a caveat.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'breadths of successive whorls along a radius in geometric progression' is tested on its equivalent for measured cross-sections: conch diameters at successive half-whorls, whose ratio is constant if and only if the whorl breadths are in geometric progression (both equal e^(pi cot alpha) per half-whorl for a logarithmic spiral). Korn's WER = (dm1/dm2)^2 is that half-whorl ratio squared, i.e. the per-revolution ratio Thompson quotes as 'about three' for Nautilus. The strict reading (a single constant ratio for the whole shell) and the approximate reading (a logarithmic spiral is a very good description) are both pre-registered so that the verdict distinguishes them. Station spacing differs by dataset (Nautilus 45 deg, ammonoids 180 deg, gastropods 180 deg); the fits use the station index, and the per-revolution ratio uses the appropriate lag (8, 2, 2). For gastropods the measured radius is the perpendicular distance of each digitised aperture's centroid from the coiling axis (Collins et al. 2021 raw tps data), the quantity Thompson's spiral describes for a turbinate shell.
tests.method: fetch.py obtains the files and writes derived station tables (committed; identical to those in thompson1917-ch11-10). analysis.py fits, per specimen, log(size) ~ station index (geometric) and size ~ station index (arithmetic) by least squares, compares their residual sums of squares on the size scale, and computes the per-revolution ratio r at each station (lag 8 for Nautilus 45-degree stations, lag 2 for half-whorl ammonoid and 180-degree gastropod stations), its within-specimen relative range (max-min)/median, and the Spearman correlation of r with station (drift). Group summaries are medians across specimens; ammonoid stations with dm < 5 mm are excluded as pre-registered.

measured.unit: median R^2 of log(diameter) vs whorl index per specimen, ammonoids (Nautilus 0.9995; gastropods 0.987)
measured.uncertainty: specimens: 93 Nautilus, 177 ammonoid species, 164 gastropods; min R^2 0.9984 / 0.9605 / 0.0867

caveats: For Nautilus and ammonoids the geometric progression is an excellent description (median R^2 0.9995 and 0.9993; the geometric model beats the arithmetic one in 100% of specimens with residuals 1-2% of the arithmetic model's) and the Nautilus per-revolution ratio is 2.87, close to Thompson's 'about three'. Strict constancy nevertheless fails: in Nautilus the ratio rises systematically through the two measured whorls (median Spearman +0.79, though only by 7% of its value), as described by Tajika et al. 2018 and later work on nautilid ontogeny.

Gastropods are where the claim is weakest: the geometric model beats the arithmetic model in only 73% of specimens (threshold 75%), median R^2 is 0.987 (threshold 0.99), and the expansion ratio of the aperture's distance from the axis declines through ontogeny in 84% of specimens (median Spearman -0.71, median within-specimen range 17%). This agrees with Collins et al. 2021, who conclude from the same material that the logarithmic-helicospiral assumptions fail in all 25 of their species.

The gastropod series are short (4-11 apertures, i.e. 2-5 revolutions) and were digitised on a single sectioned plane; short noisy series depress R^2 and make the arithmetic/geometric comparison less decisive than for the CT-based cephalopod diameters.

The ammonoid sample is biased to Palaeozoic pachyconic and globular species; Walton & Korn document multi-phase ontogenetic trajectories in these forms, so the 6% median within-species range of r is, if anything, an overestimate of constancy for ammonoids generally only in the sense that other groups could drift more.

No arithmetic-progression alternative is seriously defensible for coiled shells; the informative comparison is between a strictly constant ratio and a slowly drifting one, which is what the 'mixed' verdict records.

datasets.name: Data from: Intraspecific variation in cephalopod conchs changes during ontogeny: perspectives from three-dimensional morphometry of Nautilus pompilius
Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn)
Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods

tests.label: The constant angle of nautiloid, ammonitoid and gastropod spirals is about 80°–85°
tests.hypothesis: If whorl breadths (equivalently conch diameters one revolution apart) expand by a factor r per whorl, the constant angle is alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) (Thompson's own table: r = 1.5 -> 86.3 deg, 2.0 -> 83.7 deg, 2.5 -> 81.7 deg, 3.0 -> 80.1 deg, 3.5 -> 78.7 deg). The claim then predicts: Nautilus r about 3, alpha about 80 deg; for ordinary ammonoids and typically spiral gastropods alpha is usually between 80 and 85 deg (r between 1.72 and 3.00) and very seldom below 80 deg (r > 3.00).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (a) Nautilus pompilius: per specimen, the median whorl expansion rate WER (Korn's definition, (dm1/dm2)^2 over half a whorl, which equals the per-revolution diameter ratio r) over all measured post-embryonic stages; the median across specimens, converted to alpha, must lie in [78, 82] deg (r in 2.6-3.5). (b) Ammonoids: per species, the median WER over measured stages with conch diameter >= 5 mm (excluding the embryonic ammonitella), converted to alpha; at least 50% of species must have alpha in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% alpha < 80 deg. (c) Gastropods: per specimen (then averaged per species), the fitted per-revolution whorl expansion rate W from the Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral fits, converted to alpha the same way; at least 50% of species in [80, 85] deg and at most 10% below 80 deg. All three of (a), (b), (c) must hold for 'supports'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the Nautilus median alpha is outside [76, 84] deg, or if in either the ammonoid or the gastropod sample fewer than 40% of species fall in [80, 85] deg, or more than 20% fall below 80 deg. Anything between the pass and fail thresholds is 'mixed'. If the gastropod expansion parameter cannot be mapped to a per-revolution ratio from the dataset's documentation, part (c) is reported as not operationalizable and the verdict rests on (a) and (b) with a caveat.
tests.interpretation: Thompson defines the constant angle through the per-whorl ratio of radii or whorl breadths, r = e^(2 pi cot alpha), and reads the angle off that ratio; the test therefore measures r and converts it with his own formula rather than fitting tangent angles to outlines. Modern 'whorl expansion rate' (Korn: WER = (dm1/dm2)^2 across half a whorl; Raup: W per revolution) is the same quantity for a planispiral shell. 'Ordinary ammonitoid shells' is operationalized as the species in a large published cross-section dataset (Devonian-Jurassic), 'typically spiral gastropods' as the 25 fossil and modern helicospiral species measured by Collins et al. 2021; neither sample was chosen by the tester. Deviation from the pre-registration: Collins et al. publish no per-revolution W (their W_e is a fitted rate of aperture-area increase), so r was computed directly from their raw digitised apertures (distance of the aperture centroid from the coiling axis at 180-degree steps, r = r[k+2]/r[k]), which is Thompson's own quantity; Nautilus r was likewise taken directly as dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations rather than through WER.
tests.method: fetch.py obtains the files (Dryad downloads sit behind a browser proof-of-work challenge; they were fetched with headless Chrome and checksummed) and writes derived tables (committed). analysis.py computes, per Nautilus specimen, the median of dm[i]/dm[i-8] over the 45-degree stations (one revolution; all stations are post-hatching, first dm 18-27 mm); per ammonoid species, the median of dm[n]/dm[n-1] over half-whorl stations with dm >= 5 mm; per gastropod specimen, the median of r[k+2]/r[k] where r is the perpendicular distance of each digitised aperture's centroid from the coiling axis (apertures 180 deg apart; replicate digitisations pooled), then the median per species. Each r is converted to alpha = arccot(ln r / 2 pi) and the pre-registered band fractions are evaluated.

measured.unit: degrees, median constant angle of Nautilus pompilius (r = 2.87 per revolution)
measured.uncertainty: Nautilus IQR 80.27-80.68 deg (r 2.81-2.94); population medians 80.4 (Indonesia), 80.4 (Malaysia), 80.7 (Philippines)

caveats: The verdict follows the pre-registered rule, which fails because only 32% of ammonoid species (threshold 40%) and 46% of gastropod species fall inside 80-85 deg. The failure is one-sided: no ammonoid and no gastropod species, and only 5% of Nautilus, fall below 80 deg, so 'very seldom less than 80 deg' is strongly supported; the typical ammonoid and gastropod sits at 85-86 deg (r 1.5-1.7), just above Thompson's upper bound rather than inside it.

The Nautilus part of the claim ('in the neighbourhood of 80 deg', 'about three times') is confirmed closely: median 80.5 deg, r = 2.87, with very low scatter across 93 specimens and three populations.

The ammonoid sample (Walton & Korn 2018) was assembled to study pachyconic and globular conchs and is 82% Palaeozoic; globular Palaeozoic goniatites have low expansion rates, so it is probably biased towards high alpha relative to the Mesozoic ammonites Thompson likely had in mind (the 3 Jurassic and 6 of 11 Permian species are in band).

The gastropod sample is 26 species dominated by four struthiolariid/turritellid species from New Zealand and Australia; species were weighted equally, but it is not a random sample of 'typically spiral' gastropods. r for gastropods was measured on digitised apertures in a single sectioned plane (centroid distance from the axis), which is noisier than CT-based cephalopod diameters.
Per-species r is a median over ontogeny; whorl expansion drifts during growth (see thompson1917-ch11-08), so an adult-only or juvenile-only convention would move alpha by a fraction of a degree.

Sensitivity (not pre-registered, computed in a side check): the ammonoid in-band fraction is 0.26 with no size threshold, 0.32 at dm >= 5 mm (pre-registered), 0.29 at dm >= 10 mm, 0.26 at dm >= 20 mm, and 0.33 using only each species' last measured revolution; the median alpha stays at 85.5-85.6 deg and the below-80 fraction at 0 throughout, so the verdict does not depend on the threshold.

datasets.name: Data from: Intraspecific variation in cephalopod conchs changes during ontogeny: perspectives from three-dimensional morphometry of Nautilus pompilius
Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn)
Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods

tests.label: Dissimilar turbinate shells share similar spiral angles and differ mainly in apical angle
tests.hypothesis: If shells as different as Cerithium (pointed turbinate), Solarium (obtuse turbinate / trochiform), Natica (globose) and Planorbis (discoid) differ little in spiral angle alpha and mainly in the apical semi-angle theta, then across public specimens of these four body forms the between-form spread of alpha (computed from the whorl-breadth ratio R and theta with Thompson's own relation R = exp(2 pi sin(theta) cot(alpha))) must be small, of the order of a few degrees, while the between-form spread of theta spans most of its possible range.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For every specimen with >= 3 digitised successive half-whorl apertures (Collins et al. 2021 helicospiral gastropods) estimate per revolution the linear whorl-breadth ratio R (square root of the aperture-area ratio per 360 degrees, from a log-linear fit of area on angle) and the apical semi-angle theta = atan(d(r_outer)/d(y)) from the outward and axial displacement of the whorl per revolution (theta = 90 degrees for planispiral shells). For the discoid form, which that dataset lacks, use adult whorls of the planispiral ammonoid conchs of Korn & Walton 2018 (R = dm at whorl n+1 / dm at whorl n over the last full whorl, theta = 90 degrees). Compute alpha = arccot(ln R / (2 pi sin theta)) in degrees. Assign specimens to Thompson's four forms by family: pointed turbinate = Turritellidae (Maoricolpus; Thompson lists Turritella with Cerithium), obtuse turbinate / trochiform = Trochoidea (Zethalia, Cookia; Thompson's Solarium / Trochus group), globose = Tonnoidea (Tonna, Semicassis; Thompson's Natica / Dolium group), discoid = planispiral ammonoids. The claim is supported if the range of the four form-mean alphas is <= 10 degrees while the range of form-mean thetas is >= 45 degrees, i.e. alpha range < one quarter of theta range.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim is refuted if the range of form-mean alphas is >= 20 degrees, or if it is not smaller than the range of form-mean thetas (the forms differ as much or more in spiral angle as in apical angle). Results between these thresholds are 'mixed'. If any of the four forms has fewer than 2 usable specimens the test is inconclusive (underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's four genera are not present in any public measurement set found (Dryad, Zenodo, figshare searched), so the test follows the body forms he names rather than the genera: his table groups shells as 'pointed turbinates' (Turritella, Cerithium, theta 7-15 degrees), 'obtuse turbinates' (Solarium 50-55, Trochus 35 degrees), globose forms (Natica, Dolium, Conus, theta ~70 degrees) and 'discoids' (Planorbis, Nautilus, Ammonites, theta 90 degrees). alpha is derived exactly as Thompson derived it, from the ratio of breadths of consecutive whorls and the apical semi-angle via R = e^(2 pi sin theta cot alpha). The 2D-photograph semilandmark data of Collins et al. (apertures digitised every 180 degrees along the coiling axis) give aperture area and centroid position per half whorl; the ammonoid cross-section data give diameters per half whorl. Note that because biological R lies between ~1.1 and ~10, alpha in degrees is mathematically confined to roughly 70-89 degrees whatever theta is, so a small alpha range is partly a property of the degree scale Thompson used; the coefficient of variation of cot(alpha) (the radial-to-tangential growth ratio itself) is reported alongside as a scale-free supplement. The Korn & Walton ammonoid table was already downloaded and inspected for claim test thompson1917-ch11-05 before this pre-registration; the Collins et al. zip has not been downloaded, only its file listing, metadata/specimen tables (taxon, locality, imaging method) and processing code were read.
tests.method: The tps file was parsed; for each specimen the aperture polygons were converted to mm with the recorded scale, their areas (shoelace), centroid positions along the coiling axis (y) and outermost distances from the axis (r_outer) computed, and angle assigned as 180 degrees per successive aperture. R = exp(pi * slope of ln(area) on angle), theta = atan(|d r_outer / d angle| / |d y / d angle|) from linear fits, alpha = arccot(ln R / (2 pi sin theta)). For the 179 ammonoid species R = dm(last whorl) / dm(one whorl earlier), theta = 90 degrees. Specimens were grouped into Thompson's four forms (Turritellidae n=35, Trochoidea n=2, Tonnoidea n=2, planispiral ammonoids n=179); form means of alpha and theta and their ranges were compared with the pre-registered thresholds. The CV of cot(alpha) across form means was computed as the scale-free supplement.

measured.unit: range (degrees) of form-mean spiral angle alpha across the four body forms; range of form-mean apical semi-angle theta = 81.5 degrees
measured.uncertainty: within-form SD of alpha 0.8-1.7 degrees; trochiform and globose forms have only 2 specimens each

caveats: The named genera (Cerithium, Solarium, Natica, Planorbis) were replaced by public specimens of the same body forms (Turritellidae, Trochoidea, Tonnoidea, planispiral ammonoids), following Thompson's own grouping of shells by form in the same table; this is a reinterpretation of the genus-level statement.
Two of the four forms (trochiform, globose) rest on two specimens each, the pre-registered minimum; the pointed-turbinate and discoid forms are well sampled (35 and 179).

The apical semi-angle measured here for the globose shells (28-37 degrees) is the cone of the digitised spire whorls, not the envelope of the whole shell including the body whorl as in Thompson's table (Natica ~70 degrees); the theta range would be larger, not smaller, with his convention, so the conclusion is unaffected.

Spiral angle expressed in degrees is compressed towards 90 degrees for all biologically realistic whorl-expansion ratios, which is part of why alpha varies little; on the scale-free measure cot(alpha), the radial-to-tangential growth ratio, the forms still differ about half as much (CV 0.40) as they do in theta (CV 0.81), so the direction of Thompson's claim holds either way, but the 'very little indeed' is partly an artefact of his angle scale.

Measured alphas (76.9-85.3 degrees) are a few degrees lower than Thompson's tabulated values (82-85) for the same forms, because R here comes from aperture-area growth per revolution over the spire rather than from whorl breadths at the body whorl.
Dryad downloads are served behind a proof-of-work interstitial (Anubis); analysis.py completes it automatically and must download the 521 MB archive (only the 1.5 MB .tps inside is read).

datasets.name: Data associated with: Going round the twist - An empirical analysis of shell coiling in helicospiral gastropods (Collins, Klapaukh, Crampton, Gazley, Schipper, Maksimenko, Hines 2021, Paleobiology)
Data from: Iterative ontogenetic development of ammonoid conch shapes from the Devonian through to the Jurassic (Walton & Korn 2018, Palaeontology)

tests.label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
tests.hypothesis: In hollow-horned ruminants (Bovidae) the two horns of a pair are conjugate spirals: each is a helico-spiral of the same length, curvature and pitch as its partner but of opposite handedness, so that reflecting one horn in the skull's sagittal plane reproduces the other.
tests.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). For at least 8 bovid crania from public 3D scans spanning at least 4 genera, extract the midline curve of each horn core from the mesh, fit a helico-spiral (constant curvature and torsion in the Frenet sense, i.e. a conical helix) to each, and compare the pair: in at least 80% of specimens the signs of the torsion of the left and right horn are opposite, and the magnitudes of length, mean curvature and mean torsion agree within 15% (|L - R| / mean of the pair).
tests.fail: Pre-registered (claim refuted). In more than 20% of specimens the two horns have torsion of the same sign (both horns coiling the same way, i.e. not conjugate), or the paired magnitudes differ by more than 15% in more than 20% of specimens beyond what the same measurement applied twice to one horn reproduces. If fewer than 8 specimens or fewer than 4 genera can be obtained from public sources without authentication, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'conjugate' means mirror-image, i.e. enantiomorphic: his point is that the two horns are not two copies of one spiral but a left-handed and a right-handed version of the same spiral. The operational quantity is therefore the sign of the torsion (handedness) of each horn's midline, plus the magnitudes of its length, curvature and torsion. Horn cores (bone) rather than sheaths are used because that is what 3D scans of museum crania show; sheath and core differ in length and tip curvature but not in handedness. Asymmetry from injury, wear or captivity is expected in a minority of specimens, hence the 80% threshold. Candidate sources, in order: MorphoSource media with open visibility (bovid crania and horn cores), other public 3D specimen repositories, and any dataset giving paired left/right horn geometry. No specimen measurement has been inspected before this pre-registration; only catalogue hit counts, visibility flags and HTTP status codes.
tests.method: fetch.py queries the MorphoSource public API for bovid media (10 taxon and part searches), writes every bovid record with its visibility, file size and use-agreement type to derived/candidate_media.csv, and then tries three download routes for the two largest open crania. The API itself answers normally; every download route fails (HTTP 404 for the API download path, and an Anubis 'Access Denied' page for the web download and media pages, also when retried through a headless Chrome browser). MorphoSource downloads additionally require a logged-in account that accepts the specimen's use agreement, which this run must not create. No mesh was obtained, so there is nothing to analyse and no analysis.py.

measured.unit: bovid crania with both horn cores actually obtained (0 of 13 open candidates)

other_sources_checked.dryad_bovid_horn: 3 datasets (ontogenetic allometry of horn length; horn investment in female bovids; Pseudoryx phylogeny) - all give one horn length or body-size measures per individual or species, never paired left/right geometry
other_sources_checked.zenodo_horn_landmark_datasets: 1 hit, a dicynodont table; nothing on bovid horns

caveats: The specimens needed exist and are catalogued: 44 bovid cranium or skull media on MorphoSource, 13 of them flagged 'open' visibility, spanning 6 genera (Ammotragus, Bison, Capra, Oryx, Ovis, Qurliqnoria). What failed is access: every download route returns an Anubis bot-protection page or HTTP 404 from this host, and MorphoSource downloads require an authenticated account that accepts each specimen's use agreement. Under the pre-registered rule ('fewer than 8 specimens or 4 genera obtainable without authentication') the verdict is inconclusive, not a judgement on the claim.

Measurement datasets about bovid horns do exist (Dryad: ontogenetic allometry of horn length; horn investment in female bovids), but they record one horn length per individual or species means, so they cannot address left-versus-right mirror symmetry at all.

With an account the test as pre-registered looks tractable: the open candidates include Bison bison (15.8 MB mesh), Bison priscus, Ovis ammon polii, Capra ibex, Ammotragus lervia and Oryx gazella CT series, which would give 4-6 genera, short of the pre-registered 8 specimens unless the restricted-download items are added.

Horn cores, not sheaths, are what these scans show; Thompson's figures are of sheaths. Handedness is the same in core and sheath, but the quantitative comparison (length, curvature, torsion) would differ between the two, which the pre-registered thresholds do not account for.

tests.label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
tests.hypothesis: Within one species of sunflower, larger capitula carry higher parastichy pairs: head diameter increases in order across the successive Fibonacci pairs (e.g. 21/34 < 34/55 < 55/89 < 89/144), so parastichy numbers rise with the size of the whole structure.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. In the Turing's Sunflowers data (Helianthus annuus), restrict to heads with a recorded head (seedhead) diameter and with both parastichy counts forming an adjacent pair of a Fibonacci-type sequence (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci or F4, as defined by Swinton et al. 2016). The Spearman rank correlation between head diameter and the larger parastichy number must be positive with rho >= 0.30 and P < 0.01, and the median head diameter must increase monotonically across successive pair classes of the main Fibonacci sequence that each have n >= 10 heads.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. rho <= 0.10, or P >= 0.05, or an inversion of median diameter between adjacent main-sequence pair classes each with n >= 10 (larger pair at smaller heads). 0.10 < rho < 0.30 with P < 0.05 and no inversion is 'mixed'. If the data file carries no head-size measurement, the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'data-unavailable'; if fewer than 50 heads have both diameter and a resolved pair, 'inconclusive' with reason 'underpowered'.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'size of the entire structure' is mapped to the diameter of the sunflower seedhead as reported by the grower; 'the arrangement' is mapped to the adjacent Fibonacci-type parastichy pair, ordered by its larger member. Primary counts are the photoreviewed counts where available, otherwise the submitter's counts. The claim's extension to other composites is not tested here; only the sunflower disc, which is Thompson's named example, is.
tests.method: fetch.py obtains the two spreadsheets (Dryad serves downloads behind a browser proof-of-work challenge; files were fetched with headless Chrome, checksummed, and a 49 KB derived table committed under derived/). analysis.py keeps heads with a reported head diameter and an adjacent Fibonacci-type pair (photoreviewed counts first, submitter counts otherwise), computes the Spearman correlation between diameter and the larger parastichy number, and compares median diameters across the main-sequence pair classes 21/34, 34/55, 55/89 and 89/144 (Kruskal-Wallis as a supplementary test).

measured.unit: Spearman rho, head diameter (cm) vs larger parastichy number
measured.uncertainty: P = 1.6e-54; photoreviewed-only subset n = 257, rho = 0.700

caveats: Head diameter was measured and reported by the growers themselves (citizen science), with unknown precision and probably mixed conventions (disc versus whole head); such noise biases the correlation towards zero, not away from it.
The sample is cultivated Helianthus annuus of many cultivars; the claim's remark about other composites is not tested.
Thompson lists 34/55, 55/89 and 89/144 as occurring in one species; here the 89/144 class has only 11 heads, though their median diameter (24 cm) is well above the 55/89 class (14 cm).
Size and developmental stage are confounded in a cross-sectional sample; the claim is about size, and that is what was measured.

datasets.name: Data from: Novel Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci structure in the sunflower: results of a citizen science experiment (Turing's Sunflowers)

tests.label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
tests.hypothesis: Within one species, heads (or cones) carrying a given parastichy pair are split about equally between the two chiralities: the larger parastichy family runs clockwise in roughly half of specimens and anticlockwise in the other half, as in Thompson's 224 right-handed versus 243 left-handed among 467 five-eight spruce cones.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. In the Turing's Sunflowers data (Helianthus annuus), restrict to heads with both a clockwise and an anticlockwise parastichy count that together form an adjacent pair of one Fibonacci-type sequence (Fibonacci, Lucas, double Fibonacci or F4, as defined by Swinton et al. 2016). Define a head as right-handed when its larger family is clockwise. Pooled over all such heads, the proportion p of right-handed heads must satisfy |p - 0.5| <= 0.10 and a two-sided exact binomial test against 0.5 must give P >= 0.05. In addition, in each pair class with n >= 20 heads, |p - 0.5| <= 0.15 or the binomial P >= 0.05. Primary counts are the photoreviewed counts (author's annotation file); the submitter counts are a secondary replication.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. Pooled |p - 0.5| > 0.10 with two-sided exact binomial P < 0.01 (a substantial and significant excess of one chirality), or the same pattern in the two most frequent pair classes. Any other outcome is 'mixed' (e.g. a small but significant bias with |p - 0.5| <= 0.10) or 'inconclusive' (fewer than 100 usable heads: underpowered).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'direction' of the five-series (right- versus left-handed spiral) is mapped to the chirality of the larger parastichy family of a Fibonacci-type pair, scored as clockwise or anticlockwise in a fixed viewing convention (the seed face of the head as photographed). Thompson's own counts are of Norway spruce cones; no public per-cone table of those counts exists, so the test is a replication in another phyllotactic system (sunflower capitula), which the claim explicitly extends to ('phyllotactic systems generally'). Thompson's own 224:243 split is reported alongside for comparison but is not used as data.
tests.method: fetch.py downloads the two spreadsheets (Dryad serves them behind a browser proof-of-work challenge; the files were obtained with headless Chrome, checksummed, and a 49 KB derived table committed under derived/). analysis.py parses the photoreviewed counts (best estimate before any parenthesised range), keeps heads whose two counts are adjacent members of the Fibonacci, Lucas, double-Fibonacci or F4 sequence, and scores a head right-handed if the larger family is clockwise. The proportion right-handed is tested against 0.5 with a two-sided exact binomial test, pooled and within each pair class; the submitter counts are analysed the same way as a replication.

measured.unit: proportion of heads whose larger parastichy family runs clockwise (photoreviewed counts)
measured.uncertainty: exact 95% CI 0.465-0.586; two-sided binomial P = 0.43

caveats: The test is on sunflower capitula, not on the Norway spruce cones Thompson cites; his spruce tally is not available as a per-cone dataset and was not re-analysed.

The sample is a citizen-science collection of mostly one cultivated species grown in many gardens; counts are subjective, but handedness (which family is larger and which way it runs) is robust to small count errors.

Heads whose two counts did not form an adjacent Fibonacci-type pair (about 40% of photoreviewed heads with two counts) were excluded by the pre-registered rule; chirality in disordered heads is not tested.

The 21/34 class (n = 29) leans right-handed (20:9, P = 0.06); it passes the pre-registered class rule only through its P value, and the two large classes lean in opposite directions, consistent with chance.
The pass criterion tolerates a true bias of up to 10 percentage points; the 95% CI (0.465-0.586) excludes biases larger than about 9 points in either direction.

tests.label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
tests.hypothesis: In species-level egg measurements of birds, turtles/tortoises and crocodilians, the polar axis (egg length) is never shorter than the maximum equatorial diameter (egg breadth): no hard-shelled egg is oblate or discoidal.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each species with a mean egg length L (pole-to-pole) and breadth B (maximum equatorial diameter) in the Deeming & Ruta 2014 amniote egg compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227) and the 955-species bird egg-shape compilation (Dryad doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648), compute the elongation L/B. Groups: birds, Testudines, Crocodylia (hard-shelled, in scope); Squamata reported separately as out of scope (mostly parchment-shelled). Supports if, in every in-scope group, zero species have L/B < 1.00, and the fraction of species within 5% of a sphere (L/B < 1.05) is reported together with the minimum L/B per group.
tests.fail: Refutes if any in-scope species has a mean L/B < 0.98 (polar axis robustly shorter than equatorial diameter, beyond ~2% measurement error) in either compilation. Mixed if the smallest in-scope L/B lies in [0.98, 1.00), i.e. a species indistinguishable from oblate within measurement error.
tests.interpretation: Thompson's 'prolate, never oblate spheroid' is read as: the axis of rotational symmetry (the pole-to-pole length, which in asymmetric eggs runs through the blunt and pointed ends) exceeds the equatorial diameter. Published egg measurements record length and breadth with length along the polar axis, so L/B >= 1 means prolate and L/B < 1 would mean oblate. A limitation stated up front: because measurers conventionally record the longer dimension as length, a truly oblate egg could only reveal itself in such data as L/B at or just below 1 (an apparently spherical egg); the test therefore asks whether any species approaches that boundary, and the fraction of near-spherical eggs is reported as the zone where the data cannot discriminate.
tests.method: Downloaded the Amniote Life-History Database CSV (21,322 rows), kept rows with both egg_length_mm and egg_width_mm recorded (594 species), and computed elongation L/B per species. Species were grouped as Aves (167), Testudines (16), Crocodilia (9) in scope and Squamata (402) out of scope. For each group the count of species with L/B < 1.00 (oblate as recorded), L/B < 0.98 (robustly oblate) and L/B < 1.05 (near-spherical) was tabulated with the minimum and quantiles of L/B.

measured.unit: minimum species-mean egg length/breadth among in-scope species (Macrochelys temminckii, 38.8 x 37.5 mm); zero of 192 species have L/B < 1
measured.uncertainty: no oblate species found; in-scope L/B 1st-99th percentile 1.15-1.90

caveats: Deviation from pre-registration: the two Dryad compilations named in planned_datasets (doi:10.5061/dryad.s9227, doi:10.5061/dryad.sj3tx9648) could not be downloaded because Dryad's file downloads are gated by an interactive anti-bot (proof-of-work) challenge; the Amniote Life-History Database, which carries the same two variables (egg length, egg width) and also covers turtles and crocodilians, was substituted. Criteria and thresholds were not changed.

Coverage is modest: only 167 bird, 16 turtle and 9 crocodilian species have both egg length and width in this database, far fewer than the ~1,400 bird species of Stoddard et al. 2017. A rare oblate species could be missed; a universal negative can only be supported, not proven, by a sample.

Measurement convention limits discriminating power: because egg length is recorded along the longer (polar) axis, an oblate egg could only appear as L/B at or just below 1. The data show no species near that boundary except the alligator snapping turtle (L/B = 1.03, effectively spherical), so the data are consistent with the claim but cannot exclude an oblate egg disguised as a sphere.
One crocodilian row (L/B = 16.9) is an evident unit error in the source (width probably in cm); it does not affect the oblate count and is left as recorded.
Squamata (402 species, mostly parchment-shelled, min L/B = 1.00 in a gecko) are outside Thompson's 'hard-shelled' scope and are reported only for completeness.

tests.label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
tests.hypothesis: If lateral-spined (S. mansoni) and terminal-spined (S. haematobium) eggs are mechanical variants produced by one species, then worms assigned to S. mansoni and to S. haematobium belong to one interbreeding lineage: their mitochondrial cox1 sequences should be no more divergent from each other than sequences within either nominal species, and should not form two reciprocally separated clusters.
tests.pass: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using GenBank cox1 sequences (up to 40 per nominal species, chosen by a fixed random seed from all records >= 400 bp, hybrids excluded by title), pairwise uncorrected p-distances computed on pairwise alignments over >= 300 overlapping sites: the mean S. mansoni vs S. haematobium distance is <= 0.03, or the distributions overlap (minimum between-group distance smaller than the maximum within-group distance of either species, i.e. no barcode gap).
tests.fail: Pre-registered (claim refuted). The minimum S. mansoni vs S. haematobium distance exceeds the maximum within-species distance of both S. mansoni and S. haematobium (complete barcode gap), the mean between-group distance is >= 0.10, and that mean is at least as large as the mean distance between each of two universally recognised distinct species pairs measured the same way (S. haematobium vs S. bovis; S. mansoni vs S. rodhaini). Any other combination is 'mixed'. If fewer than 10 usable sequences per focal species can be retrieved the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's compound claim has two parts: (i) a mechanism (the lateral spine is moulded in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus), and (ii) the taxonomic conclusion he draws from it, that the two egg forms 'do not shew the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni'. Part (i) is anatomical and is not operationalizable with public data; part (ii) is tested here by genetic species delimitation, which did not exist in 1917 (modern reinterpretation: 'separate species' is read as a separately evolving, reproductively isolated lineage, detectable as a deep, reciprocally separated mitochondrial divergence comparable to that between other accepted Schistosoma species). GenBank species labels for sequenced adult worms rest on life-cycle, host and multilocus data, not only on egg-spine position, which limits the circularity noted by the assessors.
tests.method: fetch.py queries NCBI E-utilities for cox1 records of each nominal species, subsamples them with a fixed seed, and writes the FASTA (committed, 128 KB) and an accession list. analysis.py aligns every pair of sequences locally (Biopython PairwiseAligner, both orientations), computes the uncorrected p-distance over aligned A/C/G/T columns (pairs with < 300 such columns discarded; 9354 of 10440 pairs retained), and summarises distances within S. mansoni, within S. haematobium, between them, and between recognised species pairs (S. haematobium vs S. bovis, S. mansoni vs S. rodhaini, and others) for calibration.

measured.unit: mean uncorrected cox1 p-distance, S. mansoni vs S. haematobium
measured.uncertainty: range 0.1475-0.2054 over 1481 sequence pairs (40 x 40 sequences)

caveats: Only the taxonomic conclusion of the claim is tested. Whether the lateral spine is moulded in a funnel-shaped part of the ootype/uterus (the mechanism Thompson takes from Looss) is not addressed by sequence data; but since the two egg types belong to lineages about 17% divergent in cox1, more than the divergence between other accepted Schistosoma species, the egg forms cannot be variants of one species whatever their mechanical origin.

Mitochondrial distance is one line of evidence; the same conclusion is standard from nuclear genomes, chromosome structure, intermediate-host specificity (Biomphalaria vs Bulinus) and the absence of fertile S. mansoni x S. haematobium hybrids. Those were not re-analysed here.

GenBank species labels are taken at face value. A few unusually divergent 'within-species' pairs (max 7.1% within S. mansoni, 6.4% within S. haematobium, one S. japonicum sequence 25% from the rest) probably reflect mislabelled or atypical records; they make the within-species range wider, i.e. work against the verdict, which is nonetheless reached with a wide margin.
The sequenced cox1 regions vary between studies; distances were computed only on overlapping aligned columns (>= 300), and 10% of pairs with no sufficient overlap were dropped.
The test is a modern reinterpretation: Thompson (following Looss) argued from egg morphology and uterine anatomy; genetic species concepts post-date him.

tests.label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
tests.hypothesis: In normal mammalian (here human) hearts the left-ventricular wall is six to seven times as thick as the right-ventricular wall, and the left-ventricular systolic pressure is six to seven times the right, so the two ratios match.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Thickness ratio R_t = (mean LV free-wall thickness) / (mean RV free-wall thickness), computed separately for males and females from the published per-sex means of morphologically normal autopsy hearts (Westaby et al. 2022, Cardiovasc Pathol, n = 1,062); LV free wall = mean of the reported LV wall sites excluding the septum; RV free wall = mean of the reported RV wall sites excluding the outflow tract. Pressure ratio R_p = median systolic blood pressure of NHANES 2017-2018 adults aged 20-59 not taking blood-pressure medication (brachial systolic as the proxy for LV peak systolic pressure) divided by 20 mmHg, the midpoint of the healthy-subject RV systolic range 15-25 mmHg (Table 1 of PMC9487613), with the range ends 15 and 25 reported as bounds. SUPPORTS if, for both sexes, R_t is in [5.0, 8.5], R_p is in [5.0, 8.5] and R_t / R_p is in [0.75, 1.33].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. REFUTES if, for both sexes, R_t < 4.5 or R_t > 9.5, or R_t / R_p is outside [0.6, 1.67] (thickness not 'in the same proportion' as pressure). Any other outcome is MIXED. If the autopsy table cannot be obtained: inconclusive (data-unavailable).
tests.interpretation: Thompson's figures come from applying Laplace's law to the two ventricles; we test whether real hearts have the stated wall-thickness ratio and whether it matches the real pressure ratio. 'Thickness of the walls' is free-wall thickness measured at autopsy (the septum is shared by both ventricles and excluded). Peak LV systolic pressure is approximated by brachial systolic pressure (close in healthy adults without aortic stenosis); RV systolic pressure is not available as a public per-person dataset, so the published healthy range is used. Scope is 'mammalian hearts'; only human data are used, which can refute a general mammalian proportion but cannot confirm it for other species. Disclosure: before this pre-registration, web-search snippets shown while locating datasets displayed summary values from these sources (autopsy LV wall about 12 mm and RV walls about 2.7-3.6 mm; RV systolic 15-25 mmHg). The thresholds above are set from the claim's stated 6-7 with symmetric tolerance, not from those values.
tests.method: analysis.py fetches and checksums the sources, averages the published per-sex mean muscle thickness of the LV anterior, lateral and inferior walls (septum excluded) and of the RV anterior, lateral and inferior walls (outflow tract excluded) from Westaby et al. Table 2, and takes the ratio. For pressure it takes the median of each person's mean systolic reading in NHANES 2017-2018 adults aged 20-59 not taking antihypertensive medication, by sex, and divides by the 20 mmHg midpoint of the healthy RV systolic range parsed from PMC9487613 Table 1 (bounds from 15 and 25 mmHg). Ratios are compared with the pre-registered intervals.

measured.unit: ratio of mean LV free-wall to mean RV free-wall muscle thickness in normal autopsy hearts (mean of female and male ratios)
measured.uncertainty: female 4.024, male 3.936; per-site SDs 1.0 mm (RV) and 2 mm (LV)

caveats: The pressure half of the claim holds: median systolic pressure is 5.7 (female) to 6.0 (male) times the 20 mmHg RV midpoint, inside Thompson's 6-7 band given the RV range (4.6-8.0). The thickness half fails: the LV free wall is only about 4.0 times as thick as the RV free wall in both sexes (11.0 vs 2.7 mm; 12.3 vs 3.1 mm), below the pre-registered 4.5 limit, so the walls are not 'in the same proportion' as the pressures (ratio of ratios 0.65-0.71).

A Laplace-law argument predicts wall thickness proportional to pressure times radius; the RV is crescent-shaped with a larger radius of curvature, so a thickness ratio below the pressure ratio is expected physiologically. That is a reason the claim fails, not a flaw in the test.

Autopsy wall thickness is measured post mortem, when the heart is in rigor or relaxed and wall thickness can differ from life by several millimetres for the LV (Hamburg study, PMC12018510); RV values are coarse (1 mm resolution, many readings of 2-3 mm). A 1 mm error in RV thickness moves the ratio by about a third, but a ratio of 6 would need the RV wall to be about 2 mm, below the reported medians at every site.

The autopsy cohort consists of sudden-death referrals with morphologically normal hearts, not a random population sample; the pressure data come from a different (US) population, and the RV pressure is a published normal range rather than measurements in the same people.
Only human hearts were used. The claim's scope is mammalian hearts; other species were not tested.

preregistered_at is the time of the pre-registration commit (2b1e5045); the committed pre-registration carried an estimated time (21:40Z) written before committing. Data were first downloaded after that commit; criteria are unchanged.
