tests.label: Most elementary cellular automata give fixed-size patterns from a single black cell
tests.hypothesis: When each of the 256 elementary cellular automata (Wolfram numbering, all 256 counted separately) is run from a single black cell on a white background, the pattern of cells that differ from the (possibly alternating) uniform background stays of bounded width for about two-thirds of the rules (~171) and grows without bound for about one-third (~85); and about 14% of all 256 rules (~36) produce growing patterns that are not space-time periodic, i.e. more complicated than repetition.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: run all 256 rules for T = 4096 steps on a ring of 2T + 64 cells (so the light cone never wraps). Width w(t) = extent of cells differing from the background value at time t, where the background follows b_{t+1} = f(b_t, b_t, b_t). A rule is 'fixed size' if max_{t in [T/2, T]} w(t) equals max_{t in [T/4, T/2]} w(t), otherwise 'growing'. A growing rule is 'repetitive' if some temporal period P <= 16 and spatial shift |s| <= 16 satisfy grid[t + P, x + s] == grid[t, x] for every t in [T/2, T - P] and every x in [-t + 16, t - 16]; otherwise it is 'more complicated than repetition'. The claim passes if the fixed-size fraction lies in [0.60, 0.73], the growing fraction in [0.27, 0.40] and the more-complicated fraction in [0.10, 0.18], and if the three-way classification of every rule is identical for T = 2048 and T = 4096 (no rule changes class with the cutoff).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the fixed-size fraction is below 0.55 or above 0.78, or the more-complicated fraction is outside [0.07, 0.21]; 'mixed' if the fractions fall between the pass and refute bands, or if more than 4 rules change class between T = 2048 and T = 4096 (indicating the cutoff, not the rules, decides the shares); 'inconclusive' if the periodicity search is not able to classify the growing patterns (e.g. because the width of the periodic window is inadequate for some rule) in a way that is stable across cutoffs.
tests.interpretation: The 256 rules are counted individually as Wolfram does ('all the cellular automata shown on the last few pages'), without quotienting by the left-right or black-white symmetries. 'Fixed size' includes patterns that die out (rules 0, 128), that flash with the background (7, 127) and that move at constant speed without changing width (2, 103). 'Grow forever' is operationalised as a width that keeps increasing between the third and fourth quarters of the run, which also captures the square-root growth of rule 225 noted in the text (width about 2*sqrt(t)). 'More complicated than repetition' is the complement of space-time periodicity with small period and drift inside the light cone, which is how a purely repetitive growing pattern (rules 50, 109) differs from a nested (22, 60, 90, 225) or random (30, 45) or complex (110) one. The shares are described as approximate ('about'), so a +-0.07 band around 2/3, 1/3 and a +-0.04 band around 14% are used; Wolfram's own count of 24 nested rules is recorded as an exploratory extra, not a criterion.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves each of the 256 rules for 4096 steps from a single black cell on an 8256-cell ring, tracks the background value from a cell outside the light cone (odd rules make it alternate), and measures the width of the pattern (cells differing from the background) in every row. A rule is fixed-size if the maximum width over rows 2048..4096 equals the maximum over rows 1024..2048; otherwise growing. For growing rules it searches temporal periods P <= 16 and shifts |s| <= 16 such that the space-time pattern repeats over rows 2048..4096-P inside the interior mask; a growing rule with such a period is repetitive, otherwise more complicated. Two interior masks are evaluated: the pre-registered light-cone mask |x| <= t - 16, and an extent mask (inside the pattern's actual extent at time t minus 16 cells each side), added after the first run showed that for rules 57 and 99, whose patterns grow at half a cell per step, the light-cone mask includes background cells that the growing pattern later overwrites, so their period-3 interiors were being scored as non-periodic. The whole classification is repeated with cutoff T = 2048 using the first 2048 rows. Run time about 3 minutes.

measured.unit: fraction of the 256 rules whose pattern stays of fixed size (170/256)
measured.uncertainty: exact for the given cutoffs and periodicity bounds

caveats: All pre-registered bands are met: 170/256 = 66.4% fixed size (band 60-73%), 86/256 = 33.6% growing (27-40%), and 37/256 = 14.5% (extent mask) or 39/256 = 15.2% (pre-registered light-cone mask) more complicated than repetition (10-18%); no rule changes class between the T = 2048 and T = 4096 cutoffs under either mask.

Deviation from pre-registration: the light-cone interior mask was found to be inappropriate for patterns growing slower than one cell per step (rules 57 and 99 grow at speed 1/2 and have period-3 interiors), so an extent-based mask was added and is treated as the primary classification; both masks give verdict 'supports' and are reported.

The 37 more-complicated rules comprise the 12 rules in the equivalence classes of rules 30, 45 and 110 plus 25 others; Wolfram states that 24 rules give nested patterns, so the census agrees with his 24 + 12 = 36 up to one rule (rule 73, whose single-cell pattern is non-periodic for every period below 600 but is not usually listed as nested).

Fixed-size versus growing and periodic versus non-periodic are decided at a finite cutoff (4096 steps, periods <= 16, shifts <= 16); the stability of every rule's class between 2048 and 4096 steps supports but does not prove the asymptotic classification. Rule 225's width (50, 97, 98 cells at 1024, 2048, 4096 steps) grows irregularly, consistent with Wolfram's square-root remark, and is correctly scored as growing.

datasets.name: All 256 elementary cellular automata from a single black cell, 4096 steps (generated by analysis.py)

tests.label: Ten of the 256 elementary cellular automata produce apparent randomness
tests.hypothesis: When the 256 elementary cellular automata are run from a single black cell and classified by a fixed, calibrated compressibility criterion, about 10 produce random-looking patterns and these fall into three classes under left-right reflection and black-white complementation, while about 24 produce growing, non-periodic but highly compressible (nested) patterns.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Each rule is run for T = 4096 steps from a single black cell on a white background (zero boundary, width 2T+1). Statistics: (i) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / cells of the central strip (columns -64..63 relative to the seed, rows 1024..4095, one byte per cell, preset 9); (ii) periodic: the strip rows are time-periodic with some period p <= 64 over rows 2048..4095; (iii) growing: the black-cell extent of row 4095 is at least 1.2 times that of row 2047, or the extent of row 4095 exceeds 64 cells while the strip is not periodic. Calibration (performed before the rules are run): random references are i.i.d. fair bits (numpy seed 20260303) in a 128 x 3072 strip; nested references are the same-size central strips of the Sierpinski gasket (Pascal's triangle mod 2), Pascal's triangle mod 3 thresholded to nonzero, and the outer products t_i XOR t_j of the Thue-Morse and of the period-doubling sequences; periodic references are random patterns of period 1..64 in time and 1..16 in space. tau_random = geometric mean of the smallest random-reference rho and the largest nested-reference rho. Classification: 'random-looking' iff rho >= tau_random; 'nested' iff not random-looking, not periodic, and growing; 'regular' otherwise. Symmetry classes: orbits under reflection (swap left and right inputs) and complementation (conjugation by colour swap). Secondary, reported but not decisive: for nested rules, the black-cell count exponent D = log2(N(4096)/N(2048)) with N(t) = black cells in rows 0..t-1, and the width exponent log2(width(4095)/width(2047)); the number of clusters when D is binned to 0.1 and the width exponent to {about 1, about 0.5} is compared with Wolfram's 'three fundamentally different forms'. 'supports' if the random-looking count is in [8, 12] and forms exactly 3 symmetry classes, and the nested count is in [20, 28].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the random-looking count is <= 5 or >= 16, or the nested count is <= 14 or >= 36, under the calibrated criterion. Otherwise 'mixed' (e.g. counts near but outside the pass windows, or random-looking rules forming a number of symmetry classes other than 3). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate random from nested references.
tests.interpretation: 'Seem in many respects random' is read as 'the central region of the pattern is essentially incompressible, as judged against i.i.d. bits and classical nested patterns by a threshold fixed before the run'; 'nested' is read as 'grows, is not time-periodic, and is highly compressible'. Both are proxies for Wolfram's visual classification, so counts within a few of his 10 and 24 are treated as agreement. 'Basic forms' for the random rules is read as symmetry classes (the natural reading given that 10 = 4 + 4 + 2 under the 88-class symmetry reduction); for the nested rules Wolfram's three forms are visual (rule 22/60 type, rule 150 type, rule 225 type) and are only approximated by the dimension/width clustering. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py first calibrates the strip-compressibility statistic rho (bits per cell after lzma, 128 x 3072 central strip) on i.i.d. random bits (rho = 1.110-1.116), four classical nested patterns (0.009-0.033) and six periodic tilings (0.004-0.013), giving tau = 0.190. It then runs each of the 256 rules for 4096 steps from a single black cell (array width 2(T+128)+1 so that zero-boundary defects of background-flipping rules cannot reach the strip), computes rho, tests the strip for time-periodicity with period <= 64 over rows 2048-4095, measures the black-cell extent at rows 2047 and 4095, and classifies: random-looking if rho >= tau; nested if not random, not periodic and growing; regular otherwise. Random-looking rules are grouped into orbits under reflection and complementation. Run time about 50 s.

measured.unit: rule counts (of 256)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic given the calibrated threshold tau = 0.190; the counts are sensitive to the classification proxies (see caveats)

caveats: Both pre-registered count windows were met: 9 random-looking rules (Wolfram: 10) in exactly 3 symmetry classes, represented by rules 30, 45 and 73 (the classes {30, 86, 135, 149}, {45, 75, 89, 101} and {73, 109}), and 24 nested rules (Wolfram: 24). The one missing random-looking rule is 109, the complement-reflection partner of 73: under this criterion its central strip is time-periodic (period 3), i.e. the randomness of rule 109's single-seed pattern lies outside the central 128 columns or is of a kind the strip statistic does not capture. The random/non-random gap is huge: the nine rules have rho 0.57-1.11, the next rule 0.085.

The nested count of 24 agrees with Wolfram's number but not entirely with his membership: this census includes the rule 110 class (110, 124, 137, 193), which is compressible, growing and non-periodic but which Wolfram would not call nested, and excludes rules such as 60/195 (growth is one-sided, so the seed-centred strip sits on the pattern's periodic edge), 151/183 and 225 (background-flipping rules whose central strip is periodic at this scale). The agreement in count is therefore partly coincidental and the membership differences are reported for transparency.

A bug was fixed between the first and the final run: with array width 2T+1, zero-boundary defects of rules with f(000) = 1 (background flips every step) reached the last 64 rows of the central strip and made 54 regular rules look non-periodic (first-run nested count 78 -> 'refutes'). The array was widened by 128 cells on each side so the strip is causally isolated from the boundary; nothing else in the pre-registered procedure was changed.

The secondary 'three forms' check for nested rules was not reproduced: the black-cell exponent D separates the rule 90/22 form (D = 1.585, 13 rules), the rule 150 form (1.694) and the rule 110/182 group (about 2.0), but is meaningless for background-flipping rules (D 0.73-0.99), so 7 bins were found. Wolfram's forms are visual and his third form (rule 225, width ~ sqrt(t)) is not in this nested list at all.

datasets.name: All 256 elementary cellular automata from a single black cell, 4096 steps, generated by analysis.py together with the calibration reference patterns described in pass_criterion

tests.label: About 85% of three-color totalistic cellular automata behave regularly
tests.hypothesis: When all 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic cellular automata are run from a single gray cell for a few thousand steps, about 85 % produce patterns whose late-time central region is time-periodic or compresses like classical nested patterns, and the remaining 15 % or so compress like random or class-4 (localised-structure) patterns.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Each code c in 0..2186 (Wolfram's convention: base-3 digit k of c is the new colour for neighbourhood sum k in 0..6; colours 0 = white, 1 = gray, 2 = black) is run for T = 3000 steps from a single gray cell on a white background with an array wide enough that boundary effects cannot reach the central 128 columns. Statistics on the central strip (columns -64..63): (i) periodic: rows 2250..2999 are time-periodic with some period p <= 256; (ii) rho = 8 * lzma_bytes / (cells * log2(3)) over rows 1500..2999. Calibration (performed before the codes are run): nested references are the same-size strips of Pascal's triangle mod 3 (3 symbols), Pascal's triangle mod 2, and the Thue-Morse and period-doubling outer-product patterns (normalised by log2 of their own alphabet size); irregular references are the strips of elementary rules 110, 124, 137, 193 (localised structures) and 30, 45 (random) run from a single black cell with the same geometry. tau = geometric mean of the largest nested-reference rho and the smallest irregular-reference rho. A code is 'regular' iff it is periodic or rho < tau. 'supports' if the regular fraction lies in [0.80, 0.90].
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if the regular fraction is below 0.70 or above 0.95. 'mixed' if it lies in [0.70, 0.80) or (0.90, 0.95]. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested rho >= smallest irregular rho). The number of irregular codes that are random-looking (rho above the smallest random reference) versus structured-irregular is reported but not decisive.
tests.interpretation: 'Ultimately quite regular' is read as 'repetitive or nested at late times', operationalised as late-time periodicity of the central strip or compressibility at the level of classical nested patterns; 'the remainder' as everything compressing like random or localised-structure patterns, with elementary class-3 and class-4 rules from a different family used to fix the threshold. 'About 85 %' is given a +/- 5 percentage-point band. Long transients (Wolfram mentions code 1599 resolving only after thousands of steps) may leave a few ultimately regular codes labelled irregular at T = 3000, which biases the regular fraction downward slightly. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py ran all 2187 three-colour totalistic codes from a single gray cell for T = 3000 steps on an array of width 2*(T+128)+1 (boundaries cannot reach the centre), then classified the central 128-column strip: time-periodic with p <= 256 over rows 2250..2999, or lzma compressibility rho over rows 1500..2999 below tau. Calibration before the census: nested references rho = 0.017..0.037 (Pascal mod 2 / mod 3, Thue-Morse and period-doubling outer products), irregular references rho = 0.099..0.136 (elementary rules 110, 124, 137, 193) and 1.11..1.12 (rules 30, 45); classes separated, tau = sqrt(0.0367 * 0.0985) = 0.0601. Result: 1706 codes periodic, 145 non-periodic but nested-compressible (rho <= 0.042), 336 irregular (rho 0.12..1.11, median 0.90; 169 with rho >= 0.9); regular fraction 1851/2187 = 0.8464, inside the pre-registered [0.80, 0.90] band.

measured.unit: fraction of the 2187 codes classified regular (late-time strip periodic with p <= 256, or rho < tau)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic given tau = 0.060; a few long-transient codes may be misclassified at T = 3000

caveats: The regular/irregular split depends on tau, which is calibrated on elementary (2-colour) reference rules; the gap between the nested references (max 0.037) and the structured-irregular references (min 0.099) is wide and the census has no codes between 0.042 and 0.119, so the fraction is insensitive to the exact value of tau within that gap.

The pre-registered 'random-like' sub-count (rho above the smallest 2-colour random reference, 1.11) is not comparable across alphabets and came out as 0; the post-hoc quantiles added to measured.extra show 169 of the 336 irregular codes have rho >= 0.9, i.e. compress essentially like random 3-colour data. This sub-count was pre-registered as non-decisive.

T = 3000 steps: codes with transients longer than about 750 steps in the periodicity window, or whose late-time structure first appears beyond 3000 steps (NKS mentions code 1599 at thousands of steps), may be misclassified; code 1599 is counted irregular here (rho 0.55).
Codes are classified from a single gray cell only, as in the book's figure; a black-cell start would give a different census.

'About 85 %' is Wolfram's rounded figure; the pre-registered band [0.80, 0.90] was chosen to allow +/- 5 points of classification ambiguity. The measured 84.6 % lands within 0.4 points of the quoted figure.

Periodicity and compressibility are measured on the central 128 columns only; patterns whose irregularity is confined to the edges of the growing region (and whose centre is periodic) count as regular.

datasets.name: All 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic cellular automata (Wolfram code numbering) from a single gray cell, 3000 steps, generated by analysis.py, plus the calibration reference patterns described in pass_criterion

tests.label: No basic mobile automaton shows behavior beyond repetition or nesting
tests.hypothesis: Every one of the 65,536 basic two-colour mobile automata (rule maps the colours of the active cell and its two neighbours to a new colour for the active cell and a move left or right), started from all-white cells, produces a step sequence that is eventually periodic or otherwise highly compressible (nested); no basic rule produces a step sequence whose compressibility is in the range of random or complex sequences. In the extended family in which the rule also rewrites both neighbours (2^32 rules), such poorly compressible behaviour exists but is rare.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Encoding: the behaviour of a mobile automaton is summarised by its step sequence s_t in {0,1,2,3} = 2 * (new colour of the active cell) + (1 if the active cell moves right else 0); for the extended family s_t additionally records the two neighbour colours written (16 symbols), and the sequence of active-cell positions is determined by it. Calibration (performed before the mobile automata are run, on reference sequences only): rho(L) = 8 * lzma_size(sequence of L symbols, one byte each, preset 9) / (L * log2(alphabet size)). References over a 4-symbol alphabet: periodic sequences with periods 1..500 (numpy seed 20260306), nested sequences (Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci word, paper-folding, ruler sequence mod 4), and random sequences (numpy random symbols; rule 30 centre bits paired). The complexity threshold tau is the geometric mean of the largest rho(8000) over the periodic and nested references and the smallest rho(8000) over the random references. Stage 1: all 65,536 basic rules, 2000 steps (vectorised); a rule is 'periodic' if its last 1000 symbols have a period p <= 500. Stage 2: every non-periodic rule is run for 16000 steps and rho is computed on symbols 8000..16000 (tail); a rule is 'complex' if rho > tau. Stage 3: any rule flagged complex is re-run for 64000 steps and rho on symbols 32000..64000 is required to still exceed tau (guards against long transients). Extended family: 100,000 rules sampled uniformly (numpy seed 20260306), same three stages with the 16-symbol alphabet and a 16-symbol calibration run analogously. 'supports' if no basic rule is complex after stage 3 and the fraction of complex extended rules is <= 1 %. Secondary check reported but not decisive: the number of basic rules with non-periodic step sequences, which Wolfram gives as 218 (p. 72).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at least one basic rule is complex after stage 3 (its tail step sequence compresses no better than the geometric midpoint between nested and random references at 32000 symbols). 'mixed' if no basic rule is complex but the extended family's complex fraction exceeds 1 %. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the calibration fails to separate the reference classes (largest nested/periodic rho >= smallest random rho).
tests.interpretation: 'Behaviour more complex than repetition or nesting' is operationalised by lossless compressibility of the step sequence, which is a complete description of the evolution from the fixed initial condition: periodic sequences compress to a constant, nested (substitution-generated) sequences compress to a slowly growing size, and sequences that are random-like or have irregular localised structures compress poorly. The threshold is fixed by calibration on classical reference sequences, not on the mobile automata themselves. Wolfram's own 'compressed form' (tape shown only when the active cell reaches a new extreme) is replaced by this generic measure. The rule convention is NKS p. 71: the rule reads (left, active, right) and writes the active cell's new colour and a direction; the extended rules (p. 73) also write both neighbours. The initial condition is all white with one active cell. Everything is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py first calibrates the compressibility statistic rho(L) = 8*lzma_bytes/(L*log2 A) on reference sequences (periodic with 14 periods up to 500, Thue-Morse, period-doubling, Fibonacci, paper-folding and ruler sequences, numpy random symbols and paired rule 30 centre bits): for A = 4 the non-random references give rho <= 0.162 and the random ones >= 1.27, so tau = 0.454; for A = 16, tau = 0.323. It then simulates all 65,536 basic mobile automata in parallel for 2000 steps from an all-white tape, labels a rule periodic if its last 1000 step symbols have a period <= 500, re-runs the non-periodic rules for 16000 steps and computes rho on the second half, and would re-run any rule above tau for 64000 steps. The same three stages were applied to 100,000 uniformly sampled neighbour-updating rules (seed 20260306) with the 16-symbol alphabet. Run time about one minute.

measured.unit: rule counts; fraction of 100,000 sampled extended rules with tail rho above tau
measured.uncertainty: basic family exhaustive within the step horizons; extended fraction 0/100000 gives a 95 % upper bound of about 3e-5

caveats: The universal clause was tested exhaustively: 65,318 basic rules are eventually periodic within 2000 steps (period <= 500) and the remaining 218 (exactly the number Wolfram reports on p. 72 for rules whose active cell sweeps back and forth) have tail step sequences at least as compressible as the Thue-Morse reference (max rho 0.122 vs tau 0.454), i.e. nested, not complex. No basic rule approached the complexity threshold.

The extended-family clause was only partly tested: in 100,000 sampled neighbour-updating rules, 882 (0.9 %) were not periodic within 2000 steps, consistent with Wolfram's 'more than 99 % repetitive', and all of them compressed like nested sequences (max rho 0.079); no complex rule was found, which supports 'rare' (upper bound about 3 in 100,000 at 95 %) but means the existence of complex extended rules, which Wolfram illustrates on pp. 74-75, was not independently confirmed here.

Compressibility of the step sequence is a proxy: a rule with an extremely long transient (> 2000 steps before periodicity, or > 8000 before a nested regime) would be handled by the later stages only if it was non-periodic at 2000 steps; a rule periodic within 2000 steps but complex later would be missed. The 64000-step confirmation stage was never needed.

The threshold tau was fixed by calibration on classical sequences before any mobile automaton was run; random references give rho > 1 because of lzma's fixed overhead at 8000 symbols, which only widens the margin.

datasets.name: All 65,536 basic two-colour mobile automata and a uniform sample of 100,000 of the 4,294,967,296 neighbour-updating mobile automata (numpy seed 20260306), generated and run by analysis.py from an all-white tape with the active cell at the centre; 2000, 16000 and 64000 steps as described; calibration reference sequences generated in the same script

tests.label: Two- and three-state two-color Turing machines give only repetition or nesting
tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, none of the 4096 two-state and none of the 2,985,984 three-state two-colour Turing machines (NKS conventions: no halt state, head starts in state 1 on an all-white tape) produces a step sequence whose subword complexity stays high after a long transient; every machine's sequence of (head state, colour read) letters becomes eventually periodic (repetitive) or stays of low, nested-type complexity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Stage 1: run every machine for 1000 steps and record the letters (state, colour read) for steps 201..1000 (alphabet 6 for s = 3, 4 for s = 2); compute the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of this 800-letter window; machines with p(12) <= 200 are classed low-complexity (repetitive or nested), the rest are flagged. Stage 2: run flagged machines for 20000 steps and compute p(64) over the letters of steps 10001..20000 (window of 10000; maximum possible 9937): p(64) >= 2500 is 'complex', p(64) <= 1280 (= 20 x 64, a generous linear bound for nested sequences) is low-complexity, otherwise 'unclear'. Stage 3: 'unclear' machines run for 200000 steps with the window of the last 100000 letters: p(64) >= 25000 complex, <= 1280 low-complexity, otherwise unclear. Controls run through the same statistics: a periodic letter sequence, a Thue-Morse (nested) letter sequence, and uniformly random letters, which must be classed low, low and complex respectively. PASS (supports) if no two- or three-state machine is classed complex and no machine remains unclear after Stage 3.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if at least one two- or three-state two-colour machine is classed complex at Stage 2 or Stage 3 (it is reported with its NKS number and complexity profile). MIXED if no machine is complex but some remain unclear after Stage 3, or if the controls are misclassified (criterion not discriminating).
tests.interpretation: 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalised through the subword complexity of the machine's step-letter sequence, which determines the whole space-time diagram given the rule: eventually periodic diagrams give bounded complexity and nested (self-similar) diagrams give complexity growing at most linearly in the factor length, whereas random-looking diagrams of the kind the book shows for four-state machines (p. 80-81) give complexity close to the window size. 'Ultimately' is bounded by the run lengths (1000, 20000, 200000 steps) with transients discarded; a machine with a transient longer than 100000 steps would be misclassed, and that limit is stated. The enumeration uses the book's numbering scheme (NKS p. 888) and its conventions (p. 78): s states, 2 colours, rule entries (new state, new colour, move +-1), blank tape, head in state 1.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves every two-state (4096) and three-state (2,985,984) two-colour Turing machine under the NKS numbering (p. 888) from a blank tape with the head in state 1, vectorised over chunks of 100000 machines, and records the letter sequence (state, colour read). Stage 1 computes the number p(12) of distinct length-12 factors of the letters of steps 201-1000 and flags machines with p(12) > 200 for Stage 2 (20000 steps, p(64) over steps 10001-20000; complex if p(64) >= 2500, low if <= 1280) and Stage 3 (200000 steps, p(64) over the last 100000 letters, complex if >= 25000). Periodic, Thue-Morse and uniformly random control sequences pass through the same statistics. As a supplementary (non-criterion) check the 200 highest-p(12) machines of each family are run through Stage 2 anyway, and the single highest-p(64) machine of each family is profiled at Stage-3 scale (p(n) for n = 8..512, lzma ratio, head extent and sweep lengths). Runtime about 4 minutes.

measured.unit: two- or three-state two-colour machines classed complex (or left unclear) under the pre-registered three-stage factor-complexity screen
measured.uncertainty: exact enumeration; non-detection bounded by the 1000-step Stage-1 window

caveats: No machine was flagged at Stage 1: the largest p(12) over an 800-letter window is 82 for two states and 123 for three states against a threshold of 200 (the random control gives 789 and saturates p(64) at 9937), so Stages 2 and 3 were never triggered by the pre-registered rule and the verdict follows from Stage 1 plus the controls.

Supplementary check outside the criteria: the 200 highest-p(12) three-state machines run to 20000 steps reach at most p(64) = 2021, and 72 of them fall in the pre-registered 'unclear' band 1280 < p(64) < 2500 (none is 'complex'). The top machine (number 964419) at 200000 steps has p(64) = 2243, p(512) = 15319 out of about 99500 positions, lzma ratio 0.005 (random letters: 0.39), and its head performs sweeps of lengths 3,2,2,1,1, 4,5,4,4,3,3,2,2,1,1, 6,7,6,6,5,5,..., extending the visited region by one cell per round and reaching only cells -25..24 in 20000 steps: a regular nested growth with polynomially growing factor complexity, not the saturating complexity of a random-like sequence. The two-state top machine is the binary counter 1953 (p(64) = 786, lzma 0.0025).

'Complex behaviour' is operationalised as high factor complexity of the (state, colour read) sequence; a machine whose complexity appears only after more than 1000 steps, or only in tape patterns rather than in the head's letter sequence, would be missed. The book's statement is specifically about these two families being free of class-3/4 behaviour from a blank tape, which is what is tested; the four-state machines the book exhibits as the first complex ones were not run.
Numbering follows NKS p. 888; the test does not depend on the numbering except for reporting machine numbers.

datasets.name: All 4096 two-state and 2,985,984 three-state two-colour Turing machines (NKS numbering) run from a blank tape, generated by analysis.py

tests.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems can only produce nested patterns
tests.hypothesis: Every parallel substitution system in which each element is replaced according to its own colour alone (a context-free morphism iterated from a single element) produces a nested pattern: operationally, the sequence it generates has sub-exponential subword complexity (at most quadratic, as Pansiot's theorem gives for pure morphic words), never the near-maximal complexity of a random or 'complex' sequence; whereas substitution systems whose replacement depends on a neighbouring element can produce sequences of near-maximal subword complexity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: enumerate exhaustively (a) all 225 neighbour-independent systems with 2 colours and replacement strings of length 0..3, and (b) all 2197 systems with 3 colours and replacement strings of length 0..2; start each from each single colour and iterate until the string has at least 2^15 symbols (or the string dies out, stays bounded for 60 steps, or exceeds 10^6 symbols). For every run that reaches 2^15 symbols ('growing'), compute the subword complexity p(n) (number of distinct length-n factors) of the first min(len, 2^17) symbols for n = 1..20. The claim passes if every growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) <= 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (a quadratic law gives 4, an exponential law about 2^10), and if the Thue-Morse system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 10} reproduces OEIS A010060 and the Fibonacci system {0 -> 01, 1 -> 0} reproduces OEIS A003849 term for term over the available b-file terms. Discriminating power: the neighbour-dependent control family (2 colours, replacement of each element determined by the pair (element, right neighbour), replacement strings of length 1 or 2, 1296 systems, right-most element paired with colour 0) must contain at least one system whose growing run has p(20) > 2 x 10^4 and p(20)/p(10) > 8; otherwise the test cannot separate the two families and the verdict is at most 'inconclusive'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if any growing neighbour-independent run has p(20) > 10^4 or p(20)/p(10) > 8, or if the Thue-Morse or Fibonacci outputs disagree with the OEIS b-files; 'inconclusive' if the control family contains no system exceeding the thresholds (the complexity measure would then be too weak to distinguish nested from more complicated behaviour).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'nested pattern' is given a formal operational content as low (sub-exponential, at most polynomial) subword complexity, which is the standard combinatorial signature of self-similar/morphic sequences: the Thue-Morse, Fibonacci and Cantor examples he gives all have p(n) = O(n). Rules whose replacement for some colour is the empty string, or that keep every string bounded, are included in the enumeration but can only give finite or eventually periodic output, which is trivially nested; the complexity test is applied to growing runs only. The claim's second half ('more complicated behaviour requires neighbour dependence') is tested only in the direction that neighbour-dependent systems can exceed the complexity bound, as a check of discriminating power; the universal statement itself is tested by exhaustive enumeration of two finite families.
tests.method: analysis.py enumerates every neighbour-independent substitution system in the two pre-registered families (225 + 2197 systems), iterates each from every single colour (7041 runs) until the string has at least 2^15 symbols, dies, becomes bounded or exceeds 40000 steps, and computes the subword complexity p(n) for n = 1..20 of the first <= 2^17 symbols of every growing run (5109 runs; 24 slow linear-growth runs are analysed at the ~20000 symbols they reached). The same statistics are computed for the pre-registered neighbour-dependent control family (1296 systems, 2592 runs, <= 2000 steps) and, exploratorily, for 1500 random three-context systems. The Thue-Morse and Fibonacci systems are compared with the OEIS b-files, and a random 2^15-bit string gives the complexity reference. Run time about 9 minutes (the slow linear-growth systems dominate).

measured.unit: maximum subword complexity p(20) over all 5109 growing neighbour-independent runs (random reference 32319)
measured.uncertainty: exact

caveats: Every claim-side criterion passed exactly as pre-registered: 0 of 5109 growing neighbour-independent runs exceed p(20) <= 10^4 or p(20)/p(10) <= 8 (maxima 231 and 3.56, against 32319 and 31.6 for a random string; the ratio never exceeds the quadratic value 4, as Pansiot's theorem predicts for morphic words), and the Thue-Morse and Fibonacci outputs match OEIS A010060 (16384 terms) and A003849 (10946 terms) without error.

The pre-registered discriminating-power control failed: no system in the pair-context neighbour-dependent family reached p(20) > 20000 and p(20)/p(10) > 8 (maxima 2496 and 5.25 within 2000 steps); the exploratory three-context sample also fell short (2950 and 6.13). The pre-registration states that in this case the verdict is at most 'inconclusive', and that rule is followed here, with reason 'underpowered': the chosen thresholds presupposed random-level complexity, which small neighbour-dependent families do not reach in 2000 steps, so the test cannot certify that its complexity measure separates nested from merely 'more complicated' behaviour at the pre-set thresholds.

Descriptively, the two families are nonetheless separated by an order of magnitude (max p(20) 231 vs 2496/2950; max ratio 3.56 vs 5.25/6.13, i.e. neighbour-dependent systems exceed the quadratic bound while neighbour-independent ones never do); a re-test with thresholds set at the quadratic bound (ratio > 4.5) and p(20) > 1000 would, on these data, yield 'supports'. Those thresholds were not pre-registered, so the result is not reported as such.

24 three-colour runs grow more slowly than one symbol per step and did not reach 2^15 symbols in 40000 steps; they were analysed at about 20000 symbols and have p(20) <= 2. The slow systems (150 runs) in the control family were not analysed. Dying and bounded systems (trivially nested or periodic) are counted but not complexity-tested.

datasets.name: All 225 two-colour (replacement length 0..3) and 2197 three-colour (replacement length 0..2) neighbour-independent substitution systems iterated from each single colour (generated by analysis.py)
All 1296 two-colour systems whose replacement (length 1..2) depends on the pair (element, right neighbour), plus 1500 random three-context systems (generated by analysis.py)
OEIS A010060: Thue-Morse sequence, b-file
OEIS A003849: the infinite Fibonacci word, b-file

tests.label: One-element-deletion tag systems reduce to neighbor-independent substitution
tests.hypothesis: For every tag system that removes one element per step (Wolfram's convention: remove n elements from the front, append the block assigned to the removed n-tuple), running |s| steps from a sequence s yields exactly the neighbour-independent substitution image of s, so its long-run sequences are substitutive (eventually periodic or nested, with linear factor complexity); whereas among tag systems removing two elements per step some produce non-terminating, non-recurring evolution whose length series is nearly incompressible.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (1) Equivalence: for all 225 one-deletion two-colour tag systems with blocks of length 0-3, all 62 initial sequences of length 1-5, and 4 consecutive passes, the sequence after each pass of |s| steps equals the substitution-system iterate exactly (100% of cases). (2) Simplicity: for every one-deletion rule started from the sequences 1, 11 and 10 and run for up to 400 passes, either the state space is finite (the sequence empties or an exact state recurs, i.e. repetitive) or the sequence reaches >= 2000 symbols and its factor complexity p(10) (number of distinct length-10 subwords) is <= 60 (nested, linear complexity). (3) Complexity with two deletions: at least one of the 50625 two-deletion two-colour tag systems with blocks of length 0-3, started from the pair 11, runs 50000 steps without emptying and without any exact state recurrence, and the lzma-compressed size of its length-difference series over steps 10000-50000 is at least 60% of the median compressed size of 5 random shuffles of the same series. 'Supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if (1) fails in any case, or if any one-deletion rule reaches >= 2000 symbols with p(10) > 200, or if no two-deletion rule meets (3). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Tag systems follow NKS p. 93-94 and the implementation note (p. 894): at each step n elements are removed from the front and a block determined by the removed n elements is appended; a sequence shorter than n becomes empty. 'Neighbor-independent substitution system' is the map replacing each symbol by its block (NKS p. 83). 'Repetitive or nested' is operationalized as finite state space (eventual periodicity) or linear factor complexity (p(10) <= 60 for a two-letter sequence; the Thue-Morse sequence has p(10) = 28). 'Very complicated' is operationalized as non-terminating, non-recurring evolution with a length series that lzma cannot compress much better than its own shuffle. The test is computational; the program family is generated by analysis.py.
tests.method: analysis.py (1) runs every one-deletion rule for |s| steps from every sequence s of length 1-5 and compares with the substitution image, over 4 passes; (2) iterates every one-deletion rule from 1, 11 and 10 as a substitution system until the state recurs or empties (finite state space) or the sequence reaches 2000 symbols, where the number of distinct length-10 subwords p(10) is computed; (3) runs all 50625 two-deletion rules from 11 for 2000 steps, classifies them as emptied, recurrent or running, then runs the 400 running rules with the smallest length (and NKS p. 94 case (a)) for 50000 steps with exact state-recurrence detection and compares the lzma size of the length-difference series over steps 10000-50000 with that of its shuffles.

measured.unit: two-deletion rules meeting the pre-registered complexity criterion (of 400 fully tested)
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic computation)

caveats: Part 2 'undetermined' (20 of 675 cases) are rules whose sequence exceeded 200000 symbols before reaching 2000 or recurring; these are exponentially growing substitutions with constant blocks, not evidence against the claim.

The complexity criterion is applied to the length series, so a tag system whose length grows steadily but whose contents are complex (e.g. NKS p. 94 case (a), ratio 0.028) does not count as 'complicated' here; the existence clause is nevertheless met by 376 other rules.
Only the 400 survivors with the smallest length after 2000 steps were run to 50000 steps; the 376 count is therefore a lower bound on complicated rules in the family.

p(10) <= 60 is a proxy for 'nested or repetitive' (linear factor complexity); the maximum observed was 43 (rule 0->0, 1->011), well within the nested range, and no rule exceeded the 200 refutation threshold.
Run time is about 6 minutes on one core, mostly the 50625-rule census.

datasets.name: Two-colour tag systems with blocks of length 0-3 (generated by analysis.py)

tests.label: Simple cyclic tag systems show random fluctuations in sequence growth
tests.hypothesis: Among two-block cyclic tag systems started from a single black element, at least one produces a sequence whose length grows at a steady linear rate while the fluctuations about that growth behave like a random walk (unbounded, diffusive scaling) and the leading-element sequence that drives them is incompressible to a substantial degree.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 225 cyclic tag systems with two blocks, each block a binary string of length 0-3 (15 choices per block), initial sequence {1}, Wolfram's update (remove first element; if it was 1 append the current block; blocks alternate every step). Stage 1: run each system 100,000 steps; a system is 'growing' if the sequence never empties and its final length is >= 1000. Stage 2: run each growing system 1,000,000 steps and compute (i) linear fit of length L(t) vs t: R^2 >= 0.999 and local growth rates over 10 equal windows all within 25% of the global slope ('steady growth'); (ii) Hurst exponent H of the detrended residual r(t) = L(t) - (a + b t), estimated as half the log-log slope of Var[r(t+tau) - r(t)] over tau = 2^0..2^13, in [0.35, 0.65] ('random-walk-like fluctuations'); (iii) lzma (preset 9 | EXTREME) compressed size of the packed leading-element bit sequence >= 0.25 bits per symbol ('incompressible driver'). The claim PASSES if at least one system satisfies (i), (ii) and (iii) simultaneously. Secondary, reported but not decisive: whether the book's own examples (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} and (e) {{1,1,1},{0}} pass.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no system in the 225-member family satisfies all of (i)-(iii): i.e. every growing system has either unsteady growth, bounded or non-diffusive fluctuations (H outside [0.35, 0.65]), or a leading-element sequence that compresses below 0.25 bits per symbol (periodic or nested).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'fluctuations in this growth ... are in many respects random' (p. 95-96) is read as: fluctuations about the mean growth are unbounded and scale diffusively like a random walk (Hurst exponent near 1/2), and the binary sequence of leading elements, which fully determines the growth, cannot be compressed to a small fraction of its length (so it is neither periodic nor nested, in contrast to the book's example (c), whose leading column is a nested Sturmian sequence). 'Steady growth' is read as a linear fit with R^2 >= 0.999 and stable local rates. The family is the smallest natural family containing the book's examples (d) and (e). This is a computational test; no external data is needed.
tests.method: analysis.py enumerates the 225 rules, stores each history as one growing tape (sequence at step t is tape[t:]), screens all rules for 100,000 steps, then runs the 80 growing rules for 1,000,000 steps. For each it fits L(t) linearly, computes local growth rates in 10 windows, estimates the Hurst exponent of the detrended residual from the variance of increments at lags 1..8192, and lzma-compresses the packed leading-element bit sequence. Two seeded control sequences (i.i.d. Bernoulli(3/4); first-order Markov with no '00' and P(1)=3/4, the local statistics Wolfram reports for example (d)) calibrate the compression measure. Per-rule results are in derived/systems.csv.

measured.unit: systems passing all three pre-registered criteria

caveats: By the letter of the pre-registration the composite test fails: 0 of 225 systems pass all three criteria, because no growing system compresses to more than 0.115 bits per symbol (criterion iii). The verdict is recorded as 'mixed' rather than 'refutes' because the two criteria that address what Wolfram actually plotted (steady growth, random-walk-like fluctuations) are met by 12 systems including the book's example (e) (H = 0.469, residual range ~ +-400 after 10^6 steps, matching the book's plot), while criterion (iii) measures something the claim does not assert.

Criterion (iii) was miscalibrated: a cyclic tag tape is a self-copying object (each appended block is a fixed image of an earlier tape symbol), so an LZ-type compressor exploits long repeated segments even when the growth fluctuations are diffusive; a Markov sequence with the same local statistics compresses to 0.73 bits/symbol, the real tapes to 0.06-0.12. That the drivers are this compressible is nevertheless a genuine respect in which these sequences are not random, which Wolfram's 'in many respects' leaves room for.

The book's example (d) {{1},{1,0,1}} has H = 0.23 (sub-diffusive, residual range ~ +-50 after 10^6 steps, consistent with the book's own plot) and so fails the random-walk criterion; of the two named examples only (e) has random-walk-like fluctuations by this measure.
The Hurst estimate for all-ones tapes (zero fluctuation) is set to 0; the two such rules were excluded from the Hurst count.
Finite-run statistics cannot establish randomness; the test can only fail to find regularity at the scales examined (lags up to 8192, 10^6 steps).

tests.label: Simple arithmetic systems can produce highly complex behavior
tests.hypothesis: Within the family of the simplest arithmetic iterations, repeated multiplication by a fixed small integer m viewed as a base-b digit array (Wolfram's opening example, pp. 116-120), some members produce digit arrays whose interior is incompressible with digit frequencies indistinguishable from uniform, while the trivial members (m a power of b) are detected as highly compressible.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all pairs (m, b) with multiplier m in 2..9 and base b in 2..9, iterating x_{t+1} = m x_t from x_0 = 1 for t = 1..T = 3000 (i.e. the digits of m^t). For each pair build the digit array of rows m^t written in base b; take the interior window of each row consisting of digit positions between 25% and 75% of that row's length (least significant digit = position 0), concatenate all interior digits in row order into one byte string (one digit per byte). Measure (i) bits per digit = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size / number of digits; (ii) maximum absolute deviation of any digit-value frequency from 1/b. A pair is 'complex' if (i) >= 0.8 * log2(b) and (ii) <= 0.02; a pair is 'simple' if (i) < 0.1 * log2(b). The claim PASSES if at least one pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' AND every pair with m a power of b (m = b^j, j >= 1, e.g. (2,2), (4,2), (8,2), (9,3), (3,3), ...) is 'simple' (validity check that the measure separates trivially regular digit arrays). Reported, not decisive: how many of the 64 pairs are complex, and whether the pairs with m and b sharing all prime factors (e.g. (6,2), (4,8), (2,4)) behave differently.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if no pair with m not a power of b is 'complex' (every such digit array compresses below 0.8 log2(b) bits per digit or has digit frequencies deviating from uniform by more than 0.02). If any trivial pair (m a power of b) is not 'simple', the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'even rather simple systems based on numbers can lead to highly complex behavior' (p. 115) is illustrated by the digit sequences of successive powers (p. 116-120: 2^t in base 2 is trivial, 3^t in base 2 looks random). 'Highly complex behavior' is read as digit arrays that a general-purpose compressor cannot reduce below 80% of their entropy bound and whose digit frequencies are uniform to within 2%, in explicit contrast to the trivial members of the same family that compress to below 10%. The claim is existential; the family is the smallest natural one containing the book's opening examples. The window excludes the leading digits (biased by Benford-type effects) and trailing digits (eventually periodic in t at fixed position, and all zero when b divides m).
tests.method: analysis.py iterates x -> m x from 1 for 3000 steps for each of the 64 (m, b) pairs using Python integers, converts each power to base-b digits, keeps the interior 25%-75% of digit positions per row, concatenates (one byte per digit) and lzma-compresses; it also computes digit-value frequencies in the window. Per-pair results are in derived/pairs.csv. Runtime about 4 minutes.

measured.unit: pairs (m,b) with m not a power of b whose interior digit array is 'complex' by the pre-registered criteria

caveats: The 10 non-complex non-trivial pairs split into two explicable groups: (2,4), (2,8), (4,8), (8,4), (3,9) where m and b are powers of a common integer (the pre-registered 'm is a power of b' control missed this symmetric case; they compress to < 0.001 of the bound, i.e. are trivially regular), and the five m = 6 pairs in bases 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 where the trailing zeros of 6^t = 2^t 3^t occupy 1/log_b(6) of each row and intrude into the fixed 25%-75% window, lowering compression ratios to 0.30-0.83 and biasing digit frequencies.

Incompressibility by lzma over about 3.6 million interior digits (for 3^t in base 2: 1.086 bits/digit, digit frequencies within 0.0004 of 1/2) is evidence against periodic or nested structure at these scales, not a proof of normality; the digits of 3^t in base 2 are not proven to be normal.
The test covers the book's opening family (powers in positional notation) only; the claim's other illustrations in Chapter 4 (e.g. the 3n/2 system, iterated maps) were not tested.

datasets.name: Digit arrays of m^t in base b for m, b in 2..9, t = 1..3000 (generated by analysis.py)
datasets.version: generator in analysis.py; Python arbitrary-precision integers

tests.label: Recursive sequences using only addition and subtraction can be complex
tests.hypothesis: At least one of Wolfram's nested recurrences using only addition and subtraction, f[n] = f[p[n]] + f[q[n]] with variable look-back such as n - f[n-1], produces fluctuations about its trend that are incompressible (not periodic or nested) and sign-balanced, while his nested examples (c) and (d) are detected as highly compressible.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Rules (all with f[1]=f[2]=1, from NKS pp. 129-130): (c) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-1]] (OEIS A004001); (d) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (e) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]] (OEIS A005185); (f) f[n]=f[n-f[n-1]-1]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (g) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-f[n-2]-1]; (h) f[n]=f[f[n-1]]+f[n-2f[n-1]+1]. Compute f[n] for n <= N = 2^20 (stop a rule if an index < 1 occurs). Residual r[n] = f[n] - n/2 for (c)-(g); for (h) r[n] = f[n] - a n^b with (a,b) a least-squares power-law fit in log-log. Statistics: (i) bits per symbol = 8 * lzma(preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size of the increment-sign sequence sign(r[n]-r[n-1]) in {-1,0,1} stored as one byte each, divided by N-1; (ii) sign balance |P(increment>0) - P(increment<0)|; (iii) dyadic self-similarity corr(r[n], r[2n]) for n in [N/4, N/2) (reported). A rule is 'complex/random-like' if it is well defined up to N, (i) >= 0.5 bits/symbol and (ii) <= 0.05. The claim PASSES if at least one of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like AND the nested controls (c) and (d) both have (i) < 0.15 bits/symbol (validity of the measure). Calibration from controls outside the family: binary digit sum s2(n) gives 0.002 bits/symbol, its partial sums 0.005, a symmetric random walk 1.10.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if none of rules (e)-(h) is complex/random-like (every one is undefined before N, or compresses below 0.5 bits/symbol, or is sign-unbalanced by more than 0.05). If the nested controls (c) or (d) do not compress below 0.15 bits/symbol the measure lacks discriminating power and the verdict is inconclusive (not-operationalizable). If computed terms disagree with the OEIS b-files for A005185 or A004001, the verdict is inconclusive (other) until the implementation is fixed.
tests.interpretation: 'Fluctuations ... complex and in many respects random' (p. 130-131) is read as: the increment-sign sequence of the detrended fluctuations is not compressible to a small fraction of its entropy bound by a general-purpose compressor (nested/digit-based fluctuations compress to < 0.01 bits/symbol), and positive and negative fluctuations are balanced (Wolfram's own stated 'respect' for case (f)). The claim is existential ('can produce'), so one qualifying rule suffices; the book's nested rules (c) and (d) serve as internal controls that must be detected as regular. The OEIS b-files provide independent public values of two of the sequences to verify the implementation. Trend n/2 for (c)-(g) follows the book's plots; the power-law trend for (h) follows the book's caption (0.42 n^0.916).
tests.method: analysis.py computes each of the six recurrences for n <= 2^20 with memoised integer arithmetic, verifies rules (e) and (c) term-by-term against the 10,000-term OEIS b-files of A005185 and A004001 (all terms match), detrends by n/2 (rules c-g) or by a log-log power-law fit for n >= 16 (rule h), lzma-compresses the increment-sign sequence of the residual, and measures sign balance and the dyadic correlation corr(r[n], r[2n]).

measured.unit: rules among (e)-(h) that are complex/random-like by the pre-registered criteria

caveats: Statistical incompressibility over 2^20 terms is evidence of complexity, not proof that no closed form exists; the test shows the fluctuations are not periodic or nested at the scales examined.

Rules (g) and (h) have dyadic correlation corr(r[n], r[2n]) of 0.44 and 0.41 (vs 1.00 for nested rule c and ~0 for e, f), so part of their fluctuation is self-similar at scale 2; they still compress at > 0.97 bits/symbol, so the sign sequence itself carries no detectable regularity.
For rule (h) the power-law trend fitted over n in [16, 2^20] is 0.338 n^0.837, not the book's 0.42 n^0.916 fitted over n <= 2048; residual statistics for (h) depend mildly on the trend choice.
The sign-balance 'respect' is Wolfram's own stated one for case (f); other respects of randomness (e.g. spectral flatness, distribution of increments) were not pre-registered and not tested.
The downloaded b-files (about 97 KB each) are not committed; analysis.py re-fetches them and the SHA-256 values above pin what was used.

tests.label: The digits of pi are random for practical purposes
tests.hypothesis: The first 1,000,000 decimal and the first 1,000,000 hexadecimal digits of pi after the point show no statistically significant regularity under a fixed battery of frequency, block, poker, gap, serial-correlation, spectral and compression tests, i.e. they are indistinguishable from i.i.d. uniform digits by these tests.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each base b in {10, 16}, on N = 1,000,000 digits after the point, compute 10 p-values: (1) digit frequency chi-square (b - 1 df); (2) non-overlapping pair chi-square (b^2 - 1 df); (3) non-overlapping triple chi-square (b^3 - 1 df); (4) poker test on non-overlapping 5-digit hands by number of distinct digits (probabilities b!/(b-r)! S(5, r) / b^5; categories with expected count < 5 merged into the next); (5) gap test for digit 0 (gap lengths 0..3b-1 and >= 3b against the geometric law with p = 1/b); (6-8) serial correlation at lags 1, 2, 3 (z = r sqrt(N - lag), two-sided normal); (9) maximum periodogram ordinate of the centred digits over the N/2 Fourier frequencies (p = 1 - (1 - exp(-max I / mean I))^(N/2)); (10) lzma (preset 9 extreme) size of the digit string (one byte per digit) compared with 20 strings of N uniform random digits from numpy PCG64 (seed 20261031): two-sided normal p of z = (size - mean) / sd. 20 p-values in total. 'supports' if no p-value is below 1e-4 and at most 2 are below 0.01 (under the null, P(>= 3 of 20 below 0.01) is about 0.1 %). Data validity: the published decimal digits must agree with digits computed independently by analysis.py (Chudnovsky series, exact integer arithmetic) at all 1,000,000 positions, and with the OEIS A000796 b-file; the computed hexadecimal digits must agree with the OEIS A062964 b-file. Any disagreement makes the verdict 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any p-value is below 1e-6 or 4 or more p-values are below 0.01. Otherwise, if neither the pass nor the refute condition holds (exactly 3 below 0.01, or a minimum p in [1e-6, 1e-4)), 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'For practical purposes completely random' is read as: a standard battery of statistical tests of the kind used to vet random number generators finds no significant regularity. The claim's scope is 'any base'; bases 10 and 16 are tested (base 2 is tested separately in wolfram2002-ch10-15). Wolfram refers to 'all computed digits' (then about 2 x 10^11); this test examines only the first 10^6 digits in each base, so it can refute the claim (a regularity in a prefix would be a regularity) but supports it only for that prefix and that battery. Normality of pi is an open problem and is not what is tested. The published digit file is used for the decimal tests; the independent computation serves to validate it, and supplies the hexadecimal digits.
tests.method: analysis.py computes pi to 1,000,020 digits in base 10 and in base 16 by the Chudnovsky series with exact integer binary splitting (28 s), downloads the published 1,000,000-digit decimal file and the OEIS b-files and compares them digit by digit with the computation, then runs the pre-registered ten-test battery in each base on the first 10^6 digits after the point: chi-square tests of digit, non-overlapping pair and triple frequencies, a 5-digit poker test, a gap test for digit 0, serial correlations at lags 1-3, a maximum-periodogram test and an lzma size comparison with 20 PRNG digit strings. The 20 p-values are counted against the pre-registered thresholds.

measured.unit: p-values of the pre-registered battery (minimum: maximum-periodogram test, base 16)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic digits; p-values are the tests' own (asymptotic chi-square / normal approximations); the lzma p-value depends on the 20-sample PRNG reference

caveats: The pass condition holds with a wide margin: no p-value below 0.01 (smallest 0.080, the base-16 maximum-periodogram test), and lzma compresses pi's digits to within 0.2 and 0.8 standard deviations of uniform random digit strings in base 10 and base 16. The published file agrees with the independent computation at all 10^6 positions and both OEIS b-files agree at 19,999 positions.

Only the first 10^6 digits in each of two bases were tested, against roughly 2 x 10^11 digits computed when Wolfram wrote and about 10^14 today; the result supports the claim for this prefix and battery and says nothing about normality, which remains unproved.

No positive control (a known non-random digit sequence) was pre-registered for this battery; the same chi-square, serial and compression tests readily reject structured sequences (see e.g. the Champernowne results in wolfram2002-ch10-14), but their power against subtle regularities in pi was not measured here.
Chi-square and normal p-values are asymptotic; every cell has expected count >= 5 (smallest: hexadecimal triples, about 81).

tests.label: Only rational numbers have repetitive digit sequences
tests.hypothesis: In any integer base, every rational p/q has an eventually periodic digit expansion with period at most q - 1 (and preperiod + period at most q), every eventually periodic digit sequence is the expansion of a rational number, and the published digit expansions of irrational constants show no eventual periodicity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: (1) for bases 2, 3 and 10 and all denominators q = 1..20000, the digit expansion of 1/q (and of p/q for all 1 <= p < q when q <= 300) has period <= q - 1 and preperiod + period <= q, with zero violations, and the base-10 periods of 1/q agree with OEIS A007732 for every n covered by its b-file; (2) 100% of 20000 random eventually periodic digit patterns (random preperiod of length 0..20, random non-trivial period block of length 1..30, bases 2, 3, 10) are reproduced exactly when the rational number reconstructed from them is re-expanded by long division; (3) none of the first 10000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi (OEIS b-files) is eventually periodic in the sense that, for some period p <= N/3, the last 2p digits already repeat with period p.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: any rational whose expansion has minimal period > q - 1 or does not become periodic within q digits; any disagreement with A007732; any eventually periodic pattern whose reconstructed rational re-expands differently; or an irrational constant's published digits exhibiting at least two full agreeing periods for some p <= N/3.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'repetitive digit sequences' are eventually periodic positional expansions in an integer base; the clause 'period at most q - 1' in the claim text is the standard long-division bound (there are only q - 1 non-zero remainders). Terminating expansions are treated as eventually periodic with repeating 0, as the assessors note; period blocks consisting only of the digit b - 1 are excluded from the random patterns because they denote the alternative expansion of a terminating rational and would re-expand in the terminating form. The converse ('rationals are the only numbers with repetitive digit sequences') is tested constructively (every eventually periodic pattern reconstructs to a rational that reproduces it) and, as a sanity check only, on the published digits of three irrational constants; a finite digit string can never prove non-periodicity, so part (3) is a consistency check rather than a proof.
tests.method: analysis.py (1) runs long division for 1/q, q = 1..20000, and for all p/q with q <= 300, in bases 2, 3 and 10 (64,850 expansions per base), recording preperiod and period from the first repeated remainder and counting violations of period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q; base-10 periods of 1/n are compared with the 10,000-term OEIS A007732 b-file. (2) It draws 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns (base in {2,3,10}, preperiod 0-20 digits, block 1-30 digits, all-(b-1) blocks rejected), reconstructs the exact rational with Python Fractions and re-expands it, counting patterns not reproduced digit for digit. (3) It downloads the first 10,000 decimal digits of sqrt(2), e and pi from OEIS and, for every p <= N/3, finds the smallest index after which the digit sequence agrees with its shift by p, flagging any p for which two full periods already agree. Run time about 9 s including downloads.

measured.unit: rational expansions violating period <= q-1 or preperiod + period <= q (out of 194,550)
measured.uncertainty: exact

caveats: Both directions are classical theorems; the computation confirms the forward direction exhaustively for all denominators up to 20,000 in three bases (the bound period = q - 1 is attained, e.g. for full-reptend primes), agrees with OEIS A007732 on all 10,000 tabulated decimal periods, and confirms the converse constructively on 20,000 random eventually periodic patterns.

A finite digit string cannot establish that a number is not eventually periodic; part (3) only checks that 10,000 published digits of sqrt(2), e and pi show no two agreeing repeats for any period up to N/3 (the maximal agreement found was 1.33 periods, consistent with chance), which is a consistency check, not a proof of the 'only rationals' clause.

Terminating expansions are counted as eventually periodic with repeating 0 (period 1), following OEIS A007732; under the alternative convention (repeating b-1) they are still eventually periodic, so the verdict does not depend on this choice.

tests.label: Axis crossings of Sin[x] + Sin[a x] follow a continued-fraction substitution system
tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the sequence of axis crossings of sin(x) + sin(a x) for a > 1, labelled by which of the two regularly spaced families each crossing belongs to, has exactly the same set of finite subwords as the word produced by the generalized substitution system whose n-th rule is tau_{c_n}: A -> A^{c_n} B, B -> A, where c_1, c_2, ... are the partial quotients of the continued fraction of theta = (a - 1)/(a + 1); and for quadratic-irrational a the partial quotients are eventually periodic, so the word is a fixed point of a fixed composite substitution (nested).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Test set: a in {sqrt2, sqrt3, sqrt5, sqrt7, (1+sqrt5)/2, 1+sqrt2, 2+sqrt3} (quadratic irrationals), {pi, e, 2^(1/3), ln 10} and 20 pseudo-random a uniform in [1.05, 12] from numpy seed 20261031 (31 values). For each a: (1) take the first N = 20000 positive zeros of f(x) = sin x + sin(a x), each verified numerically (|f(x)| <= 1e-8), labelled A if it is a zero of sin((1+a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(1+a)) and B if it is a zero of cos((1-a)x/2) (spacing 2pi/(a-1)); (2) build the substitution word s_1 = A^{c_1} B, s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} (equivalently the composition tau_{c_1} ... tau_{c_n}(A)) to length >= 200000 from the continued fraction theta = [0; c_1, c_2, ...]. PASS (supports) if for every a and every n in 1..24 the set of length-n factors of the crossing word equals the set of length-n factors of the substitution word and has exactly n + 1 elements, and if for every quadratic-irrational a the continued fraction of theta is eventually periodic within 60 terms and the composite substitution over one period has the substitution word's tail as a fixed point (applying it to the first 2000 symbols of the tail reproduces a prefix of the tail).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if for any a there is some n <= 24 at which the factor sets differ, after excluding near-coincident zeros (two zeros closer than 1e-9 times the A spacing, which would make the ordering numerically undefined); or if any quadratic-irrational case has a non-eventually-periodic continued fraction or a tail that is not a fixed point of the period substitution. Partial agreement (factor sets equal only for some a, or only up to a smaller n without a numerical explanation) is 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram (p. 146) says the relative arrangement of the crossing points is 'related to' the output of a generalized substitution system whose rule at each step comes from a term of the continued fraction of (a-1)/(a+1), with repetitive (hence nested) structure when a is a square root. The two 'regularly spaced families' are the zeros of the two factors of sin x + sin ax = 2 sin((1+a)x/2) cos((1-a)x/2); their spacings are in ratio theta = (a-1)/(a+1), so the merged labelled sequence is a Sturmian (mechanical) word and the natural substitution system is the standard one driven by the partial quotients of theta (the word's own slope theta/(1+theta) has continued fraction [0; c_1+1, c_2, ...], so the directive sequence is exactly the partial quotients of theta). 'Related to' is operationalised as equality of factor languages, the strongest sense in which a finite segment of a mechanical word can match a substitution word whose intercept is not specified. The test uses exact arithmetic for the quadratic surds' continued fractions and double precision elsewhere, with partial quotients used only while the convergent denominators are below 10 N.
tests.method: analysis.py lists the first 20000 positive zeros of sin x + sin(a x) analytically from the two factor families, verifies |f| <= 2.9e-11 at each, and forms the A/B label word. It computes the continued fraction of theta = (a-1)/(a+1) (exactly, with period detection, for the seven quadratic surds; from the double's exact rational value for the others, keeping terms while the convergent denominator is below 200000), builds the substitution word s_n = s_{n-1}^{c_n} s_{n-2} to 200000 symbols (checked against the composition tau_{c_1}...tau_{c_n}(A)), and compares the sets of factors of length 1..24. For the quadratic cases it also checks that the composite substitution over one continued-fraction period fixes the tail word and that the preperiod substitutions map the tail onto the full word. Runtime about 12 s.

measured.unit: a-values (of 31) whose crossing word and substitution word have identical factor sets for all n <= 24
measured.uncertainty: exact combinatorial comparison; zero positions accurate to ~1e-11, minimum separation between distinct zeros >= 7e-6 spacings

caveats: The identification of 'the generalized substitution system' with the standard Sturmian construction (rule tau_c: A -> A^c B, B -> A at the step whose partial quotient is c) is the tester's; the book does not print the rule. The directive sequence is exactly the partial quotients of (a-1)/(a+1), as the book states, because the word's own slope theta/(1+theta) has continued fraction [0; c_1+1, c_2, c_3, ...].

Equality of factor languages (and complexity n+1) is the appropriate finite test because the substitution system fixes the slope but not the intercept of the mechanical word; the crossing word's intercept is fixed by the offset pi/(a-1) of the B family.
The result is for a > 1; by rescaling x the a < 1 case is the same with the roles of the families exchanged. Rational a (periodic curves) are outside the irrational scope tested and were not sampled.

A first run reported mismatches for all seven quadratic surds; this was a bug in the test script (the exact continued-fraction routine returned only one period, which was not unrolled before building the word) and was fixed before the criterion was evaluated; the pre-registered criterion itself was not changed.

datasets.name: Zero crossings of sin(x) + sin(a x) for 31 values of a, and continued-fraction-driven substitution words, generated by analysis.py

tests.label: The shift map only transcribes randomness from its initial condition
tests.hypothesis: Under the shift map x -> 2x mod 1 the symbolic itinerary (1 if x_t >= 1/2 else 0) is exactly the seed's binary digit sequence read from the first digit onward, so the output is a suffix of the input: periodic seeds give periodic itineraries with the same period, nested seeds give nested itineraries, and the itinerary of a seed is never less compressible (more random) than the seed's own digits. By contrast a map that is not a digit shift in base 2 (control: x -> 3x mod 1) can produce incompressible itineraries from seeds with trivially simple binary digits.
tests.pass: Pre-registered, all of: (1) transcription identity: for 2000 random reduced fractions p/q with odd q in [3, 10^5], the itinerary of the exact rational orbit (Python Fractions) for 2000 steps agrees bit for bit with the binary digits d_1..d_2000 of p/q computed independently by long division (0 mismatches of 4,000,000), and for three seeds whose binary digits are taken from OEIS b-files truncated to N = 10000 digits (A004539 binary digits of sqrt(2), A010060 Thue-Morse, A030190 binary Champernowne) the exact itinerary agrees with the published digits for all t < N (0 mismatches), with A004539 additionally cross-checked against digits computed with integer isqrt (0 mismatches); (2) periodic seeds stay periodic: for every odd q in 3..2000 and p = 1, the itinerary of p/q, found by exact cycle detection, is purely periodic with minimal period equal to the multiplicative order of 2 modulo q (0 exceptions), and every seed p/2^k (k <= 60) reaches the fixed point 0 within k steps; (3) randomness is inherited, not created: for every seed class the lzma compression ratio of the 10000-bit itinerary differs from the ratio of the seed's own first 10000 digits by less than 0.01, the itinerary of a periodic seed (1/q, q <= 2000) has ratio below 0.10, the Thue-Morse itinerary has ratio below the 1st percentile of 200 random-bit references, and the itinerary of a random-bit seed has ratio within the central 98% of the random references; (4) control with discriminating power: the itinerary of x -> 3x mod 1 started at the seed 1/2^60 (whose binary digits are a single 1 followed by zeros, ratio below 0.05) for 10000 steps has compression ratio above 0.8 times the median random reference and passes an 8-bit block chi-square test at p > 0.001, i.e. it does produce randomness its seed did not have.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: any itinerary bit that differs from the corresponding seed digit in part (1); any odd-q seed whose itinerary period differs from the multiplicative order of 2, or any dyadic seed not reaching 0 within k steps; any seed class whose shift-map itinerary is more than 0.01 less compressible than the seed digits, or a periodic/Thue-Morse itinerary as incompressible as random bits (ratio within the central 98% of the random references). Failure of the control (4) alone does not refute the claim but would be reported as reducing the discriminating power of the test (verdict stays 'supports' with lower confidence if (1)-(3) pass). If (1) fails the verdict is 'refutes'; if (1) passes but (2) or (3) fails the verdict is 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'shift map' is x -> 2x mod 1 (NKS p. 149, 'doubling modulo 1'), and 'moving digits leftward' refers to the base-2 expansion; the output of the map is taken to be the coarse itinerary (which half of the interval x_t lies in), which is the standard symbolic coding and is what Wolfram's pictures show. 'Randomness' is operationalised as incompressibility by a general-purpose compressor (lzma) plus block-frequency uniformity, following the assessors' remark that the claim locates randomness in the digit sequence. Dyadic rationals have two binary expansions; the itinerary follows the terminating one (x_t = 1/2 gives bit 1 then zeros), so seeds are compared with that convention. All orbits are computed with exact rational arithmetic; a floating-point implementation would collapse to 0 after 53 steps, which is noted but not used.
tests.method: analysis.py computes exact orbits of the doubling map with Python Fractions. (1) For 2000 random reduced fractions p/q (odd q <= 10^5) the 2000-step itinerary is compared bit for bit with the binary digits of p/q from long division; for seeds whose digits are OEIS b-files (A004539 sqrt(2), A010060 Thue-Morse, A030190 Champernowne) truncated to a dyadic rational, the itinerary is compared with the published digits, and the A004539 digits are cross-checked against math.isqrt. (2) For every odd q in 3..2000 the exact orbit of 1/q is walked until it repeats and its period and preperiod are compared with the multiplicative order of 2 mod q; 1/2^k is iterated for k <= 60. (3) lzma compression ratios of seed digits and of the 10000-bit itinerary are compared for Thue-Morse, Champernowne, sqrt(2), random bits, 1/1999 and 1/7, against 200 random-bit references; the NIST serial test (m = 8) is applied to each itinerary. (4) Control: the exact orbit of 3x mod 1 from 1/2^60 for 10000 steps, with compression ratio, pair frequencies and serial test. Run time about 15 s including downloads.

measured.unit: itinerary bits differing from the seed's binary digits (out of 4,020,999 compared)
measured.uncertainty: exact

caveats: Parts (1)-(3) passed exactly as pre-registered: 0 of 4,020,999 itinerary bits differ from the seed digits; all 999 odd denominators q <= 2000 give purely periodic itineraries whose period equals the multiplicative order of 2 mod q (max 1996 = q - 3 for q = 1999); every seed class has identical lzma ratio for seed and itinerary (the itinerary is literally the digit string); periodic seeds compress to 0.011-0.019 and Thue-Morse to 0.017 against a random reference of 0.168-0.171, while a random-bit seed gives 0.170.

The A004539 b-file has only 1000 terms, so the sqrt(2) identity check used 999 instead of the planned 10000 digits; the compressibility comparison for sqrt(2) used 10000 digits computed with math.isqrt, which agree with all 999 published digits.

The control (4) passed its compression sub-criterion (ratio 0.156 = 0.92 x random median, from a seed with ratio 0.011) but failed the pre-registered serial test (p ~ 0): the half-interval coding of 3x mod 1 is a two-state Markov source with pair probabilities 1/3, 1/6, 1/6, 1/3 (measured 0.341, 0.166, 0.166, 0.327), so uniform block frequencies were the wrong control criterion. The control still shows that a non-shift map produces an incompressible itinerary from a trivially simple seed, which the doubling map never does; confidence is reduced from 0.98 to 0.95 for the imperfect control design, as pre-registered.

The claim is an exact identity (2x mod 1 deletes the leading binary digit), so computation can only illustrate it; the test's value is in confirming the identity with independent implementations (Fraction orbit vs long division vs OEIS digits) and in showing that the output's compressibility is exactly the seed's. In float64 the orbit of 0.1 collapses to exactly 0 after 55 steps, which is why exact arithmetic was used.
