tests.label: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles
tests.hypothesis: The two-dimensional 8-neighbour outer totalistic cellular automaton with code 746 (the example Wolfram gives on p. 178), started from a row of 7 black cells, grows a pattern whose outer boundary stays close to a circle: the radial profile of the boundary has small relative spread and no appreciable fourfold (square-lattice) anisotropy, at the 400 steps shown in the book and at three times that many steps.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Run code 746 (a white cell becomes black iff exactly 3 of its 8 neighbours are black; a black cell stays black iff it has 0-4 black neighbours and becomes white with 5 or more; Wolfram's outer-totalistic numbering, bit index 2*s + c) from a horizontal row of 7 black cells for T = 400 and T = 1200 steps on a grid large enough that the pattern never touches the edge. Take the centroid of all black cells as centre, bin all black cells by polar angle into 360 one-degree bins and let r(theta) be the largest centre distance in each bin (outer boundary profile). Compute CV = std(r)/mean(r) and the anisotropy ratio A = mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four axis directions divided by the mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four diagonal directions (a square gives A = 0.707, a diamond 1.414, a circle 1). 'supports' if at T = 1200 both CV <= 0.03 and |A - 1| <= 0.03, and at T = 400 both CV <= 0.05 and |A - 1| <= 0.05. Measurement validation (not part of the verdict): the same statistics for the control rule 'a cell becomes black if any of its 8 neighbours is black' (which grows a square) must give A < 0.8 and CV > 0.06, otherwise the method is declared broken and the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at T = 1200 CV >= 0.06 or |A - 1| >= 0.06 (the outline is at least as far from a circle as a regular octagon is from its circumscribed circle in CV terms, or shows a clear square or diamond bias). Any intermediate outcome -> 'mixed'. Growth rate: the mean radius divided by T is reported and compared with Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t', but does not enter the verdict.
tests.interpretation: 'Overall shape' is taken as the outer boundary of the set of black cells (interior holes ignored), and 'closely approximates a perfect circle' as a boundary whose radius varies by at most a few percent around the pattern and shows no lattice-axis bias. The claim is existential ('it is even possible to find cellular automata that ...'), so one rule suffices; the rule tested is the one Wolfram himself exhibits (code 746, p. 178, with the stated initial condition and the 400-step figure). The 1200-step run checks that the circularity is not an artefact of the particular time shown. The pattern is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves Wolfram's 8-neighbour outer totalistic code 746 from a row of 7 black cells on a 500x500 (T = 400) and 1100x1100 (T = 1200) grid with numpy, asserting that the pattern never reaches the grid edge. All black cells are binned by polar angle about the centroid into 360 one-degree bins and the largest radius per bin forms the outer profile r(theta); CV = std/mean of that profile and A = mean radius within 5 degrees of the lattice axes over the mean radius within 5 degrees of the diagonals. A control rule in which any black neighbour makes a cell black (which grows a square) was run with the same initial condition to validate that the statistics detect lattice anisotropy.

measured.unit: CV = std/mean of the 360-bin outer radial profile; A = axis/diagonal mean radius (circle = 1, square = 0.707)
measured.uncertainty: deterministic computation; lattice discreteness contributes about 0.5/mean_r = 0.001 to CV at T = 1200

caveats: Both pre-registered thresholds were met with margin: at T = 1200 the boundary radius varies by 1.2 % (CV) around the pattern and the axis/diagonal ratio is 1.014; both statistics improved between T = 400 and T = 1200, so the circularity is not a transient of the time shown in the book. The control square gave CV = 0.108 and A = 0.736 (ideal square: 0.707), so the statistics do detect lattice anisotropy.
The measured growth rate is 0.36 cells per step, close to Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t'.

The claim is existential and only the rule Wolfram himself exhibits was tested; nothing is said here about how common circle-growing rules are. A small residual fourfold anisotropy (A = 1.014, slightly diamond-leaning) persists and is not zero, so 'closely approximates' rather than 'is' a circle is the supported reading; whether A tends to 1 as T grows further was not tested beyond 1200 steps.
The outer boundary profile ignores interior holes and surface roughness below the one-degree binning scale.

datasets.name: Two-dimensional 8-neighbour (Moore) outer totalistic cellular automaton, Wolfram code 746, generated by analysis.py; initial condition a row of 7 black cells on a white background; T = 400 and 1200 steps; grid 1100 x 1100 with the pattern kept away from the edges; control rule (code with all 'any black neighbour -> black' bits set) run with the same initial condition and T

tests.label: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors
tests.hypothesis: The 8-neighbour outer-totalistic 2D cellular automaton 'a cell becomes black when exactly three of its eight neighbours are black, otherwise it is unchanged' (NKS code 174826, Life-like notation B3/S012345678), started from a row of eleven black cells, keeps growing for 1000 steps while the normalised outline of the whole pattern keeps changing on the scale of the pattern itself and never settles to a simple geometric form (circle, square, diamond or octagon), whereas simple growth rules settle to a fixed simple outline.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Run the rule for T = 1000 steps from a row of 11 black cells. Let rho_t(theta) be the outer radius of the occupied set from the pattern centroid in 360 angular bins, normalised by its mean, and D(t1,t2) the mean absolute difference between rho_t1 and rho_t2. PASS (supports) if all three hold: (a) growth continues: mean radius R(1000) >= 1.5 * R(500) and the population is larger at step 1000 than at step 500; (b) the outline keeps changing: D(500,1000) >= 0.05 and D(750,1000) >= 0.03, while both control rules (8-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a square, and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a diamond) give D(500,1000) <= 0.02; (c) the outline at step 1000 is not a simple form: the minimum over the reference family {circle, axis-aligned square, 45-degree square, regular octagon at 0 and 22.5 degrees} of the mean absolute difference between rho_1000 and the reference profile is >= 0.05, while for each control rule the same minimum is <= 0.03.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if growth stops (population unchanged over steps 900-1000) or if the outline converges to a simple form: D(500,1000) < 0.02 and the minimum simple-shape distance at step 1000 is < 0.03. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. shape still changing but growth slowing, or controls not behaving as expected, which would mean the descriptor is not discriminating).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's claim (pp. 176, 181) is existential: this one rule from this one seed produces an overall shape that 'seems continually to go on changing, with no simple overall form'. 'Overall shape' is mapped to the normalised angular outer-radius profile of the occupied set, so interior texture is ignored; 'no simple form' is mapped to distance from a small pre-declared family of simple convex shapes and to non-convergence of the outline between steps 500, 750 and 1000. 'Continually' can only be bounded by the run length; a finite run cannot exclude eventual regularity. Code 175850 (the '3 or 5 of 8' rule from p. 177, row of 7), which the book says is rough on small scales but smooth on large scales, is run as an additional comparison but is not part of the criterion.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves NKS code 174826 (B3/S012345678) from a row of 11 black cells for 1000 steps on a dynamically padded numpy grid, and at 8 checkpoints records population, mean radius, convex-hull solidity and the normalised outer-radius profile rho_t(theta) in 360 angular bins about the pattern centroid. It computes D(t1,t2) = mean |rho_t1 - rho_t2| between checkpoints and the distance from rho_1000 to five reference profiles (circle, two squares, two octagons). The same pipeline is run on two simple-growth controls (8-neighbour and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black') and on code 175850 from a row of 7 for comparison. Runtime about 20 s.

measured.unit: mean |rho_500 - rho_1000| (dimensionless, normalised radius)
measured.uncertainty: exact deterministic computation; descriptor resolution 1 degree

caveats: A 1000-step run bounds 'continually' but cannot exclude eventual regularity of the outline; growth was still linear (mean radius 128 -> 251 cells between steps 500 and 1000, about 0.25 cells per step) and the outline change between checkpoints showed no downward trend (0.08-0.39).

'Simple form' was operationalised as a pre-declared family of five convex shapes plus convergence of the outline; a shape could in principle be 'simple' in a sense not covered (e.g. a fixed irregular polygon), but the outline also failed to converge (D(750,1000) = 0.16), which no fixed limiting shape allows.
The outline descriptor is the outer radius per angular bin, so interior holes (solidity 0.49 of the convex hull) are ignored, as the claim requires.

The comparison rule code 175850 behaves as the book describes (D(500,1000) = 0.0066, closest to a circle at distance 0.025), which supports the discriminating power of the descriptor but is not part of the criterion.

tests.label: Neighbor-independent geometric replacement rules always give nested fractals
tests.hypothesis: Every two-dimensional substitution system in which each cell is replaced by a fixed block depending only on its own colour produces, from a single cell, a pattern that is exactly nested (decomposes at every scale into the patterns grown from single cells) and has at most quadratic block complexity, whereas rules in which the replacement depends on neighbours can violate both.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Neighbour-independent families: F1 = all 256 two-colour rules replacing each cell by a 2 x 2 block; F2 = 2000 random three-colour 2 x 2 rules; F3 = 2000 random two-colour 3 x 3 rules (numpy PCG64, seed 20261031). Each is iterated from a single cell of colour 1 for n steps (n = 9 for 2 x 2 rules, 512 x 512 cells; n = 6 for 3 x 3 rules, 729 x 729). Measures: (1) exact nesting: for every j = 1..n-1, P_n equals P_{n-j} with each cell of colour c replaced by P_j^(c), the j-step pattern grown from a single cell of colour c; (2) block complexity: the number N(k) of distinct k x k sub-blocks of P_n satisfies N(k) <= s^4 b^2 k^2 for k = 4 and 8 (s colours, b x b blocks; this bound follows from (1), since any k x k window lies in a 2 x 2 group of level-j supertiles with b^(j-1) < k <= b^j; a random s-colour image of this size has N(8) close to the number of positions, about 2.5 x 10^5). Control (validity): 2000 random two-colour neighbour-dependent 2 x 2 rules, where the block replacing a cell depends on its own colour and the colours of its right and lower neighbours (outside the pattern = colour 0), iterated and measured identically; at least 20 of them (1 %) must fail (1) or (2), and a Bernoulli(0.5) 512 x 512 image must fail (2), showing the measures can detect non-nested patterns. 'supports' if every rule in F1, F2 and F3 satisfies (1) and (2) and the control condition holds.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any neighbour-independent rule in F1-F3 fails (1) or (2). If the control condition fails (fewer than 20 neighbour-dependent rules flagged, or the random image not flagged), the measures are judged unable to discriminate and the verdict is 'inconclusive' (reason 'other').
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'completely regular nested structure' is formalized as exact hierarchical self-similarity: the pattern after n steps is the pattern after n - j steps with every cell replaced by the pattern grown in j steps from a cell of that colour, for every j. This holds for neighbour-independent rules by construction (the substitution acts cellwise and commutes with composition), so this test is a computational verification of a mathematical statement across an enumerated and a sampled rule space, plus a check that the formalization and the complexity bound genuinely discriminate (neighbour-dependent controls, as on NKS p. 191). Scope is limited to grid substitution systems with uniform b x b blocks (b = 2, 3; 2 or 3 colours); 'geometric replacement rules' of traditional fractal geometry with arbitrary affine maps, including overlapping ones, are covered by Hutchinson's theorem on self-similar sets in the literature but are not computed here.
tests.method: analysis.py grows every rule's pattern from a single cell of colour 1 (9 steps for 2x2 rules, 512 x 512; 6 steps for 3x3 rules, 729 x 729), checks the nesting identity P_n = sigma^j(P_{n-j}) with sigma^j given by the single-cell patterns P_j^(c) for every j = 1..n-1 by exact array comparison, and counts distinct 4 x 4 and 8 x 8 windows (exact 64-bit codes, or a 64-bit multiplicative hash for three-colour 8 x 8 windows) against the bound s^4 b^2 k^2. The same measures are applied to 2000 neighbour-dependent rules and a random image. Run time 3 min.

measured.unit: count of rules failing the nesting identity or the block-complexity bound
measured.uncertainty: exact except that three-colour 8 x 8 window counts use a 64-bit hash (collision probability ~1e-8 per pattern, which could only lower a count)

caveats: All 4,256 neighbour-independent rules satisfy the exact nesting identity at every scale and stay at or below 18 % of the quadratic block-complexity bound (largest 748 distinct 8 x 8 blocks against a bound of 4,096), while 1,982 of 2,000 neighbour-dependent rules break the identity, 1,799 exceed the bound (up to 9.7 times), and a random image has 255,025 distinct 8 x 8 blocks.

For neighbour-independent rules the nesting identity is a theorem (the substitution acts cell by cell, so sigma^n = sigma^j composed with sigma^(n-j)); the computation verifies the formalization and its implementation on an exhaustive and a sampled rule space rather than discovering an empirical regularity. Its non-trivial content is that the formalization discriminates: the neighbour dependence Wolfram introduces on p. 191 destroys it in 99 % of sampled rules.

Scope: uniform b x b grid substitutions with b = 2, 3 and 2-3 colours, from a single seed cell. Geometric replacement rules with arbitrary affine maps (traditional IFS fractals), including overlapping ones where the drawn union can look solid, were not computed; their self-similarity is Hutchinson's theorem. 'Nested' here includes degenerate cases (18 of the 256 two-colour rules give all-white or all-black patterns), which are trivially nested.
Before the full run the functions were exercised on three hand-chosen or differently seeded rules and one random image to check the code; this did not involve the pre-registered rule samples.

tests.label: Networks of identical two-connection nodes can form arrays of any dimension
tests.hypothesis: Directed networks in which every node is of one type and has exactly two outgoing connections can realize, through the connection pattern alone, structures equivalent to d-dimensional arrays for every d, as well as trees and nested (fractal) structures. 'Equivalent to a d-dimensional array' is taken in Wolfram's two senses: (i) grouping nodes into identical blocks yields exactly the d-dimensional grid (each block connected to its 2d neighbouring blocks), and (ii) the number of nodes reachable within r connection steps grows like r^d (the network dimension criterion of NKS chapter 9).
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (1) Arrays: for d = 1..6 construct the network by one uniform rule: each lattice point x of Z^d is a block of d nodes (x, i), i = 0..d-1, and node (x, i) has exactly two outgoing connections, to (x + e_i, (i+1) mod d) and (x - e_i, (i+1) mod d). Verify (a) every node has out-degree exactly 2 and the rule is identical for every node; (b) exact structural equivalence: on the torus (Z_L)^d with L = 5, contracting each block to a point gives a multigraph whose edge set equals the d-dimensional grid's edge set {x <-> x +- e_i} with every block connected to exactly 2d distinct neighbouring blocks (exact set comparison); (c) dimension criterion: breadth-first search along connections from one node of the infinite network, counting N(r) = nodes within r steps; the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d must lie within 0.5 of d for d = 1, 2, 3, 4 (so that it rounds to d), and is reported (not scored) for d = 5, 6. (2) Trees: the infinite binary tree (node k connects to 2k+1 and 2k+2) has N(r) = 2^(r+1) - 1 for r <= 15 (exact). (3) Nested: the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3 corner nodes of degree 2, all others of degree 4) is given an Eulerian orientation along an Euler circuit plus a directed 3-cycle through the corners, which must give every node out-degree exactly 2; its undirected growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 64 from a corner must lie within 0.3 of log2(3) = 1.585, the gasket's dimension. 'Supports' if (1a), (1b), (1c), (2) and (3) all hold.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if the uniform construction fails structurally for some d <= 6 (out-degree not 2, or the block quotient is not the d-dimensional grid), or if the measured growth exponent for some d <= 4 rounds to an integer other than d, or if no out-degree-2 orientation of the gasket exists. 'Mixed' if arrays pass but the tree or nested construction fails its criterion. 'Inconclusive' is not expected: the test is a self-contained computation.
tests.interpretation: The claim is constructive and existential: one explicit family of networks suffices for each d, plus one tree and one nested example. The block-quotient check is the exact sense of 'equivalent to an array'; the growth exponent is Wolfram's own operational notion of network dimension (NKS p. 479 and notes) and adds a check that the effective geometry is d-dimensional without reference to the blocks. Blocks of d nodes connected to 2d neighbouring blocks follow the description on NKS p. 195 ('every block of nodes is connected to four rather than two neighboring blocks'). Growth exponents at finite radius are biased low (the lattice ball itself has local exponent below d at radius ~20), hence the +-0.5 window; the exact quotient check is the decisive part.
tests.method: analysis.py builds the d-dimensional block network from the single rule in the pre-registration for d = 1..6 and checks, on the torus (Z_5)^d, that every node has two outgoing connections and that contracting blocks gives exactly the grid's edge multiset with 2d distinct neighbouring blocks per block. It runs a breadth-first search along connections on the infinite network from node (0,0) and computes the growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) at R = 20 d (d <= 4) or 8 d (d = 5, 6), alongside the same exponent for the plain L1 lattice ball at radius R/d as a finite-size reference. It checks N(r) for the infinite binary tree and constructs the level-7 Sierpinski gasket graph (3282 nodes), orients its 6561 edges along an Euler circuit (Hierholzer) and adds a directed 3-cycle through the corners so that every node has out-degree 2, then measures the growth exponent from a corner (undirected and directed).

measured.unit: growth exponent log2(N(R)/N(R/2)) of the out-degree-2 block network for d = 1..6 (pre-registered window: within 0.5 of d for d <= 4)
measured.uncertainty: exact counts; the exponent is biased below d at finite radius exactly as the plain lattice ball is (reference values given)

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration: for d = 5 and 6 (reported, not scored) the BFS radius was reduced from 20d to 8d because the 20d search for d = 6 visited 13 million nodes (68 s and several GB in a first run; it gave exponent 5.756 and the d = 5 run at radius 50 gave 4.815). At radius 8d the exponents are 4.74 and 5.65, still rounding to d and above the plain lattice ball's finite-radius exponents (4.26 and 4.96), so the conclusion is unchanged.

The claim is existential and is settled by the exact quotient check for d <= 6 together with the uniform rule, which is defined for every d (the same code runs for any d; only the search radius limits the computation). The growth-exponent check is Wolfram's operational notion of dimension and confirms the effective geometry without using the block structure; its finite-radius bias is quantified by the lattice reference.

One construction per structure type is tested (block arrays; binary tree; Eulerian-oriented Sierpinski gasket). The gasket orientation plus corner 3-cycle is one way to get out-degree exactly 2 for every node; the undirected growth exponent 1.612 and directed 1.594 are both within 0.03 of log2(3), the gasket's Hausdorff dimension.

Whether the resulting networks are 'equivalent' to arrays in any stronger sense (e.g. as substrates for network cellular automata, NKS p. 1031) was not tested; the block-quotient isomorphism and dimension are the two senses stated in the pre-registration.

tests.label: One-dimensional local constraints can always be met by a repetitive pattern
tests.hypothesis: For every one-dimensional local constraint system (a set of allowed length-w colour words over k colours) that admits any bi-infinite satisfying arrangement, there is a purely periodic satisfying arrangement, and its period can be taken at most V = k^(w-1).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated or sampled constraint systems, every system that admits a valid word of length 4V + w (the operational test of satisfiability, independent of any cycle argument) also admits a periodic arrangement u^infinity with |u| <= V whose every cyclic window of length w is allowed; and every system with no such long valid word has no periodic arrangement either. Zero violations in both directions.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: at least one constraint system admits a valid word of length 4V + w but no periodic arrangement with period <= V (this would refute the claim as stated, since the shortest possible periodic solution is bounded by V); or the two satisfiability indicators disagree in the other direction, which would indicate a broken test.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'local set of constraints' on a one-dimensional array of coloured cells (p. 210-211: each cell's neighbourhood must be one of a given set of allowed configurations) is a one-dimensional subshift of finite type: a set of allowed words of a fixed window length w over k colours. 'Can be satisfied at all' is read as the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement all of whose windows are allowed; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of arbitrarily long valid finite words, and operationally it is tested by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w (any valid word longer than V must revisit a de Bruijn vertex, so this length is far beyond the threshold, and the check is done by a reachability iteration, not a cycle search). 'Simple and purely repetitive arrangement' is read as a periodic configuration, found by brute-force enumeration of all period words u with |u| <= V = k^(w-1) and checking all cyclic windows. All constraint systems are enumerated exhaustively for (k, w) in {(2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2)} and sampled with a fixed seed for (2,5) and (3,3).
tests.method: analysis.py encodes each constraint system as a bitmask of allowed length-w words. Satisfiability is decided by iterating a reachability vector over the k^(w-1) de Bruijn vertices for 4V + 1 edge steps (existence of a valid word of length 4V + w). Independently, every period word u with |u| <= V is enumerated (sum of k^p over p = 1..V candidates, each stored as the bitmask of its cyclic length-w windows) and u^infinity is accepted iff its window mask is contained in the allowed set. The two indicators are compared for all 138,856 systems (exhaustive for (k,w) = (2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,2), (4,2); seeded samples of 2000 and 5000 for (2,5) and (3,3)); minimal periods are tabulated. Run time about 3 s.

measured.unit: fraction of satisfiable constraint systems that have a periodic solution with period <= k^(w-1)
measured.uncertainty: exact for the exhaustive families; the two sampled families are 2000 and 5000 seeded draws

caveats: The claim is a theorem (a non-empty one-dimensional shift of finite type contains a periodic point, from a cycle in its de Bruijn graph); the computation confirms it exhaustively for all two-colour constraints with windows up to 4 and all four-colour constraints with window 2, and by sampling for windows 5 (two colours) and 3 (three colours). The maximal minimal period found (8 for k = 2, w = 4; exactly the two de Bruijn-cycle constraint sets) matches the bound V = k^(w-1).

Satisfiability was operationalised by the existence of a valid word of length 4V + w; by compactness this is equivalent to the existence of a bi-infinite arrangement, but the equivalence itself relies on finiteness of the vertex set, so the two indicators are not logically independent even though they are computed by different algorithms.
Wolfram's 'simple' is read as 'periodic'; the observed minimal periods are small (at most V), but 'simple' is not otherwise quantified.

tests.label: 3x3 template constraints can force a rule 30–like random pattern
tests.hypothesis: The set of 56 allowed 3x3 templates shown on NKS p. 221 is satisfied by a shifted rule-30 space-time pattern (with the boundary structures shown in the figure), uses all 56 templates, encodes rule 30 in its interior templates, and admits no spatially periodic pattern containing the first template, consistent with the pattern being forced.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (T) Templates: the 56 templates are read automatically from the figure image fig-c.png of p. 221 (14 x 4 grid, 3 x 3 cells each, dark fraction of a 9 x 9 pixel patch at each cell centre > 0.5 = black); the extraction must yield 56 distinct templates listed in strictly decreasing order of their 9-bit binary value (Wolfram's usual ordering), which is the check that the transcription is sound. (A) Realisability and exhaustiveness: the candidate pattern is defined as follows, with rows indexed downward and columns rightward. Rows 0 and 1 are black for all columns <= C+1 and white for columns > C+1; columns C and C+1 are black in every row >= 0; every other cell with row < 2 or column > C+1 is white, and all cells above row 0 are white; interior cells (row t >= 2, column x <= C-1) are a(t, x) = rule30(a(t-1, x), a(t-1, x+1), a(t-1, x+2)), i.e. rule 30 shifted one cell to the left per step, using the black columns C, C+1 as fixed neighbours. On a window of 300 rows and 300 columns to the left of and below the corner (plus a white margin of 3 cells above and to the right), every 3 x 3 block must be one of the 56 templates, and every one of the 56 templates must occur. (R) Rule identification: a template is 'interior' if neither of its 3-cell rows is a boundary row (rows 0-1 or the two black columns); the test reports how many templates satisfy the relation middle-left = rule30(top row) and bottom-left = rule30(middle row), and lists the remaining templates. (U) No periodic alternative: for every horizontal period w = 1..9, build the transfer graph whose nodes are pairs of consecutive rows (r0, r1) on a cylinder of circumference w and whose edges (r0, r1) -> (r1, r2) exist when all w cyclic 3 x 3 blocks of (r0, r1, r2) are allowed; a valid pattern periodic horizontally with period w exists iff this graph has a cycle, and such a pattern contains template 1 iff some edge inside a non-trivial strongly connected component (or a self-loop) has template 1 among its w blocks. The claim PASSES if (T) holds, (A) holds in both directions, and (U) finds no cycle edge containing template 1 for any w <= 9. (R) is reported, not decisive.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. If (U) finds a cyclic (doubly periodic) pattern containing template 1 the uniqueness part of the claim is REFUTED (a second pattern satisfies the constraint). If (T) fails the result is 'inconclusive' (reason: transcription). If (A) fails in the subset direction (the candidate pattern contains a disallowed block) the result is 'inconclusive' (the pattern definition inferred from the templates is wrong, not the claim), unless the failing blocks are interior rule-30 blocks, in which case the templates do not encode rule 30 and the claim is refuted. If (A) holds as a subset but not all 56 templates occur, the verdict is 'mixed' (the figure's template set is larger than needed).
tests.interpretation: The caption on p. 221 states that only the 56 templates may occur anywhere, that the first template must appear at least once, and that the pattern required is a shifted version of the rule-30 evolution. Uniqueness on the infinite plane cannot be verified by finite computation; this test checks (i) that the published template set is actually satisfied by, and derived from, a shifted rule-30 pattern and (ii) the strongest finite consequence of uniqueness that is cheap to check: no spatially periodic competitor exists for periods up to 9 (a doubly periodic pattern containing template 1 would be a counterexample). Disclosed calibration before this pre-registration: the templates were extracted once to design the extraction check (56 distinct, strictly decreasing); a tally found 46 of the 56 templates satisfy the left-target shifted rule-30 relation; and constraint propagation from two black rows over a 45-column window determined rows 2-4 of the pattern (the double black column with white to its right and the rule-30 growth to its left), which is how the candidate pattern above was inferred. No pattern beyond row 4, no exhaustiveness count and no periodic search was computed before pre-registration.
tests.method: analysis.py downloads fig-c.png (46,304 bytes), reads the 56 templates from the 14 x 4 grid by sampling 9 x 9 pixel patches at the 3 x 3 cell centres, checks that they are distinct and strictly decreasing as 9-bit numbers, builds the candidate pattern (two-row black band, two-column black wall, interior shifted rule 30) on a 300 x 300 window, enumerates its 3 x 3 blocks, tallies the shifted-rule-30 relation over templates, and for horizontal periods w = 1..11 builds the transfer graph on pairs of cylinder rows (4^w nodes), finds strongly connected components with scipy and counts cycle edges containing template 1. Outputs in derived/templates.csv and derived/periodic_search.json; runtime about 4 minutes (w = 11 dominates).

measured.unit: number of cycle edges (doubly periodic valid patterns, periods 1-9) containing template 1; 0 = no periodic competitor
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive for periods 1-9 (pre-registered) and 10-11 (supplementary)

caveats: Pre-registered decision: all three decisive parts hold. (T) The automatic transcription yields 56 distinct templates in strictly decreasing binary order with no ambiguous cells. (A) The candidate pattern (two-row black band, two-column black wall below its right end, interior a(t,x) = rule30(a(t-1,x), a(t-1,x+1), a(t-1,x+2)) growing leftwards from the wall) contains exactly the 56 templates on a 300 x 300 window: no disallowed block and no unused template, so the published set is precisely the block set of this shifted rule-30 pattern. (U) No horizontally periodic valid pattern of period 1-9 (and, supplementary, 10-11) contains template 1.

(R) 46 of the 56 templates satisfy the shifted rule-30 relation in both row pairs; the 10 others (templates 1, 2, 3, 10, 45, 46, 47, 51, 52, 53) are the band, wall and corner templates, consistent with the construction being 'derived from rule 30' plus boundary structures.

Uniqueness on the infinite plane is not finitely verifiable; what was shown is that no spatially periodic alternative with period <= 11 exists. Periodic patterns without template 1 do exist for every period tested (e.g. the all-white plane; 47 distinct templates appear on cycles), which is why the caption requires template 1 to appear at least once. The pattern is unique only up to translation, and its interior is 'largely random' in the sense that rule 30 from this boundary is (not separately tested here).

The candidate pattern was inferred from the templates by constraint propagation over rows 2-4 before pre-registration (disclosed); the exact figure layout (band thickness, wall) was read from the inset of fig-a and confirmed by (A). Template extraction depends on fixed pixel coordinates for this image version (sha256 recorded).

tests.label: Finite discrete deterministic systems must eventually repeat
tests.hypothesis: For every finite deterministic discrete system we enumerate, every orbit (from every possible state) becomes eventually periodic, and its eventual period is at most N, the total number of possible states of the system (and the transient plus period is also at most N).
tests.pass: Pre-registered: across all enumerated systems and all initial states, 100% of orbits satisfy period <= N and transient + period <= N (zero violations), where N is the exact number of distinct global states of the system.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: at least one orbit of at least one enumerated system has eventual period > N, or never repeats within N + 1 steps (impossible to observe without a period > N, so equivalently a measured period exceeding N).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'system of limited size that involves discrete elements and follows definite rules' is read as a deterministic map f on a finite set of N global states, so 'definite rules' means the next state depends only on the current state. 'Eventually exhibit repetitive behavior' is read as: the orbit s, f(s), f(f(s)), ... is eventually periodic, with the eventual period (cycle length) at most N; the text's surrounding argument (p. 255) gives exactly this bound. Three concrete families of finite systems from the book's own repertoire are enumerated: the 256 elementary cellular automata on cyclic rings of n cells (N = 2^n), the 4096 two-state two-color Turing machines on cyclic tapes of n cells (N = 2 * n * 2^n: head state x head position x tape contents), and the modular multiplication maps x -> m x mod n (N = n). For every system every state is used as an initial condition, so the test is exhaustive within the enumerated sizes. The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle); the computation checks that the stated bound is never exceeded in these families and records how close observed periods come to it.
tests.method: analysis.py builds, for each enumerated system, the complete transition map on its N global states and computes for every state the transient length and the eventual period from the functional graph (in-degree peeling to find cycle nodes, cycle walking for periods, vectorised relaxation for transients). It then counts orbits with period > N or transient + period > N. Families: 256 ECA x ring sizes 1..12 (3072 systems, 2,096,640 orbits), 4096 two-state two-colour Turing machines x cyclic tapes 1..5 (20,480 systems, 2,113,536 orbits), and x -> m x mod n for n = 2..200 (20,099 maps, 2,686,699 orbits). Total 43,651 systems and 6,896,875 orbits; run time about 4 s.

measured.unit: fraction of orbits with eventual period <= N and transient + period <= N
measured.uncertainty: exact (exhaustive enumeration, no sampling)

caveats: The claim is a theorem (pigeonhole principle on a finite state set), so a finite enumeration can only fail to refute it; the enumeration here covers three concrete families exhaustively up to the stated sizes and finds the bound tight (period = N in degenerate 1-cell systems, period = N - 1 for x -> 3x mod 199).
Wolfram's bound is on the eventual period; the test also checks the slightly stronger transient + period <= N, which is what the pigeonhole argument actually gives, and it held in every orbit.
Systems whose next state depends on more than the current state (external input, randomness, unbounded memory) are outside the claim's scope and were not tested.

tests.label: Class 3 randomness can arise without randomness in initial conditions
tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the centre column of rule 30 started from a single black cell (an initial condition with no randomness) passes a standard battery of statistical randomness tests as well as the centre column of rule 30 started from a random initial condition and as well as a pseudo-random reference stream, whereas a nested deterministic sequence (Thue-Morse) fails the same battery.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Sequences of N = 2^20 bits: (S1) rule 30 centre column from a single black cell; (S2) rule 30 centre column from a random initial row (numpy seed 20261031, width 2N+1, so that the column is exactly the random-initial-condition case); (S3) numpy PCG64 bits, seed 20261031; (S4) the Thue-Morse sequence. Battery of 10 tests, each giving a p-value with pass meaning p >= 0.01: monobit frequency; block frequency (M = 128); runs; longest run of ones (M = 10000, K = 6); serial (m = 16, minimum of the two p-values); approximate entropy (m = 10); cumulative sums (minimum of forward and backward); discrete Fourier transform spectral test; autocorrelation (lags 1..64, Bonferroni-corrected normal p-value of the largest |r|); and a 16-bit non-overlapping block chi-square uniformity test. Also record the lzma compression ratio of the packed bits. PASS (supports) if S1 passes at least 9 of 10 tests and has lzma ratio >= 0.99, S2 and S3 each pass at least 9 of 10, S4 fails at least 4 tests, and the first terms of S1 agree exactly with the OEIS A051023 b-file over the whole length of the b-file.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if S1 passes 7 or fewer of the 10 tests or has lzma ratio < 0.98 (an exploitable regularity), or if S1 disagrees with OEIS A051023 (then the generator is wrong and the test is aborted as inconclusive/other). If S1 passes exactly 8, or S4 fails fewer than 4 tests (battery not discriminating), the verdict is 'mixed'. If the OEIS file cannot be fetched the OEIS cross-check is dropped and reported, and the verdict rests on the generated sequences.
tests.interpretation: 'Random behaviour' is read as the book itself reads it (practical randomness, pp. 261 and 1085 ff.): the sequence passes standard statistical tests and is incompressible, not algorithmic randomness, which no finite test can establish. 'No randomness in initial conditions' is realised by the single-black-cell seed; the book's own comparison (p. 261) is with random initial conditions, so S2 is the matched control and S4 is a control for a deterministic but nested (non-random) sequence that the battery must reject for the test to be discriminating. Rule 22 is also mentioned in the claim's context but its single-cell pattern is nested; only rule 30, the book's example on this page, is tested.
tests.method: analysis.py generates the rule 30 centre column for 2^20 steps from a single black cell (S1) and from a seeded random row of width 2^21+1 (S2) using big-integer bit operations, a PCG64 stream (S3) and the Thue-Morse sequence (S4), checks S1 against all 100001 terms of the OEIS A051023 b-file, and applies ten NIST SP 800-22-style tests (monobit, block frequency M=128, runs, longest run M=10000, serial m=16, approximate entropy m=10, cumulative sums, DFT, Bonferroni autocorrelation over lags 1-64, 16-bit block chi-square) plus the lzma compression ratio to each. Runtime about 5 min, dominated by the two 2^20-step evolutions.

measured.unit: randomness tests passed (p >= 0.01) by the rule 30 single-cell centre column, out of 10
measured.uncertainty: at alpha = 0.01 per test a truly random sequence fails at least one of 10 tests with probability about 0.10

caveats: Passing a finite statistical battery is practical randomness, the sense the book uses; it does not establish algorithmic randomness or exclude a regularity invisible to these tests (the sequence is of course computable).

The 16-bit block chi-square test has expected count 1 per cell, so its chi-square p-value is approximate (the true null variance of the statistic is about 1.5 times the chi-square value); the same approximation is applied to all four sequences and S1 passed it with p = 0.26.

S1's smallest p-value is 0.037 (approximate entropy, m = 10); with ten tests at alpha = 0.01 a single marginal value is expected. S2 (random initial row) had its smallest p-value at 0.018 (cumulative sums). Both rule 30 columns are statistically indistinguishable from the PCG64 stream in this battery, while Thue-Morse fails 7 of 10 tests and compresses to 0.4% of its size.
Only rule 30 was tested. Rule 22, also named in the claim's context, gives a nested pattern from a single black cell, and the book's example on p. 261 is rule 30.

tests.label: Additive rule 90 only transmits randomness from its initial conditions
tests.hypothesis: Rule 90 is additive (linear over GF(2)): its local rule is l XOR r, so every evolution is the XOR superposition of shifted copies of the single-cell nested (Pascal mod 2) pattern. Consequently a biased random initial condition leaves a permanent trace: at every time t = 2^k each cell is the XOR of exactly two initial cells, so the density returns to 2p(1-p) forever for initial density p, and the single-cell pattern itself is nested, not random. Rule 22 (non-additive, class 3) instead forgets the initial density: from any initial density the density converges to one common value.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Additivity: the rule-90 local map phi satisfies phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) for all 64 pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods, and the rule-22 map does not; (B) superposition: for 50 random initial conditions on a cyclic lattice of width 513 run for 256 steps, the rule-90 evolution equals the cellwise XOR of the shifted single-cell evolutions exactly (100% of 50*256 rows); (C) single-cell pattern: for rule 90 from one black cell the row at t = 2^k (k = 0..10) has exactly 2 black cells and the row at t = 2^k - 1 has 2^k black cells (nested, Pascal mod 2); (D) persistence in rule 90: with initial densities p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} on a measured window of 100000 cells (array padded by 1024 cells on each side so boundaries never reach the window), the measured density at t = 2^k for k = 0..10 is within 0.01 of 2p(1-p) in all 33 cases, and at t = 1024 the three densities differ from the p = 0.5 density by more than 0.1; (E) loss of memory in rule 22: with p in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5} on the same windows, the time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 differ from one another by less than 0.01 (max minus min). 'Supports' requires A-E.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A or B fails in any case (rule 90 is not additive / not a superposition), or if in D the rule-90 density at t = 1024 for p = 0.1 lies within 0.05 of the p = 0.5 density (the low-density effect has been forgotten), or if in E the rule-22 late-time densities spread by more than 0.05 (rule 22 remembers the initial density). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim has an algebraic clause (additivity, superposition) and an empirical clause (density persistence in rule 90 versus rule 22, the quoted sentence on p. 265). Additivity is checked exhaustively on the local rule and by exact superposition on random configurations. 'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is operationalized by the exact nested structure of the single-cell pattern plus the superposition identity: everything in a rule-90 pattern is a XOR of shifted copies of that nested pattern. 'Low initial density persists forever' is operationalized by the density at times 2^k, where rule 90 reduces to x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) and the density must equal 2p(1-p) at arbitrarily late times; 'no long-term effect' in rule 22 is operationalized as late-time density independent of the initial density. Random initial conditions are Bernoulli(p) with fixed seeds; the lattice is a finite array measured only in a window unaffected by the boundaries within the run length. Rule numbering is Wolfram's standard code (rule 90 = l XOR r; rule 22 = exactly one of l, c, r black).
tests.method: analysis.py: (A) checks phi(a XOR b) = phi(a) XOR phi(b) over all 64 neighbourhood pairs for rules 90 and 22; (B) evolves 50 random rows on a 513-cell cyclic lattice for 256 steps under rule 90 and compares every row with the XOR of the single-cell evolution shifted to each initially black cell; (C) counts black cells in the rule-90 single-cell pattern at t = 2^k and 2^k - 1; (D, E) evolve Bernoulli(p) rows of 100000 + 2*1024 cells for 1024 steps under rule 90 (p = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5) and rule 22 (same p) with zero boundaries, measuring the density in the central 100000 cells, which the boundaries cannot influence within 1024 steps; D compares rule-90 densities at t = 2^k with 2p(1-p), E compares the rule-22 time-averaged densities over t = 512..1024 across p.

measured.unit: largest |density(t=2^k) - 2p(1-p)| over p in {0.05,0.1,0.2}, k = 0..10 for rule 90 (threshold 0.01)
measured.uncertainty: sampling: ~0.0015 (100000 correlated cells per row)

caveats: Part C initially failed for a trivial reason unrelated to the claim: the single-cell array was two cells too narrow and the fixed-zero boundary cells coincided with the two black cells at t = 1024. The array was widened by one cell on each side (commit history shows the change); no threshold or criterion was changed.

The densities of 100000 cells in one row are correlated (in rule 90 at t = 2^k, cells 2^(k+1) apart share an initial cell), so the binomial standard error (0.0012 for p = 0.1) understates the sampling error; the pre-registered 0.01 tolerance was chosen to absorb this and the largest deviation observed was 0.0031.

Rule 22's late-time density of about 0.351 from all four initial densities agrees with the known asymptotic density of rule 22 from random initial conditions; convergence is complete by t ~ 128 even for p = 0.05.

'Cannot generate randomness intrinsically' is interpreted structurally (every pattern is a superposition of the nested single-cell pattern); whether XOR-superposed nested patterns count as 'random' under some statistical test is not what is being tested. Rule 90 from a p = 0.5 random row does look random and has density 0.5 at all times, consistent with 'randomness from the initial conditions'.

Finite run: 1024 steps and times up to 2^10; 'forever' follows from the identity x_t(i) = x_0(i-2^k) XOR x_0(i+2^k) at t = 2^k, which holds for all k by additivity (verified in A and B), so the finite check is of the mechanism, not a substitute for the proof.

tests.label: Spatially periodic initial conditions always give repetitive behavior
tests.hypothesis: For every cellular automaton tested and every block of n cells repeated forever as the initial condition, the evolution is eventually time-periodic with period at most k^n (k = number of colours; 2^n for two colours), and the infinite repeated-block configuration evolves exactly as a cyclic ring of n cells.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: (1) across all (rule, block) pairs enumerated, 100% have eventual temporal period <= k^n (zero violations); (2) for every (rule, block) pair in the equivalence sample, the central block of a long line made of repeated copies of the block evolves identically to the n-cell ring for all simulated steps (zero mismatching cells).
tests.fail: Pre-registered: any (rule, block) pair whose eventual period exceeds k^n, or any pair for which the repeated-block line evolution differs from the ring evolution inside the region unaffected by the line's ends.
tests.interpretation: 'Initial conditions which consist just of a fixed block of cells repeated forever' is a spatially n-periodic configuration on the infinite line. 'Simple repetitive behavior' is read as eventual time-periodicity of the configuration, and the stated bound 2^n is read, following Wolfram's own reasoning and the assessors, as k^n for k colours (2^n in the two-colour case the text has in mind). 'Any cellular automaton' cannot be enumerated, so three families are tested: all 256 elementary rules exhaustively (n = 1..12), all 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic rules (n = 1..6, bound 3^n), and a fixed-seed random sample of 500 two-colour range-2 (5-neighbour) rules out of 2^32 (n = 1..10). The reduction 'each block evolves like a finite cyclic system' is tested separately by simulating the actual repeated-block line and comparing it with the ring.
tests.method: analysis.py treats a block of n cells repeated forever as an n-cell ring, builds the ring's transition map on all k^n states for each rule and computes the eventual period of every state's orbit from the functional graph (cycle detection by in-degree peeling). Families: all 256 ECA for n = 1..12 (2,096,640 rule-block pairs), all 2187 three-colour totalistic rules for n = 1..6 (2,388,204 pairs, bound 3^n), and 500 seeded random range-2 binary rules for n = 1..10 (1,023,000 pairs). It then checks the reduction itself: for all 256 ECA and all 32,256 blocks of n = 1..6, a line of repeated copies of the block is evolved for 2*2^n steps and its central copy compared cell by cell with the ring evolution (15,845,376 cells). Run time about 18 s.

measured.unit: fraction of (rule, block) pairs whose eventual temporal period is <= k^n
measured.uncertainty: exact (exhaustive within each family; the range-2 family is a seeded sample of 500 of 2^32 rules)

caveats: The claim quantifies over all cellular automata; three rule families (one exhaustive over all 256 elementary rules, one exhaustive over all 2187 three-colour totalistic rules, one a 500-rule sample of range-2 rules) were tested, and the general statement rests on the finite-state argument that the line-vs-ring check confirms empirically for the elementary rules.

The bound k^n is attained only in degenerate cases (n = 1, rules that cycle through every state); for n >= 2 the overwhelming majority of periods are below k^n / 10 (see the histogram), so the bound is loose but never violated.
Wolfram writes 2^n for two colours; the three-colour family tests the natural k^n generalisation that the assessors and the book's own argument imply.

tests.label: Additive rules self-emulate; rules 90 and 150 are the only elementary ones
tests.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata, every rule that is additive (linear over GF(2)) can emulate itself with blocks of cells and yields an exactly self-similar (nested) pattern from a single black cell; after removing trivial rules and identifying rules related by reflection or by the sublattice (shear) relation between rules 60 and 90, exactly two additive classes remain, represented by rules 90 and 150; self-emulation among the remaining 248 rules is uncommon, but rule 184 has it with blocks of three cells.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Definitions: a rule f is additive iff f(x XOR y) = f(x) XOR f(y) for all pairs of 3-cell neighbourhoods x, y (which forces f(000) = 0). Rule f self-emulates with block size b >= 2 and t >= 1 steps iff there are two distinct b-cell blocks B0, B1 such that for every arrangement of 2k+1 blocks (k = ceil(t/b)) drawn from {B0, B1}, running f for t steps leaves the centre block equal to B_{f(c-1, c0, c1)}, where c-1, c0, c1 are the bits represented by the three central blocks; this is the block-emulation notion of NKS pp. 269-271 and note p. 1118, which allows t != b. The search covers b in {2, 3, 4}, t in {1, 2, 3, 4} and all block pairs. Trivial rules: 0, 204 (identity), 170 and 240 (shifts). Equivalences for 'fundamentally different': reflection (rule 60 <-> 102) and the sublattice relation p90[t, 2j - t] = p60[t, j], verified computationally on the first 256 steps from a single black cell. Nested: the single-cell pattern p satisfies p[2t, 2i] = p[t, i] for all 0 <= t < 256 and |i| <= t. Clause A passes if every additive rule self-emulates with b = t = 2 and every non-trivial additive rule is nested in this sense. Clause B passes if the non-trivial additive rules fall into exactly two equivalence classes, one containing 90 and one containing 150. Clause C passes if rule 184 self-emulates with b = 3 for some t <= 4 and the fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one self-emulation in the searched range is <= 0.25. 'supports' if A, B and C all pass.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if clause A or clause B fails (an additive rule that does not self-emulate with b = t = 2, a non-trivial additive rule that is not nested, or a third inequivalent non-trivial additive class). 'mixed' if A and B pass but C fails (rule 184 does not self-emulate with 3-cell blocks within the search, or self-emulation is found in more than 25 % of non-additive rules, so 'rather rare' would be an overstatement).
tests.interpretation: 'Additive' is read as linear over GF(2) (Wolfram's own definition on p. 264: patterns from two initial conditions can be superimposed by XOR). 'Emulate itself' is read as block emulation with 2 to 4 cells per block and 1 to 4 steps per emulated step. 'Fundamentally different' is read as 'not related by left-right reflection and not related by the sublattice/shear relation that maps the rule 60 pattern onto the even sublattice of the rule 90 pattern'; without the second identification rule 60 (and its mirror 102) would be a third additive rule, which the test records explicitly. 'Rather rare' is given the threshold 25 % of the non-additive rules. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py tests all 256 elementary rules for GF(2)-linearity over all 64 neighbourhood pairs, then searches exhaustively for block self-emulations with b = 2, 3, 4 cells per block, t = 1..4 steps and all ordered pairs of distinct blocks, checking every arrangement of 2k+1 blocks (k = ceil(t/b)) so that the centre block's light cone is covered. Nesting of the non-trivial additive rules was checked as exact scale-2 self-similarity p[2t, 2i] = p[t, i] of the single-black-cell pattern over 256 steps, and the sublattice relation p90[t, 2j - t] = p60[t, j] was verified over 256 steps before being used to merge rules 60/102 with 90. Equivalence classes of non-trivial additive rules were formed by union-find under reflection and the verified sublattice relation.

measured.unit: rule numbers; fraction of the 248 non-additive rules with at least one block self-emulation (b <= 4, t <= 4)
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive finite check; exact within the searched block sizes and step counts

caveats: All three pre-registered clauses passed: exactly 8 additive rules exist, each self-emulates with 2-cell blocks and 2 steps (the Frobenius identity f^2 = f at stride 2 over GF(2)) and the four non-trivial ones are exactly self-similar at scale 2; after identifying 60/102 with 90 through the verified sublattice relation the additive rules fall into the two classes {60, 90, 102} and {150}; rule 184 self-emulates with the 3-cell blocks 010/101 and 3 steps, as Wolfram says, and only 15 of the 248 non-additive rules (6 %) have any block self-emulation in the searched range.

'Fundamentally different' required an interpretive choice: rule 60 (and its mirror 102) is additive and nested but is not related to 90 by reflection or colour complement; it is the rule 90 pattern restricted to the sublattice i + t even. Without that identification the claim's 'precisely rules 90 and 150' would be 'rules 60, 90 and 150'. The test records this explicitly.

The 15 non-additive self-emulating rules are the affine rules 15, 51, 85, 153, 165, 195 (complements/XOR with 1), the AND/OR-type class-1 rules 128, 136, 192, 238, 252, 254, 255, the shift-like rule 226 and rule 184. Larger blocks or more steps (b > 4, t > 4) might reveal further self-emulating rules; 'rather rare' is confirmed only within the searched range.

The claim's sub-clause that additivity implies self-emulation in general (for any number of colours and neighbours) was tested only for the elementary rules; the argument via the Frobenius endomorphism is standard but was not checked beyond them.

datasets.name: All 256 elementary cellular automata (Wolfram rule numbering), generated by analysis.py: additivity tables, exhaustive block self-emulation search (b = 2..4 cells, t = 1..4 steps, all block pairs), and 256-step single-black-cell patterns for the self-similarity and sublattice checks

tests.label: Maximal-period linear congruential generators still show strong nonrandomness
tests.hypothesis: Widely deployed linear congruential generators x_{n+1} = (a x_n + c) mod m that were chosen to have maximal period nevertheless produce consecutive d-tuples lying on a small number of parallel hyperplanes (Marsaglia 1968: at most (d! m)^(1/d)), a gross deviation from uniform randomness that is visible at sample sizes far below the period and that standard empirical tests detect.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Generators (all full period for their class): RANDU (a=65539, c=0, m=2^31; period 2^29, maximal for a multiplicative generator mod 2^31), ANSI C example rand (1103515245, 12345, 2^31), Numerical Recipes ranqd1 (1664525, 1013904223, 2^32), Borland C (22695477, 1, 2^32), VAX MTH$RANDOM (69069, 1, 2^32), Park-Miller minimal standard (16807, 0, 2^31-1), C++11 minstd_rand (48271, 0, 2^31-1), POSIX drand48 / java.util.Random (25214903917, 11, 2^48); for comparison Knuth's MMIX generator (6364136223846793005, 1442695040888963407, 2^64) and a cryptographic source (os.urandom). (1) Lattice: the exact spectral test on the dual lattice gives, for every generator with m <= 2^32 (7 generators), a family of at most 3000 parallel planes containing all consecutive triples of the whole period (minimal L1 norm of a nonzero dual vector in d = 3 at most 3000; Marsaglia's bound (6 m)^(1/3) is 2953 for m = 2^32), and at most 93000 parallel lines containing all consecutive pairs in d = 2 ((2 m)^(1/2) = 92682). (2) Visible deviation: projecting 2^20 consecutive triples (coordinates x/m) onto the minimal dual vector u and reducing mod 1, each of those 7 generators yields at most 3000 distinct values (<= 0.3% of 2^20) while os.urandom yields at least 99% distinct values under the same projection and rounding (1e-9). (3) Standard empirical test: the two-dimensional birthday-spacings test (L'Ecuyer and Simard 2001 setting: n = 2^15 points (x_i, x_{i+1}) in 2^21 x 2^21 cells, expected collisions lambda = 2, 32 independent replications from different seeds; total collisions compared with Poisson(64)) rejects (two-sided p < 1e-6) at least 6 of the 8 historical generators, while os.urandom and MMIX are not rejected (p > 1e-3). 'Supports' requires (1), (2) and (3).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if any of the 7 generators with m <= 2^32 has triples on more than 3000 planes (the lattice theorem would be wrong), or if the projection of the LCG triples gives more than 50% distinct values (the structure is not visible at 2^20 samples), or if fewer than 3 of the 8 historical generators fail the birthday-spacings test. Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'Constructed to have maximal repetition period' is operationalized as the set of full-period historical generators listed, with RANDU included as maximal for its multiplicative class (it is Wolfram's own example in the NKS note). 'Very substantial deviations from perfect randomness' is operationalized as (i) the exact lattice structure (number of covering hyperplanes, Marsaglia/Knuth spectral test), (ii) its visibility at a sample size (2^20) far below the period, with a cryptographic source as the randomness baseline under the identical statistic, and (iii) rejection by a standard test from the TestU01 family that random sources pass. The lattice is analysed on the full state recurrence; generators that output only high-order bits (ANSI C, drand48) are analysed on the state, which is the sequence whose stripes Wolfram's pictures show. The MMIX 64-bit generator is outside 'over the years' up to 2002 as a deployed generator and is reported for contrast only.
tests.method: analysis.py: for each generator builds the dual lattice of consecutive d-tuples (basis (m,0,..), (-a^i mod m, e_i)), LLL-reduces it exactly and enumerates all short vectors (Fincke-Pohst) to obtain the exact spectral test value nu_d, the normalised figure of merit S_d and the minimal L1 norm (number of parallel hyperplanes containing every d-tuple of the whole period) for d = 2, 3, 4; generates 2^20 consecutive states from seed 12345, projects each triple (x_i, x_{i+1}, x_{i+2})/m onto the minimal-L1 dual vector and counts distinct values (rounded to 1e-9), repeating the same projections on 2^20 64-bit words from os.urandom; runs the two-dimensional birthday-spacings test (32 replications of 2^15 non-overlapping pairs in 2^21 x 2^21 cells, expected 2 collisions each, total compared with Poisson(64)) on every generator and on os.urandom.

measured.unit: largest number of parallel planes containing all consecutive triples, over the 7 historical generators with m <= 2^32 (threshold 3000; each has 2^29 to 2^32 triples)
measured.uncertainty: exact (lattice computation)

caveats: Borland's generator is listed with modulus 2^31 by Wikipedia and 2^32 by other sources; 2^32 was used as pre-registered (both are full period and share the low 31 bits).

The claim says generators 'one after another' deviated substantially; the set tested is the eight most widely deployed historical generators, not a random sample. The one that passed the birthday-spacings test at this sample size (drand48, period 2^48) still shows its lattice: its 2^20 triples project onto only 83834 distinct values (8%) of a possible 2^20, versus 99.996% for os.urandom; L'Ecuyer and Simard's rule predicts birthday-spacings failure for it at n of order 16 * 2^16 points, not tested here.

Knuth's 64-bit MMIX generator (post-dating most of the historical generators) passes both empirical tests at these sample sizes, as pre-registered for the contrast; it still has a lattice (about 2.9 million planes in 3 dimensions). The claim as stated concerns deployed generators up to 2002.
Spectral values agree with published ones where known (RANDU: 15 planes, S_3 = 0.008; Park-Miller: S_2 = 0.34 as in Knuth TAOCP 3.3.4), which checks the lattice code.

The birthday-spacings statistic is applied to the full generator state; ANSI C and drand48 output only high-order bits, which does not remove the lattice (the hyperplane statement holds for the state sequence) but changes which empirical tests fail first.

tests.label: Rule complexity does not determine behavioral complexity
tests.hypothesis: Across exhaustively enumerated families of simple programs, measures of the complexity of a rule's definition are at most weakly rank-correlated with measures of the complexity of the behaviour it produces; some rules of minimal definitional complexity produce behaviour in the top quartile of behavioural complexity, some rules of maximal definitional complexity produce behaviour in the bottom quartile, and a non-negligible fraction of rules that differ in a single table entry differ greatly in behavioural complexity.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Families: (F1) the 256 elementary cellular automata; (F2) the 2187 three-colour nearest-neighbour totalistic cellular automata (Wolfram codes 0..2186). Rule-complexity measures: F1: (a) number of monomials in the algebraic normal form over GF(2), (b) minimal number of two-input gates (AND, OR, XOR, with negation free) computing the rule, found by breadth-first search over truth tables; F2: (c) Shannon entropy in bits of the 7-entry code table, (d) number of table entries that differ from the table's most frequent value. Behaviour-complexity measures: (e) lzma-compressed size (preset 9) of the space-time diagram, one byte per cell, from a random initial condition (width 300, periodic boundary, numpy seed 20260720, steps 200..600 after a 200-step transient); (f) the same for the single-seed pattern (one black / one gray cell, 400 steps, width 801, zero boundary). Statistics: Spearman rank correlation rho for each (rule measure, behaviour measure) pair within each family (8 pairs). 'supports' if max over the 8 pairs of rho <= 0.30, and in each family at least one rule at the minimum value of each rule measure has behaviour measure (e) in the top quartile of its family while at least one rule at the maximum value has (e) in the bottom quartile, and at least 5 % of F1 Hamming-distance-1 rule pairs (1024 pairs) differ in (e) by more than half of the family's range of (e).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any of the 8 Spearman correlations is >= 0.60 (a direct, monotone correspondence between rule complexity and behaviour complexity) or if in either family no rule at minimal rule complexity reaches the top quartile of behaviour complexity. Otherwise (e.g. 0.30 < max rho < 0.60, or the Hamming-neighbour fraction below 5 %) -> 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: 'Complexity of underlying rules' is operationalised by syntactic measures of the rule table (ANF size and minimal circuit size for Boolean rules; entropy and non-default entries for totalistic codes), and 'complexity of behaviour' by lossless compressibility of the space-time diagram, which treats both random-looking and structured-but-irregular behaviour as complex (Wolfram's usage also counts class 3 randomness as complex). 'No direct correspondence' is read as the absence of a strong monotone association (rho < 0.3 weak, rho >= 0.6 strong) plus the existence of the counterexamples Wolfram describes. The extension 'and by extension natural systems' is not tested. All patterns are generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py enumerates the 256 elementary rules and the 2187 three-colour totalistic codes, computes the rule-complexity measures (ANF monomial count by Moebius transform; minimal two-input gate count by breadth-first search over all 3-input truth tables with free negation; table entropy; non-default entries) and runs each rule from a random initial condition (width 300, periodic, seed 20260720, 200-step transient, 400 recorded steps) and from a single seed (400 steps, width 801), compressing each space-time diagram with lzma preset 9. Spearman correlations were computed for the 8 (rule measure, behaviour measure) pairs, quartile counterexamples were listed, and the 1024 Hamming-distance-1 pairs of elementary rules were compared on the random-IC compressed size. Run time about 4 minutes.

measured.unit: Spearman rho between rule complexity and lzma size of the space-time diagram; fraction of 1024 Hamming-1 ECA pairs whose random-IC lzma sizes differ by more than half the family range
measured.uncertainty: one random initial condition per rule; lzma sizes in bytes (ECA random-IC range 152..17028)

caveats: The pre-registered decision rule is degenerate and the verdict is therefore recorded as inconclusive rather than as the 'refutes' it literally produces: the rule required a rule 'at the minimum value of each rule measure' to reach the top behavioural quartile, but the minimum of every measure is attained only by constant rules (rule 0; the three constant totalistic codes; for the gate count, the eight 0-gate projections/negations), which cannot produce complex behaviour under any definition. The condition therefore tests nothing about the claim. This is an error in the pre-registration, discovered only after the run.

Post hoc (not pre-registered): at the lowest non-constant complexity levels there are rules in the top behavioural quartile, as the claim asserts: with 2 ANF monomials rules 60, 90 and 102 (nested), with 1 gate the same rules plus 153, 165, 195, and with 2 gates rules 30 and 45 (random-looking, essentially incompressible: 16952 and 16932 bytes vs a maximum of 17028). At the highest gate count (4) rules 77, 104, 232 and 233 sit in the bottom quartile, and 65 maximum-entropy totalistic codes do likewise. Rules differing in one table entry differ by more than half the behavioural range in 19.2 % of the 1024 pairs (e.g. 14/30, 6/22, 2/18), far above the pre-registered 5 %.

All eight Spearman correlations are positive but weak to moderate (0.13 to 0.41; the four elementary-rule correlations are 0.13 to 0.41 and the four totalistic ones 0.30 to 0.38). None reaches the pre-registered 0.60 'direct correspondence' threshold, but the maximum (0.41, ANF monomials vs single-seed compressibility) exceeds the 0.30 'weak' threshold, so under the pre-registered thresholds with the degenerate clause removed the outcome would have been 'mixed': there is some statistical association between rule and behaviour complexity, but nothing like a monotone correspondence, and the counterexamples Wolfram describes exist.

Compressibility of a random-initial-condition diagram is a poor proxy for behavioural complexity for shift-like class 2 rules (e.g. rule 15 transports the random input and so compresses badly) and for additive rules; the single-seed measure corrects this for those cases but conflates nested with random behaviour less well. Only one random initial condition per rule was used. The 'natural systems' extension of the claim was not tested.

tests.label: Simple cellular automaton markets generate random-looking price series
tests.hypothesis: Among the 256 elementary cellular automata run from random initial conditions, (almost) every rule in which a single-cell perturbation spreads to an ever-growing set of cells produces a black-minus-white count series that is non-periodic and incompressible relative to its own increment distribution.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules (Wolfram numbering), two colours, nearest neighbours. Propagation test (per rule): 20 trials; lattice of 1601 cells (non-wrapping: cells outside are fixed to the random background and the lattice is wide enough that the perturbation cannot reach the edge in 400 steps), random initial condition with density 1/2 from a fixed seed, second copy with the centre cell flipped; after 400 steps the damage width w = (rightmost differing cell - leftmost differing cell + 1) is recorded (0 if no cell differs); a rule is 'propagating' if w >= 100 (= 0.25 x 400, i.e. the damaged region grows linearly rather than staying bounded or merely moving) in at least 10 of 20 trials. Price-series test (per rule): ring of N = 400 cells, random initial condition density 1/2 from a fixed seed, discard 1000 transient steps, record d(t) = (#black - #white) for W = 4096 further steps; d(t) is 'significantly random' if (R1) it is not exactly periodic with any period p <= W/2 within the window and (R2) the first differences D(t) = d(t+1) - d(t), stored as int16, have plug-in marginal entropy H >= 1 bit and lzma (preset 9|EXTREME) compressed size >= 0.5 x H bits per sample. Calibration on controls: i.i.d. binomial counts give ratio 1.35, an AR(1) series 1.40, a period-97 series 0.09, a noiseless sinusoid 0.47. The claim PASSES if at least 90% of propagating rules are significantly random. Reported, not decisive: the fraction of non-propagating rules that are significantly random, and the list of propagating-but-not-random rules.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if fewer than 75% of propagating rules are significantly random (several counterexamples to 'essentially inevitable' inside the stated family). Between 75% and 90% the verdict is 'mixed'. If fewer than 5 rules are propagating under the definition the test is underpowered (inconclusive).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's market model (p. 431-432) is a one-dimensional CA of buy/sell agents, with 'price' the running difference of black and white counts; his figure uses rule 90. 'Information will eventually propagate from one entity to all others' is read as damage spreading in the sense he uses in Chapter 6: the set of cells affected by a one-cell change grows without bound (linear growth of the damage width), which excludes pure shifts and travelling defects whose influence merely moves. 'Significant randomness' of the running totals is read as non-periodicity plus incompressibility of the increments of the black-minus-white count. 'Essentially inevitable' is read as at least 90% of the propagating rules. The claim is a universal statement over the family, so the test looks for counterexamples.
tests.method: analysis.py evaluates all 256 rules. Damage spreading: 20 seeded random initial conditions on a 1601-cell open lattice, centre cell flipped in a copy, damage width after 400 steps; propagating if width >= 100 in >= 10 trials. Price series: ring of 400 cells, seeded random initial condition, 1000 transient steps, d(t) = #black - #white for 4096 steps; exact-periodicity scan over periods <= 2048; lzma compression of the int16 first differences compared with their plug-in marginal entropy. Per-rule values in derived/rules.csv; runtime about 1 minute.

measured.unit: fraction of propagating rules whose black-minus-white series is significantly random
measured.uncertainty: 40 propagating rules; 33 random, 7 not

caveats: The measured fraction 0.825 (33/40) falls in the pre-registered 'mixed' band (0.75-0.90). The converse direction, which the claim does not assert, is clean: 0 of 216 non-propagating rules has a significantly random count series, so propagation is at least necessary for randomness in this model.

The 7 counterexamples form two equivalence classes under mirror/complement symmetry. Rules 41, 97, 107, 121 spread damage during their long transient on the open lattice but settle on the 400-cell ring into a period-4 cycle within 1000 steps, so d(t) is exactly periodic; whether such rules count as 'information eventually propagating to all others' is a definitional question the pre-registration resolved in favour of counting them. Rules 124, 137, 193 (the symmetry partners of rule 110) are non-periodic but their increments compress to 0.37-0.40 of the marginal entropy, below the 0.5 threshold, because on a 400-cell ring few gliders survive and d(t) is nearly periodic with small fluctuations; rule 110 itself passed with ratio 1.03 from a different random seed, which shows the class-4 verdicts are seed- and size-sensitive.

Conclusions depend on the finite ring (400 cells) and horizon (4096 steps after 1000 transient); on an infinite lattice class-4 rules would keep producing gliders and the period-4 rules might not settle. 'Significant randomness' is operationalised by non-periodicity and increment incompressibility only.

The damage-width definition of propagation excludes shifts and single travelling defects (e.g. rules 170, 184), whose influence reaches every cell on a ring but does not spread; under a footprint definition those rules would be additional counterexamples (their d(t) is constant).
