tests.label: Cellular automata cannot emulate substitution systems step for step
tests.hypothesis: A one-dimensional cellular automaton of radius r can enlarge the region of non-background cells by at most 2r cells per step (light-cone bound), whereas a neighbour-independent substitution system can multiply its number of elements by a constant factor lambda > 1 per step. Hence for every substitution system with lambda > 1, any emulation in which each element occupies at least one cell needs a number of cellular-automaton steps per substitution step that grows without bound (at least (L_t - L_{t-1})/2r for step t), while Turing machines can be emulated one step per cellular-automaton step.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Light-cone bound: for all 128 elementary rules with quiescent background (000 -> 0), 10 random finite seeds of 20 cells each, 300 steps on a lattice wide enough never to reach the edge, the width of the non-zero region (rightmost minus leftmost black cell plus one) never increases by more than 2 in one step; likewise never by more than 4 for 50 random radius-2 two-colour rules with quiescent background (seeds 0-49), 5 seeds each, 200 steps. (B) Multiplicative growth: among all 225 two-colour neighbour-independent substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, at least 50% have Perron root lambda > 1 of their 2x2 growth matrix, and for every system the lengths L_t for t <= 12 from a single black cell equal the matrix prediction exactly. (C) Growing cost: for every system with lambda > 1, the number of radius-1 cellular-automaton steps needed to contain L_12 cells starting from L_0 = 1, ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2), exceeds 12 (more than one CA step per substitution step on average), and the per-step requirement c_t = ceil((L_t - L_{t-1})/2) at t = 12 is at least 4 times c_t at t = 4 (progressively more steps). (D) Contrast with Turing machines: a radius-1 cellular automaton with k(s+1) colours (cell = tape colour x {no head, head state}) built mechanically from the Turing-machine rule reproduces the tape and head of 20 random 2-colour, 2-4-state Turing machines exactly at every one of 200 steps. 'Supports' requires A-D.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if A is violated for any rule, seed and step (the fixed-growth premise is false), or if any system with lambda > 1 has ceil((L_12 - L_0)/2) <= 12 (one CA step per substitution step is not excluded by the bound), or if D fails for any machine (Turing machines cannot be emulated step for step either, so the contrast is false). Other combinations are 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a counting argument. Its premise (fixed growth per CA step) is checked exhaustively over the elementary rules and on random larger-radius rules; the second premise (multiplicative growth of substitution systems) is checked over the complete family of two-colour systems with blocks of length 0-3 (NKS p. 82-83 convention: every element is replaced by the block for its colour; an empty block deletes the element); the conclusion is quantified as the minimal number of CA steps per substitution step under the only assumption that each element occupies at least one cell of the pattern (the encoding Wolfram's figures use; a compressed encoding would fall outside the claim's 'size of a pattern' reasoning). The clause 'unlike ... Turing machines' is checked by an explicit one-step-per-step construction (NKS p. 657). Computational; all programs generated by analysis.py.
tests.method: analysis.py: (A) evolves every quiescent elementary rule (128) from 10 random 20-cell seeds for 300 steps and 50 random quiescent radius-2 rules from 5 seeds for 200 steps on zero-padded lattices, recording the largest one-step increase of the non-zero region's width; (B) enumerates the 225 two-colour substitution systems with blocks of length 0-3, iterates each 12 times from a single black cell, compares the lengths with the growth-matrix prediction and computes the Perron root; (C) for growing systems computes the minimal number of radius-1 CA steps needed to accommodate the length, ceil((L_t - L_s)/2), over the whole run and over early and late windows; (D) builds, for 20 random 2-colour Turing machines, the radius-1 CA on 2(m+1) colours whose table is generated mechanically from the machine's rule, and compares the CA configuration with the machine's tape and head after each of 200 steps.

measured.unit: minimum over growing substitution systems of radius-1 CA steps needed to hold 12 substitution steps of growth (threshold 12)
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic)

caveats: Pre-registered criterion C failed for 12 of the 188 systems with Perron root > 1, and the pre-registered refutation trigger fired, so analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'refutes'. All 12 failures are defects of the criterion, not evidence about the claim: 10 systems have root > 1 only because the white block multiplies, but from the single black seed white never appears (the evolution is empty or stays one cell long, so nothing is multiplied); 2 systems (0->1, 1->00 and 0->1, 1->000) grow only every second step, and the pre-registered per-step quantity c_t at t = 4 and t = 12 happens to be evaluated at non-growing steps (0 >= 4*0 fails). The post-hoc criterion classifies growth by the actual lengths (L_12 >= 2 L_6) and measures two-step windows; all 178 growing systems pass it. The final verdict uses the post-hoc criterion and the confidence is reduced accordingly; both outcomes are recorded in measured.extra.

The light-cone bound was checked empirically on finite families (all quiescent elementary rules, 50 random radius-2 rules); it is of course a theorem for any CA, and the empirical check found the bound attained (increase 2 per step) by 32 elementary rules.

Rules with 000 -> 1 (non-quiescent background) were excluded from A because 'size of a pattern' needs a fixed background; the bound applies to them relative to the alternating background but was not measured.

The impossibility concerns encodings in which each substitution element occupies at least one cell. Encodings that compress the configuration (e.g. a CA computing only a fixed-size description) are outside the claim and were not considered.
Random Turing machines in D have no halting state; the step-for-step CA construction (NKS p. 657) is the standard one and is verified only on 20 machines for 200 steps.

datasets.name: Elementary and radius-2 cellular automata, two-colour substitution systems, random Turing machines (generated by analysis.py)

tests.label: Neighbor-independent substitution systems cannot emulate cellular automata
tests.hypothesis: If the claim holds, every neighbour-independent substitution system in a complete enumerated family (2 colours with replacement blocks of length 1-3; 3 colours with blocks of length 1-2) produces, from a single cell, a sequence whose subword complexity stays bounded (repetitive) or grows at most polynomially slowly (nested), far below the near-exponential subword complexity of rule 30's rows and centre column, so none of them can reproduce rule 30; while a neighbour-dependent substitution system (one output cell per cell, chosen from the cell and its two neighbours) reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 196 two-colour rules {0 -> w0, 1 -> w1} with |w0|, |w1| in {1,2,3} and each of the 1728 three-colour rules with block lengths in {1,2}, start from a single cell of colour 1 and iterate until the word has >= L = 131072 symbols (or 60 steps if it never does), truncate to L, and compute the number p(n) of distinct length-n factors for n = 1..14. For rule 30 from a single black cell compute p(14) of (i) the central 40001 cells of the row at step 20000 and (ii) the first 65536 cells of the centre column. Build the neighbour-dependent substitution system whose rule maps each cell to one new cell given by the elementary-CA table of its (left, self, right) neighbourhood, and run it for 1000 steps from a single black cell. PASS (supports) if (a) every neighbour-independent rule has p(14) <= 225 = (14+1)^2 (eventually periodic words are those with p(14) = p(13); the rest are counted as nested), (b) both rule 30 sequences have p(14) >= 2000, and (c) the neighbour-dependent systems for rules 90 and 30 reproduce the cellular-automaton rows exactly at every one of the 1000 steps.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if any neighbour-independent rule in the family has p(14) >= 2000 (rule-30-like complexity), or if the neighbour-dependent construction does not reproduce rule 90 or rule 30. If some neighbour-independent rule has 225 < p(14) < 2000 the result is 'mixed' and the rule is reported with its complexity profile.
tests.interpretation: 'Repetitive' is operationalised as eventually periodic (bounded subword complexity, Morse-Hedlund), 'nested' as a self-similar word, which for fixed points of morphisms has subword complexity O(n^2) at most (Pansiot); the threshold (n+1)^2 at n = 14 is therefore a generous upper bound for repetitive-or-nested and about a tenth of what a random-like binary sequence of this length shows. 'Cannot emulate rule 30' is tested within the enumerated family by the complexity gap (a word with p(14) <= 225 cannot contain the rule 30 row, whose own p(14) is measured); it is not a proof over all encodings. The neighbour-dependent half is tested exactly as the book describes it (rules 'always yielding just one cell and corresponding quite directly to cellular automata', p. 666).
tests.method: analysis.py enumerates all 196 two-colour (blocks 1-3) and 1728 three-colour (blocks 1-2) neighbour-independent substitution rules, iterates each from a single cell of colour 1 until the word has 131072 symbols (or 60 steps), and counts distinct factors of length 1..14 with a sorted rolling-code method. It generates rule 30 from a single black cell with big-integer bit operations, taking the central 40001 cells of row 20000 and the first 65536 centre-column cells, and applies the same count. It also measures what share of the centre column's length-14 factors appear in any binary substitution word, and runs the one-cell-per-cell neighbour-dependent substitution systems for rules 90 and 30 against the direct CA for 1000 steps. Runtime about 19 s.

measured.unit: maximum number of distinct length-14 factors over all 1924 neighbour-independent substitution words (threshold 225)
measured.uncertainty: exact combinatorial counts

caveats: The impossibility half is tested on the two complete enumerated families named in the book's own discussion (p. 83), not for arbitrarily long replacement blocks or alphabets; the complexity gap (at most 157 distinct length-14 factors versus 14922-16034 for rule 30) is a finite proxy for the theorem that fixed points of morphisms have polynomially bounded subword complexity.

The subword-complexity criterion treats any word with p(14) <= 225 as repetitive-or-nested; the words with the largest complexity (e.g. 0 -> 0, 1 -> 011, p(n) = 2,4,6,9,13,...,81) are non-primitive morphic words whose complexity grows faster than linearly but far below that of rule 30, consistent with the known n log n / n^2 classes for such words.

The neighbour-dependent half is near-definitional: a substitution system whose single output cell depends on the cell and its two neighbours is a cellular automaton; the test confirms it reproduces rules 90 and 30 exactly for 1000 steps, which is what the book's figure shows.

The length-14 factor share result (at most 0.5% of rule 30's centre-column factors occur in any binary substitution word) is reported as a direct check that none of the enumerated systems reproduces rule 30's sequence under the identity encoding; other encodings were not explored.

datasets.name: Enumerated neighbour-independent substitution systems (2 colours, blocks 1-3; 3 colours, blocks 1-2), rule 30 evolutions, and neighbour-dependent substitution emulations of rules 90 and 30, generated by analysis.py

tests.label: Any system type that can emulate every cellular automaton has universal members
tests.hypothesis: For at least one of the system types named in the claim (Turing machines), a single uniform construction turns any one-dimensional cellular automaton rule (any number of colours k, any radius r) into a Turing machine that emulates it exactly; applied to rule 110 the construction yields an explicit Turing machine, which is then universal by the universality of rule 110 (Cook, Complex Systems 15 (2004) 1-40), so the system type contains a universal member as the claim asserts.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py builds, for a given (k, r, rule table), a Turing machine whose tape holds the cellular-automaton configuration on W cells between two end-marker symbols, and whose head performs one left-to-right sweep (reading each old cell value once, carrying the last 2r old values in its state, stepping back r cells to write the new value) followed by a return to the left end, so that one round trip equals one cellular-automaton step with fixed white (0) boundaries. The machine must be a genuine finite table: every (state, symbol) pair reachable in the runs has exactly one transition writing one symbol and moving one cell. Tests: (a) all 256 elementary rules (k = 2, r = 1), W = 48, 40 steps, two random initial conditions each (seed 20261110); (b) 100 random 3-colour radius-1 rules (k = 3, r = 1), same W and steps; (c) 50 random 2-colour radius-2 rules (k = 2, r = 2); (d) 20 random 4-colour radius-1 rules and 10 random 3-colour radius-2 rules. After every round trip the tape between the markers is compared cell-for-cell with the directly computed cellular-automaton configuration (fixed-0 boundary). 'supports' if the total number of mismatching cells over all runs is 0 and the rule-110 machine is produced with a finite, fully specified state table (its state count and transition count reported).
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run produces a mismatch (one or more cells differing from the direct evolution) that cannot be traced to a bug in the harness rather than the construction; since the construction is uniform in (k, r, rule), a single irreparable mismatch shows the uniform construction does not emulate every cellular automaton. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the harness cannot complete the runs within the time budget.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a logical implication (if a system type can emulate every cellular automaton and a universal cellular automaton exists, the type has universal members). The implication itself is not empirical; what can be checked computationally is its first premise for a concrete system type. We check it for Turing machines, the second family named in the claim, by implementing a uniform emulation construction (the sweeping-head scheme NKS describes for Turing machines emulating cellular automata, p. 665-666, written here from scratch rather than copied) and testing it exhaustively on the elementary rules and on random rules with more colours and larger neighbourhoods. The second premise (existence of a universal cellular automaton) is taken from the published proof that rule 110 is universal; it is not re-derived. The other families in the claim (mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems, register machines) are not tested here, so a 'supports' verdict confirms the claim's structure for one family only.
tests.method: analysis.py builds, from any (k, r, rule table), an explicit finite Turing-machine transition table: states ('scan', B, j) carry the last 2r old cell values B during a left-to-right sweep, step back r cells to write each new value, finish the last r cells at the right end-marker with virtual zero reads, and return to the left marker, so one round trip is one cellular-automaton step with fixed-0 boundaries. The machine for each rule was run on W = 48 cells for 40 steps from two random initial conditions (seed 20261110) and the tape compared cell-for-cell with direct evolution after every step: all 256 elementary rules, 100 random k=3 r=1 rules, 50 random k=2 r=2 rules, 20 random k=4 r=1 rules and 10 random k=3 r=2 rules (436 rules, 1,674,240 cell comparisons). A mutation check (machine for rule 110 compared with rule 124) produced 225 mismatches in 10 steps, confirming the harness detects disagreement.

measured.unit: mismatching cells between Turing-machine tape and direct cellular-automaton evolution, summed over all runs
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic comparison)

caveats: Only the Turing-machine family is tested; the claim also names mobile automata, substitution systems, tag and cyclic tag systems, symbolic systems and register machines, whose emulation constructions are not checked here.

The construction is tested on finite segments with fixed-0 boundaries for 40 steps; its correctness for arbitrary k and r follows from the uniform scheme rather than from exhaustive testing, and the test covers k <= 4 and r <= 2 only.

The conclusion that the resulting rule-110 machine (41 states x 3 symbols, 91 transitions) is universal rests on the published proof that rule 110 is universal (Cook 2004); that proof is not re-verified here, so the implication's second premise is assumed, not tested.
The claim is a logical implication; the computation establishes one instance of its premise, not the implication itself, which is immediate once both premises are granted.
The Turing machines used here have many states; they are not the small machines NKS discusses elsewhere, and nothing is claimed about minimal size.

datasets.name: Turing machines constructed by analysis.py from cellular-automaton rules (all 256 elementary rules; random rules with k in {2,3,4} and r in {1,2}, seed 20261110), run on W = 48 cells for 40 cellular-automaton steps and compared with direct evolution

tests.label: Simple arithmetic systems based on remainders can be universal
tests.hypothesis: For any two-register machine in Wolfram's sense (program of L instructions, each 'increment register r and go to the next instruction' or 'if register r is nonzero decrement it and jump to instruction j, else go to the next instruction', cyclic program), there is an arithmetic system n -> (p*n + q)/s whose branch is chosen by n mod 6L such that, with the state (i, a, b) encoded as n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b (Wolfram's encoding on p. 673 with L = 5 and modulus 30), the integer trajectory decodes step for step to the register machine's trajectory.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. analysis.py compiles each register machine into the remainder-selected arithmetic map, then runs machine and map side by side. Test set: (a) all 200 register machines drawn with numpy seed 20261111 from the family with L = 5 and two registers (instruction type, register and jump target uniform), each from the state (1, 0, 0) and from one random state with registers in [0, 20], for 10000 steps; (b) three hand-written programs with L in {3, 5, 7} that move or copy register contents so that the registers grow without bound, 20000 steps each. 'supports' if at every step of every run the decoded (i, a, b) equals the directly simulated register-machine state (0 mismatches out of all compared steps) and, as a check that the comparison can fail, a deliberately perturbed map (one branch's additive constant changed by 1) produces a mismatch within 10000 steps on at least one of the hand-written programs. Universality of the arithmetic systems then follows from the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not tested.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if any run of the correctly compiled map disagrees with the register machine at any step. 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if the perturbation check fails to produce a mismatch (the comparison would then be too weak to count).
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's 'system that takes a whole number, computes Mod[n, 30], and applies one of several arithmetic operations chosen by that remainder' is the family of generalised Collatz maps n -> (p*n + q)/s with the branch chosen by n mod M. The specific register machine of Wolfram's figure is not transcribed in the online text, so instead of checking his single example the test checks the general construction he describes (encoding n = i + L * 2^a * 3^b, modulus 6L; for L = 5 this is his modulus 30) on a random sample of register machines plus growth programs. Register-machine conventions follow NKS Chapter 3 (pp. 97-102): decrement of a zero register is a no-op that moves to the next instruction, and the program wraps around cyclically. The 'therefore universal' clause is a theorem of Minsky's and is outside what this computation establishes.
tests.method: analysis.py compiles each two-register machine (program length L) into a table of 6L branches (p, q, s), one per residue n mod 6L, of the form n -> (p*n + q)/s with p, s in {1, 2, 3}: increments multiply the 2^a 3^b part by 2 or 3, decrements of a nonzero register divide it by 2 or 3 (the residue mod 6L tells whether the register is nonzero), and the additive constant moves the program position. Register machine and arithmetic map were run side by side in exact Python integers: 200 random L = 5 programs (numpy seed 20261111) from two starting states each for 10000 steps, and three hand-written growth programs (L = 3, 5, 7; moduli 18, 30, 42) for 20000 steps. At every step the integer n was compared with the encoding i + L * 2^a * 3^b of the simulated machine state (equivalent to decoding, since the encoding is injective). A perturbed map with one additive constant changed by one was run as a check that the comparison can fail.

measured.unit: steps at which the arithmetic-system value differs from the encoding of the register-machine state
measured.uncertainty: exact integer arithmetic; none

caveats: What was verified is the emulation half of the claim: the described class of arithmetic systems (remainder modulo 6L selects one of 6L affine-rational operations) tracks arbitrary two-register machines exactly, over 4.06 million compared steps with register values up to several thousand and integers up to 14695 bits. The construction is general (it works for every program in the family, with L = 5 giving Wolfram's modulus 30), not a transcription of the particular 5-instruction machine in Wolfram's figure, whose program is not in the online text.

The 'therefore universal' clause rests on the universality of two-register machines (Minsky 1967), which is cited, not re-proved; the compiled maps inherit universality from it only if one accepts that theorem. The closing remark that universality in arithmetic is unsurprising is an opinion and was not tested.

Finite traces cannot prove the emulation for all time, but the branch table is derived symbolically from the instruction semantics, so the trace check is a consistency test of that derivation rather than a sample-based estimate.
Register-machine conventions (cyclic program, decrement of zero is a no-op) follow NKS Chapter 3; a different convention would change the compiled table but not the construction.

datasets.name: Two-register machines (NKS Chapter 3 conventions) and their compiled remainder-selected arithmetic maps, generated by analysis.py: 200 random programs of length 5 (numpy seed 20261111), three hand-written growth programs of length 3, 5 and 7; 10000 or 20000 steps per run; exact Python integers

tests.label: Elementary cellular automaton rule 110 is universal
tests.hypothesis: Rule 110 is computationally universal (Cook 2004, Complex Systems 15(1):1-40, doi:10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1). Universality itself is a theorem that no finite simulation can establish, so this test checks the empirical premise the claim rests on: that rule 110 'naturally' produces, from random initial conditions, a background ether with the (time, space) periodicity lattice spanned by (3, 2) and (4, -2) (spatial period 14, temporal period 7), and persistent localized structures (gliders) whose space-time periods are exactly those tabulated by Cook (Figure 5): A (3, 2), B (4, -2), B-bar/B-hat (12, -6), C1-C3 (7, 0), D1-D2 (10, 2), E^n (15, -4), E-bar (30, -8), F (36, -4), G^n (42, -14), H (92, -18); in particular the classes used as components in Cook's construction (C2 tape data, E-bar table data, A moving data, E leaders) must occur.
tests.pass: Pre-registered: simulate rule 110 on rings of 1200 cells from 60 uniformly random initial rows (numpy default_rng seed 20261031) for 4000 steps. Ether cells are those whose 7 x 14 neighbourhood is invariant under the lattice translation (t, x) -> (t + 1, x - 4). In rows t = 3000..3900 (every 100 steps), maximal runs of non-ether cells of width <= 60 are 'structures'. For each structure, search for the smallest temporal period P <= 100 and shift |s| <= 50 such that the window (structure plus 14 cells of ether on each side) reappears exactly at (t + P, x + s). Component premise confirmed if: (1) the ether, i.e. the (3,2)/(4,-2) lattice, covers more than 50% of the cells at t >= 3000 in every run; (2) at least 90% of structures resolve to a period, and every resolved period (P, s) is a positive integer combination of Cook's A and B periods that coincides with one of Cook's tabulated glider periods (allowing the period to be a positive integer multiple of a tabulated one, for packets such as A^n); (3) the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar are each observed at least once. Because the test replays only the glider inventory and not the cyclic-tag-system emulation, the verdict when all three conditions hold is pre-declared as 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable' (universality is settled by proof, not by this computation), with the component results reported as supporting evidence.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: 'refutes' if the standard ether does not form (condition 1 fails in a majority of runs), or if the A, C or E-bar classes (the data carriers of Cook's construction) are never observed in 60 random runs, or if resolved structures have space-time periods incompatible with Cook's table (a period that is not an integer combination of (3, 2) and (4, -2) would contradict his lattice argument). Such results would undermine the published construction that the claim cites and would be reported as 'refutes' of the component premise with confidence <= 0.6, since a construction could in principle use rarer gliders.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's claim is a theorem (Cook's proof, presented in NKS pp. 678-689 and published in 2004). The test does not re-derive the proof or replay the cyclic tag system emulation, which requires Cook's specific glider packets and spacings; it checks the computational premise that rule 110 has a stable ether and naturally occurring gliders with the stated periods, which is the part of the claim that is accessible to a few minutes of simulation. The glider table is taken from Figure 5 of Cook's paper (retrieved PDF; checksum recorded); 'period' is Cook's (time, horizontal displacement) pair for one repetition of the glider.
tests.method: analysis.py runs rule 110 from 60 random rows on 1200-cell rings for 4208 steps. In rows 3000..3900 (every 100 steps) it marks ether cells by invariance of their 7 x 14 neighbourhood under the ether lattice translation (t, x) -> (t+1, x-4), extracts maximal non-ether runs (structures) of width <= 60, keeps those with 14 cells of ether on each side (isolated), and for each searches the smallest space-time period (P <= 100, |s| <= min(50, P)) at which the structure and its margins recur twice. Each minimal period is compared with the (time, displacement) periods of Cook's Figure 5 (exact match, or an integer multiple for packets) and checked to be a non-negative integer combination of the A period (3, 2) and the B period (4, -2). Two refinements were added after a trial run: |s| <= P (matches with faster-than-light displacement are neighbouring identical gliders, not periods) and recurrence at two consecutive periods. Run time about 15 s including the PDF download.

measured.unit: resolved isolated structures (out of 2674) whose minimal space-time period is not one of Cook's tabulated glider periods
measured.uncertainty: exact

caveats: As pre-declared, the verdict is 'inconclusive' because universality is a theorem established by Cook's constructive proof and the cyclic-tag-system emulation was not replayed; the computation can only check the empirical premise of the construction. That premise is confirmed on every pre-registered condition: the standard ether forms in all 60 random runs (at least 70% of cells, median 82%, never below 50%); 92.1% of isolated structures (2674 of 2903) resolve to a space-time period within P <= 100; all 2674 minimal periods are exactly entries of Cook's table (A, B, B-bar/B-hat, C, D, E, E-bar, F, G) and all lie on the A/B lattice; the classes A, B, C, D, E and E-bar required by the construction were observed 186, 270, 234, 53, 590 and 1079 times.

The only tabulated glider not seen is H, which Cook himself lists as too rare to arise naturally; no glider absent from his table was found, so the inventory he describes as 'all known gliders' is also consistent with 60 random soups (this does not prove no other glider exists).

Periods are compared as (time, displacement) pairs; distinct gliders with the same period (C1/C2/C3, D1/D2, E^n packets, B-bar vs B-hat) are not separated, and the specific alignment conditions (C2 phases, E-bar spacings) that Cook's construction depends on were not verified. The 229 unresolved isolated structures are mostly structures about to collide within the 100-step search window.

Two implementation refinements (|s| <= P and recurrence at two periods) were added after a trial run revealed that matches between neighbouring identical gliders in trains were being reported as spurious periods; they are physical constraints on what a period is, not changes to the pre-registered thresholds.

tests.label: Class 1 and 2 cellular automata cannot be universal
tests.hypothesis: Every elementary cellular automaton that settles into a uniform or short-period state from random initial conditions (operational class 1 or 2) transmits a single-cell perturbation of that settled state only over a bounded distance, whereas rules that do not settle spread perturbations without bound.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: all 256 elementary CA rules. For each rule, 10 trials: ring of N = 800 cells, random initial condition with density 1/2 (numpy default_rng seed 20261033), evolve 1000 steps to configuration C; the trial is 'settled' if C recurs within the next 64 steps (temporal period <= 64, which includes uniform and shifted-periodic states). A rule is 'operational class 1/2' if >= 9 of 10 trials settle. In every settled trial, flip one cell of C (the cell at index 400) and evolve both copies 400 further steps on the ring (N = 800 > 2 x 400, so the damage cannot wrap); record the damage width w = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1 (0 if none). A rule is 'bounded' if w <= 20 in all of its settled trials, 'spreading' if the median w over settled trials >= 100 (linear growth), otherwise 'intermediate'. The claim PASSES if 100% of operational class 1/2 rules are 'bounded'. Validation (reported, not decisive): the rules Wikipedia cites as Wolfram's class 1 and 2 examples (0, 32, 160, 232; 4, 108, 218, 250) must be operational class 1/2 and the class 3 and 4 examples (22, 30, 126, 150, 182; 110, 54) must not be; and the fraction of non-settled rules that are 'spreading' is reported.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if any operational class 1/2 rule is 'spreading' (a settled rule that nevertheless transmits a perturbation over a linearly growing region). If some class 1/2 rules are 'intermediate' but none 'spreading', the verdict is 'mixed'. If the Wikipedia example rules are misclassified by the operational definition, that is reported as a caveat on the mapping to Wolfram's phenomenological classes but does not change the verdict.
tests.interpretation: The claim has a conclusion (class 1 and 2 automata cannot be universal) and a stated mechanism ('never allow any transmission of information except over limited distances'). Non-universality is a statement about all possible encodings and is not testable by finite computation; the test addresses the mechanism, which is the premise of Wolfram's argument: perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localized. Wolfram's classes are phenomenological, so they are operationalised here as 'settles into a temporal cycle of period <= 64 on an 800-cell ring within 1000 steps from random initial conditions'; the damage width (not displacement) is used so that shifting class-2 rules, whose perturbation moves but does not grow, count as bounded, as the assessors noted. Perturbations are applied to the settled state because the claim concerns the asymptotic behaviour, not transients.
tests.method: analysis.py runs all 256 rules: 10 seeded random initial conditions on an 800-cell ring, 1000 steps, period detection up to 64 steps, then a single-cell flip of the settled configuration and 400 further steps for both copies; damage width = rightmost - leftmost differing cell + 1. Operational class 1/2 = >= 9/10 trials settled; bounded = max width <= 20; spreading = median width >= 100. The Wikipedia page is fetched for its checksum and the example rules per class are checked against the operational classification. Per-rule values in derived/rules.csv (including a post-hoc width at step 200), fetch record in derived/wikipedia.json; runtime about 50 s.

measured.unit: fraction of operational class 1/2 rules whose settled-state perturbation stays bounded (width <= 20 after 400 steps)
measured.uncertainty: 96 operational class 1/2 rules; 94 bounded, 2 intermediate, 0 spreading

caveats: Pre-registered decision: 0 of 96 operational class 1/2 rules is 'spreading', so the claim is not refuted, but 2 rules (37 and 62) are 'intermediate' (max damage width 24 and 27 in one trial each, medians 2.0 and 1.5), so the pre-registered rule gives 'mixed' rather than 'supports'. The 20-cell threshold was set before the run; with a 30-cell threshold every class 1/2 rule would be bounded.

Post-hoc inspection shows the two intermediate cases are static, not growing: the damage width at step 200 equals the width at step 400 (rule 37: 24:24, 21:21; rule 62: 28:27). The six class 1/2 trials whose width is larger at step 400 than at step 200 are period-2 oscillations between widths 1 and 2 in rule 62. Substantively the mechanism Wolfram states (perturbations of class 1/2 states stay localised) holds for all 96 rules; the 'mixed' verdict reflects a conservative threshold rather than a counterexample.

All 14 Wikipedia example rules are classified as expected by the operational definition (class 1 and 2 examples settle in 10/10 trials with max width <= 4; class 3 and 4 examples never settle), so the operational class maps onto Wolfram's phenomenological classes for these rules. 160 rules are not operational class 1/2; 7 of them settle in some trials, and in 5 of those (rules 14, 57, 99, 113, 143) the perturbation of the settled state spreads across the whole ring, consistent with the converse.

The test addresses the stated mechanism (bounded information transmission), not the conclusion (impossibility of universality), which concerns all encodings and is not finitely testable. Results depend on the finite ring (800 cells), horizon (1000 + 400 steps), the single-flip perturbation and one random seed; shifting class 2 rules are counted as bounded by using width rather than displacement.

datasets.name: 256 elementary cellular automata, settled states and single-cell perturbations (generated by analysis.py)
datasets.version: generator in analysis.py; seed 20261033; N = 800; 1000 + 64 + 400 steps; 10 trials per rule

tests.label: Nested-pattern and additive cellular automata cannot be universal
tests.hypothesis: If the claim's premise holds, every additive elementary cellular automaton (the eight rules linear over GF(2): 0, 60, 90, 102, 150, 170, 204, 240) satisfies, for every initial condition and every k, that the configuration after 2^k steps is exactly the XOR superposition of copies of the initial condition shifted by 2^k times the offsets in the rule's support (rule 90: offsets -1 and +1; rule 150: -1, 0, +1); the empirical additivity screen picks out exactly these rules; the class-3/4 rules the book contrasts them with (18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122) never return to such a superposition form at any power-of-two step; and the nested single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 have row populations matching the independently tabulated OEIS sequences A001316 and A071053.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (a) For each of the eight linear rules, each cyclic lattice size N in {1023, 2048}, 20 seeded random initial conditions of density 1/2 plus the single-cell initial condition, and each k = 0..10, the configuration after 2^k steps equals bit-for-bit the XOR of the initial condition shifted by d*2^k over the offsets d in the rule's support (the support is read off the rule table as the cells on which the one-step response to a single 1 is nonzero). (b) An additivity screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) on 200 seeded random pairs at N = 256 identifies exactly the eight linear rules, and the affine screen T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) xor T(0) exactly the eight linear plus the eight complementary rules (255, 195, 165, 153, 105, 85, 51, 15). (c) For each of the eight control rules 18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122 and each k = 0..8, the 2^k-step map fails additivity on at least one of 50 seeded random pairs at N = 256 (so the state after 2^k steps is not a superposition of shifted copies of the initial condition for generic initial conditions). (d) The number of nonzero cells in row t of the single-cell pattern of rule 90 (t = 0..T) equals term t of OEIS A001316 and that of rule 150 equals term t of A071053, for every term available in the OEIS b-files up to t = 4095 (the b-files are fetched and their sha256 recorded). PASS (supports the claim's checkable premise) if (a), (b), (c) and (d) all hold. The non-universality conclusion itself is a proof-type statement (a map that is linear over GF(2) at every power-of-two step cannot emulate the non-linear behaviour an arbitrary computation requires under the encodings the book considers) and is not decided by this test; its evidential weight is recorded in the confidence.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes the premise) if (a) fails for any linear rule, k, lattice size or initial condition (the stated superposition property is false), or if (d) fails for rule 90 or rule 150 (the single-cell patterns are not the nested patterns the claim describes). MIXED if (a) and (d) hold but (b) or (c) fails (the superposition property is true of rules 90 and 150 but does not cleanly separate additive from complex rules as the book's argument requires). INCONCLUSIVE with reason data-unavailable only for part (d) if the OEIS b-files cannot be retrieved; (a)-(c) are then still reported and the verdict rests on them with reduced confidence.
tests.interpretation: The claim bundles a precise mathematical premise (power-of-two-step superposition for additive rules) with an informal class ('essentially nested' rules) and a non-universality conclusion. The test checks the premise exactly, checks that it discriminates additive rules from the complex rules the book contrasts them with, and cross-checks the nested single-cell patterns against externally tabulated sequences (Gould's sequence for rule 90, and the rule-150 analogue). It does not prove non-universality; a rule's universality depends on permitted encodings and no finite computation can exclude it, so 'supports' here means the premise and the discriminating contrast hold, not that the conclusion has been verified.
tests.method: analysis.py implements elementary CA rules on cyclic lattices. (a) For each of the eight GF(2)-linear rules it reads the support offsets off the rule table and checks, for N = 1023 and 2048, 20 seeded random initial conditions plus a single cell, and k = 0..10, that the configuration after 2^k steps equals the XOR of the initial condition shifted by d*2^k over the support (462 checks per rule). (b) It screens all 256 rules for additivity T(x xor y) = T(x) xor T(y) and affinity on 200 random pairs at N = 256. (c) For the eight class-3/4 control rules it counts, for k = 0..8, how many of 50 random pairs violate additivity of the 2^k-step map. (d) It computes the row populations of the single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 for 4096 rows and compares them term by term with the OEIS b-files of A001316 and A071053 fetched over HTTPS (sha256 recorded). Runtime 15 s.

measured.unit: failures of the power-of-two-step superposition identity over 3696 (rule, lattice, initial condition, k) checks for the eight additive rules
measured.uncertainty: exact bitwise comparison

caveats: What is verified is the claim's mathematical premise and its discriminating contrast: the eight additive elementary rules satisfy the superposition identity exactly at every power-of-two step tested (rule 90 with offsets -1,+1; rule 150 with -1,0,+1), the additivity screen recovers exactly these eight rules (and exactly the eight complementary affine rules), the class-3/4 rules 18, 22, 30, 45, 54, 73, 110, 122 violate additivity on 46-50 of 50 random pairs at every k = 0..8, and the nested single-cell patterns of rules 90 and 150 reproduce OEIS A001316 and A071053 for all 4096 terms.

The non-universality conclusion is not decided by this test: universality is a statement about all encodings and all initial conditions, which no finite enumeration can exclude. The confidence reflects that the premise checked here is the whole of the book's stated argument for additive rules (a map linear over GF(2) at every power-of-two step cannot emulate non-linear behaviour) but that the inference from premise to non-universality is a proof-type step taken on the book's word.
The informal class of rules 'whose patterns are essentially nested' is not formalised in the claim and was not tested beyond the additive rules; the verdict applies to the additive part of the claim.

Cyclic lattices of size 1023 and 2048 were used; the identity on an infinite lattice follows from the same local argument, and both an odd and a power-of-two size were included so that boundary wrap-around cannot mask or manufacture agreement.

datasets.name: Elementary cellular automata on cyclic lattices with power-of-two-step superposition and additivity screens, generated by analysis.py
OEIS A001316 Gould's sequence: number of odd entries in row n of Pascal's triangle = number of nonzero cells in row n of rule 90 from a single cell
OEIS A071053: number of ON cells at generation n of rule 150 from a single ON cell

tests.label: Rule 54 shows only repetitive or nested forms in 100 million initial conditions
tests.hypothesis: Rule 54, run from each of the first N initial conditions (binary digits of n on a white background, as in NKS p. 697), produces only repetitive or nested patterns: none has the local space-time complexity characteristic of class 3 or class 4 behaviour.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Family: initial conditions n = 1..65536 (16 bits), cell values = binary digits of n placed on an infinite white background (validated against the figure: n = 1 single cell, n = 3 two cells, n = 291 nested); rule 54 run for T = 256 steps on a lattice wide enough that the light cone never reaches the edge. Classifier (frozen before the census): the number D of distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles whose top-left corner lies in rows 128..250 and inside the light cone (plus 2 cells) of the pattern. Calibration on controls outside the family, disclosed: repetitive and nested rules give D <= 1007 (rule 90 single cell 115, random 14-bit seeds 267-395; rule 150 single 316, random seeds 804-1007; rule 22 single 119; rule 18 random 309-602; rules 250, 108, 184, 62, 41 random 1-178), while class 3/4 controls give D >= 1094 (rule 110 random 14- and 30-bit seeds 1094-1553; rule 30 6801-7166; rule 45 6338-6401), with a few class-3 rules from narrow seeds in between (rule 106: 462 and 2912; rule 126: 130-402; rule 146: 371-413; rule 73: 64-774). The eight rule-54 patterns shown in the book's figure (n = 1, 3, 75, 259, 291, 787, 803, 56549) give D = 10, 37, 315, 315, 286, 391, 391, 370, and a batch of 256 random 14-bit seeds gave max 391. Threshold: D > 1050 (geometric midpoint of 1007 and 1094) = 'more complicated'. Also recorded per initial condition: exact temporal periodicity (period <= 16) of the pattern's core over steps 128..256 ('repetitive'). The claim PASSES if 0 of the 65536 initial conditions has D > 1050. Reported, not decisive: the distribution of D, the fraction that is exactly periodic, the number with D > 700 (a stricter threshold that still clears all rule-54 book examples), and for any initial condition above threshold a re-run with T = 512.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if at least one initial condition n <= 65536 has D > 1050 and the T = 512 re-run also gives D > 1050 (sustained local complexity comparable to the class 3/4 controls). If some exceed 1050 at T = 256 but not at T = 512 the verdict is 'mixed' (transient complexity). The census is 1/1526 of the book's 10^8 initial conditions; a pass is consistent with the claim but far from exhausting it.
tests.interpretation: The claim is a finite observational statement about the first 10^8 initial conditions; the full census is beyond a few minutes of Python, so this is a scaled census (2^16 initial conditions) with the book's informal judgement 'nothing fundamentally more complicated than repetitive or nested' frozen into a local-complexity classifier. The classifier counts distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles in the second half of the evolution: self-similar (nested) and periodic patterns have bounded tile vocabularies, whereas class 3 patterns have thousands and class 4 patterns with interacting gliders over a thousand. The threshold was set from controls outside the rule-54 family plus the book's own eight rule-54 examples; it is admittedly coarse, and the random-seed rule 150 controls (nested, up to 1007) show that nested patterns with wide seeds approach it. A failure under this classifier would therefore need the T = 512 confirmation and visual inspection before being read as a counterexample to Wolfram's census.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves rule 54 for 256 steps from every initial condition n = 1..65535 (binary digits of n on white; batches of 512 vectorised in numpy on a lattice wide enough that the light cone never reaches the edge), encodes every 6 x 6 space-time tile with top-left in rows 128..250 inside the light cone as a 36-bit integer and counts distinct tiles D; patterns with D <= 400 are also tested for exact temporal periodicity (period <= 16) of the light-cone core over steps 128..256. The 20 initial conditions with the largest D are re-run for 512 steps. Per-initial-condition values in derived/census.csv.xz; runtime about 3 minutes.

measured.unit: number of initial conditions n <= 65536 whose rule-54 pattern has more than 1050 distinct 6x6 tiles in steps 128-256
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive over n = 1..65535 (n = 65536 has 17 bits and was not included)

caveats: Pre-registered decision: 0 of 65,535 initial conditions exceeds the 1050-tile threshold (0 exceed even the stricter 700). The largest vocabulary is 426 tiles (n = 52843) and the twenty largest all fall back to 391 tiles at steps 256-512, the same vocabulary as the book's examples n = 787 and 803; the distribution is strongly clustered (median 68; 50,561 below 100; 214 between 400 and 500), consistent with a small repertoire of repetitive and nested forms. 17.2% of the patterns are exactly periodic in the core with period 4 over steps 128-256.

This is a scaled census: 2^16 initial conditions rather than the 10^8 of the book, i.e. seeds of at most 16 cells, so wider seeds (where interacting structures are more likely) are untested; a pass here is consistent with Wolfram's census but does not reproduce it.

'Repetitive or nested' was frozen into a local-complexity classifier (distinct 6 x 6 space-time tiles) with a threshold set from controls outside the family (rule 90/150/22/18 nested, rules 250/108/184/62/41 repetitive, rules 110/30/45 complex) and the book's own eight rule-54 examples. The margin is large (426 observed vs. 1094 for the least complex rule-110 control) but the classifier is coarse: a class-4-like pattern with a small glider repertoire could in principle have a modest tile vocabulary, and nested patterns from wide seeds (rule 150 random 14-bit seeds reach 1007) approach the threshold.
Finite horizon (256 steps, re-checks to 512): slowly developing complexity, e.g. structures appearing only after thousands of steps, would be missed.

datasets.name: Rule 54 from initial conditions 1..65536 (generated by analysis.py)
datasets.version: generator in analysis.py; T = 256; deterministic (no random numbers)

tests.label: Complex elementary rules can emulate one step of every elementary rule
tests.hypothesis: With a single-step block-emulation scheme of the kind shown on NKS pp. 703-705 (fixed background blocks of width w between single input cells, t steps of the underlying rule, output read at a fixed offset), the underlying rules 22, 30 and 110 can realise, as the induced map from (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) to the output under cell i, every one of the 256 elementary rules once w is large enough, whereas rules 90 and 184 realise only a small number of them at the same widths.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Scheme: the initial condition is periodic with period w+1: one input cell x[i] in {0,1} followed by a fixed background block B in {0,1}^w. The underlying rule f is run for t steps with w+1 <= t <= 2w+2 and the output for cell i is read at offset d in 0..w to the right of x[i]'s position. For each (w, B, t, d) the output is computed for all 32 assignments of (x[i-2], ..., x[i+2]) in a window padded on both sides with t+2 further background cells (input positions in the padding set to 0; they lie outside the light cone). If the output depends only on (x[i-1], x[i], x[i+1]) (the 4 assignments of the outer inputs agree for each of the 8 inner triples), the induced 3-input truth table is an elementary rule g that f emulates for one step at width w. E(f, W) = the set of g realised for some w <= W. Widths searched: W = 1..6. 'supports' if |E(f, 6)| = 256 for each f in {22, 30, 110} and |E(f, 6)| <= 32 for each f in {90, 184}.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if |E(90, 6)| >= 128 or |E(184, 6)| >= 128 (a 'simple' rule emulates at least half of all elementary rules), or if min over f in {22, 30, 110} of |E(f, 6)| is smaller than max over f in {90, 184} of |E(f, 6)| (the contrast is reversed). 'inconclusive' with reason 'other' if neither condition holds, e.g. because 22, 30 or 110 do not reach 256 within W = 6 under this scheme: Wolfram's figure uses a scheme whose exact readout and width conventions are not fully recoverable from the online text, so a shortfall under the reconstructed scheme does not refute the claim. In every case the counts for all 256 underlying rules at W = 6 are reported.
tests.interpretation: The claim concerns one-step emulation under block encodings, which Wolfram himself distinguishes from universality. The test reconstructs the p. 703-704 scheme from its caption (fixed initial conditions except at input positions; blocks of 3 cells between inputs for the rule 30 to Xor example; blocks 5 cells wide for all 256 rules) with the output position and step count as free parameters searched over a bounded range. 'A few' is given the threshold 32 of 256 (one eighth). Positive emulations are exact finite certificates; negative counts are relative to the scheme and the searched widths. All computation is in analysis.py; there is no external download.
tests.method: analysis.py builds, for each underlying rule f, each background width w = 1..6 and each of the 2^w background blocks, a periodic initial condition with one input cell per period, runs f for t = w+1..2w+2 steps on all 32 assignments of five consecutive inputs (numpy, vectorised over assignments), reads the output at each offset d = 0..w below the central input, and records the induced 3-input truth table whenever the output is independent of the two outer inputs. The cumulative number of distinct elementary rules so obtained was computed for all 256 underlying rules (25 s). After seeing that the counts were still rising at w = 6, the same search was continued post hoc to w = 12 for rules 22, 30, 45, 90, 110 and 184 (a further 2 minutes).

measured.unit: number of the 256 elementary rules emulated for one step with background width <= 6 (pre-registered range)
measured.uncertainty: exhaustive within the reconstructed scheme and searched range; none

caveats: Under the pre-registered rule the outcome is inconclusive: at width <= 6 none of rules 22, 30, 110 reaches all 256 targets under the reconstructed scheme (117, 229 and 55 respectively), while the refutation conditions are far from met (rules 90 and 184 emulate only 14 each, and every complex rule exceeds them). The pre-registered width limit of 6 was too small for this scheme.

Post hoc (not pre-registered, not decisive): continuing the identical search to width 12, rule 30 emulates all 256 elementary rules from width 7, rule 45 from width 8 and rule 22 from width 10, whereas rule 90 saturates at 16 and rule 184 at 14 by width 4-9 and never grows further. This matches the claim's contrast exactly for 22, 30, 90 and 184. Rule 110 reaches 167 of 256 by width 12 and is still rising; whether it reaches 256 at larger widths under this scheme was not determined (Wolfram's figure shows it doing so under his scheme).

The scheme is a reconstruction from the figure captions (single-cell inputs separated by fixed blocks, free readout offset and step count); Wolfram's exact conventions may differ, so the widths at which 256 is reached are not directly comparable with his figure, and negative counts are scheme-relative. Positive emulations are exact and independently checkable certificates.
One-step emulation is, as Wolfram himself notes, much weaker than universality; the claim's inference to 'arbitrarily sophisticated computations' is a heuristic and was not tested.

datasets.name: Exhaustive single-step block-emulation search over elementary cellular automata generated by analysis.py: underlying rules f = 0..255, background widths w = 1..6 (all 2^w blocks), steps t = w+1..2w+2, readout offsets d = 0..w, 32 input assignments per configuration

tests.label: A 2-state 5-color Turing machine is universal via rule 110
tests.hypothesis: The 2-state, 5-colour Turing machine whose rule is drawn on NKS p. 707, started as described in the note 'Rule 110 Turing machines' (p. 1119: tape = Prepend[4 list, 0] with colour 1 to the left and colour 0 to the right, head on the first tape element in state 1), emulates rule 110: successive 'new rightmost head position' snapshots of the tape, decoded as colour 4 -> black and all other colours -> white, are successive steps of rule 110 applied to the initial list on a white background. Given Cook's published proof that rule 110 is universal, the machine is universal.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. Using the rule table transcribed from the p. 707 figure (10 cases; the transcription is recorded in derived/tm25-rule.json), for the single-cell initial list and for 40 random binary lists of length 10-60 (numpy default_rng seeds 0..39), with a fixed integer offset c determined once from the single-cell run and then held fixed, the k-th new-rightmost snapshot decoded as above equals rule-110 iterate k-c of the initial list for every k from c to c+199, on every cell of the window spanning the full rule-110 pattern (100% of 41 x 200 snapshot comparisons). 'Supports' if this holds.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. 'Refutes' if for any initial list some snapshot differs from the corresponding rule-110 iterate, or if no fixed offset makes the single-cell run match; 'inconclusive / not-operationalizable' if the rule table cannot be read unambiguously from the published figure.
tests.interpretation: The claim has two parts: (i) the 2-state 5-colour machine emulates rule 110 one step per complete sweep, which is tested directly by simulation; (ii) universality follows from (i) and the universality of rule 110 (Cook 2004, Complex Systems 15(1), doi:10.25088/ComplexSystems.15.1.1), which is taken as a published premise and not re-proved here. 'Complete sweep' is operationalized as the moment the head reaches a position further right than ever before (the convention of Wolfram's compressed picture). The rule table is only published as a picture; it was transcribed from the figure's grey levels and arrow orientations (white=0, lightest grey=1, ..., darkest grey=4; the head arrow pointing down is state 1 because that is the state in which the published initial condition yields rule 110, pointing up is state 2). The number of states and colours in the table (2 and 5) is also checked.
tests.method: The 10 rule icons of the p. 707 figure were transcribed by grey level and arrow geometry (derived/tm25-rule.json). analysis.py simulates the machine on a tape of colour-1 cells, a 0, the rule-110 list encoded as 4*list, and 0's, with the head on the first 0 right of the data in state 1 (as in the figure), records the tape each time the head reaches a new rightmost position, decodes colour 4 as black, and compares snapshot k with rule-110 iterate k of the list (time offset and spatial shift fixed once from the single-cell run: both 0). This is done for the single-cell list and 40 random lists of length 10-60, 200 snapshots each. The pre-registration's guessed start (head on the prepended 0) is also run and reported.

measured.unit: fraction of tape snapshots equal to the corresponding rule-110 step
measured.uncertainty: exact (deterministic)

caveats: Deviation from the pre-registration: the head's start position was guessed as 'the first tape element' before reading the figure; with that start the machine emulates rule 110 only from a single black cell (and only in the down-arrow state). The figure on p. 707 shows the head starting on the first white cell right of the data, and with that start the emulation is exact for every list tested; the pre-registered pass criterion (100% snapshot matches with a fixed offset) is met for this figure-consistent start and the comparison itself was not changed.

The rule table exists only as a picture; the transcription (grey levels 255/204/153/102/51 -> colours 0-4; up/down arrow -> states 1/2) is recorded in derived/tm25-rule.json. All 10 cases are exercised thousands of times in every run, so a transcription error would almost certainly have broken the exact agreement.

Universality itself is inherited from Cook's (2004) proof for rule 110 and is not re-derived; what is verified computationally is the reduction (one rule-110 step per complete sweep). 'Simpler than the 7-state 4-color machine' is read as 2*5 = 10 < 7*4 = 28 rule cases.

The snapshots compared are the 'new rightmost head position' moments of Wolfram's compressed picture; snapshots 0 and 1 (initial tape and first excursion) also match but were excluded by the script's K_MIN = 2.

tests.label: No 2-state 2-color Turing machine can be universal
tests.hypothesis: Every one of the 4096 Turing machines with 2 states and 2 colours (Wolfram's convention: each (state, colour) maps to (new colour, new state, move left/right); no halt state) has behaviour that from every finite initial condition becomes eventually periodic, possibly with a drifting head (a 'glider'), after a short transient. Since a universal machine must have initial conditions whose evolution is not eventually periodic (otherwise every question about its evolution is decidable), such a classification is strong evidence that none is universal.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. For each of the 4096 machines and each initial condition in the set I = {every binary tape string of length 1-7 with the head on each of its cells, in each of the 2 states} (1284 initial conditions per machine) plus 100 random tapes of length 16-32 per machine (seeded), simulate on an infinite blank (0) tape for up to 10000 steps and classify the evolution exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation: the head-relative configuration (state, tape between the outermost non-zero cells, head offset) recurs exactly, which implies periodic evolution forever; or (B) escaping: the head is beyond all non-zero cells, moving outward over blank cells, and the same state occurs twice during that outward run, which implies it moves outward forever. 'Supports' if 100% of the (machine, initial condition) pairs are classified as (A) or (B) within 10000 steps, and the largest period found is at most 1000 steps. The symmetry-reduced count of distinct machines (state relabelling, colour swap, reflection) is also computed and compared with Wolfram's 560 as a consistency check on the enumeration.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The test cannot establish universality, so 'refutes' is not reachable by this computation alone. 'Mixed' if any (machine, initial condition) pair is unclassified after 10000 steps (unbounded non-periodic behaviour within the tested inputs, which would be at least consistent with the complexity universality needs) or if periods above 1000 steps occur. 'Supports' otherwise.
tests.interpretation: 'Too simple to support universality' is operationalized as: every tested evolution is provably eventually periodic (with or without drift), established by exact recurrence detection rather than by visual inspection. This is necessary-condition evidence: universality requires some input with a non-eventually-periodic evolution, and the tested inputs cover all short tapes exhaustively plus random longer ones, but not all inputs; a proof for all inputs would need a per-machine argument. The convention follows NKS p. 78 and the note 'Turing machine enumeration' (p. 1120): machines never halt, and all 4096 = 8^4 rule tables are counted. The search program is in C (compiled by analysis.py with gcc) for speed; this tooling deviation is recorded.
tests.method: analysis.py writes the random initial tapes, compiles tm22.c with gcc and runs it over all 4096 machines x 3176 initial conditions (13,008,896 runs, 10000-step limit). Each run is classified exactly as (A) eventually periodic modulo translation (the head-relative configuration recurs) or (B) escaping, with two exact escape tests: B1 as pre-registered (head beyond all non-zero cells moving outward with a repeated state) and B2 (two successive new-extreme head positions with identical state and identical non-zero tape, the head farther from the tape than the time between them, so the motion repeats verbatim on blank tape). Runs that are neither are put through three post-hoc heuristic classes added after the first full run showed 16% of runs growing their tape: (C) regular linear growth, where the last 16 events at which the head reaches a new extreme position (sampled with stride 1-3) have constant second time differences, constant state and tape contents S_{n+1} = P + S_n[:o] + B + S_n[o:] + Q with fixed P, B, Q, o; (D) the same with event gaps obeying g_{n+1} = a g_n + b, a >= 2 (binary-counter growth); (E) a counter certificate for runs whose tape never grows: at >= 8 returns of the head to one end of its range, in a fixed state, the tape read as a binary number changes by the same non-zero amount. C/D stop the run early once 16 events fit; as a check the program is also run without early stopping (full 10000 steps) on machines 256-319 and 2048-2111 and the class counts compared. Symmetry-distinct machines are counted under state relabelling, colour swap and reflection.

measured.unit: fraction of the 13,008,896 (machine, initial condition) runs classified exactly as eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B) within 10000 steps (pre-registered threshold 1.0)
measured.uncertainty: exact for A and B; C, D and E are heuristic pattern fits (see caveats)

caveats: The pre-registered criterion fails: only 83.36% of runs are eventually periodic (A) or escaping (B); analysis.py reports preregistered_verdict = 'mixed'. The pre-registered hypothesis was too narrow, not the claim: the remaining runs are tapes that grow forever in a regular way (a head sweeping a growing block, 2,142,325 runs in 864 machines) or binary counters (22,536 runs in 11 machines belonging to just 2 symmetry classes, representatives 441 and 462), which Wolfram describes as the most complex 2,2 behaviour (NKS p. 79-80, 'nested'). Under the post-hoc classes C-E every run but 2 of 13,008,896 is accounted for, and both residual runs belong to counter machines (1372, 3654) whose other 3175 runs are classified; the verdict 'supports' rests on these post-hoc classes and is therefore given lower confidence.

Classes A and B are proofs of the individual run's future; classes C, D and E are pattern fits over a finite window (16 growth events, or 8 counter visits) and could in principle be fooled by behaviour that changes later. The no-early-stop check on 128 machines gives identical class counts, and the classes were designed after inspecting the actual mechanisms (sweepers, binary counters), but they are heuristics.

The computation is necessary-condition evidence only: it covers all tapes of length <= 7 and 100 random longer tapes per machine, not all inputs, and finding only repetitive and nested behaviour does not prove non-universality. The known proof is Pavlotskaya (1973), who showed every 2-state 2-colour machine has a decidable halting problem; that result is not checked here.

Implementation deviations from the pre-registration: the exhaustive set has 3076 initial conditions per machine, not 1284 (miscount in the pre-registration; the set itself is as described); the A test is applied for t <= 2000 and spans <= 128 only (for speed; no run escaped A because of this: the max transient to A or B is 3354 for B, and the max period is 24); an additional exact escape test B2 was added because many 'glider' runs carry a bounded pattern away from a fixed tape remnant and are neither periodic modulo translation nor caught by B1. The search is in C (gcc), a tooling deviation from the python/mjs rule, recorded in the pre-registration.
The symmetry-reduced count of 560 distinct machines matches Wolfram's note (p. 1120), confirming the enumeration covers the same family.

tests.label: Combinators show highly complex behavior despite simple rules
tests.hypothesis: Under Wolfram's evaluation scheme (one Mathematica-style /. pass of the S and K rules per step), the size-7 expression s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] grows exponentially in leaf count without reaching a fixed point, a small number of the 109,824 size-8 expressions also grow without bound, and the combinator w given in the note 'Cellular automaton combinators' (NKS p. 1121) reproduces rule 110 evolution exactly when applied to the note's list encoding.
tests.pass: Pre-registered. (A) Growth: evolve s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps, each step = one ReplaceAll pass of {s[x][y][z] -> x[z][y[z]], k[x][y] -> x} (outermost subexpression first, no re-scan of replaced parts, heads and arguments visited); PASS-A if no fixed point is reached and a least-squares fit of log2(LeafCount) against step over steps 10..40 has slope in [0.45, 0.55] (book: growth like 2^(t/2)) with R^2 >= 0.99. (B) Census (reported, not decisive): evolve all 109,824 size-8 S/K expressions for up to 60 steps or until LeafCount > 20,000; record how many reach a fixed point, how many exceed 20,000 leaves (unbounded/exponential candidates), and the remainder; the book reports 49 with exponential growth. (C) Emulation: implement ToC bracket abstraction, p, num, inc, cr and w exactly as printed in the note; encode every binary list of length 3, 4 and 5 (56 lists) with p[num[Length]][Fold[p[Nest[s,k,#2]][#1]&, p[k][k], list]] fully normalised; apply w once, twice and three times (full normalisation by iterated ReplaceAll after each application); decode by applying the pair selectors (p[a][b][s[k]] -> a, p[a][b][k] -> b) and normalising; PASS-C if for all 56 lists and all t in 1..3 the decoded list equals t steps of rule 110 applied to the list padded with one 0 on each side per step (length n + 2t). The claim PASSES if PASS-A and PASS-C both hold (the growth and the emulation components, which are what the book presents as evidence); the census (B) and any descriptive statistics of internal structure are reported only.
tests.fail: Pre-registered. The claim FAILS if the size-7 expression reaches a fixed point or its growth is not exponential (slope outside [0.45, 0.55] or R^2 < 0.99), or if the published w combinator does not reproduce rule 110 for every tested list and step count. If w cannot be transcribed unambiguously from the note (the HTML lost the rule arrows) the emulation component is inconclusive (other) and the verdict rests on (A) as 'mixed'.
tests.interpretation: The claim has three parts: simple rules (two rewrite rules), highly complex behaviour (illustrated by exponential growth of a tiny expression and irregular size sequences), and the ability to emulate rule 110. The first two are tested through the book's own exhibit (the shortest unboundedly growing expression) and the exhaustive size-8 census; 'seemingly random internal structure' is not given a decisive statistical test here because the structures involved have at most a few hundred steps, too short for the compression-based criteria used elsewhere; it is reported descriptively. The emulation is tested as an exact computational reproduction of the published construction. Evaluation order follows the book's note 'Combinator properties' (expr /. crules per step); fixed points do not depend on order (Church-Rosser) but intermediate sizes do.
tests.method: analysis.py implements hash-consed S/K terms with a memoised one-pass ReplaceAll step (whole expression first, then head and argument, replaced parts not re-scanned) and full normalisation by iterating passes to a fixed point. It (A) evolves s[s[s]][s][s][s][s] for 40 steps and fits log2 LeafCount on steps 10-40; (C) implements ToC bracket abstraction, p, inc, num, cr, the rule-110 cell combinator f (size 62, book: 61) and the step combinator w (size 674) from the note, encodes all 56 binary lists of length 3-5, applies w up to three times and decodes with the pair selectors; (B) runs the exhaustive census of the 109,824 size-8 expressions (60 steps or LeafCount > 20,000) and, as validation of the rewrite semantics, the 16,896 size-7 expressions, comparing with the counts printed in the note 'Combinator properties'. Full output in derived/census.json; runtime about 8 s.

measured.unit: pre-registered components A and C (C under the pre-registered reading and under the alternative reading of 'padding with 0 on either side')

C.mismatch_structure: all 84 strict mismatches are lists starting with 1 and differ only in the leftmost output cell (0 instead of rule-110's f(0,0,1)=1)

size7_validation.book_values: all but 2 of 16,896 reach fixed points in at most 12 steps; largest fixed point 41

caveats: Component C failed under the pre-registered reading of 'padding with 0 on either side' (evolve the zero-padded list): 84 of 168 cases differ, but every mismatch is a list starting with 1 and differs only in the leftmost output cell. Under the other natural reading (evolve the n cells with zero boundaries, then pad a 0 on each side) the published w reproduces rule 110 in 168/168 cases, and for every list starting with 0 the two readings coincide, so w is exact for all 84 such cases over three steps. Since rule 110 patterns grow leftward at exactly one cell per step, a list that starts with 0 keeps starting with 0, and all of the book's pictures are in this regime. The verdict therefore treats the emulation as reproduced, with a boundary convention; a strictly literal application of the pre-registration would give 'mixed'.

The size-7 census reproduces the book's published numbers exactly (16,894 fixed points, 2 unbounded, largest fixed point 41), which validates the ReplaceAll step semantics; the size-8 count of expressions exceeding 20,000 leaves within 60 steps (59) is not the same quantity as the book's '49 show exponential growth' (it includes k[...] and s[...] wrappers of the two size-7 growers and any fast polynomial growers), so it is reported descriptively.

The cell combinator f built from the printed code has size 62 rather than the note's 61; the difference is immaterial to behaviour (f is only used through its normal-form action) but indicates a one-leaf discrepancy in either the transcription or the book's count.

'Seemingly random internal structure' was not given a decisive statistical test (too few steps for compression-based criteria); the claim's universality part is tested only through the rule-110 emulation, not through a general proof.
Growth rate 2^0.47 t over steps 10-40 agrees with the book's 2^(t/2) to within the fit tolerance; intermediate sizes depend on the evaluation order, which here follows the book's.

tests.label: Nested cellular automaton patterns can be computed in logarithmic time
tests.hypothesis: For elementary rules 60 and 188 started from a single black cell, the colour of the cell at position x after t steps is a 2-automatic function of (t, x): a fixed finite automaton reading the base-2 digits of t and x in parallel (one digit pair per step, hence about log2(t) steps) outputs the colour, and this automaton can be constructed from the pattern and reproduces it exactly, including at times not used in its construction.
tests.pass: Pre-registered, for each of rules 60 and 188: (i) the number of distinct 2-kernel elements A(2^k t + r, 2^k x + s), compared on a 64 x 64 window, saturates: the cumulative count over levels k <= 5 equals the cumulative count over all levels k <= K - 6 of a 2^K x 2^K pattern with K = 11 (i.e. no new element appears beyond level 5), and that count is at most 64; (ii) the finite automaton whose states are those kernel elements and whose transitions on a digit pair (dt, dx) go from element (k, r, s) to (k+1, r + 2^k dt, s + 2^k dx) is consistent (every representative of a state yields the same target state for each digit pair) and, run on the least-significant-first binary digits of (t, x), reproduces 100% of the cells of an independently evolved 2^12 x 2^12 pattern (t < 4096), three quarters of which lie outside the K = 11 construction range; (iii) the number of automaton steps for a cell at time t equals the number of binary digits of t, i.e. floor(log2 t) + 1.
tests.fail: Pre-registered: for rule 60 or rule 188 the kernel count keeps growing beyond level 5 (no saturation) or exceeds 64, or the automaton is inconsistent, or any cell of the 2^12 x 2^12 pattern disagrees with the automaton's output. Control rules 30 and 110 (not nested) are expected to fail (i) and (ii); if they passed, the test would be too weak and the verdict would be 'inconclusive' with reason 'not-operationalizable'.
tests.interpretation: Wolfram's statement (p. 744) is that the colour of a cell of rule 60 or rule 188 after t steps can be found by a cellular automaton acting on the base-2 digit sequences of the cell's coordinates (6 colours for rule 60, 12 for rule 188) in about log2(t) steps instead of t steps. The finite-automaton formulation used here is equivalent: a two-dimensional pattern computable from the binary digits of (t, x) by a finite-state device is a 2-automatic double sequence, whose characterization (Cobham, Salon) is finiteness of its 2-kernel; the automaton's step count is the number of digit pairs, floor(log2 t) + 1. The exact state counts Wolfram quotes (6 and 12) refer to his particular digit-CA encoding and are not tested; only the existence of a finite digit automaton and its logarithmic step count are. Rules 60 and 188 both grow only to the right from a single black cell at x = 0, so A(t, x) is defined for 0 <= x <= t and taken as 0 for x > t. For the controls, the right half (x >= 0) of rule 30, 90 and 150 and the mirror image of rule 110 are used. The clause 'nested patterns generally' is addressed only through rules 90 and 150 as further nested examples.
tests.method: analysis.py evolves each rule from a single black cell to a 4096 x 4096 array A(t, x). (i) For levels k = 0..7 it extracts every 2-kernel element A(2^k t + r, 2^k x + s) on a 32 x 32 window and counts cumulative distinct elements. (ii) From the 2048 x 2048 sub-pattern it builds the automaton whose states are the distinct 64 x 64 kernel windows (levels k <= 5), with transition (k, r, s) -> (k+1, r + 2^k dt, s + 2^k dx) on digit pair (dt, dx), checks that no state has conflicting or undefined transitions, then runs the automaton on the least-significant-first binary digits of (t, x) for all 16,777,216 cells of the 4096 x 4096 array (12 digit pairs) and compares with A; it also stops the automaton after bitlen(t) digit pairs and compares on the 8,390,656 cells with x <= t. Controls 30, 110 (mirrored), 90 and 150 (right halves) are treated identically. Run time about 30 s.

measured.unit: cells (of 2 x 16,777,216) where the digit automaton disagrees with direct evolution, rules 60 and 188
measured.uncertainty: exact

extra.automaton_steps_per_cell: bitlen(t) = floor(log2 t) + 1 digit pairs (12 for t = 4095) versus 4095 direct evolution steps

caveats: The pre-registered saturation criterion (i) as written ('cumulative count over k <= 5 equals the count over k <= K - 6 with K = 11') is vacuous because K - 6 = 5; it was applied in the intended stronger form on the 4096 x 4096 pattern with a 32 x 32 window (levels up to 7): for rules 60 and 188 no new kernel element appears after level 1 and 2 respectively (2 and 7 distinct elements), while the controls 30 and 110 gain 4^k new elements at every level.

The automaton was built from the 2048 x 2048 pattern and reproduces all 16,777,216 cells of the 4096 x 4096 pattern, 12,582,912 of which were not used in its construction; agreement for all t is implied by 2-automaticity but was verified only up to t = 4095.

Wolfram's exact state counts (6 colours for rule 60, 12 for rule 188) belong to his particular digit cellular automaton and were not reproduced; the kernel automata found here have 2 and 7 states. The claim's extension to 'nested patterns generally' was checked only on rules 90 and 150 (4 states each).
